column121: Coming into Scottsdale from ZZZ; we were cleared direct to DSERT for the DSERT2 RNAV (Area Navigation) arrival; then given instructions to cross YOLOW at 7;600 ft. and 250 kts. I put the altitude and speed in the FMS (Flight Management System) and the PF (Pilot Flying) set the AAD to 7;600 ft. and initiated the descent. Prior to reaching YOLOW; we acquired the runway at SDL and informed Approach; who simply acknowledged our transmission. We crossed YOLOW at 7;600 ft. and 250 kts; and shortly after were cleared for the visual approach to Runway 21 and instructed to contact Tower. The PF (Pilot Flying) began slowing the aircraft by reducing throttle and extending speed brakes while I activated the secondary flight plan containing the DSERT visual Runway 21 approach and activated the leg from YOLOW to EEDGR. The PF put 3;400 ft. into the AAD and activated VS (Vertical Speed) and dialed in a descent rate to reach 3;400 ft. at EEDGR. The PF directed me to extend the gear to assist with the descent and speed. Just prior to EEDGR we received a SINK RATE alert; and the PF shallowed the descent slightly; so we crossed EEDGR at approximately 200 kts and 3;600 ft. At the appropriate speeds; I extended the flaps; and shortly above 1;000 ft. AGL (Above Ground Level) we received a TERRAIN PULL UP alert; at which point I called for a go-around; which the PF executed. We climbed to 3;000 ft; ran the appropriate checklists; and then made a normal visual approach and landing.As we crossed EEDGR; the PF dialed the AAD to TDZE (Touch Down Zone); allowing the aircraft to continue descending while we attempted to get on profile.The PF and I were both distracted attempting to configure the aircraft and meet the profile of the approach. We both felt that the altitude and airspeed assignment at YOLOW made the switch to the REQUIRED visual approach with RNAV waypoints very difficult; and if we had simply flown a normal visual approach (which we've been doing for 15 years); we would have been fine. We were unable to configure early due to the ATC (Air Traffic Control) clearance; and the extra altitude carried past YOLOW forced a potentially unsafe descent rate. In the future; I will refuse a clearance to cross YOLOW at 7;600 ft and 250 kts if I expect to fly the visual to Runway 21. I feel the [Company] procedure as published actually reduces safety by drawing one or both pilots' attention into the cockpit during a critical phase of flight.

column121: I was on the Local Control position and traffic was light. Initially coordinated with Approach Control; Aircraft X was approved for a late frequency change to tower as it would be number two behind Aircraft Y. With this coordination I was expecting Aircraft Y to be first followed by Aircraft X; but Aircraft X came to tower first approximately two miles north of the VOR. At this time Aircraft Y was still outside of 10 miles from the field and I cleared Aircraft X to land. Approximately on a two mile final; Aircraft X requested a left 360 due to him still being too high. I asked Aircraft X to verify they had the field in sight; but there was no response. The CIC (Controller in Charge) responded to me that he requested a left 360. I observed outside the window that Aircraft X was in his left turn executing a 360 prior to my approval. At this time; Aircraft Y was approximately 8 to 9 nm north of the field. Immediately we coordinated this with Approach letting them know Aircraft X was too high and needed to execute a 360 and was instructed a missed approach; but at the time Aircraft X was just completing his left 360 with Aircraft Y approaching approximately a five mile 5 mile final. With coordination for the missed approach and Aircraft X nearly completing a 360; I advised Aircraft X of the inbound traffic and instructed him to turn northbound and to contact Approach Control. During this time; separation between both aircraft was lost.I believed what led to this event was initially the miscommunication between tower and approach with the sequence of the inbound. I was preparing for Aircraft X to be shipped late behind Aircraft Y; but there wasn't any communication that the sequence has changed.  We are a VFR tower and I haven't had the experience with dealing or the knowledge on how to deal with such a situation; but this incident was definitely a learning experience. I believe Aircraft X also went below the MVA; which is 3000 ft. and they were at 2000 ft. I have not seen or experienced this situation.In my opinion; I believed this occurred because of the miscommunication and both the lack of knowledge from both my position and the pilot in command of Aircraft X. I am aware of the required separation and that IFR procedure. With the last minute decision of Aircraft X to execute the 360 on his own led me to approve his request when I know he must break of the approach and cancel IFR; otherwise they should execute the published missed approach. I would recommend for this VFR tower to include the rare; but possible situations that could occur during training. This situation was unexpected and rare; but it did happen. I would recommend to go over the separation needed for IFR aircraft and the MVAs surrounding the airport. Prior to this situation; I should've noted the altitude; this would have prevented the situation.

column121: At gate X in ZZZ; filed to ZZZ1 on the ZZZX Departure. The flight plan after the SID started at ZZZ.  We requested log-on from ZZZ2 for the departure clearance 30 minutes prior to push.  Flight plan (legs) verification accomplished per SOP.  First Departure clearance came about 20 minutes prior to push indicating a new clearance for the ZZZZZY; ZZZZZ [Intersection]; as filed.  Started to update flight plan to account for this.  While editing flight plan; another Departure Clearance came in for ZZZX; ZZZ [VOR]; ZZZZZ [Intersection]; AF.  Started editing flight plan again to account for reversion to original flight plan and SID.  Completed another flight plan verification from ZZZ.  Completed briefing. Standard push back and taxi for [Runway] XXR.  Completed before takeoff checklist; inclusive of the 'runway confirm.'  Both the FO and myself think we both saw the correct runway on the ND during the final check; as well as the departure brief.   On takeoff; very early after liftoff; switched to Departure Control.  Very early in climb; 'NAV' engaged; catching me off guard as it seemed like we were below 400 feet; commanding a hard right turn.  I instinctively followed the flight directors initially.  In the turn; still below thrust reduction altitude (1;000 feet); I realized from my briefing that the turn should have been to the left; not the hard right turn the flight directors were commanding.  I started to correct back to the left.  I did not see any traffic in our immediate vicinity on TCAS. ATC then assigned us a heading of 350.  As we were in the turn to Heading 350 ATC mentioned that we were supposed to turn left. I believe were around a northerly heading when we hit 1;000 feet; our thrust reduction altitude.  We apologized to ATC and inquired if there was a traffic conflict; which he replied 'no.'  He handed us off.  About 60-90 minutes into the flight we were notified over CPDLC of a possible pilot deviation and to call TRACON.  I called TRACON and the Supervisor was very cordial.  He explained what they had seen; and we also told him what had happened on our end.  He told me they had been seeing this event a fair amount lately.  Coincidentally; on the same aircraft yesterday for the outbound flight to ZZZ; we had to have maintenance reset the FMC's on the ground in ZZZ1 because both with; and without; a Flight plan in the FMC; as soon as the flight directors would be turned on the lateral 'NAV' mode would engage and command a hard right turn.  We tried resetting everything; inclusive of the ADIRS; swapping the nav data base; and the same thing kept happening.  After maintenance reset the FMC's problem went away.  Caught/detected by myself (PF) below thrust reduction altitude of 1;000 feet.  Correction applied.First flight and operation into a busy complicated airport in over 6.5 months due to the COVID situation.  Numerous cockpit distractions during cockpit setup.  Several ATC digital clearances within a short period of time.  External stresses caused by current state of affairs currently going on within our country and our company.  Potential aircraft navigation technical issue; however; I cannot rule out pilot error.  Possible pilot error scenarios would be; departure procedure in the FMC jarred/messed up by the second CPDLC clearance route uplink; and subsequently not caught during second flight plan verification.  Potentially wrong runway set in FMC during cockpit setup. The FO and I don't believe it is the incorrect runway scenario because we did the Flight Plan verification; briefing; and final runway confirmation approaching the runway threshold as per SOP; and we believe we saw the digital representation of the runway on the ND.  But I have to admit this is a possibility.  At all times all SOPs were adhered to the best of our knowledge.
column123: It was a busy morning out of ZZZ. Our flight plan called for the ZZZX Departure. The automatic upload for the flight plan wasn't working so my Captain was manually loading the flight plan. Bottom line SOPs were followed to best of our knowledge. Verify; verify; verify.

column121: From the ZZZZZX arrival approach gave us a clearance direct to ZZZZZ on the ILS XXL approach. The PM selected the ZZZZZ fix from the DIR FMS page and asked if I agree; I visually verified that direct ZZZZZ was selected and replied I agree and to execute the change. The PM then stated we need to make the 176 course big; and I agreed. After the change was made I verified on PFD1 that the aircraft was in white needles with NAV captured and the fix was ZZZZZ. A few moments later approach asked us if we were going direct to ZZZZZ; and again I verified on PFD1 that the aircraft was in white needles; navigating to the fix ZZZZZ. The PM confirmed that we were direct ZZZZZ. Approach then gave us a HDG to the right of our flight path to fly. I dialed in the requested heading (I think it was 125) and selected HDG on the FCP and verified on the PFD1 that the aircraft was now in HDG mode. Trying to determine what had happened and why we need a course correction I noted the flight path on PFD2 that showed we had been tracking the last heading as an intercept for the extended LOC course outside of ZZZZZ. A brief discussion of what had happened with the PM was conducted and we both agreed that we should not have entered the course; which tells the FMS that you want this heading to intercept; and that it should have been left as the course direct to ZZZZZ as this was the clearance. The approach was conducted without further incident.This was my first flight as Captain after almost X years. I had just completed IOE the previous week; which had multiple interruptions including being taken off line because my IOE Check Airmen had been exposed to COVID. I flew one turn as an FO the previous day; and this flight. I believe my concern to be open to correction caused my response to want to agree with the PM; and this was a common error I had made during training as well; not making the inbound course 'BIG' to have the FMS adjust the flight profile for an intercept as opposed to flying to a specific course. Just because I had made this error before; does not mean that I will make it again; I should have stated out loud why I did not initially ask to make the course big; because I heard the clearance as direct to the fix; not intercept; which we were primed for; due to our position in the flight. Additionally when ATC questioned if we were going direct to ZZZZZ; I check PFD1 to read the status of our navigation; and seeing ZZZZZ as the fix; and NAV captured and in white; believed this could only be the case. In all my time flying this type aircraft; I don't know if I have ever been aware that this shows when intercepting the course; as you would usually see HDG mode to capture. Additionally; the slight difference in the flight path was not great as displayed on PFD2 in the map. This will definitely change the way I verify the mode the aircraft is in; to include tracing the flight path on PFD2.
column123: We were on descent via ZZZZZX Arrival.  We were cleared Direct ZZZZZ before the last fix of ZZZZZX Arrival on the Visual back it up with (ILS) for Runway XXL. column121: While enroute to GTF; the CA (Captain) who was PM (Pilot Monitoring) requested direct DATSA with Center in order to set up for RNAV (RNP) Z RWY 21. As we neared DATSA; Approach Control gave us a vector towards the northeast for sequence. After a few minutes we were given a vector towards the southeast and the controller asked if we still wanted the RNAV Z Approach. We said yes.  He gave us a clearance direct to 'DRIFT'. I pushed DTO (Direct To) and used the FMS to fly direct to the fix DRFTR (I thought the controller was simply using a different pronunciation of the same fix). Shortly after; the CA realized that there was another fix on the approach: DRYFT; which was not in our flight plan in the FMS since we had used DATSA as our IAF. He queried the controller who confirmed that he had cleared us to DRYFT. At this point I had the airport in sight and  we requested a visual approach. We were cleared for the Visual to RWY 21 and performed a stable visual approach.The lesson I learned is to listen more carefully to the spelling of the fix the controller is giving us and not just assume it's the fix that sounds close to what he said. I recommend that one of these two fixes DRFTR and DRYFT be changed to something different. These two fixes are close to each other on the approach and the spelling and pronunciations are similar enough to cause confusion.

column121: TCAS RA while flying inbound on ILS XXR ZZZ. Exceptionally busy local ZZZ Tower Controller with multiple VFR in pattern and adjacent Class D airspace including helicopter operations. Listening to [the] Controller manage multiple; busy aircraft in [the] pattern including one helicopter; [I] slowed [the] aircraft to 180 kt.; downwind pattern entry. Numerous call outs additionally for traffic just outside control zone led to heavy workload for crew entering pattern. Called out airport in sight and given visual clearance on 8-mile left base XXR. Joined localizer inbound. [A] low level helicopter in pattern was consuming [the] majority of [the] Tower Controller instructions either due to training occurring in [the] helicopter; or [an] inability to comply with Tower instructions and widening their pattern out for [the] landing jet - us. Continuing inbound at the marker; I elected to stay one dot above glide slope due to [the] continuing inability of [the] helicopter to comply with Tower instructions to turn away from final approach course for us. Inside the marker one dot high; [I] received [a] TCAS RA from [the] helicopter turning base early towards us. PNF (Pilot not Flying) had helicopter in sight [the] entire time. Immediately started to arrest descent when TCAS RA abated. Continued [the] approach; reestablishing glide slope intercept without unusual maneuvering required; to an uneventful landing. ZZZ during VMC weather is always an exceptionally busy airport with mix of high and low speed traffic in addition to multiple flight schools based there. Slowing the aircraft significantly assisted us and likely ATC Tower with sequencing for landing XXR and smaller aircraft; XXL. Estimate [there was] one dozen aircraft in pattern; with more nearby. Additionally; staying high on glide slope using situational awareness VFR likely provided further altitude separation for this eventual encounter. Non-complying VFR pattern helicopter to Tower instructions for whatever reason; highlights perils at this airport and necessitates good crew situational awareness and CRM. I did not follow up with ZZZ Tower with non-complying instruction helicopter; deeming [the] encounter a good learning lesson for all of us.

column121: We were conducting a long cross country for the student's commercial pilot requirements. This required us to deviate west and south of course due to not being cleared into the Class Bravo airspace and Class D airspace. We had a near miss with a powered parachute. The other operator was slightly below us; heading westbound. Our altitude at the time was 3500 feet eastbound; with flight following. Weather conditions were VMC; clear and unrestricted. Both I and the student were actively scanning for traffic outside due to the busy Bravo environment and using ADS-B to aid us. Since he was slightly below us; we did not see him until close; less than 1 mile separation and probably closer. I directed the student to immediately turn left to pass behind; but he started turning slowly; so I took controls to avoid the situation. The powered parachute passed behind; and we continued without further incident. The parachute's color caused it to really blended in until we were close. We were attempting to spot all traffic visually; but did not see them until late. I'm unsure if the parachute operator ever saw us; as we would've been coming out of the sun off his roughly 3 to 4 o'clock. I did not report this to Approach; mainly since we ourselves were getting into a high workload environment since we were close to our destination. Additionally; with the traffic was behind us; I was more concerned with flying the airplane and watching for other traffic; especially since it is a busy general aviation airport. That was probably my biggest self recommendation; is trying to report that if able to approach to warn other aircraft. The only other recommendation for myself is to be a little clearer when I need to assume controls.

column121: On arrival into ZZZ; descending via on the ZZZZZ3 Arrival just before the ZZZZZ waypoint; we checked on with approach; and they responded 'Company XXXX; cleared ILS X.' I had programmed the ILS X for our arrival; but didn't select any transition on the approach. The ZZZZZ3 STAR has the note to cross ZZZZZ at 6;000 feet; expect ILS or LOC Runway X. On receipt of the clearance; I paused for a moment as there was a discontinuity in the box after ZZZZZ and before ZZZZZ1 [waypoint]; and the remaining points on the ILS X. ATC had not given us a heading or guidance for after the last fix on the STAR; just cleared ILS X. I looked at my EFB to see what the text of the STAR said; and my Captain seeing my confusion; said 'you're cleared for approach; how about direct ZZZZZ1?' He had also queued up ZZZZZ1 in the box; and was poised to execute it. I still wasn't sure; but he seemed positive. I said 'OK;' he executed it and we began direct to ZZZZZ1. Within a few seconds; Approach queried us 'I show you left of course; what [are you] doing?' The Captain replied; 'we're direct ZZZZZ1 cleared for ILS X; is there something else you would like?' ATC responded that there was a ZZZZZ transition to the ILS X; and in future that is what he meant when he cleared us ILS X - to fly the ZZZZZ transition on the ILS from the STAR. Had I looked closer at the approach plate; and not just the STAR chart; after the issuance of the clearance; the ATC clearance intention would've become obvious to me. I let my Captain cause me to second guess my hesitation; and disregard my uncertainty over our clearance. I should have requested he ask for clarification from ATC instead of allowing him to execute a path I was unsure of. I have felt a bit slow in the cockpit lately; due to having flown very infrequent this year (light schedules/hindsight/scheduled time off) and I believe I made the false assumption I was missing something and he was correct. A simple query to ATC would have cleared up the matter.I should have taken a moment longer to review the appropriate charts to clarify the appropriate flight course; and failing that answering my question; I should have queried ATC for clarification. When programming the approach; closer examination of the plate would have shown the available lead in transition from ZZZZZ. I should have trusted my hesitation upon receipt of the clearance and not assumed I was wrong in needing clarification.

column121: It was from ZZZ1 to ZZZ IFR flight. Our flight plan and clearance was from ZZZ1..ZZZZZ5. ZZZ. On the ground; [the] Captain; and I reviewed the route including every fix in the arrival and programmed [the] FMS for Runway XXL in ZZZ. From takeoff until descend via ZZZZZ 5 Arrival; flight was uneventful. Captain and I took off from Runway XXL at ZZZ1 and then instructed to go direct ZZZZZ shortly after instructed go to direct ZZZZZ1 which is [the IAF] of [the] arrival. We were instructed to descend via ZZZZZ5 Arrival in to ZZZ with both altitude and airspeed restriction as stated in the STAR. During the descend; the ZZZ Approach Controller gave instruction to switch our runway to XXR. Captain and I programmed [the] FMS and switched our planned runway to XXR as well as review the fixes along the route. However; as we approach the fix ZZZZZ2; LNAV autopilot was switched to lateral mode [and the] airplane was late to turn to [the] final [approach] fix which is ZZZZZ3. As soon as Pilot Flying noticed the mode change in autopilot; Pilot Flying used heading bug to make a left turn to rejoin the course for the rest of arrival. After the arrival; flight crew flew rest of flight uneventfully and land safely at Runway XXR. Next time; we will review the fixes more carefully after making any changes on the runways or arrivals and make sure if there are any fixes that are duplicated; we will deleted it.
column123: On arrival to ZZZ we were descending via ZZZZZ5. Our dispatch release had planned [Runway] XXL and we had already briefed our approach prior to the beginning of the arrival as is common for preparation and safety. As an LCA (line check airman) I have been flying our route structure for over X;XXX hours in the left seat and this is common practice for myself. However; I am still trying to understand the traffic flows in ZZZ and as time progresses I am positive the other crews and I will get better at selecting runways based on flow and approaches utilized over time. ZZZ Approach Control gave us instructions for XXR somewhere after ZZZZZ5 I believe. I was the pilot monitoring. So I immediately went to work resetting FMS verifying ZZZZZ3 had now changed to ZZZZZ2. Altitudes were correct at said waypoint. Getting new landing data. Resetting both navigational aids for the correct runway. And since my FO (First Officer) was fairly new to the plane I began briefing his approach to him out loud; highlighting changes and re-briefing all pertinent information. It was in the middle of this brief that I heard the lateral NAV disconnection chime. The plane had entered ROL mode and within a second I and the FO were both reaching for the heading bug. He made the correction on the FGC (Flight Guidance Computer) about as quickly as anyone could. We recaptured the LNAV course to ZZZZZ2 and were given a number to call.I have been operating with this company for over X years; almost Y are as an LCA. In all my time I have never seen what I described above. After the fact I am aware of exactly what happened and I will explain and make suggestions to correct. Upon loading the runway change to XXR the FMS duplicated the ZZZZZ fix. I know this because the pilot observing told us when we got on the ground what he had witnessed and told us it was a current trend within our airline and they were trying to troubleshoot. I understand why that might happen in the mind of the FMS as it is trying to separate the arrival into parts. Initial arrival segment versus approach segment. However; reloading approaches or fielding runways changes are common in our route structure and not once in four years has this happened anywhere else. ZZZZZ4 in ZZZ2. Landing north transitions to ZZZZZ6 at 7000. Landing south your next fix might be ZZZZZ7 at 7000 for XXC. But never in four years has a reassigned runway and a reload of the approach caused ZZZZZ4 to duplicate. This is specific to ZZZ2. This is why we are just now seeing this throughout the pilot group in this airspace. I know there is verbiage within our books that states duplicated points must be removed for this very reason. However; in this event I was unable to catch the duplicated fix due to workload and I had never seen the issue before so my mental radar so to speak was focused on threats I have seen: monitoring our descent rate; monitoring speed control for arrival compliance; re-briefing navigational aid frequencies; briefing go-around and missed approach for the new runway. All the things I have seen cause errors in our flight on a normal day. So when this lateral break happened I was as stunned as the FO. I will say to his credit he corrected in the quickest fashion and made the correct adjustment for the situation. There was nothing more we could have done. I did not feel safety was at stake nor that the violation was hugely significant. I however do see that as a systemic issue the implications of this are massive and need to be corrected ASAP which is why I have my recommendations. I spoke with a sim pilot who was able to recreate the event and he confirmed what I had already suspected. Pilots need to be aware that this is common in ZZZ2. When receiving a new runway or a change to the approach. Look for duplicate fixes!

column121: I was Captain and the flying pilot for arrival into IAH. We were descending in VMC conditions on the LINKK1 Arrival for the assigned Runway 27. We had completed our Approach to Landing above the line and as we were approaching 10000' we were running our Approach to Landing checklist Below the Line when we were cleared by the Approach Controller for the ILS 27 Approach and to maintain 240 knots.I put on the appropriate lights and we finished our checklist. However I did not - in hindsight - set the lower 1500' at which we were to cross the FAF at REDOC. Between RDFSH and GEYGR we were queried as to whether we were going to make our crossing restriction of 4000 at GEYGR. We realized the error and started to descend on the approach. Shortly after not complying with the crossing restriction at GEYGR; we were broken off the approach and vectored back around-slowed to 210 and descended to rejoin the approach. We were given a phone number to call HOUSTON TRACON. We then completed the approach and landing. The error started when I did not select the lower altitude for the FAF of 1500. The timing of our clearance was a contributing factor but the error was in the failure to set lower FAF altitude. Typically we are double checking each other and we missed it. Greater vigilance would have eliminated this error. We were also discussing the fact we were at 240 as assigned still inside of RDFSH was also a factor. We debriefed this all on the ground in detail. I later spoke with TRACON about this. They informed me that there were no separation issues and he did note the timing of the clearance when they reviewed the tape.
column123: We were flying the LINKK 1 Arrival; runway 27 to IAH. We confirmed all points in the MCDU and set the altitude down to 6000 we both confirmed the altitude we were then given a speed of 240kts with a clearance of descend via the STAR. I believe we were between RDFSH and GEYGR and the controller asked if we were going to make the crossing restriction at GEYGR which was supposed to be 4000; at this point I looked at the distance to GEYGR and it showed 4.2 miles and we had 2000ft to lose. We both looked at each other to confirm everything before we started to descend down immediately. There was not enough time to report that we were not going to make the crossing restrictions at 240kts and also the altitude. We both realized at this time that the altitude had not been changed for the lower altitude of 1500ft. at REDOC. The controller gave us a 360-degree turn back on course as we lost our altitude. At this point we realized our error. The controller called back with a number to call Houston for TRACON; we completed the approach and landed. Timing of the clearance was a factor; as well as not selecting lower altitude for the FAF of 1500 or double checking each other. Also should have discussed that we were inside of RDFSH and still at 240. We talked when on the ground in detail.

column121: Aircraft Y was at 2;000 feet MSL; and issued a climb to 3;000 feet to avoid converging VFR traffic who I was not talking to (squawking 1200) observed at approximately 1;700 feet MSL. Sector complexity was high due to IFR/marginal VFR conditions as well as an increase in usual volume we have seen over the past months. I was working 2 different frequencies as well. When I issued a climb to 3;000 feet to Aircraft Y; he read back 3;000 feet; and then I moved on to other priorities. The next time I observed Aircraft Y's altitude; I observed 3;400 and told him to stop his climb and issued a turn away from conflicting IFR traffic (Aircraft X at 040). I also turned Aircraft X away from Aircraft Y and issued traffic. I did not issue a Brasher warning.This was the busiest session; both traffic and complexity wise I have worked in many months due to decreased traffic volume due to COVID-19. I feel like if I had scanned better I would have caught Aircraft Y's altitude bust before I did. If my workload increases to this level in the near future; I feel asking for a split from the departure sector; or even calling someone over to act as a coordinator; or a '2nd set of eyes' when I feel task saturation is causing my scan to break down would be beneficial. I feel that both of these actions could prevent this from occurring again.Another important take away from this event in preventing [a] re-occurrence is to not have an expectation bias assuming a pilot will comply with your instructions; even if he reads it back correctly. A constant scan is absolutely critical at all times; (busy or slow) to ensure pilots are doing exactly what you told them and to prevent separation/deviation errors due to complacency and/or expectation bias.

column121: We were just outside the MNARK waypoint descending via the TBARR1 into Denver when I requested an unrestricted descent in order to expedite down through some turbulence. ATC granted my request and cleared us to descend and maintain 14;000 FT. I took the aircraft out of the managed descent mode and used open descent to descend to 14;000 FT. ATC subsequently amended our clearance as follows; cross BDIVN at or above 14;000 FT then descend via the TBARR1. The Pilot Monitoring (PM) put 13;000 in the FCU as the bottom of the TBARR1 is 13;000 FT at LDORA which is the next waypoint after KUSHH. I acknowledged the change to the altitude in the FCU but failed to put the aircraft back into a managed descent. We were between BDIVN and KUSHH when Denver Center switched us over to approach. As the PM checked in with approach I was expecting the aircraft to level off at 14;000 FT in order to meet the restriction by KUSHH. Just as the aircraft approached 14;000 FT two things happened simultaneously. One; I realized the aircraft wasn't leveling off as I expected; and two; approach cleared us to descend to 10;000 FT and turn left to a heading of 040. I don't believe there was an altitude deviation but I was certainly very fortunate that approach gave us a lower altitude when they did.

column121: I read the company e-mail concerning Runway 16 at AVL being closed. At the time I didn't realize I had a trip coming up to go there. During the flight over to AVL; my FO (First Officer) and I looked over the special airport qualification pages for AVL. Pages indicated that the closed Runway 16-34 was completely torn up; and just dirt. I forgot the e-mail I had read that stated that the runway was actually almost finished. It was hazy in the AVL area. I had not landed there in several years; so we decided to do the RNAV approach to Runway 17. I expected to see just one runway as shown on Jeppesen 19-3 chart. We got the airport in sight and the Tower cleared us to land. When fully configured and below 1;000 AGL; Runway 16 was much more prominent than Runway 17. We both thought 16 was 17. Both of [us] saw a small light flash on the runway that looked like an aircraft taxing onto the runway. I saw the flash again; and it looked like a very small 'X'. I reported that to the Tower; and they instructed us to go around; which we did. After talking to the Tower and being vectored back around we saw our error; and successfully landed on Runway 17. I blame myself for not putting the information together and noticing that there was a discrepancy between what the e-mail stated and the Jeppesen charts. It would be nice if Jeppesen could keep their airport qualification charts updated.
column123: We were going to Asheville North Carolina which was my first time going there. I asked the Captain to request the RNAV approach going into Asheville since there were mountains and I'm not familiar with the airport; we have reviewed the special airport on the Jepp chart which was showing one runway and the runway [that] was shown was much torn up and under construction. When we were on final; I noticed there was an X on the runway which I thought was an airplane. I did not see another runway next to it even though there was. But the runway that was next to it; was very small; narrow; short and nothing like the runway [that] was showing on the [Jepp] chart. I realize that's not an airplane on the runway but it was an X flashing. I asked the Captain to let Tower know what's going on. Tower said go around; and after completing the go around procedure Tower has informed us that the main runway is closed and we are supposed to land on the adjacent runway. The adjacent runway is nothing like what was showing on the special airport chart. The picture that was showing in the special report chart is very different than what is in real life. People need to be aware that the predominant runway is not the runway that is used.

column121: In Cruise Flight at FL380 approaching ZZZZZ north boundary of ZZZZ airspace we were denied right deviations for active military airspace. Left deviations at that point were no longer an option and appeared worse. We were on the western edge of a line of weather moving East we were deviating just slightly left of our course to go through what appeared to be the thinnest area of weather on our radar. I had made a PA and had all passengers and Flight Attendants seated. We experienced a brief 10 to 15 seconds of Moderate Turbulence which cause our Altitude to drop 200 ft. to about 37;800 ft. and the a gain of about 300 ft. to about 38;100 ft. and then settled back to level at FL380. We also experienced some airspeed loss and then gain briefly as well as some left bank. It felt much like wake turbulence briefly. Just then MIA center told us to maintain FL380 and contact ZZZZ; before leaving the frequency I stated we had experienced some moderate turbulence which had caused some altitude loss; a couple hundred feet; and that we were now level at FL380 and we were told 'roger' contact Center which we did. The remainder of the flight was uneventful and smooth to destination. [The cause of the event was that] a deviation 100's of miles earlier to the left would have been a better choice and I believe a couple of aircraft behind us after hearing my report to MIA Center deviated into the Military Airspace. I do not know if the aircraft behind me declared an Emergency to do so or not; as we were changing frequency to next center during the radio discussions. That may have been a better choice but I did not expect the turbulence to be that bad; but was very glad I sat the Flight attendants down prior; as well as making a very clear PA to the passengers that we were going to experience some Turbulence since we had to fly in the area of some weather and insisted that they be seated with their seatbelts securely fastened. An earlier plan for weather deviations 100's of mile away if necessary would have helped knowing any right deviations would be denied.
column123: Level at 380 approaching XXXXX; there was some weather close to the intersection. Requested right deviation and Center informed that Warning Areas were active so unable right deviation. We encountered some moderate turbulence in the clouds for a few seconds. The airplane descended 200 ft. before returning to level. Miami informed to maintain 380 and to contact next center over ZZZZ which we did. Flight continued uneventfully.The cause of deviations was not being able to deviate due to Center's instructions.I suggest deviating ahead of time if known that no deviations allowed.

column121: This report covers two events generated from the same aircraft condition.  At FL370; I; as pilot flying received an Engine 1 EPR (emgine pressure ratio) Mode fault.  The FO (First Officer) ran the ECAM procedure and we selected N1 modes on and ran the autothrust manually.  We almost had to ask for a descent because the speed was bleeding off.  I managed to correct the speed; and noticed the thrust levers were quite split.  I needed to transfer aircraft control to the FO so that I could call Dispatch and Maintenance.  I explained the split throttle situation to the FO and gave him the aircraft and radios.  Shortly afterwards; he said we needed to descend.  I saw the speed deteriorating and immediately said to start down; we were going below green dot and into the hook.  I took back the radio; and we descended. Our fuel situation was such that at the lower altitude we couldn't continue on to ZZZ1; so we coordinated to divert to ZZZ2.  Everything was non eventful until we started the approach.  I had the FO flying because he was handling the split thrust levers well and I thought it would be best for him to continue.  He asked for a longer final then they were vectoring us for and ATC gave us a long final.  When cleared for the Visual; the FO decided to descend from 8000 feet to 7000 feet. I should have told him to maintain 8000 feet. I wanted him comfortable on the approach and let him descend early.  ATC called us with a low altitude alert; stating the MDA was 7500 and we climbed back to that altitude and intercepted the glide slope and landed without incident.The cause of the low altitude alert was that I had already told the FO how to make the descent with the throttle situation and didn't want him to feel like I was flying while I was Pilot Monitoring; and we were visual so I knew we were safe as far as terrain and obstacles; but we were definitely dragged in.  Normally when FO's ask to descend early on visuals I mention class B airspace or terrain; but this time I wanted him to be comfortable just working the split thrust levers. I've thought about this for about a day now; and what I've come up with is try to keep things as normal as possible even in an abnormal situation.  The extended final was fine.  It actually made it easier to accomplish what he was trying to accomplish and made the descent totally unnecessary.  I also want to mention that the mechanic who greeted us asked why we hadn't applied the MEL; which would have helped us with our power settings.  We don't reference the MEL in flight; but either the QRH should address the thrust situation or it should mention to refer to the MEL because it would have been helpful.
column123: During cruise at FL360; in the vicinity of the ZZZ VORTAC; flight experienced a Master Caution and a following ECAM warning message of ENG 1 EPR MODE FAULT. The CA (Captain) who was the Pilot Flying (PF) stated 'My Aircraft' and I; the FO who was the Pilot Monitoring (PM) immediately began the procedures to address the ENG 1 EPR MODE FAULT caution. After referencing the Quick Reaction Card (QRC) we determined this was not a Quick Action or ECAM exception; and after concurrence between the PF and the PM began the ECAM Actions for ENG 1 EPR MODE FAULT. After completion of the ECAM actions; and the aircraft was stabilized we both noted the trust levers were split in their position to maintain corresponding N1 and N2 engine settings. The CA (PF) then transferred the aircraft and ATC communications to me and I became the PF. The CA began an aircraft wifi internet phone call to company Dispatch and Maintenance and began to discuss follow-on options. I then informed ATC Center that the flight would be diverting due to 'engine issues' but the divert destination was not yet determined and we did not require any priority handling at that time. The decision to divert was made and ZZZ1 was determined the best place to divert. Once the CA completed coordination with Dispatch and Maintenance; he assumed the ATC Communications and assumed the PM duties and I remained the PF. During this time we noticed the power setting; as to not exceed any N1 engine limitations; were not sufficient to maintain the desired airspeed at FL360; and I notified the CA (PM) we needed an immediate descent out of FL360. The CA (PM) attempted to communicate with Center for the immediate decent; but was not able to establish communication due to frequency saturation from other radio calls. I (PF); in order to maintain airspeed; immediately disconnected the autopilot and began a shallow descent out of FL360. The CA (PM) made a call and notified Center of our descent out of FL360 and we were requiring a lower altitude. Center immediately responded to call and then cleared us to FL340; I estimate our altitude to be 35;850 feet when Center responded to call. The flight continued; uneventfully; to land at XXR a ZZZ with a visual approach.

column121: Had been issued a block altitude clearance and been changing altitude as needed within that block (related to turbulence) for several hours. Requested deviation around weather. ATC granted 50 NM. During deviation; descended from FL370 to FL360 due to turbulence. When ATC requested that we confirm altitude; signaled that something was amiss. Reread the deviation message...both of us had previously missed the cancellation of our block clearance- we both thought we still had one. Climbed back to FL370 and flight continued normally to destination.There were several [causes]; speaking only for myself. This was my first flight after nearly X months off due to COVID. I still feel confident; but out of practice. [I] was in seat 5+ hours when event occurred; energy was waning a bit. New to the X type aircraft fleet and just consolidated prior to extended time off. Had only crossed Ocean X twice and unfamiliar with 'the norms' (Didn't know that ATC tends to cancel block clearances in conjunction with another instruction/clearance over Ocean X.) Expected that an altitude clearance/cancellation would be communicated on its own; not included with weather deviation. Due to aforementioned factors; regrettably didn't register the block cancellation. Captain evidently didn't either.I admit and sincerely apologize for the error; however; altitude clearances are critical to our safety and should be given separately from any other clearance or instruction. One CPDLC message sounds (one chime in the flight deck) - I believe it's human to expect the message to address one thing; not two. It's easier to miss the 2nd item if clearances are combined; especially after many hours sitting with low activity. My suggestion is to send the weather deviation clearance as one message (one chime) and the block altitude cancellation as a separate message (2nd chime.)

column121: My pre-departure clearance was the Bluegrass 4 SID; Lexington transition. I received a 'line up and wait' instruction; shortly followed by a takeoff instruction for runway 27. My concern was that these instructions were given very soon after the departure of a Boeing 737; and I was worried about wake turbulence; especially in light of the young passengers in the cabin. After liftoff; I initiated an expedited climb; followed by a turn to the southwest in an attempt to sidestep the flight path of the Boeing ahead of me. Covington tower handed me off to Cincinnati Approach; who then cleared me to the Kenlan intersection; which was the next waypoint on the departure. After receiving that clearance; the Departure Controller queried us as to the turn that we made on departure; and I explained that we were attempting to avoid wake turbulence. I heard no further word on the matter.Looking back; I never should have accepted the takeoff clearance that quickly after the departure of the Boeing. I'm sure that the Controller was following procedure; but I was not comfortable with the situation. I should have either rejected the takeoff clearance; or asked for an immediate turn to the southwest in order to avoid the 737's flight path.

column121: Aircraft X checked on inbound at 13;000 feet descending to 9;000 feet. I told him to expect vectors for the ILS as that was what was being advertised and issued a heading of 130 and descended him to 3000 ft. He stated he did not want to go southeast bound because of weather south of the field. I was only showing small areas of light precipitation building 15 miles south of the field. After his request I told him an approach to the opposite runway circle to land will probably be okay but I will need time to get it approved as I was busy and a few other aircraft were deviating and one was having some radio issues. He then says he'll take a vector to the southeast for the ILS Approach. Once he is about 10 miles southwest of the field he reports the airport in sight. I clear him for the Visual Approach and call the tower to tell them of the change. I switched him to tower. I noticed him turning and figured he was either turning directly towards the field or deviating for weather since he was complaining about it before. He suddenly made a sharp left turn heading due north and descended to 1;000 feet. The low altitude alert goes off and I called the tower to issue it. They informed me he had lined up for the wrong airport. Tower handed him back off to me and I climbed him the 3;000 feet; re-vectored him for the ILS Approach and he landed safely. The pilot seemed rushed or impatient. I should have verified the azimuth and distance to the field even though he called the field in sight himself. The private airport should be displayed on the main map instead of a random roadway emergency map.

Just as FO was heading YY0 and approaching 2;500 feet altitude we received a climb to 6;000 feet and a heading of 0Z0 degrees which was more than XA0 degrees to the right. I acknowledged clearance and reset MCP to 6;000 feet with VVM sop. I then started to slowly spin the heading knob to heading of 0Z0 so as not to induce a left turn because it was more than XA0 degrees from our current heading. While maintaining traffic watch and setting the new heading the FO went through 6;000 feet and I saw the 300 feet amber warning and an altitude of 6;380 as the FO was already correcting. This all occurred within a 30-45 second time frame. The remainder of departure was uneventful.Once at altitude we debriefed as a crew and outlined contributing factors:1. Pre-departure issue with COVID-19 deadheading crew members and airline's poor handling and pressure was a distracting and still on top of mind.2. PM while setting MCP with ATC instructions was distracted and missed the sop 1;000 feet call (5;000 feet approaching 6;000 feet)3. column121: During descent to ZZZ for visual approach; FO PF (First Officer Pilot Flying); CA PM (Captain Pilot Monitoring). Crew called the airfield in sight and was frequency changed to tower. Once on tower frequency; we heard Tower call a Seneca directing them to clear the approach path of runway XX. The next call was to a departing aircraft calling out our aircraft for separation which they did not see us. TWR then called our aircraft saying traffic 12 o'clock 3600 ft. north northeast bound. We responded with leveling and we have them on TCAS. Noting on TCAS the aircraft climbing toward us and it's very close proximity and rapid closure rate; we leveled our aircraft. The approaching TCAS target continued climbing from less than 1;000 ft. below us at our 12 o'clock into our flight path rapidly. TCAS quickly displayed a climb for the RA OF 3;000 fpm. The PF added thrust to TO (Takeoff) power and climbed with the RA at 3;000 fpm. The PM called tower notifying them we were responding to an RA. The TCAS target continued climbing passing 400 ft. directly under the aircraft from the 12 o'clock position to the 6 o'clock position. After the RA was complete; the crew began the descent again coordinating with tower for a right 360 degree turn in order to reestablish the approach. The crew landed on runway XX without further incident. No heavy aircraft loading during climb and no passenger complaints on landing. No PA's were made to passengers [in] reference [to] this event.Frequency changed from approach to tower at 10 miles for the visual without any traffic notifications. Contacting tower we were given a traffic advisory with less than a 1;000 ft. separation descending while traffic climbed with a rate of closure of at least 400 knots.Before being given a frequency change by approach control crews should be given traffic advisories in the area in order to build situational awareness.
column123: While descending into ZZZ out of approximately 3500 ft. MSL; and on about a 10 mile left base for XX; we received an advisory and then an RA to climb. We had been talking to approach and had just reported the field in sight. We were cleared for the visual and advised to switch to tower frequency. The FO (First Officer) was the PF (Pilot Flying). I switched to tower and heard the tower advising another aircraft to stay clear of the approach area. I checked in and was cleared to land. The tower then advised a Seneca that he needed to clear the approach area due to our approach and was advised to turn left. We then received a traffic advisory from the tower that was simultaneous with TCAS traffic alert; followed shortly by a RA to climb. I was looking outside and did not see the conflicting aircraft. The FO advised it passed underneath approximately 400 ft. below us. The entire event took less than 15 seconds as best I can recall. At that point we advised the tower we had complied with an RA and that we were high and needed a right 360 to re-establish on the approach. The tower responded that where we were was class E airspace and that the opposing Aircraft was not under radar control; and words to the affect that we were not in his airspace. He cleared us for the maneuver and again cleared us to land. Once on the ground we advised the tower via ground frequency that we would be filing a report for a near miss.Changed from approach control to tower after reporting field in sight without being given any traffic advisories before the frequency change. Also departing conflict aircraft departing along approach corridor.Approach controller should coordinate with tower to ensure approach path is clear prior to allowing frequency change.

column121: Filed flight plan about 20 minutes before calling to see if flight plan was in the system. I informed Ground Control that I would pick it up in the air but was just checking to see if it had arrived.  Ground did not have flight plan so I started up and taxied to runway figuring it would be out by the time we were at the hold line. Called at the runway hold line and still no flight plan - Ground suggested I just take off and have the Departure Controller enter one for me.  Just to be safe I quickly filed another one on my phone; did my checks and when I called for takeoff they told me it had just come through.  I had filed NAVHO intersection then BLD VOR on the first flight plan; then just direct BLD VOR on the second - rest of route to ZZZ the same for both plans.On VFR climb I skipped NAVJO because I thought it was the second flight plan that had popped up on the system.  Phoenix Approach was in a long conversation with a VFR plane so couldn't contact until I was at 14;500 feet - climbing to 16;500.  They told me I was almost out of their airspace and to call ABQ Center.  Level at 16;500 I called ABQ and they cleared us to ZZZ as filed.  Here's where there was a problem.  Just to be safe I asked if I should be going direct NAVHO then BLD and the controller said 'affirmative' as I was climbing to FL280.  I knew I wasn't at NAVHO yet so entered it in as 'NAVJO' (incorrect).  I noticed that the needle pointed over 30 degrees to the right as I engaged NAV - figuring something was wrong I disengaged NAV and turned back to something close to direct BLD and asked if I could just go direct BLD which I was given.  NAVHO was pretty much on a direct line from FLG to BLD so I was doing okay before entering 'NAVJO' which is way up to the North.Looking at the track log I never was more than 17 degrees off and that was for as long as it took to reverse the turn; but this was embarrassing.  Don't want to do this kind of thing when departing a NY Metro area airport.  Contributing factors:  Flight plan late arriving at FLG.  My desire to do a quick turn and keep the boss happy - this was a fuel stop.  Misspelling 'NAVHO' because I was rushing - trying to keep the controller happy.  Two flight plans in the system; each with a different initial fix.  I neglected to enter NAVJO because it would be departing VFR and it was pretty close to the airport. Ways to prevent this from recurring:  File my flight plans earlier just in case - even if I'm not sure we will use it.  I thought we may be able to make it all the way to ZZZ so didn't file the plan for departing from FLG (fuel stop).  Don't be so quick to engage NAV - make sure it looks correct first.  Don't rush when entering waypoints - if I had entered with the correct spelling there would not have been more than a few degree turn to the left involved.  Enter all the fixes when departing VFR - don't assume you won't get one of them.

They had a properly programmed FMS with no modifications to the waypoints. The airplane behaved unexpectedly with a continual turn passing the first waypoint PIKIL and deviating from the magenta course line. They appropriately downgraded from the highest level of automation to correct the error. The RF2; who was the PM; captured the POS REPORT page when time allowed. The operating crew requested updated winds aloft around XC:00Z and were made available and executed around the time of PIKIL. Perhaps the new winds caused the FMS anomaly and shouldn't be requested anywhere near the first ocean entry point. This was stated as a known anomaly with the B767 FMS.

column121: Unanticipated GPWS warning on approach requiring crew action. We were flying the freighter (tail); second leg ZZZ-ZZZ1 (1.5 hr delayed at start of day); 5-6 hours into the flight duty period (~XA:00 pm local time). Night IMC w/moderate to heavy rain showers in vicinity. I was Pilot Flying PF (Captain).Clearance was ZZZ...ZZZ1. On the ground at ZZZ we planned and briefed the departure and RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from the ZZZZZ1 transition. De-iced; taxied; departed; climbed to cruise at FL280.Enroute to ZZZZZ1 at cruise; Center warned of areas of moderate to extreme precipitation from ZZZZZ1 fix to the airport and advised of better weather to the Northeast. After discussing a change to the arrival; we both agreed to request radar vectors to the approach segment from ZZZZZ (IAF). Center agreed to vector us around and down to put us on the published portion of the arrival with the stated intention of joining us to the approach path at ZZZZZ2. FO (First Officer) made the changes in the FMS and we briefed and then ran the Decent Checklist Change Triangles.Radar vectors included a descent and vectors resulting in established on published segment near ZZZZZ2 at 5000 and given approach clearance from center (I had directed PM to reset FMS Cruise Alt to 8;000 feet when we were on vectors). Once established near ZZZZZ2 at 5;000 cleared us for the approach. I engaged LNAV/VNAV and set airport elevation; but was high on the vertical path. I continued to slow to final configuration (gear down; Flaps 40) by ZZZZZ1; stable; but still 1;400 feet above the path in VNAV SPD (vertical navigation speed). After the turn at ZZZZZ1 I set 1;600 feet in the MCP ALT window (FAP 1;600 MSL) and at approximately 2;300 MSL; engaged Vertical Speed down in order to regain the VNAV Path before the FAP. As I approached the path; I reset MCP altitude to airfield elevation and engaged VNAV while pitch mode was in ALT ACQ (altitude acquire); resulting in an unrecognized mode change to V/S (2;100 ft/min) and projected vertical path well before the airport. It was at this point; we received a GPWS 'Caution Terrain' followed shortly by GPWS Warning 'Terrain Fly UP.'  I immediately executed an escape maneuver/go-around; climbing and flying the go-around flight path to ZZZ2 and mistakenly climbed to 5;000 MSL (missed approach alt 3;000 MSL); entering the hold as published. I requested and was given a descent to 3;000 MSL in holding.We then built and briefed the RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from ZZZ2; ran the Descent Change Triangles; received our approach clearance; and executed the approach to landing uneventfully. The FO and I thoroughly debriefed the events of the flight. I then called the Duty Pilot and DISPATCH to report the incident. I should have requested radar vectors ZZZZZ1 for the best opportunity to acquire the VNAV path. I allowed the Controller to compress and to keep me high on my approach; and reducing my situational awareness. I configured very early; but it still wasn't enough to regain the VNAV path. In the future; I will not allow the ATC Controller to dictate the terms of my energy management and will give myself the Flight Handbook recommended 3 miles per 1;000 descent planning as a minimum starting point.Because we compressed our arrival and ended up high above the VNAV path I attempted to use the Vertical Speed method on LNAV/VNAV Approach rules to regain VNAV path prior to the FAP. Had I cross-checked my FMA after selecting VNAV; I would have noticed the V/S mode and perhaps executed an uneventful go-around. In the future; I will make sure to always verify my FMA mode on the PFD after making a selection on the MCP.Lastly; after fully configuring and still not descending to the path; I might have been able to acquire VNAV path prior to the FAP using Speed Intervention. There was chance we were light enough (low Ref Speed) to accelerate the idle pitch descent to regain the path; ensuring the pitch FMA remained in VNAV and avoiding the unrecognized and inadvertent V/S mode descent that caused the GPWS Warning. Recommend expanding the understanding of VNAV speed during initial and continuing qualification training in the B737.
column123: Escape Maneuver occurred at approximately (time) local time on (date). Flight conditions at the time were night; IMC; rain; light turbulence.Leg 2 of a planned 4 leg day. Leg 1 was delayed 1 hours due to cargo loading. The flight was uneventful. Deiced in ZZZ after aircraft pushback. Filed route was ZZZ...ZZZ1. We planned and briefed the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZZZ. Cruise was at FL280. PF (pilot flying) MFD was in WX Radar mode due to significant weather in the area. PM (pilot monitoring) was in TERR (terrain) mode with VSD (vertical speed) displayed. Cruise was at dusk. Shortly after starting the descent; ATC notified us that he saw an area of Moderate to Extreme precipitation ahead of us. ATC said it looked clearer to the north and asked if we would like vectors to the north for an approach via ZZZZZ1. We responded yes and he started vectoring us north. PF flew while PM loaded the arrival from ZZZZZ1 (via IAF ZZZZZ1). PM briefed the new approach and called for change triangles; which we accomplished. ATC had us do intermediate level-offs at 8;000 feet; then 7;000 feet. PF asked PM to reset the cruise altitude to provide an accurate flight path. In anticipation of being high on flight path; PF configured early to flaps 40. PM was actively monitoring the VSD and flight path; and requested lower when able from ATC. ATC said he would give us lower in a few miles. He then gave us a short vector prior to ZZZZZ2 with a descent to 6;500 feet. At approx 0.5 miles before ZZZZZ2 at 6;500 feet; ATC cleared us 'to cross ZZZZZ2 at or above 5;000 feet; cleared RNAV Rwy XX at ZZZ1'. When cleared for the approach over ZZZZZ2; PF dialed in field elevation in the MCP and descended towards the flight path. Flight conditions were night; IMC; rain; light turbulence. Approximately 1 mile prior to ZZZZZ3; we were still high on flight path so PF verbalized and set Vertical Speed down and reset MCP to 1;600 feet. PM saw the downward vector on the VSD and monitored it for approaching the flight path. Almost immediately thereafter; we received a 'Caution; Terrain' and the depicted island terrain went yellow on PM's MFD. This was quickly followed by a 'Terrain; Pull up' and the depicted terrain on the MFD went red. PF called for go-around and executed the escape maneuver. After aircraft was climbing; PF asked PM to reset MCP for missed approach altitude of 3;000 feet. PF initially had difficulty verifying the missed approach altitude on the EFB due to turbulence; transition to nighttime; and prioritizing monitoring the aircraft state while performing aircraft cleanup. PF put and verbalized 5;000 feet in the MCP window; thinking 5;000 feet was better in case 3;000 feet was incorrect. PMs intent was to devote more brain cells to performing the aircraft cleanup items and monitoring the safe aircraft state as we climbed. Aircraft was cleaned up; leveled at 5;000 feet and continued to holding at ZZZ2. We then queried ATC for a descent to 3;000 feet; setup the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZ2. Approach was briefed by Captain; flown; and landed uneventfully. Once the aircraft reached parking and shutdown at ZZZ1; Captain and FO debriefed the events. Captain called and briefed Duty Officer; who approved continuing to the remaining 2 destinations. Captain also called and spoke with Dispatch. The remaining flights to were flown with minimal changes. Post flight; the Captain called Quality Assurance to see what they could tell us; so that we could learn further from this experience.Stay on the magenta line; and if vectored off; get back on it as early as possible. Even though the controller had plans to vector us back onto the RNP approach; a better outcome likely would have resulted if we started at the IAP. This way we would have been able to descend on a normal flight path; with adequate time and pacing; vs. having to stay higher due to the controllers higher vectoring altitudes. Request the IAP next time.At nighttime in IMC; I need to have a faster response timecalling for the escape maneuver/go-around. I should clarify this maneuver more; particularly the triggers. I should have been the first to call for it since the Captain was the PF. Instead of trying to salvage a bad or difficult approach; make the decision to go-around earlier. Memorize the missed approach altitude prior to each approach; or ensure my EFB chart is not zoomed-in so far that I cannot see it without a quick glance.Clarify various 'what-if scenarios' on RNP approaches; Escape Maneuvers; Go-Arounds. If I haven't flown as much recently; spend extra time clarifying. Communicate with Center that 6;500 feet at ZZZZZ2 creates a very difficult approach to accomplish. Recommend to them that vectoring to the IAF is likely a better option.

column121: Runway XXR was NOTAMed closed for 2 hours due to a crane on the departure end of the runway. Runway XXL was in use. Aircraft inbound from the west was given a right downwind entry for Runway XXL. The aircraft was sequenced to follow multiple aircraft ahead. On short final; I noticed that he appeared to be lined up for the closed runway (Runway XXR). I instructed the pilot to go-around and re-enter right traffic Runway XXL and emphasized to the pilot that Runway XXR is closed. When I cleared him to land Runway XXL; he again appeared to be lined up for XXR. I verified if he was lined up for the correct runway and on very short final; he appeared to maneuver for the correct runway.Background: all controllers at ZZZ have been on 6 day work week for the last few months due to a shortage in staffing. Our facility has also been experiencing roughly a 20% increase in traffic volume compared to last year. In September; our traffic count index has reached the numbers for us to qualify for a level 8 upgrade. If we sustain our traffic numbers for the next couple of months; level 8 at ZZZ will become a reality once it gets approved by the National Validation Team.We are all fatigued from the increase in traffic and the amount of overtime we have all been working. This is no doubt affecting our performance on position. Morale is down and controllers are becoming more and more impatient with pilots as a result of being over-worked. I worry that this will impact safety by increasing the possibility of human error.I felt noticeably fatigued towards the end of my work week. If I had not been as fatigued; I may have been able to recognize the aircraft lined up for the incorrect runway sooner. Thankfully; I recognized it at the last second; but it was very close.Yesterday; I was working CIC combined with GC. Traffic was busy. A Controller who was finishing an overlap in the back of the cab was on the phone with someone and relayed information to me. I was in the middle of working a lot of traffic on ground and what I thought I heard was to have the pilot of an Aircraft X with an XXXXX tail number call the airport manager when he lands. It turned out that the airport manager wanted us to call him when the aircraft landed.  Had we had more staffing and CIC was de-combined; this information would have been properly relayed to me. I would have been able to figure out that we had to call the airport manager and not have the pilot call. Again; my lapse in judgement may have also been due to fatigue from prolonged 6 day work weeks.For the safe of safety; the agency needs to take our staffing situation seriously. In the midst of the pandemic; our tower hours have changed to XC:00am to XO:00pm. Even though we have a staffing issue; due to the compressed tour hours; there is a good amount of overlap between controllers so we can keep LC split into 2 positions. In a little over a week; we will be going back to our normal hours which are XA:00am until XQ:00pm. column121: The VFR Aircraft; Aircraft X; was cleared on the [published VFR route] to maintain 5;500 feet. He was southbound and converging over the VOR with Aircraft Y who was IFR and descended to 5;000 feet and told about the 5;500 feet traffic that was at the time 4 miles north of the VOR. Everything was fine and it was a normal everyday situation. I was cleaning up some loose ends giving headings to other aircraft and traffic advisories; many traffic advisories. I had an aircraft report getting an RA but its resolution told him to stay where they were because there were just so many VFR's. Then I hear the Traffic Alert start which isn't uncommon for aircraft 500 feet apart in this airspace and as I look up the Aircraft Y tells me he's responding to an RA and his voice is clearly strained.I incorrectly said what I was thinking which was 'Aircraft X what are you doing! Climb immediately to 5;500' as I'm watching him descend through 5;200 feet right on top of Aircraft Y. He responds that he 'thought they were on a collision course'. To which I informed him that his actions caused the collision course. He also turned right which would have been fine if that's all he had done and stayed at 5;500 feet; but the descent made it a near or for sure mid-air if Aircraft Y hadn't taken evasive action. I issued a Brasher Warning to the pilot of Aircraft X because he 100% cause a perfectly separated situation to become a very ugly situation. Both aircraft were in the Class Bravo airspace and the VFR aircraft had no right or reason to descend at all.Over the top of LA is just a busy place where aircraft are routinely separated by 500 feet; that's just life. If they move the VFR areas where Special Flight Rules is to somewhere else then we would definitely have more altitudes to use to separate people by greater than 500 feet. but; until that happens it's just going to be what it's going to be.
column123: While on a Class B clearance through the Class Bravo airspace on published VFR Route southbound at 5;500 feet; I received a traffic notification from Approach for traffic at 11 o'clock; opposite direction; at 5;000 MSL a conflict for traffic that was approaching nearly head-on. I continued to visually scan for the traffic in front of me; and when I finally spotted the oncoming traffic it was at my 11 o'clock to 11:30 position in my windscreen; at eye level. I was unable to discern any relative motion of the target relative to my windscreen. The only change I could see in the target was that it was getting larger in my field of view; and that it appeared to be some type of small jet aircraft. I immediately initiated a turn to my right in order to avoid the oncoming traffic. The turn that I initiated was done very quickly; and was probably on the order of a 30 to 35 degree angle of bank. As a result of this turn; I lost approximately 250 feet of altitude from my cruising altitude of 5;500 feet. My change in heading was approximately 45 degrees; and once my turn was completed I was able to discern relative motion of the target with respect to my windscreen and left side window. The traffic was now moving to my left; and the separation between the two of us was increasing.The opposite directly traffic passed well behind me. At that point the TRACON Controller called me and admonished me for deviating from my assigned heading and altitude. I responded to the controller with an apology; and explained that the opposite direction traffic appeared to be on a collision course with me; and it required me to take evasive action. The controller provided me with a toll-free number to call after I landed. After landing I called the toll-free number and spoke to an individual at SOCAL who asked me to describe the occurrence from my perspective. I described the occurrence in an identical manner to what I have written here. The individual was very courteous and listened carefully to my explanation; and thanked me for calling. The call ended with no indication to me that any further action would be forthcoming.It is extremely difficult to estimate lateral and vertical separation of traffic; especially when a target has no apparent relative motion and is approaching head-on. Any vertical separation that does exist between two aircraft in this situation will not be perceptible until the aircraft are very close together; when there is very little time to take evasive action if it is required. In this particular case; the opposite direction traffic was probably traveling at least twice as fast as my aircraft; resulting in an effective rate of closure of at least 400 MPH. A vertical separation of 500 feet is very small; and when possible sources of altitude error are included; it is possible that the actual vertical separation between our two aircraft was less than 500 feet.  Approximately ten minutes after this occurrence; I was in the vicinity of another airport and was in contact with another sector of the TRACON. This Controller provided me with a traffic advisory regarding jet traffic inbound from the west at 5;000 feet; and gave me instructions to climb and maintain 6;000 feet for separation purposes. I initiated the climb and leveled off at 6;000 feet; and observed the jet traffic passed well below me. After the jet traffic had crossed my flight path; the Controller cleared me back down to 5;500 feet. I have included a description of this action on the part of Approach as an example of prudent traffic management.In summary; I should have been more diligent in maintaining my assigned altitude of 5;500 feet during my turn to avoid the oncoming traffic. However; it was my belief that there was insufficient separation between the flight paths of our two aircraft; and seeing no relative motion of a target that was at eye-level in my windscreen; as pilot-in-command of the aircraft I took evasive action in the interest of collision avoidance.

column121: This event was a complex setup with numerous contributing factors that led to a slight and uneventful course deviation on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Having spent 30+ years in the part of the US I was quite familiar with the dynamics of the environment. In preparing the flight; I ran a prelim flight plan which recommended a route I would expect; a SID that meshed with the ZZZZZ3 arrival to ZZZ1. For arrivals from the south into ZZZ1 it is customary and without exception have flown the ZZZZZ3 which runs with the arrivals and departures to several airports. There were numerous TFR's along and around the route of flight this day. I filed a flight plan using app which recommended a different route; a SID to Victor airways; no STAR into ZZZ1. It was presumed this route was preferred to accommodate the numerous TFR's. I know for certain in the app I had selected FL230 as I wanted to either be rerouted as necessary for the TFRs or be above as the TFRs were below FL180. These issues were disclosed; briefed between the two pilots prior to filing flight plan; discussed verbally in the takeoff briefing; and even added extra fuel for possible reroute. When our clearance was obtained to depart ZZZ; it was for the SID and Victor airways as filed with app; further reinforcing the presumption that it was ATC preferred due to the TFR's. The final altitude cleared was 17;000 feet due to the Victor airways chosen; not FL230 as was desired.As we began our taxi; we were expecting Runway XX for departure which was a fairly long taxi. Traffic was light; and Ground Control stated Runway XXC was available which we accepted. This now being a very short taxi. I stated to the copilot would taxi slowly to allow time to load new departure runway in FMS; the SID chart was retrieved; compared to the FMS; and the takeoff briefing verbally amended accordingly. In doing these things; we verified only page one of the flight plan in the FMS. At this point we were not aware that in reloading the departure RW; the FMS had on the second page not only inserted a discontinuity; but had deleted two waypoints; the last one on the SID and first point on the filed Victor airway.As we were flying the departure and level at 15;000 feet; we crossed the second to last waypoint on the SID. At this point when the FMS sequenced; the discontinuity appeared on page one. This FMS has known issues and several Service Information Letters (SIL's) from the manufacturer regarding runway changes with SIDs and STARs. Having seen the occurrence a vast number of times for arrivals when changing or loading the arrival runway after the STAR; the resolve had always been to delete the discontinuity as no waypoints had ever been seen deleted and verify altitude/speed restrictions. When the discontinuity appeared on page one of the FMS flight plan; it was simply deleted without verifying the fix meshed with the filed route. As two waypoints had also been deleted; this created the issue at hand. Soon after we crossed the waypoint in question; ATC asked if we were beginning our RH turn. This exchange revealed the error at hand and we were given a vector. Believe it was just prior to that waypoint that ATC asked if we could join the ZZZZZ3 arrival; to which we stated yes. The Controller stated this will be vectors to join the ZZZZZ3 and cleared us to 17;000 feet. At this point we inserted the missing waypoints and queried ATC to confirm our currently assigned route. ATC again stated expect the ZZZZZ3 without confirming assigned route; and did not provide an expect to waypoint to join the ZZZZZ3. A level of uncertainty remained as the ZZZZZ3 has six (6) transitions into the arrival. We briefed and had STAR displayed to deal with the coming short notice for the join waypoint as the fixes along this arrival are close together with several altitude and speed restrictions. Throughout this event; we could hear ATC transmitting to other aircraft; but never heard other aircraft respond; thus the controller was obviously working multiple frequencies/sectors with a resulting high workload likely contributing to not providing and expect to waypoint. This also presented a certain level of distraction on our part. Once we were cleared to a waypoint on the ZZZZZ3; and with a descend via clearance; the remainder of the flight was uneventful. The slight deviation actually took us further away from the TFRs; no restricted airspace was encroached; and there were no traffic conflicts.

column121: On the DRLLR5 Arrival into IAH the aircraft went into a roll mode configuration at DOMNO; displaced the NAV mode and maintained its course on the RNAV arrival without turning to the next fix (SKLER). I immediately went on heading mode; turned the aircraft towards SKLER the next fix on the RNAV and my First Officer updated the aircraft simultaneously towards the next fix (SKLER). A few seconds later; the controller asked us if were making a turn towards the next fix. We replied yes and continued the flight on the arrival. The event took less than 10 seconds. Once heading in the right direction we then re-engaged NAV mode and continued on the arrival with no further incidents. This incident has been very frequent on our airplanes on the same Arrival on the final turn on the arrival; we followed every single procedure on our SOPs and training bulletin by double checking our fixes to make sure we had no duplicates and by waiting till we get a runway assignment before we load any runway on the FMS; still we still had the same issue.On landing at IAH the tower control advised us of a possible pilot deviation and issued us a phone number; after the flight on our debrief we then concluded it will be wise to submit an incident report. Since we followed every single procedure and training bulletin and still ran into the same issue; my suggestion is for the company to find out why the FMS and autopilot keep getting confused at this fixes; for the mean time I will always be ready and alert on this said arrivals and fixes to reduce or completely eliminate any deviation.
