column121: I was operating as First Officer and Pilot Monitoring on our flight. In cruise approximately 15-20 mins prior to touchdown we were talking to Center. When we checked in with them they advised us to expect the visual for Runway XX. Being night time; we advised them that we needed the ILS. The controller then cleared us to ZZZZZ to do the NDB procedure turn for the ILS [Runway] XX. We told the controller that we couldn't find this in our box and asked for direct to ZZZZZ1 which would eliminate the procedure turn and give us more space to set up for the approach. The controller asked us why we couldn't just tune in the NDB and fly it. We ended up just asking for direct to the field while we looked at the box and tried to set up what the controller was asking. We were approved as requested. Still having trouble setting up the box we asked the controller for direct ZZZZZ1 several times for the ILS [Runway] XX. He finally cleared us direct ZZZZZ1. We were told to descend and maintain 4;100 feet until established on a segment and then cleared for the ILS [Runway] XX. Being at 4;100 feet so close in left us a little high for the approach. Approximately 1-1.5 miles from ZZZZZ1 and approaching on a 300 heading; the Captain disconnected the auto pilot. I reminded him that we were instructed to maintain 4;100 feet until established and that we were cleared for the ILS. The Captain was navigating in pink needles and I had green needles on my side so that the Captain could reference the glide slope. We were showing approximately a dot and a half above the glide slope. At that point the Captain began to descend to catch up to the glide slope and proceeded to turn inbound. As far as I could tell he started doing this prior to being established inbound. Once we were finally established inbound we were at approximately 3;800 feet and descending which was above the minimum altitude for that segment however we were instructed to maintain 4;100 feet until established on a segment. At this point the controller switched us over to advisories. The flight continued normally. The controller did not advise us of any issues. This was all under visual conditions. I don't believe the altitude was a problem. I think we were within the normal tolerances for being established on the inbound course however I am uncertain. This report is being filed because the Captain prematurely descended below our assigned altitude as well as both the Captain and I feeling as though the controller was very unprofessional and unhelpful in aiding us in flying the plane the safest way possible. The Captain and I realized that we couldn't find the appropriate fix for the procedure turn in the box and did the right thing by telling the controller and trying to work with him. He was not very receptive to helping. As I said this created confusion in the cockpit trying to figure out how to make the procedure turn happen. As mentioned; after asking several times we were finally cleared direct ZZZZZ1. Approaching ZZZZZ1 at 4;100 feet and seeing we were high; the Captain disconnected the autopilot and started descending. That's when I reminded him that we needed to maintain 4;100 feet until established and weren't quite at ZZZZZ1 yet. He responded by saying he had the field and that it was ok to start descending. The root cause of all of this was the controller refusing to accommodate our requests to start the ILS [Runway] XX at a fix that would eliminate an NDB procedure turn. All of the back and forth created a lot of confusion for us in the cockpit. The end result was us getting a compromise for flying the approach we needed however it left us high which lead the Captain to descend early to catch the glide slope. As mentioned we reacted by asking the controller several times to work with us. We weren't asking for much. All we wanted was to be cleared to a fix to give us space to set up and [eliminate] the procedure turn. As far as the Captain possibly starting his descent early; I reacted by speaking up and telling him that I didn't think we were established inbound yet. He elected to continue to descend despite the concerns. This was a one leg day. Day one of a four day trip. Starting your first leg at XA:00 is tough for anyone. Being tired from sitting around all day waiting to go to work; we figured the safest option was to ask for a solution that eliminated the NDB procedure turn. We were both confused in trying to set up the box and asked for a different fix; ZZZZZ1; which seemed like a good option. This was the right decision. We did not expect so much push back from the controller. The last time I did any NDB procedures was almost five years ago in a simulator. With GPS waypoints and our FMS; the safest option was to avoid trying to experiment with an NDB procedure turn while conducting a revenue flight at night. Additionally; although instructed to be at 4;100 feet at ZZZZZ1 which would leave us slightly high; it would have been a better option if the Captain had let the auto pilot turn inbound and as soon as we were established then he could have initiated the descent to catch up to the glide slope. This way there would have been no question about our altitude.

column121: This was a post maintenance test flight after ventilation system had been partially dismantled trying to troubleshoot a noise from vents.Departed ZZZ VFR and requested from Approach to depart to the southwest and climb to FL250 for post maintenance flight to check pressurization. Was given an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1 and eventually handed off to Center. Center cleared me to FL250 and was directed to maintain current heading...basically towards ZZZ1. Upon reaching FL250 I determined that the noise had not been resolved and I requested from ATC that I was done and would like to head back to ZZZ. Immediately there was a 'pop' and the aircraft began to rapidly depressurize followed by the cabin pressurization Master Warning light and buzzer. Everything happened before the controller could give me a new heading or altitude. I immediately pulled power back to idle; banked approximately 45 degrees to left and began a rapid descent. The controller stated that he 'noticed' I was in a left turn to which I replied that I was having some pressurization issues and needed to get lower. The controller asked if I wanted to declare an emergency to which I declined and stated that it's ok I just needed to get lower. I was then cleared to 17;000 feet and then handed off to Approach control. Remainder of flight back to ZZZ was uneventful.Although the controller did not call me out for altitude or heading deviation; I was concerned that I had initiated a turn and altitude change without clearance from the controlling ATC. My main concern was to fly the plane and handle the situation prior to advising ATC. The sky condition was unlimited visibility and ceiling and there was little to no traffic in the area. The time from the onset of the depressurization; me configuring the aircraft for a rapid descent and communicating with ATC was maybe 5-10 seconds.It was later determined that the shop had not securely reinstalled pressurized ducting in the nose of the aircraft and upon reaching FL250 that ducting separated from it's connection and vented pressurized air from the cabin to the outside.

column121: While descending on the ZZZ1 arrival we were cleared to FL290.  While passing FL300 ATC issued a pilot discretion descent clearance to 17;000 feet.  My PNF waited to set 17;000 feet until the autopilot went into ALT CAP and began to capture FL290.  Upon setting 17;000 feet I noticed the autopilot no longer holding FL290 and disconnected the autopilot and manually held altitude and then selected manual ALT to hold FL290.  At that point the autopilot was forgotten to be reengaged; and the aircraft slowly climbed to almost 29;800 feet before the PF noticed it and manually initiated descent to 17;000 feet.  ATC was notified of the correction and that we were beginning our discretion descent from current altitude to 17;000 feet.  ATC did not say anything about the brief climb and only verified we were beginning our descent to cross ZZZZZ [Intersection] at 17;000 feet.Human factors of disconnecting the automation while correcting for the unanticipated non capture; manually setting ALT hold without resetting the ALT selector caused no bug to appear on the altitude tape and the action of selecting ALT hold caused the PF to be the live autopilot; holding altitude; although only the FD was since the autopilot had not been reengaged.  Usually we would correct an autopilot behavior such as this while still engaged by resetting the ALT selector and using VS or Pitch mode; but that level of automation had been removed.  Problem was identified and quickly discussed and understood by the flight crew to ensure better communication and pilot automation interface in the future. A likely contributing factor is lack of flying hours in the recent 6 months for both crewmembers due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

column121: While on the ZZZZZ4 [arrival]; approaching ZZZZZ we were given a vector to the North.  We were asked if we had the river in sight; which we responded; 'Yes.'  We were cleared the ZZZZZ visual to Runway XX.  CA wanted to cross ZZZZZ1 at 3;000 feet; so CA selected Flt Lvl Chg and proceeded down.  Upon reaching the fix; CA failed to re-select VNAV as we commenced the approach.  LNAV was selected and we were tracking correctly.  Between ZZZZZ2 and ZZZZZ3; CA realized we were too low.  CA saw the '1;700' at ZZZZZ3; we were at approximately 1;100 feet.  CA clicked off the auto pilot and leveled the aircraft at 1;000 feet.  We were given a 'low Altitude' alert from the Tower.  We maintained our altitude and tracked the approach.  We landed without any further incident.  We were below the charted altitudes at ZZZZZ3 and ZZZZZ4; possibly ZZZZZ5.I believe currency was a significant factor.  The CA had a total of 55 hours in the preceding 5+ months and the FO had just come back from 6 month leave.  Because this was an RNAV approach; briefing the importance of verifying both LNAV/VNAV on the FMA would have reminded both pilots to look for this upon the commencement of the approach.
column123: We were descending for the ZZZZZ Visual approach to [Runway] XX. We had the RNV-F approach selected in the FMS. Descending through approximately 5;000 feet ATC had given us a lower altitude so the Captain selected LVL CHG. A short time later ATC asked if we had the river in sight; we did; so we were cleared for the visual approach. We set our briefed minimums for the approach and continued our descent. However we had not gone back to VNAV and confirmed VNAV PATH. As we approached 1;000 feet we both realized we were too low. The Captain disengaged the autopilot. Stopped the descent until we were reestablished on the path. From there we continued the approach to landing.This was my first leg back from a six month leave and the captain is on reserve and had not flown in two months. We had briefed before the flight that our biggest threat was our lack of recent flying. This proves that even when a threat is identified and discussed; it does not go away.The company and [union] need to continue to stress as more of us return to work that observance to SOPs is vital to the priority of safety.

column121: During our preflight the Captain and I discussed how recently we had each flown.  I had not flown for about 5 weeks and the Captain had just done landings class at training after not flying since March; as I recall.  This was the Captain's first trip since then.After takeoff; Captain was hand flying the airplane and I was performing PM duties.  We were on the ZZZZZ2 departure and I had checked in with ZZZ Departure.  They told us about a storm directly to our south that other flights were having to leave the departure route to avoid.  ATC said we could continue to the west and turn to a 150 heading when able.  After looking at the radar return I acknowledged the instruction and added we would have to go about another 10 miles west.  ATC acknowledged and cleared us to climb to 12;000 feet.I should also mention this was in a very compressed time line.  Tower turned us over to Departure; I was doing the After Takeoff Check and making FMC modifications under the Captain's instructions; and checking in and talking with ATC.  The plane was also very light; so we were climbing rapidly.  I was interrupted three times while trying to read the After Takeoff Checklist and I think we were nearly at 10;000 feet by the time I was able to accomplish the checklist.  I guess; what I'm trying to say is; I felt that I was very busy; and surprisingly so.  ZZZZZ can get busy; apparently even now; but the thunderstorm and the communication and coordination involved with that probably took us to task saturation.After being cleared to 12;000; we got another frequency change and ATC cleared us to 14;000 feet.  I set it in the MCP and saw the flight director was still in LNAV and commanding a left turn.  I asked if Captain wanted HDG SEL and Captain did which I accomplished.  ATC then asked us about the turn to the south and I answered we still were going to have to go further west; but the tops were lowering and I thought the turn could be made soon.  ATC then amended our cleared altitude to 12;000 feet again.I reset the MCP again and got acknowledgment from the Captain.  ATC then cleared us to go direct to ZZZZZ1 when we were able.  I put it in the FMC to see how the course looked compared to the radar return.  I looked out the window to see how the tops were looking.  I heard the altitude alert chime then looked at our altimeter and saw we were climbing through 12;000 feet.  I immediately exclaimed we were cleared to 12;000 feet and I think the Captain swore and immediately reversed the climb.ATC then informed us we were cleared to 12;000 feet.  I re-acknowledged the altitude clearance and we descended back to 12;000 feet.  I don't think we got above 12;600 feet.I wish I could remember when we were re-cleared to 12;000 feet; because I don't remember hearing the approaching altitude alert chime.  I think the altitude may have been above 11;000 feet so we were already within the 900 foot alert window.  When the chime did sound; I thought it was the 900 feet to go; but it was really the 300 foot off warning.
column123: We were on the departure and had been told to maintain a heading due to weather. Altitude clearance was to 14;000 feet. column121: We were departing from Pittsburgh Airport. We took off on runway 28R and were assigned runway heading.Our flight plan first fix was AHTIY (then to BURGS). We briefed the route during preflight and of course verified that the course looked like it should.Shortly after takeoff; we were given a turn to the left to 'eighty' which I know from prior experience is how they pronounce that first fix; AHTIY. We brought that point up in our flight plan; inserted it into the FMS (Flight Management System) direct; agreed; then activated. The turn was a very sharp left. Once we realized we were turning toward the airport and away from our course; we briefly discussed amongst ourselves that the seemed strange. I immediately called up to verify that our clearance was a left turn direct 'eighty' (or AHTIY.) ATC (Air Traffic Control) confirmed but immediately told us to turn right to a heading of 180 'one eighty'. We started a turn to 180 but it only added to the confusion because now I thought that perhaps when I had heard 'eighty' earlier maybe I misunderstood and it was actually a heading of 'one eighty'.Once we were on that heading; we were cleared again 'direct AHTIY'. I read it back very slowly and asked to confirm that we would make a right turn direct to the fix. He said; 'Affirmative... Direct Alpha Hotel Tango India Yankee.' It was then that I realized that the point I had on my flight plan in the FMS had the T & the I switched... AHITY. I proceeded to type in the correct spelling; we agreed and flew toward AHTIY. At this point; I thought that the point AHITY actually existed over the top of Pittsburgh Airport. I found that to be a really strange placement for such a closely spelled GPS (Global Positioning System) fix to AHTIY. Upon beginning this report; I looked at my charts to verify where that fix was located. The fix doesn't seem to exist. I racked my brain to try to figure out how the fix existed in that plane but not on my chart. Then I remembered that pilots can create their own waypoints. Normally; if a fix does not exist; the FMS pulls up an option to create a pilot waypoint. I can tell you with 100% certainty but this did not happen to me when I was entering the flight plan. However; because it took my false waypoint without the prompt to create it; I can deduce that someone created that way point in that database prior to my typing it. At this point; someone must have created a misspelled version of AHTIY as AHITY. It was then that I remembered a detail that I had deemed unimportant prior to this. When we began entering the flight plan; the First Officer was holding the paperwork. He had started to enter the flight plan and then stopped. When I asked if he was doing it or if he wanted me to; he said that he decided to stop and get the ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) first so I could do it. He spelled the first point for me as AHITY and I typed it. I then picked up the other copy of the flight plan and told him I would use that for the routing if he wanted to get the ATIS. I continued with BURGS and so on. I wanted to confirm my suspicions about this waypoint so I looked up the crew for the outbound flight on that aircraft. The First Officer happens to be a friend of mine. I called her and I asked her to pull up the pilot created waypoint list. She did; and sure enough there was a fix called AHITY. I had her take a photo of the coordinates for that point and send it to me. I also asked her to please delete the point from the database. I spoke with my First Officer today about user created waypoints. He says he did not create AHITY. Either way; it was a point in the pilot waypoint database and thus allowed me to use it in my flight plan.An unfortunate series of events seems to have led up to us turning toward a non-existent point. Luckily there was no mention of pilot deviation or loss of separation with any aircraft; but a mistake was still made.In the future; I will make apoint to double check the spelling of all waypoints along the route myself. We did not catch it on our verbal route review because we read it as the first fix despite the 2 letters being switched. It didn't look much different. I have certainly learned a lot from this experience; and will do my best to ensure that this does not happen again to me or anyone that I fly with. The only suggestion I have is perhaps to request that the company send a reminder to the pilot group to refresh everyone about pilot created waypoints. I would emphasize that if you do create a waypoint; you should only do it if you are doing it purposefully and using the coordinates on your chart. Then; after the flight; you should delete that point so that we don't have non-existent points in our database.

column121: Vectored off of ZZZZZ 4 STAR and directed to descend to 5;000 feet and proceed direct to ZZZZZ and intercept the Runway XXL LOC. Loaded ZZZZZ in FMS; selected LNAV and armed LOC. While on a roughly southwest heading and proceeding direct to ZZZZZ in LNAV/VNAV; but still well east of Runway XXL we experienced a false LOC capture and the AFDS turned the aircraft to a heading of 176 degrees. Disconnected AFDS and de-armed the LOC and then used HDG Select to turn back to ZZZZZ. While in the process of turning back to ZZZZZ; Approach Control called us and said 'Flight AAAB I need you direct to ZZZZZ; turn right heading XXX.' We proceeded direct to ZZZZZ and landed uneventfully.PF and PM both recently returned to flying after long layoffs and that may have contributed. I knew for sure not to arm the Approach (APP) mode too early due to the aircraft either climbing to join the glide slope or descending on the glide slope before being established on the localizer; and was aware of the possibility of false localizer capture; but had never experienced a false LOC capture before.Using LNAV to intercept the LOC is a normal procedure; but possibly don't arm not only the APP mode; but also the LOC until within a few degrees of the ILS final approach course.  However this procedure could cause its own set of problems/conflicts by setting you up for flying through the LOC if you forget to arm the LOC.
column123: We were assigned 5;000 feet; and given direct to ZZZZZ with instructions to join the localizer for [Runway] XXL there. Captain selected ZZZZZ and we proceeded direct in LNAV mode. He also armed LOC. About 8-10 miles northeast of ZZZZZ the aircraft falsely captured the localizer and began a turn south. Captain tried to select heading mode; but it initially would not select due to the false LOC capture. When we realized what happened; he deselected the LOC mode and began our turn back to ZZZZZ. About halfway through the turn back; ATC called and said he needed us direct ZZZZZ. We informed him we were in the turn; proceeded to ZZZZZ; and completed the approach without incident.The main cause was the premature capture of the localizer. I have not seen the aircraft do this before; and don't recall a warning or admonishment that it may. I don't plan on selecting LOC until closer to the intercept fix from now on; but I still don't believe this to be a crew error except that a slightly more timely response to the errant capture probably could have happened. The delay in response may have been quicker with a bit more recency of experience as both the Captain and I had recently returned from months long absences.Delaying LOC arming until closer to intercept is what I plan to do; though I don't think that is a perfect solution. I will study my manuals to try to determine why it happened; and a closer monitoring of the system should catch the fault earlier in the errant turn.

column121: The Captain and I discussed not doing a Visual Approach. Passing through about 9;000 feet; we were going direct to the FAF; conditions where ceiling and visibility unlimited. Approach cleared us for a Visual Approach. We accepted and started descending to 7;000 feet; the altitude for FAF. At about 7;300 or 7;200 feet ATC advised us the Minimum Vectoring Altitude was 7;500 feet. The Captain immediately stopped descending and went to 7;500 feet until just outside the FAF. We made a normal stable approach.We didn't want to do a Visual Approach when we briefed it. We were lured in by the visual conditions and the fact that that everything was stable and non rushed. It was late. Lesson is; do not do night visuals at airports that you are not to familiar with; try to do what you brief especially around terrain. I did get distracted when I lost my flight deck WiFi when I was trying to pull up a new ATIS on iPad. Don't do visual approaches at night; especially near terrain. Fly what you brief.
column123: While descending on the arrival and approximately 10 miles south of ZZZ; ATC asked us to report the field in sight. It was clear and unlimited visibility. So we called it. I felt that we were within the airspace; but when descending to the FAF altitude of 7;000 feet and at approximately 7;200 feet; we got a call from ATC saying altitude alert. Climb to 7;500 [feet] min vectoring altitude. We immediately climbed to 7;500 [feet] and continued approach. ATC handed us to Tower and nothing else said.During cruise; my First Officer and myself went through all company pages and arrival and approach plates. We discussed terrain and even said that we shouldn't accept a visual approach since it was night time. However; we got direct to FAF and not a usual vector outside the FAF. ATC asked us to report the field. We both evaluated that we were comfortable accepting the visual. We should have stayed with the plan because after being cleared approach; we descended below the ATC min vectoring altitude. Bottom line; be conservative and when flying approaches at night; I will no longer accept a visual approach.

column121: While flying at FL230; we began experiencing some moderate turbulence. The plane began an uncontrolled descent for 500 feet; and we reported it to ATC who then cleared us to FL220. The aircraft was controllable at FL220; but were still encountering moderate turbulence. We requested lower and were given FL210; and no more moderate turbulence was encountered. Turbulence in the flight levels was the primary causal factor. There was also active MOAs and crossing traffic that required us to stay higher. Upon getting the flight release I used my personal software of Foreflight to realize we were filed through a SIGMET for severe turbulence. We were then filed lower after talking with the Dispatcher. When talking to Center; they said there weren't any severe SIGMETS for our route of flight. I am not sure where the disconnect was; but I would suggest providing Dispatch the tools for greater awareness of flight through severe turbulence; as this was the second time in two days where we were filed through severe turbulence SIGMETS. Also; there were MOAs that we were being vectored over by one sector of Center; and then another sector said they were cold. This could have possibly been coordinated better to allow for lower altitude to stay out of turbulence.

column121: During operation of Aircraft X at FL340 we began having GPS navigational issues. Beginning in an area approximately 40 miles SE of ALS (Alamosa VOR) along our route to approximately 80 miles SW of RSK (Rattlesnake VOR); approximately 160-200 miles; we experienced intermittent 'GPS PRIMARY LOST' messages. As we began to troubleshoot the issue we discovered that both GPS #1 and #2 were erratically receiving GPS signals; varying from 0 to 9 satellites. The system cycled rather rapidly between the GPS 1 & 2 signal strength and navigational capability; losing all GPS capability at times.  We referred to the QRH but began to surmise that given the unusual operation of the receivers that there was nothing wrong with the onboard equipment and there must be an external issue like 'jamming'. We were discussing a plan: return to land base NAV and advise ATC or request ATC temporary headings when ATC asked if we were going direct to 'DAFNY'. We advised him that we were experiencing various NAV downgrades and asked for heading verification. He gave us a heading correction of 5 degrees left. Immediately after that transmission another aircraft reported the exact same issue with GPS NAV. After a few minutes the controller advised us that there were GPS jamming exercises going on in the area around White Sands. Therefore; we updated our heading with ATC as we progressed. A subsequent controller cleared us direct to 'ZZZZZ' and advised us we appeared to be slightly north of a direct route to 'DAFNY'. Shortly thereafter 'GPS PRIMARY' returned and normal operations ensued. We continued the arrival while checking our radar position with ATC. No further anomalies were encountered. Landed without further incident in ZZZ. I can only presume that the US Government (Military) was performing 'GPS Jamming' exercises as the controller said such activities were happening around the White Sands area. How about a NOTAM!
column123: At FL340 we began to get several GPS Primary Lost indications. Navigation reliability was in question so we got vectors from ATC for the fix that we were cleared to. Multiple other aircraft in the vicinity were reporting the same issues with their GPS. ATC informed us there was 'jamming' going on at nearby White Sands. When our GPS finally seemed to be working again; we were several miles off course going to the assigned fix. We reported that our GPS seemed to be working again and we were cleared to a different fix. No further anomalies were encountered but I am writing this report because were were off course for a short amount of time. White Sands jamming of GPS reported by ATC.

column121: During vectors into OKC from the east; the Approach Controller assigned us Runway 17R differently from the one we had setup (17L). After re-configuring for the ILS 17R; I asked the Pilot Monitoring to brief the approach so I can concentrate on flying (Approximately 14;000 feet MSL and descending to 4;000 feet). During the brief a bright shining white light; like a spotlight shined at us; caught our attention and cause a distraction. We still conducted the briefing; including the highest elevation figure. As I kept flying I was paying attention if the light shined us again; in the event it was a laser that needed to be reported. I had the terrain page setup from the previous briefing and both pilots were aware of the obstacle northeast of the airport (Antenna 2758 feet MSL). After the briefing was complete; we were given a vector (a 90 degree angle) for the approach within a close proximity of the Final Approach Fix (minimum altitude at FAF 3;000 feet MSL). This vector would have flown us south of the obstacle depicted in the plan view section of the approach chart. Approximately 18NM from the airport the Approach Controller queried the visual contact of the airport. Pilot Monitoring told me he had contact with it and after I picked it up in sight I asked to call for it if he still had it. At that point the Approach Controller cleared us for the visual approach for [Runway] 17R. Slightly after; the Approach Controller notified us of traffic on the approach to the parallel runway. Both pilots were trying to ID the traffic since it was below our altitude and we had to cross his approach path. We seemed clear of the traffic; but a strong wind from the south was drifting us north which cause a concern for us due to the known obstacle. The aircraft was just approaching 4;000 feet of altitude and started to level off; when I set 3;000n in the Altitude Select box. The aircraft transitioned into a shallow descent instead of holding 4;000 since it wasn't fully captured. While having a discussion about the wind I adjusted my heading and kept the descent to 3;000 feet so we could be close to level and slow when we intercepted the course outside of the FAF. Around 3500 feet we both remembered the obstacles when we saw its lights ahead and below us. I already started a transition into a climb when the Pilot Monitoring verbally reminded me of the obstacles. During the climb we got a 'Caution Obstacle'; due to the projected descent; which was removed shortly since we were already compensating. We were 500 to 700 feet above the highest obstacle. The obstacle represented on the MFD was not the highest elevation figure on the IAP chart. This depicted obstacle was part of another group of towers not depicted on the chart but they can be seen on the VFR chart in the Jeppesen app. Since it was a visual approach; I had focused on maintaining the airport inside; and started to descend and slow down so we could be on a good position for the stable approach. Following the event; we landed with no issues and had a discussion at the gate on how we could have mitigated our error. We were below the MSA and had loss awareness of the obstacles due to other distractions and the tight vector to the approach with the visual approach. Several factors played key roles for the loss of situational awareness that led us to be at a lower altitude for our location. Flags:-A night Visual approach into an airport were an obstacle is a threat.-A night Visual approach to an airport were the elevation of the airport is higher than we are normally used to.-An arrival consisting of an extended base into a visual approach rather than a downwind arrival.-The change of runway that led to a new setup and briefing.-The distractions caused by the wind-drift; traffic; and the bright light.-The tight vector given and accepted for the original approach. Our error was the premature descent to 3000 feet with the goal of not being high once we intercept the final course with short distance to the final fix. Although the setup for the approach included the awareness of terrain and using the terrain displayed as an aid; we should have use TEM to establish a plan to avoid the premature descent. A briefed plan of using the last assigned altitude of 4;000 feet until intercepting would have avoided this. During the approach brief; I should have asked my Pilot Monitoring to intervene in the event I set a lower altitude while maneuvering for the visual (mitigation plan in the vent of losing SA). I realized that our briefings cover informational items that could be threats but we should discuss mitigating plans for them. Other actions that could have been taken are: 1) denying the visual at night due to the obstacle; 2) requesting a vector for the visual; and 3) querying if a lower altitude was needed which would have led the Controller to keep us at 4;000 feet.
column123: I was Pilot Monitoring. Approximately 20min out we were giving the option to change our landings intentions from [Runway] 17L to 17R which we took. Captain asked me if I could brief the approach which I did and then we performed the runway change items from the checklist. During this briefing moment we both noticed a bright light from about a 12 o'clock position which caught our attention. Captain was aware of the obstacles to the northeast of the airport (antennas) and turned on the terrain. At approximately 18 miles out we were asked if we had the airport in sight. We both saw it and were cleared for the visual approach Runway 17R. Winds were out of the south at approximately 26kt pushing us to the north since we were coming from the east. We were at 4;000 ft. and began a gradual descent. ATC advised us of traffic at 11 o'clock landing on the parallel runway. Looking for the traffic we began to noticed the red lights of the obstacles (towers) on the northeast of the airport. I pointed them out as [did] the Captain. The altitude window was set for 3;000 ft. we were currently at 3;400 ft. Captain turned off the autopilot and began a climb. As we were climbing we received a Caution for the obstacle but it cleared quickly since the Captain had already began the climb. Once cleared we continue to intercept the final approach course and perform a normal landing. We both had a long discussion after the flight and both agreed that we should had mitigated this by simply staying at 4;000ft when cleared for the visual approach since we knew about the MSA which is 3;800 ft. Also the parallel traffic played a role on this since we started looking for it due to it being in our path for intercepting the final approach course of [Runway] 17R. As a Pilot Monitoring I should had advised the Captain that selecting 3;000 ft. and continuing the descent once cleared for the visual would had put us close to the highest obstacle stated in the approach plate. I will keep this in consideration for future flights to come ensuring we are not at a lower altitude than the MSA not established on a final approach course as well as keeping in mind obstacles around us at all times.

column121: Aircraft X [flight] got handed off from ZLC they passed along that they were low fuel. Aircraft X was a flight of 6. With the weather being poor and the visibility being 4 miles an instrument approach is what they were requesting. That being said; their TACAN and ILS were both out of service. The only way they were getting in was a visual to [Runway] XXR. So I vectored the flight behind the [civilian] aircraft coming from the south. Giving them block altitudes above the MVA so they had proper spacing amongst themselves. As I was stepping Aircraft X down they kept wanting lower and lower in order to get the visual approach. I stepped them down to 5000 and they descended to 4800; I gave them an LOA (low altitude alert). Then after fixing that issue I gave them 4500 once they were in the 4500 MVA. Turned them to final and I noticed that they dropped below 4500. So I gave them another LOA and told them to maintain 4500. I asked them numerous times if they had the airport in sight. They said no so I climbed them to 8000 and told them to fly heading 100. Aircraft X flight 2-5 reported the field in sight and at that point I cleared them for the visual. Aircraft X 6 didn't get the airport so I turned him away from the mountains and climbed them. After that I gave him a new squawk code and split Aircraft X 1 and Aircraft X 6 up. After clearing Aircraft X 6 to ZZZ and verifying his altitude I sequenced the two flights to get the visual behind another arrival. When we have airplanes that are low fuel and have no approaches we need to get those approaches fixed. Tech ops or who ever was fixing them need to understand the situation on hand.

column121: Aircraft X was on heading 360 and instructed to descend to 6;000 ft.  I observed Aircraft X descend through 6;000 and at 5;800 I issued a low altitude alert; the MVA was 5;600.  Aircraft X did not respond and kept descending.  I issued another low altitude alert; climb and maintain 6;000 immediately and when their data block displayed 5;100 they reported level at 6;000.  I told them altitude indicates 5;100; they asked to verify altimeter 30.25 and I gave them the current altimeter 29.24.  After a couple miles they showed a climb and climbed to 6;000.It was apparent watching the replay that Aircraft X check on indicating 12;100 and reporting level at 13;000.  For some reason I did not catch it.  I even descended them to 8;000 and they leveled at an indicated 7;000 and I did not notice.  I think this is because 7;000 is a normal altitude that I would descend them to at that location but I had left them a little higher.  When I descended them to 6;000 and they indicated lower it was apparent something was wrong and I was immediately concerned about the MVA so I issued a low altitude alert before they went below the MVA and a climb to 6;000.A snowstorm had just blown through the airspace and there was still stiff winds out of the west gusting to 30 kts.  I had a sequence developing for ZZZ and Aircraft X was near the front of it.  I recall planning ahead; looking at strips; using the STARS (Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System) to determine how much the wind was pushing the vectors.  Also ZZZ had many taxiways closed from the snow so I was vectoring for much greater distance than usual (10 miles on final).  I must not have looked at Aircraft X's altitude when they checked on and just used the reported altitude.  While I am happy I got a low altitude alert out when they were near terrain; I wish that I had caught it on check-on.I found it strange that their altitude in STARS was accurate but not in the cockpit.  I thought the altimeter setting would change what STARS reported. I have to be diligent to verify altitudes when the aircraft check on; so altimeter discrepancies can be caught early.
column123: Descending into ZZZ through FL 180 we completed the Approach Checklist and verified 30.24 altimeter setting. On vectors to final as we were leveling off; Approach Control asked us to climb to 6;000 ft. We were indicating 6;300 at that time; so the clearance just sounded odd. The Approach Controller said that we were at 5;200 and for us to climb to 6;000 and turn to a heading of 030. I immediately clicked the autopilot/auto-throttles off and started my turn towards 030 heading and started climbing; as my Pilot Monitoring verbalized that we had the wrong altimeter setting of 30.24 instead of 29.24. We leveled off at 6;000 on a 030 heading; and at that time I engaged the autopilot and auto-throttles. We got vectored for approach and landed uneventfully on Runway XX. We were asked to contact TRACON on landline by the Ground Controller as we taxied to the gate. We realized that we had unintentionally set altimeter setting of 30.24 in error instead of 29.24 which directly led to the altitude deviation. We failed to catch our error during crosschecks as we ran the checklist due to expectation bias. Lack of digital ATIS was also a contributing factor; however; we should have trapped this error as we updated the new weather. We needed to be more vigilant to trap these kind of errors.

column121: We briefed the route and departure; to include the [engine failure] procedures. We confirmed the route in the FMS. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; We turned to heading 189 and hit moderate or greater turbulence and mountain waves; which significantly affected us. I had trouble communicating with ATC and performing cockpit duties due to turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 AGL; Tower said switch to departure. Upon contacting departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to a fix'; but the radio quality of the transmission was poor and we couldn't clearly hear the name of the fix. I realized the mountain was on our path and for an immediate left turn to avoid terrain. The Spokane Departure Controller cleared us direct to a fix by name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling; which I couldn't understand due to significant turbulence and poor radio quality. We continued normal flap retraction callouts and takeoff profile. We were given heading a 120; to which we turned; and it took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. We were mistakenly trying to navigate to ENY VOR which caused us to be confused and task saturated. Once we got the correct identifier for HIA and entered into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. This caused the controller to get a low altitude alert although we did not receive any terrain avoidance warnings from our aircraft. In retrospect; the controller admitted on our phone conversation afterwards that this situation is very common. There are a lot of risks and stressors associated with this MZULA.MSO RWY12 and I feel like our outside resources did not help the flight crew. We accept full responsibility for allowing this situation to develop; but changes to this procedure will greatly increase safety in the future.First our Jeppesen charts had no verbal narrative and left us needing FAA charts to understand the procedure. It would be a great help if the procedure could be simplified or the controller's expectations that are outside the procedure could be communicated before we hit significant turbulence. The controller was clearly frustrated with us which only made our situation worse by trying to give us a phone number during a high stress and high workload phase of flight in significant turbulence. This shows the controllers are not fully aware of what human factors the flight crews have and how to help safety of flight. Having poor radio transmission quality was also a significant factor.
column123: I was the First Officer and Pilot Flying departing MSO. I received and read back the clearance from ATC which included the MZULA5 Departure MSO transition. I programmed this into our FMS and the Captain and I thoroughly reviewed the route in the FMS and on our Jeppesen plates. We also briefed the procedure for engine failure departure. In my takeoff briefing I again described the departure we were assigned. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; I turned to heading 189 as charted. Immediately we began to encounter moderate turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 ft AGL; Tower said switch to Departure. Upon contacting Departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to ________ ' but it was very turbulent and we did not clearly hear the name of the fix. I immediately realized the flight director was not commanding a left turn in accordance with the charted procedure. The Captain asked to say again the fix; and the controller said the name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling. At 1;000 ft AGL; I called out 'flight level change'; followed by the normal flap retraction callouts and told him we needed a left turn since I knew from the charted SID that's what we were supposed to do. Meanwhile the Captain was trying to get clarification on the fix to which we were to proceed. We knew it would be a left turn so he asked for a left turn and we were given heading 120; to which we turned. During this entire time it was very turbulent and took a lot of effort and concentration to focus on safe flying. It took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. Once we got the correct identifier and entered it into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However; this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. During this time; we had terrain radar displayed on our MFD and were well aware of our surroundings and the location of rising terrain; and at no time did we ever get a terrain caution or warning.Although the SID was correctly programmed into the FMS; for unknown reasons the Flight Director did not command the left turn to intercept the MSO 159 radial. The extreme turbulence and difficulty understanding ATC instructions caused a delay in turning to the assigned fix; resulting in a course deviation. First of all; given our route of flight; it would have made much more sense if; in the pre-departure clearance; we would have been given the Salmon transition. This fact was even stated by the ATC supervisor on the phone when I called him after we landed. He further stated they have had frequent problems with pilots and aircraft not following the procedure we were assigned. Second; I could have anticipated a potential issue; and tuned the MSO VOR in NAV 1 and 2; along with the radial to intercept prior to takeoff. If I return to MSO in the future; I will definitely do that as a backup in case this kind of thing should happen again. I realized we were supposed to be turning left; which is why we asked for a left turn in the interim while trying to get the identifier for the fix and get that loaded in the FMS. The significant turbulence and the communication difficulties with ATC were definitely contributing factors in this temporary deviation. Nonetheless; as a pilot it is my responsibility to safely and correctly fly the plane; so I will ensure I have a backup navigation source programmed and ready in the future. And if I go back there again and get assigned that same SID; I will ask for the Salmon transition rather than the MSO transition; as suggested by the ATC supervisor. Finally I will brief my Captain on what happened previously so we can be vigilant and prepared.

column121: We had just switched on to approach frequency and were given a heading and altitude for the visual approach. We both heard the altitude clearance as 5;000 ft. and the PM read back 5;000 ft. A few min after we had leveled off at 5;000 ft. ATC asked us to confirm altitude and gave us the altimeter. We responded with 5;000 ft. and verified we had the correct altimeter. ATC then responded the minimum vectoring altitude was 5;300 ft. for that area. As the PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to clarify we read back 5000 ft. in the initial clearance; I started a climb to 5;300 ft. ATC then asked if we had the field in sight which we did and then we were cleared for the visual approach using the GPS 14 approach plate as guidance. We landed normally.The cause of this event was a miscommunication with ATC. We both heard 5;000 ft. in the initial clearance not 5;300 ft. The PM read back 5;000 ft. and we didn't hear a correction from ATC. A contributing factor in my opinion was the fact that we were experiencing light to occasional moderate turbulence for most of the flight including the descent and that could have caused us to miss hear the original clearance and potentially the read back was hard for ATC to hear due to the PM's mic being jostled.In cases such as this we could have requested clarification if the altitude didn't sound correct but in my estimation the clearance seemed to make sense based on our position and the airport elevation and the location of obstacles and terrain which were not a factor from the direction we were arriving and they also seemed to be similar to the altitudes we would expect if on the GPS approach we were using as a backup. But it would be prudent in the future especially in turbulence to verify clearances considering the effect turbulence could have on radio transmissions.
column123: We had just checked in with approach and they gave use a heading to turn to for vectors and an altitude to descend to. I thought I had remembered reading backing 5;000 ft. as the captain who was the PF put 5;000 ft. in the FMA and we both confirmed the 5;000 ft. once set. After reaching 5;000 ft. the controller asked us to verify our altitude and I read back 5;000 ft. The controlled returned with 'the MDA is 5;300 in that sector do you have the field in sight?' We had the field in sight but the question led us to believe we descended to the wrong altitude. The controller didn't clarify the altitude at this point and said were cleared for the visual using the RNAV GPS 14 approach plate for guidance.The cause of the event was a miscommunication with ATC and I could have possibly read back a different altitude and thought that 5;000 ft. was what he said instead; after we had set 5000 ft. Also; we were in light to moderate turbulence during the entire flight and it might have caused me to mishear the controller or misread the altitude.I should have asked for clarification from the controller after we had set the altitude in the FMA. From where we were; the altitude of 5000 ft. made sense so it did not cue me to ask for clarification. We had briefed the approach plate as well and the higher rising terrain was on the other side of the field and we determined it would not be a factor for the altitude of 5000 ft. Where we were seemed to coincide with the altitudes on the approach plate as well.

column121: On a relatively calm and clear day at ZZZ1; I departed southbound toward ZZZ. The takeoff was uneventful; I contacted Approach for flight following. Throughout the climb to 9;500 ft.; there was constant light to moderate turbulence; typical for this segment of flight throughout this area. Upon reaching cruise the severity increased to consistent moderate turbulence; again not abnormal for the route of flight; the aircraft was slowed. I reported the ride conditions to Approach; and they stated that a Cessna 208 had reported similar conditions and opted for lower. The airplane began to experience downdrafts; exceeding over 1000 fpm and airspeed fluctuations of +/- 20 knots. I elected to descend to 7;500 ft. based on the ride conditions reported by the aircraft in front of me. At 7;500 ft. I experienced consistent moderate to severe turbulence; with consistent up and downdrafts; accompanied by fluctuations in airspeed. Occasionally; I nearly hit my head on the ceiling of the airplane. I queried [ATC] and they stated that the aircraft had reported a better ride at 6000 ft.; at that time I descended to 6000 ft. At 6000 ft. the ride was much more manageable; and I was able to make it to ZZZ safely. I made the decision that the airplane did in fact fly through severe conditions and required an inspection. I wrote the airplane up and contacted Maintenance Control. The unstable nature of the valley I was flying over and the absence of weather reporting in the valley make it difficult to gauge the ride conditions. I should have slowed the airplane down; and descended to more manageable flight conditions.A solution would have been flying the airplane above the valley to avoid possible severe turbulence. I talked with my pilot supervisor and he advised that flying at 15;500 ft. over the valley is a viable option. This particular route is very abnormal; with respect to mitigating risk. This is a prime example of how quickly things can change when flying. The more we can do to try to mitigate these risks as a whole; the safer it will become.

column121: After passing waypoint GILLL on the LINKK1 arrival into IAH; we were cleared runway 27 ILS approach. The next waypoint on the flight was RDFSH then GEYGR. GEYGR was to be passed at 3000' while we were around 3600'. Being cleared the ILS approach; we were to comply with crossing restrictions that were still in place on the approach. The restriction was noted on the approach as a small note; and we announced it too late. The approach controller alerted us high on the crossing restriction and we were then able to comply with the rest of the crossing restrictions. After being swapped runways late in an arrival; we should still review all notes and restrictions applicable to the approach. The note indications are easy to miss; but I am well aware now of specific crossing restrictions instead of waypoint floors on an approach. I believe it would be beneficial to have these notes and restrictions in different colors or noted right below the waypoint name to make it more obvious to the pilots. The constant change in runway assignments late in arrival makes it easy to miss small annotations on approach plates that are important for traffic separation.

column121: After a diversion to our planned alternate we had a routine enroute and descent phase. We contacted Tower on about a 10 mile final. We were approximately 5 miles in trail of a B737; and we heard them check in as well. I overheard tower tell them about a Medevac helicopter who was operating to the east of the airport and transiting to the west. Once we were on about a 5 mile final; tower provided us with a traffic call for the same helicopter. The first call we received was traffic at our 10 o'clock and about three miles; and that the traffic had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation. Due to the lights of the city; I did not see the traffic; and it was not yet showing up on our TCAS.Inside of a 4 mile final; at approximately 1200 ft. we received a Traffic Alert for the traffic. On TCAS it showed him at 200 ft. above us and inside a mile. I immediately saw the traffic visually and told the first officer that I had the traffic in sight. Based on the traffic's track and altitude; I very quickly suspected that we might receive an RA. I instructed the first officer to go slightly below the glide slope to increase our separation. Very shortly after that; at 1050 ft. we received a 'DESCEND DESCEND' TCAS Resolution Alert. The First Officer followed the TCAS guidance and I informed ATC. Due to the switch at 1000 ft. to Traffic Alert only we never received a clear of conflict; but we were able to visually identify that we were clear of conflict at about 800 ft. We were one dot low on the glide slope but correcting and all other approach criteria were stable so I quickly asked the First Officer if he felt stable. He responded that he did; so we agreed that we were okay to continue the approach. At our closest point; the helicopter was directly above us and approximately 200 ft. above; leading to a significantly reduced margin of separation.This event was caused by several factors. The helicopter pilot had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation; but in our opinion; the separation provided was not adequate. I was not able to visually identify the traffic until the Traffic Alert occurred; and at that point there was very little we could do to avoid a loss of separation. I do not believe we should have been sequenced by air traffic control to pass directly underneath the medevac's flight path. After landing I communicated my concerns to tower and he said that once the helicopter reported maintaining Visual Separation; he had no further responsibility to separate us. If that is correct; I believe it is a fundamentally unsafe procedure. In this event it led to us receiving a descending RA at 1000 ft. leaving us with very little maneuvering room. I should have made more of an effort to find the traffic prior to receiving a Traffic Alert; but with the city lights it was difficult. This was at the end of a very high workload; 3 hour blocked flight with significant weather; holding; a diversion; and fuel considerations. I believe that this type of event could have been prevented with better planning from air traffic control. There was clearly a difference in expectations between the helicopter pilot and us; and the helicopter pilot may have been comfortable with 200 ft. of separation; but we were not.
column123: We diverted due to weather. On final approach we received a TCAS Resolution Alert due to a medical helicopter crossing the final approach. I was Pilot Flying for the approach. When we received the Traffic Alert; I initially assumed it was an aircraft on a parallel approach. The Pilot Monitoring reported the aircraft in sight. The helicopter had also reported us in sight. Only moments before the Resolution Alert did I realize the aircraft was going to cross directly in front. We received a descending Resolution Alert. I complied with the Resolution Alert. The helicopter passed approximately 200 ft. above. I don't recall ever hearing a clear of conflict call. We descended below 1000 ft. and the TCAS went into Traffic Alert Only mode.A medical helicopter was crossing approximately 3 mile final at approximately 1200 ft. while we were on approach. I was manually flying a challenging approach due to high winds and did not recognize the threat until a few seconds before the Resolution Alert.

column121: I am a flight instructor I was on the ground observing the traffic pattern. I had just sent my student on his first solo flight. There were three Citabrias in the pattern; all same company. My solo student was Aircraft X. Aircraft Z was on ½ mile final. Aircraft Y was on an extended downwind. My student; Aircraft X; was abeam midfield in the downwind. All traffic was in a left pattern. Tower called and told my student 'traffic to follow ahead in the downwind'. My student replied with 'traffic in sight'. My student had mistaken Aircraft Z on final as the traffic he was following; instead and of seeing and following Aircraft Y in the downwind. Tower proceeded to clear my student 'follow that traffic; clear to land Runway XX'. Because my student was following the wrong aircraft; he turned base (about a half mile) in front of Aircraft Y and cut him off. Aircraft Y was on a 1 mile final at the time. Aircraft Y saw the error and made appropriate maneuvers. Tower noticed when Aircraft X had turned final in front of Aircraft Y and proceeded to tell both aircraft to go around. No further events took place. The pilot in Aircraft X did not see or follow the correct traffic and turned base accordingly. He unintentionally deviated from the ATC clearance. The plot of Aircraft Y noticed and took evasive actions as necessary. I was on the ground and all distances are highly estimated.
column123: I was given traffic information by ATC while on downwind leg of pattern; a Aircraft X in the pattern ahead and to my left. I saw an aircraft matching ATC description on short final approach and responded that I had the traffic in sight. ATC gave landing clearance with instructions to follow that aircraft; so when I had sufficient distance behind I began my turn to the base leg of the pattern. Upon turning I spotted another aircraft ahead and to my right at about 500 feet clearance on final approach. I took a hard left turn to evade and was told by ATC to go around and that the aircraft I flew in front of was the traffic I was originally advised of and that I had cut them off. I continued in the traffic pattern and landed without further incident.

column121: We exceeded 250 knots below 10;000 and were on speed by 9;600. I (PM) was looking at weather and the STAR and when I went to monitor the aircraft displays I noticed we were doing 300 knots at about 9;760 feet. I said check speed and the PF disengaged the autopilot; reduced power; deployed speed brakes; and leveled off. He had the speed window open and we both failed to monitor the speed window. He is very good about VVM (Verbalize; Verify; Monitor) and not doing something without informing the PM; so I feel I'm just as much responsible for the incident. I believe the speed window was open from a previous instruction from a Controller.
column123: On the ZZZZZX south of ZZZZZ [Intersection]; we exceeded 250 knots below 10;000 feet.ATC had originally asked us to cross ZZZZZ at 15;000 feet leaving us high for the next restriction (ZZZZZ1 at 8;000 feet and 250 knots). I was using speed intervene (300 knots) and flight spoilers to make the anticipated restrictions at ZZZZZ1 while descending from 15;000 feet. The FMA switched from VNAV SPD to VNAV PATH at approximately 12;500 feet. At this point; I began focusing more attention on small build-ups and ensuring the flight attendants were seated. Upon crossing 10;000 feet; the PM called out 'speed' and we quickly corrected to 250 knots by 9;650 feet. ATC passed us off to Approach without commenting about the speed deviation.The FO did a great job as the PM. However; we did debrief that; despite verbalizing the use of speed intervene; we ended up below 10;000 feet above 250 knots. The error is mine and I own that; but recency of experience may have been contributory as well.

column121: On an early evening flight to IAH we were descending via the DRLLR 5 RNAV arrival being set up and briefed for the RNAV Y 26R with our altitude set to 6000'. When checking on with the approach controller we were told to expect the runway 26L transition. We selected the new runway in the FMS but failed to reset our altitude selector to 7;000' at that time. As we neared ZOEEE Drag Required appeared on the FMS scratchpad and the Captain said; 'Careful not to be too hot at ZOEEE'. I deployed the speed brakes and slowed us to 210kts and checked the FMA and we were still in VNAV PATH. Shortly after passing ZOEEE; I noticed the FMA showed VNAV SPEED as we were leveling at 6;000' and I no longer showed SKLER as a waypoint on the screen. I then looked more closely at the DRLLR 5 chart and noticed the point we'd briefed as the lowest altitude on the arrival had (Runway 26R) beside it and thought we should've stopped at 7;000'. I brought it to the attention of the captain who then queried ATC. The ATC response was that we were ok and to now descend to 5;000'. We started the descent and shortly after were told by what sounded like a different voice on the radio to maintain 6;000'. We reversed the approximately 200' descent and returned to 6000'.The rest of the approach and landing were uneventful and the flight ended safely at the destination. I believe we should've stopped at 7;000' but am unsure since the controller didn't have a problem with us being at 6;000' so I listed the event as a possible altitude deviation.

column121: We were assigned the ZZZZZX RNAV departure off Runway X at ZZZ.  The clearance was to climb via the SID; top altitude of FL230 was set in the MCP. All the fixes and altitude restrictions were correct in the FMC; I was the PM; the airplane was light; so we had a good climb rate. The PF was hand flying as we approached the first fix which has a crossing restriction of at or below 10;000. LNAV/VNAV and VNAV PTH was selected. Close to the first fix the PF called for the autopilot as the airplane started its turn to cross the fix that placed the sun directly into our face which affected our visibility. As I turned my head to get my sunshade; ATC asked if we were going to stop at 10;000 feet; we got as high as 10;300 the PF turned the autopilot off and went down to 10;000.  In this situation I think turning the autopilot on earlier would have helped. Also anticipating the sun and take steps earlier to mitigate the effects of the sun would have helped us to maintain better situational awareness.
column123: Our departure SID was the ZZZZZX.  Our departure plan was for Runway YYR per the ATIS.  During taxiout our runway assignment was changed to Runway X with the same SID.  My First Officer ran the runway change checklist and briefed me on the changes to the SID departing Runway X.  During the climbout I called for the autopilot sometime prior to 10;000 feet.  There is a fix named ZZZZZ that has a crossing altitude of 10;000 or below.  Our automation level was LNAV/VNAV with the autopilot engaged.  Approaching 10;000 feet I noticed that the FMA went to VNAV PTH.  About that time; I also got a face full of morning sunrise.  It briefly made it hard to see and I had not deployed my sunshade or put on my sunglasses yet.  When my vision adjusted to the glare of the sun I noticed that the aircraft did not level at 10;000 feet.  It overshot the altitude by 300 feet.  I disengaged the autopilot and returned to 10;000 feet.  The Controller did query us on our altitude during the overshoot.  One other piece of useful information is that the aircraft was very light.  I'm wondering if the system was respecting a G-Load vs. an altitude because I have no other explanation as to why it did not level at 10;000 feet.  Factors that I feel contributed to this event were the runway change on the ground; high airport elevation; sunrise; fatigue and maybe our light weight.  Next time I will not accept the immediate line up and wait from ATC.  Instead I would re-brief the SID so that my situational awareness would be better.

column121: ATC cleared us for a visual approach to Runway 16R into Denver after turning us on to a right base approximately 5 miles from MERYN intersection on the ILS 16R. After being cleared for the visual approach the First Officer (FO) selected the approach mode and a selected a slower speed. The FO was slow to turn towards MERYN and over shot the final approach course. I instructed to FO to turn immediately toward the runway and then back to the final approach course. The approach controller asked if we need a vector and I declined. The FO had previously briefed the ILS to 35R. During the approach briefing we discussed threats that included high elevation; an MEL that restricted RNAV approaches; and that we were tired. The flight was cleared to descend via the TBARR 1 RNAV Arrival with the Runway 16R transition. The transition ends at CLFFF intersection at 11;000' with a speed of 210 knots. ATC was informed that we could not accept an RNAV approach and we were told to expect a visual approach; which we backed up with the ILS approach. The flight was turned to a right base heading at 210 knots. While turning the FO requested a slower speed which ATC approved. ATC asked if we had the airport insight. When I replied that we had the runway insight we were cleared for the visual approach. The FO selected the approach mode. As the FO was selecting a slower speed I mentioned that she should turn toward MERYN intersection. She slowly selected a heading toward MERYN and over shot the final approach course. I think this was due to the angle in which the course was intercepted. I would suggest adding a discussion about accepting visual approaches to the approach briefing; as a possible threat.

column121: I had just descended through IMC and was worried about the potential icing and high winds. I hand flew the approach and due in part to lack of recent experience (rustiness due to 2020/COVID); I inadvertently descended to ~2;100 feet MSL between ZZZZZ (IF) and ZZZZZ1 (FAF) on the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ; about 200 feet lower than the 2;300 feet minimums. I recognized my error and climbed back to 2;300 feet by ZZZZZ1 then continued to an uneventful landing. I should not have hand flown the approach given my rustiness--despite having done well in an IPC (Instrument Proficiency Check) a week or so ago--as I was preoccupied with studying wings for evidence of icing in the fast approaching twilight/dusk; and I was fighting strong winds that had me watching airspeed more than altitude.  All in all; it was 100% my fault and reemphasized to me that currency does not equal proficiency.

column121: There was a line of storms crossing ZZZ.  We were told to expect holding at ZZZZZ.  We ended up holding.  We did one turn and then we got sent back on the arrival.  We ultimately got vectors from ZZZZZ1 and were following one Company aircraft.  The plan was to fly northeast about 30 miles at 5;000 ft to go around the weather and then come back south to land.  We couldn't get in front of it or through it.  Company turned around to try to get around the weather from the other direction.  We did the same thing.  We got a 270 heading and a descent to 4;000 ft and an assigned speed of 170 knots.  On that vector; I noticed airspeed decreasing and added some power.  Then the airspeed dropped to approximately 140 knots and the autopilot and autothrottles were disconnected.  I announced to the PM (Pilot Monitoring) that we were in windshear and I added power and started a climbing turn to the left.  The aircraft started accelerating and climbing; and we retracted the flaps.  The highest speed I saw during the recovery was 220 knots.  During this period; airspeed; pitch attitude and altitude was very difficult to control and we encountered what we believed to be severe turbulence.  The PM told ATC that we had severe turbulence and windshear and that we were turning to the left and climbing.  We tried to level at 5;000 ft and flew southwest.  ATC told us to climb to 6;000 ft for traffic.  I added power and the aircraft responded poorly.  Eventually; we got a climb going; but we were unable to stop the climb at 6;000 ft.  The aircraft continued to about 6;450 ft and ATC asked us what altitude we were going to.  PM told them that we were trying to get to 6;000 ft but were having a difficult time maintaining altitude with the turbulence.  On our way back down to 6;000 ft we got a TCAS TA for traffic at our 1-2 o'clock at 700-800 ft above us.  I continued down to about 5;800 ft to make sure we avoided that traffic.  We continued southwest and diverted to ZZZ1. If we had asked to stay in holding until we saw that the line had passed even further northeast of the field; it would have prevented this.  We had about 13.0 of fuel when we entered holding; so we had the time. [We were] unable to maintain assigned altitude; heading; and airspeed due to windshear and severe turbulence.

column121: We were navigating between coordinates at FL410 and M.80 assigned.  We received a CPDLC clearance that said; 'Resume normal speed'.  We reviewed the Europe Jeppesen Airway Manual section entitled 'Operations Without an Assigned Speed' to review this relatively new procedure. After agreeing on what it meant we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC at XA:03z via CPDLC 'Present speed .83'.  ATC responded at XA:13z with 'Do you want M.83'.  We responded; 'Received normal speed CLNC and advising our speed is .83'.  At XA:17z ATC sent; 'You may want to read up on that. Resume normal speed means plus or minus mach .01 from cleared mach.'  We immediately changed speed to Mach .81 and replied; 'Roger speed now is .81 requesting M.83' (XA:18z). At XA:19z ATC sent 'Maintain .83M'. All communications were done via CPDLC. The rest of the flight was uneventful.  We disagree with the controller's interpretation of the 'Resume normal speed' clearance and request clarification from the company. Page 668 of the Jeppesen Airway Manual (Europe) says; 'If the aircraft then receives RESUME NORMAL SPEED (via CPDLC or Voice); the flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However; the flight crew shall advise ATC if; as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message; they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed.'  Furthermore; in the operational example given on page 688 it says; '...message RESUME NORMAL SPEED will be sent.  The flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However; the flight crew shall advise ATC if; as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message; they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed. In this case; with a previously assigned speed of .81; they must inform ATC if the flight either slows to M.79 or less or speeds up to M.83 or more.'  Finally; in the North America Jeppesen Airway Manual it says; ' When adherence to an assigned 'MACH' setting is no longer required; pilots will receive a controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) message to 'RESUME NORMAL SPEED;' at which point the flight crew can continue at their cost index. Refer to aeronautical information circular (AIC) 1/20 Operations Without an Assigned Fixed Speed (OWAFS) in the North Atlantic for more details.'  In looking at the ICAO NAT OPS Bulletin (2019_001); the text mimics what is published in the Jeppesen Airway Manual. In conclusion; I believe we were in full compliance with the 'Resume normal speed' clearance when we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC but since the controller has a different understanding of the situation I would like to get clarification from the company.
