column121: I am a contract pilot and an on-call simulator instructor on the various Falcon EASy airplanes. The PIC is an experienced large airplane pilot. His current experiences are on numerous types of Boeings; etc. He became the manager/pilot of the subject -900EASy and has roughly 6 flights with this aircraft; most with me. His type training was about 3 months ago and he did not fly the airplane until roughly 1.5-2.0 months after his check ride (guesstimate). I have been providing SIC support (until the other full-time pilot can accomplish his type training) as well as IOE on the airplane and especially on the EASy avionics. The pilot's 'airliner avionics' background has generated system misunderstandings that I have corrected. This includes incorrect use of Flight Guidance selection choices. While arriving on the STAR into ZZZ we were advised to 'descend via the STAR'. The Captain highly prefers to use VNAV for virtually all climbs and descents and as he was selecting such I was reprogramming our waypoints for altitude crossings. The Captain then questioned me as to 'how best to set up the VNAV function'. I explained various ways to do so; i.e. VNAV versus minimum altitude to select; using the vertical profile 'laser pointer' to start the descent or to use for constant descent without stair-stepping through crossing altitudes; how to change the descent angle utilized on the FMS avionics page; etc. However; after some time I noticed that the VNAV was not capturing and that the 'laser pointer' was moving away from the target setting; i.e. waypoint selected for crossing. This happened a few times. I even showed him how to do a 'Direct Vertical Descend To' but it also did not work. The Captain was complaining about the EASy system compared to the Boeings he flies and couldn't understand why it was not capturing. During this time I was acquiring the ATIS and setting up for the approach to be utilized. However; when I once again noted that we were still not descending correctly I stopped doing my functions and spent more time analyzing the situation. That is when I noticed that the airplane was west of the intended course (I would guess about 4-5 miles). I then informed him that somehow he had lost LNAV guidance. As such; the VNAV would not be correct. Although he asked me to now give him direct to the waypoint I told him he instead needed to rejoin the arrival and advised him to use HDG (heading) or TRCK (track) to perform a turn back to rejoin. He said he understood but I noticed his confusion and delay in doing so. I again advised him that he needed to get back on course and almost simultaneously ATC noticed our discrepancy. Because of our course deviation we did not descend accordingly. As such; ATC gave us a direct to ZZZZZ and cross at 10;000. I performed the 'direct to' and advised the Captain to start an immediate descent which he slowly did; however; the eventual angle was high and as such the airspeed increased. He complained about the increasing speed and I told him that he needs full airbrakes to check the speed increase (twice). He looked confused and delayed the extension of the airbrakes until the speed had already climbed; i.e. he now had to reduce the speed he had allowed to increase during the initial descend maneuver. Therefore; we exceeded the 250 knots below 10;000 feet for roughly 600-700 feet (I think we were back at 250 before 9;300 ft.) The remainder of the flight was uneventful. I should note that during a post debrief the Captain was noting how only one person should be touching the guidance panel. He was; in my opinion; somewhat deflecting responsibility for the loss of the LNAV function (after I asked him if he knew how we lost LNAV guidance). However; I did not manipulate the panel. I pointed to what and where he needed to go for his choice of modes. This is especially true during the initial mistake. Although I cannot guarantee my thought I think that the Captain inadvertently disconnected LNAV after passingZZZZZ1 while we were setting up for the descent. He has previously chosen the wrong button before; e.g. he once switched guidance to the non-flying pilot during his attempt at setting-up another choice. At that time I saw his action and corrected him immediately (that time I did change the setting myself). It was in a very high workload moment and I did not have the time then to explain to him what he had done. In that situation I needed to get the guidance back to the pilot flying which necessitated a minimum of three button selections. After a little time; and after I had completed what I was doing as the SIC; I attempted to explain what he had done but prior to such he said he understood his mistake so I did not delve deeper into it. Since aircraft traffic in the ZZZ area was light there was no deviations and ATC did not 'appear upset'. However; I felt it important to write this ASRS Report. This Captain is very confident of his methods (he is very experienced) and strives to be as efficient as possible. He chooses to carry the minimum fuel required for a trip; always flies at Long Range Cruise power setting; requests as many short cuts as possible; and wishes to start the airplane moving as quickly as possible after engine starts. As such; he has often questioned me in relation to after start tests that need to be performed for each flight versus those that only need to be performed once a day; or maybe even once a week. He does not like sitting with engines running. Therefore; we are sometimes somewhat in a hurry. Being the SIC and as a contract pilot I have acquiesced to his overall style as it is not illegal or unsafe; although it is not the method I prefer. For a pilot new to an airplane I would recommend that the pilot 'go slow' and diligently learn the process of the new airplane but a pilot's prior experiences can alter that process. This is especially true when the pilot has a vast (many years) experience flying numerous large airplanes worldwide. I have suggested that this Captain fly as the SIC for a bit to truly learn the airplane but he noted that during his training he only got experience in the left seat. His comment was that he wants to become familiar with the left seat before trying the right seat. As the SIC can be busy it is hard for an experienced pilot (in a particular airplane) in that role to provide guidance to an inexperienced pilot (in a particular airplane) while doing both instruction; IOE overview; and normal duties simultaneously. My recommendation is that regardless of experience that a pilot 'to a new airplane' be limited to the SIC duties for a minimum of 5 flights (segments; not hours) before transitioning to the left seat. What is required is the 'muscle and mental memory' performing the numerous tasks associated with the various sections of a flight.

column121: On descent into ZZZ; we momentarily exceeded Vmo by approximately 1 knot for less than 3 seconds. I later completed an AML entry and notified Maintenance Control. When we were next cleared to descend; I elected to go into Vertical Speed Mode; selecting 2000 FPM in order to recapture the VPATH. The task saturation over the next few seconds took my scan away from our airspeed; and we surpassed and we surpassed XXX knots; our 'barber pole' airspeed. I immediately disconnected the AP; overrode the autothrottles and raised the nose of the aircraft. The max airspeed reached [was] XXY knots for a second or two; before returning to green numbers. There appeared to be no adverse effect on the aircraft or passengers. I later completed an AML entry and notified Maintenance Control. I had not flown in 3 weeks; due to my inactivity on reserve status. I now know that I must be more diligent on my scan; especially when I have not flown in a while. column121: We were on arrival into ZZZ and on vectors with Approach Control. Prior to switching over to Approach Control ATC advised us that we could expect moderate turbulence; I believe from 9;000 to 12;000 feet; on descent. We were higher up on our descent when they notified us that we could expect the moderate turbulence in the lower altitude structure. We were switched over to approach control.  I remarked to approach that we were picking up moderate turbulence; again I believe we were at or above 6;000 feet to give them a heads up. We were given a left northerly turn to 010 degrees and a descent to 5;000 feet.  The Autopilot was engaged. It was very turbulent. We received an Alts Cap which is a normal indication on the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) that the autopilot is now armed to capture the selected altitude. We were getting bumped around pretty good by now; full continuous moderate turbulence. It was at that moment when the autopilot was capturing the altitude that the upset occurred. The aircraft was rocked to a 45 to 50 degree left bank and a sinking drop occurred similar to what you would receive in an airliner if you ever have hit an air pocket. This exceeded the limits of the autopilot and it kicked off. I took over manually to right the airplane and that is when we received what I would call a severe bump which led to the second upset that did the same thing; left bank to 45 to 50 degrees and a pitch downward.  I was already in the process of advancing power from the first upset but this time I went to full thrust; TOGA power if you will; to initiate the unusual attitude recovery.  I was aggressive in the recovery; put some G on the aircraft; airspeed bled down from 250 to about 180 or 190 at that moment which is still a safe flying airspeed in our type aircraft; well above stall.  I traded airspeed for altitude to expedite the recovery.  We recovered to altitude shortly after.This all happened so quickly.  Severe turbulence upset coupled with automation exceedance were contributing factors.  Lessons learned are significant. Turbulence is always a threat.Constance vigilance is always required.  Secondly we stress at our company to never fully rely on automation and that it will not always work in all situations.  We also stress that situations can happen to anyone regardless of experience. An Incident/Hazard Report has been filled out as part of our Safety Management System (SMS) program and submitted to the Director of Safety at our company. We train for upset situations every X months as part of our X month continuation qualification and training. I've flown many types of aircraft as well as fighter type aircraft and have never experienced a situation such as the one described above.

column121: Takeoff and initial climb from DCA; Runway 01. Captain Pilot Monitoring; First Officer Pilot Flying. Pre-flight duties completed and route review completed at gate. Engine start and taxi was normal to Runway 01; before takeoff checklist completed to the line before crossing Runway 04; below the line after crossing Runway 04. As we taxied to runway; Aircraft Y was cleared to cross Runway 04 before us on another taxiway then into the box. As we were approaching Runway 01; Tower Controller asked Aircraft Y if they were ready for departure; Aircraft Y responded they needed 2 minutes. Tower asked if we were ready for departure and we responded we were ready; completed final checklist items. We lined up on Runway 01 and were cleared for takeoff. I do not recall checking FMA for NAV annunciation as we taxied on to the runway and checked final for traffic. Light passenger load/light takeoff weight. After takeoff; aircraft climb was rapid with a quick change to Departure frequency. We were at clean-up altitude quickly after takeoff. After thrust set to climb power and frequency change to departure (prior to check-in on frequency with departure) I noticed FMA annunciation was RWY TRK and we had not yet initiated a left turn for the departure. I told the First Officer to turn left; which he accomplished; initially coming left to approximately a 290-300 degree heading. I cross checked Nav Display for 1 NM circle around point PLVIA and outside references. I do not believe we entered Prohibited Area 56A or Prohibited Area 56B. After initial left turn; we then turned back to the right to rejoin the departure. A turn to point ADAXE would have required an aggressive right turn; so we turned to rejoin the departure between ADAXE and BEBLE After turning to rejoin departure I checked-in with departure control when they asked if we were on frequency. Remainder of the flight was uneventful.This was my (Captain) first flight back on the line after several months away due to combination of leave of absence and quarantine for close contact with [someone] with COVID-19. I had just completed recurrent training the week before this flight. In the pre-flight briefing the First Officer had noted that with light passenger loads the aircraft takeoff and climb would happen quickly. Given my lack of recent flying; I should not have accepted departure prior to the aircraft in front of us on the ground; even though I felt I was in the green. I was slow to notice we had not initiated left turn on the departure where I would normally expect to begin a turn; possibly due to lack of recent line flying experience; the combination of quick climb after takeoff to acceleration altitude and frequency change slowing my monitoring and recognition of aircraft not being in NAV mode. Though I did direct the pilot flying to make a left turn; if I had done so earlier we would have been able to maintain the departure track without tracking close to Prohibited Area 56.The time from takeoff to overshooting the departure turn on takeoff from Runway 01 at DCA happens fast! I would like to see a similar event during simulator training to illustrate just how quickly you can get close to Prohibited Area 56 after takeoff from DCA when combining a timely distraction with lack of aircraft going in to NAV mode. PLVIA with 1 NM ring on NAV display did assist me as a barrier for this event.

column121: On Aircraft X to ZZZ; we were given a turn to base for a visual approach to XR inside the final approach fix 600 feet above the FAF.  We realized we weren't going to be able to complete the approach under the stable approach criteria so I called the go-around at 1;000 feet AGL. Once we got the aircraft climbing I called ATC saying that we are going around. ATC said climb and maintain 3000 feet; we were already climbing and had a high rate of climb because we only had about XX people on board.  While we were cleaning up the aircraft and setting up the FCP; I realized our Climb rate was high and we were approaching 3;000 feet quickly. I said 'watch your altitude' and asked ATC if we could get 3;500 feet. ATC denied it and said to maintain 3;000 feet and contact departure. Unfortunately; the correction of bringing the nose down and power back happened too late and we climbed through our altitude by about 200 feet. The correction came and we corrected our altitude back to 3;000 feet. On the second attempt approach tried to do the same thing to us again however we denied it and asked to be vectored for the ILS.  ATC turned us to intercept the final approach course too close and I told them we won't be able to do it due to us having a tailwind; and that we are going to need to intercept it from the other side. I told ATC the intercept we would need. On that attempt we completed the approach successfully and landed with no further complications.Due to having a poor vector for the approach; and no warning of a close approach; we ended up high on a visual approach to Runway XR. For that reason we decided to go-around. The altitude assigned to us was only about 1;200 feet above the altitude we decided to go-around at. By the time we got the aircraft configured for the go around and contacted ATC we were even closer to that altitude. Due to having a high workload in that environment; a light weight; and being already close to the altitude assigned to us the climb rate was too high when I made the call out to the Captain. I also tried to rectify the situation before it happened by asking ATC for a higher altitude but was denied.Deny the visual approach and ask ATC to just fly the ILS to give us more time. Say unable instead of asking for a higher altitude.
column123: Today on Aircraft X to ZZZ we were given a turn inside of the FAF for Runway XR into ZZZ. ZZZ Approach had us at 3;000 feet. The FAF is 2;400 feet. column121: Received numerous ATC clearances via CPDLC while enroute. First cleared us down to 38;000 ft; was accepted by Pilot Flying.. Next was a route clearance. First line of free text said 'Cleared to NIKLS'. Pilot Flying changed the Legs page with verification from me. After a few minutes ATC sent another CPDLC that said descend to 34;000 ft and then another clearance came in a couple moments later clearing us to 31;000 ft. column123: ATC gave us a 90 degree plus vector for Runway XXR and asked us to call the field. We had it in sight and were cleared for the visual. The glideslope didn't capture and we were then low on the glide slope as we passed through it from above. We leveled off; slowed down and finished configuring. Approach was closed and Denver center was handling approach.Don't be pressured into accepting a visual at night with mountainous terrain. Go-around if an approach is feeling uncomfortable. Slow down earlier when at a higher elevation airport.

column121: On [Date]; I was acting as Pilot in Command (PIC) of a UH-60 L Army National Guard Helicopter conducting a round-trip air movement of crew and passengers from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. I was sitting left seat; my Co-pilot (PI) sat right seat. I had two crewmembers in the gunner's seats (Row 2); and one passenger in Row 3. Total: 5 souls on board.Earlier in the day; we had flown IFR from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 for a fuel stop before heading to ZZZ. We had received a military weather briefing and were aware of an AIRMET Zulu for moderate icing along the route. We monitored PIREPS and determined as a crew that the risk of anything beyond moderate icing was minimal; as the few PIREPS observed were for light rime ice at flight levels above our planned flight altitude.The conditions observed on the flight from ZZZ2 to ZZZ were very stable. There was a stratiform cloud layer; approximately 1;000 to 2;000 ft. thick; that we either flew below or above the cloud layer the entire way to ZZZ. We observed no icing.We were on the ground for approximately two hours after landing at ZZZ. I continued to monitor weather conditions; and it appeared they had not changed from the time we landed. I observed the same AIRMET Zulu and a couple of PIREPS reporting light rime above our planned flight level.Prior to departure; my crew and I conducted de-ice checks in accordance with our aircraft's technical manual; which all passed.After an uneventful climb to our requested flight level of 7;000 ft. MSL; we leveled off. At this time the annunciator panel gave us a warning of 'MR ICE DETECTED'. We had discussed this as an expected possibility; acknowledged the caution; and monitored our ice rate meter; which read 'Light Icing Detected'.At this time; I asked ATC if they knew where the cloud tops were. We were informed that they were at approximately 8;000 ft. MSL. Faced with the decision to climb approximately 1;000 ft. through visible moisture; or descend approximately 4;000 ft. through visible moisture; I requested to climb to 10;000 ft. MSL. ATC gave a clearance to 9;000 ft. MSL. We began our climb.In approximately 1.5 minutes; our icing condition worsened. Our ice rate meter pegged out at its maximum indication of severe icing. The helicopter began to shake; and we lost a dangerous amount of our main rotor RPM (a true [anomaly]). I immediately pressed down on the collective to preserve our rotor RPM; took the controls from my co-pilot; [advised ATC] by announcing 'PAN PAN PAN' on ZZZ Approach frequency. I asked the controller to help me get out of the icing situation and was ultimately cleared down to 2;500 ft. MSL.My crew and I flew the helicopter well; in a level attitude at approximately 2;500 ft. per minute. We maintained 100% rotor RPM during our decent and exited the cloud layer at approximately 3;000 ft. MSL. I tested the controls as we got closer to the surface to ensure I would be able to arrest the helicopter's rate of decent. Upon exiting the clouds; the icing condition improved; and the rest of the flight home was uneventful and under VFR conditions.Chain Of Events:How the problem arose: The problem arose from the unexpected encounter into severe icing.How it was discovered: The severe icing was detected by on the on-board ice detection system; severe vibrations were felt by the crew; and the low rotor warning alarm sounded.Corrective actions: The Good: The crew responded to the [situation] well by manipulating the flight controls to preserve rotor RPM; communicating the [anomaly] to ATC; and flying the aircraft out of the icing conditions.The Bad: The crew did not respond correctly to the initial 'ICE DETECTED' caution. In accordance with the UH-60 Operators Manual; 'The ice rate meter activates the ICE DETECTED caution when the BLADE DE-ICE POWER switch is turned off; informing the pilot of the requirement to turn on the system'. Contributing Factors:Neither the UH-60 Operating Manual or checklist clearly emphasizes the immediatememory item actions required in the event of an icing [situation].An updated -1 weather brief was not obtained from the Air Force Operational Weather Squadron by the Pilot in Command.Human Performance Considerations:The perception of the Pilot in Command that the 'AUTO' function on the ice rate meter meant that the system will 'automatically operate upon detection of ice' was incorrect.The perception of the Pilot in Command that the weather conditions would be the same on the return flight as they were on the first portion was incorrect.The actions of both the Pilot in Command and Co-pilot ultimately saved the lives of the crew; however their inaction to turn the de-ice system on was detrimental to the safe operation of the aircraft.Factors affecting the quality of human performance:Neither the Pilot or Co-pilot complained of fatigue or other exogenous factors prior the flight. Both had a good night's rest and were well within the confines of their duty day at the time of the incident.Recommendations:Ensure aircrew are intimately familiar with the de-ice equipment and capabilities on their aircraft. Recommend that changes be made to the UH-60 Operator's Manual and checklist to emphasize the seriousness of an icing [situation] and the immediate response required. This should be an underlined step. Once the ICE DETECTED caution appears; the immediate action required is for the blade de-ice switch to be turned ON.

column121: I was returning to BED from the West. It was dark. I tuned in the ATIS. The current ATIS was broadcasting that BED was 'landing and departing Runway 23.' After copying the ATIS; I called BED Tower and reported my position as near Minuteman Airport (6B6) and informed the Tower that I was inbound landing with ATIS. The Tower Controller initially cleared me to enter a right downwind for Runway 29.  This confused me because the ATIS had stated that BED was 'landing and departing Runway 23.' I asked the Controller for confirmation of the runway assignment and he acknowledged that he had 'made a mistake' and told me to enter a right downwind for Runway 23. After I entered the control space; and near the airport; I noticed the high intensity runway lights and landing traffic was on Runway 29; while runway 23 had their lights on 'dim'.  Since the ATIS had not mentioned simultaneous operations to intersecting runways; I became disoriented. I mistook Runway 29 for Runway 23. I was so concerned that I even called the Tower and asked the Controller: 'Is the Aircraft Y lined up with the right runway?'The Tower Controller realized that something was not right and called me and asked me to confirm that I was setting up for right downwind 23 and offered me a clearance to enter a right downwind for Runway 29. I told him that I thought I could still correct; but I ended up flying through the final for Runway 23 and ended up on a left downwind for 23. At about this time; another aircraft; which I later learned was Aircraft Z arriving from the west had also turned inbound to Runway 23 from the north. The Tower Controller told me to turn 20 degrees further right which I did to widen out my downwind leg. Thanks to the Controller; the Aircraft Z was able to land safely and so was I.I now realize that several other factors contributed to my confusion.  I was more tired than I realized. I had a very long work week; yet this night was an opportunity to start flying more night flights; after being absent from this experience for over 16 months.  The pandemic means hazard [but not] if I bring an instructor to help me re-acquaint to night flying.   I allowed myself to be fooled by the warm weather; the light winds and the great visibility into thinking that it would be a good night to re-acquaint myself to cross-country night flying.  Tonight; with the lights dimmed in the cockpit; and the high intensity lights on Runway 29; a plane landing on 29; the lights dimmed on Runway 23; and my lack of night flying practice did this happen.I now realize that I had vastly underestimated the combined effects of fatigue; distraction and 'rust.' Added to that; my confusion resulting from the initial mistaken clearance to enter a right downwind for 29; the combination of bright runway lighting on a conflicting runway without any warning that such operations were being conducted; and traffic operating in unexpected directions all combined to make for a much more confusing situation than I ever would have expected.The controllers explained to me that even when Runway 23 is the operating runway; they still allow traffic to land and depart Runway 29 because Runway 23 is too short for some aircraft that use the field. Nevertheless; I believe that safety would be greatly improved if; during nighttime operations; the ATIS included the warning concerning operations being conducted simultaneously to conflicting runways. This is especially true at BED where runway alignment issues are already an issue. I believe that such a warning would have eliminated my confusion at seeing traffic landing and departing on Runway 29 and then mistaking it for Runway 23.

column121: I was doing pattern work at ZZZ between XA:00 and XB:00. The airfield had a large amount of arriving traffic during the hours I was flying. After a touch & go on RWY XX; I was asked to extend the upwind before flying a right pattern. About mid-field on the downwind; tower requested a left-360. After my first 360; I was instructed to extend my downwind. A second plane [Aircraft Y] was approaching the airport from the northwest. Aircraft Y was asked to 'make a right 270; keep it tight and get ready to line up behind a [jet]'ATC then asked me to widen out my downwind and look for Aircraft Y making the right 270. At this point it was at my 11 o clock; 3 miles. About 5 seconds later I was able to identify the aircraft; let tower know that I had them in sight and was preparing to line up behind them. About 15 seconds later; tower called me up again; asking 'Aircraft X - extend it out a little bit; actually just follow behind and I'll call your base you will have to follow a jet behind on final'. I read back and confirmed.About 30 seconds later; tower called me up again; 'Aircraft X just so I don't get you too far from the field; make a left 360'. I read back the instruction and began my left 360. At this point; I was already thinking about Aircraft Y as I was planning on how I would get back on the downwind and line up behind them. I believe Aircraft Y was just about to finish its right 270 as I was about 90 degrees into my 360. I was able to spot and track the plane on Foreflight with Sentry; but since I had to make a 360 I lost visual when I initiated my turn. Tower; likely receiving a traffic alert called the other plane to make them aware of me: 'Aircraft X about a mile south making a left 360 - he has you in sight'. I do not think he asked them to confirm that they had me in sight and I can't tell from the live-ATC recording whether they read it back. The added statement 'he has you in sight' was extremely dangerous and could have been fatal. Yes; I had the traffic in sight when I was heading toward it and planning to get behind them; but once I started my left 360 there was no way of maintaining a visual with the other plane since I was now heading the opposite direction. I immediately recognized the potential conflict and started looking both outside the plane and on Foreflight trying to spot and track the other plane's relative position. The other plane did not make a 270 turn; but instead kept turning toward the airport/runway i.e. cutting into my path.As I was about 270 degrees into my 360 turn tower called 'Aircraft X - as you are coming out of that 360 turn do you still have Aircraft Y in sight?'At this point; I was already banking hard left in a steep turn trying to pull away from the converging traffic that I saw coming closer toward me. Turning right was not an option as it would have put me in the middle of final with jets arriving. I do not think the other plane confirmed whether or not they had me in sight. If they did; they flew way too close to me for my comfort and should have initiated an avoidance maneuver. In response to tower's question I responded 'Aircraft X unable' because I had to focus on flying the airplane away from the other traffic. We then passed by each other with much less separation than I feel comfortable. The other plane heading toward the runway; and me pulling hard left to the North-West; initiating a climb up to gain altitude. It is hard to tell exactly but horizontal distance could have been less than 500 feet Vertical distance was virtually the same. It happened very quickly. If I had not realized the potential conflict and mitigated by tracking on foreflight and pulling hard left this could have been a really really bad situation. The biggest mistake here; in my opinion; was ATC communicating to the other plane that I had them in sight AFTER I started my 360. There is no way one can maintain visual during such a maneuver while also flying safely and ATC shouldunder no circumstances make that statement. I also think that having two planes completing maneuvers in a way where their exit paths can conflict (right 270 and left 360) in close proximity should be prohibited.There were multiple safer options here. Aircraft Y could have flown a proper base rather than cutting it short onto final. I could have been asked to fly west; or I could have been asked to fly another 360 right after the first one. The fact that ATC changed its instructions relative to how I should fly behind/around the other traffic 3 times in a minute indicates to me that they were not planning ahead but rather responding to/running behind.In the future; I will call out if ATC tells other people that I have them in sight when I don't (i.e. after starting my left 360). I am also surprised nobody (tower/the other plane) complained about how close this was. I am glad to be back on the ground.  I hope this helps keep other people safe in the future!

About 3 miles from KAFKA; and the approach mode in the armed position; the airplane selected the LOC mode on the PFD and began to turn towards Runway 2. I turned the autopilot off; and manually continued to fly towards the KAFKA waypoint to lose more altitude. The airplane was about 2;300 feet; with 1;700 feet selected in the altitude selector. I continued the approach; and we landed safely. My First Officer questioned the Tower as to why this would happen. The Tower stated that both the Runway 34; and Runway 2 localizers were operational. However the Dispatcher rerouted us to fly from 140W bypassing 130W to begin an arrival using the RYDER arrival. This confused not only us but departure Area Control who had our original flight plan in their system. We departed the gate with the correct uploaded ATC flight plan but possessed on our iPads the amended flight plan from Dispatch... in addition our FO (First Officer) refused to coordinate with Dispatch to revise our our flight plan to its original format which resulted in erroneous flight progress forms from ACARS. To be clear the flight plan only deviated towards the latter end of the flight with the confusion resulting from the Dispatcher uploading an erroneous flight plan to remove a bend in the flight however that was not loaded to the PACOTS east routing for the day. Our FO contacted SFO radio to confirm our routing was correct with our FMS but neglected to inform Dispatch who thought we were still flying the amended route he had given us. It would be helpful if the company would provide guidance regarding how procedurally they would prefer crews coordinate changes to flight plans with ATC. Do they prefer we coordinate with ATC directly or would they prefer that we contact Dispatch and ask that they upload the correct route and that we check it with ATC. It would seem there is a loophole in regards to keeping Dispatch up to speed on changes to flight plans. I believe there is language in the FOM regarding any changes to the flight plan to notify Dispatch of those changes. In this case the changes were minimal however the arrival time differed by about 6-8 minutes from the original flight plan and the amended one from Dispatch. Dispatch was unaware that this stub flight was not flying the amended flight plan they sent us. When I; as the relief pilot; arrived from my break on the flight deck I noticed the erroneous flight progress forms and notified Dispatch who then sent us the revised flight plan. Dispatch was unaware that we were back on our original PACOTS routing. This was accomplished 2+45 into the flight. However if I had not done this it would not have gotten done as the FO refused to contact Dispatch to clear up the confusion. please advise. The First Officer refused input from both the Captain and myself; the relief pilot; to contact Dispatch and get them in the loop regarding discrepancies from filed flights from amended ones. Stub flights caused more confusion than necessary. Clear guidance is needed from company on how they prefer the crew to remedy route discrepancies from Dispatch versus filed. Do they prefer the crew to contact ATC and fix the problem ourselves or do they prefer Dispatch to get involved and fix the discrepancy.
column123: Just prior to pushback; we received a message from Dispatch with regards to a change in our flight planned route. We delayed pushback until receiving new flight plan. Only change was to end of route after waypoint at 140W. We then called Clearance Delivery and did a full route verification. They still only had the original; unchanged route. Since the only discrepancy between the flight plans was at the end of the flight; we opted to depart. After departure; we received the flight progress report that showed the modified route (after 140W). During flight; after checking in with San Francisco ARINC; we asked for a verification of our cleared routed. ARINC verified it was the original flight planned route. We then sent a message to Dispatch with our cleared route and received an update. Dispatch believed we requested a look at modifying our route to remove a 'dog leg' segment from our route which we hadn't.  We were a STUB flight and that might have been a factor as the original flight was near to the arrival time. The change to our flight plan wasn't requested and wasn't essential to safety. Unless critical to flight safety; last minute changes to flight plans (especially international) can cause miscommunications and errors in navigation and should be avoided.

column121: During climbout on a heading of east on the ZZZZZ2 SID while passing 8;000 feet between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 we got a TCAS TA regarding traffic descending off ZZZZZ3 on the ZZZZZ4  flowing south at 1 o'clock; 3-5 miles ahead that was no factor.  This is something we see every day on climb out or descent in and out of ZZZ due to climb and descent rates.   ATC then called traffic at our '10-11 O'clock 3 miles descending to one one (11) thousand I called 'traffic in site no factor; they're passing above and behind us.'  ATC then asked our Altitude.  I replied 'level 10;000 feet.He asked our altitude again; I replied 'Level 10;000 feet; he said he saw us at 10;500 feet and gave us an updated Altimeter setting; and cleared us to climb to 17;000 feet.  Passing 12;000 feet he asked us what altitude we were passing.  I replied '12;000 feet.'  He then replied 'That's what we show as well.  For some reason I had you at 10;500 feet back there. I have a phone number to copy when you are ready.'  We took the number down; and he said 'Call us when you get to your destination to discuss a possible pilot deviation.'The Captain called when we got to ZZZ1.  The Controller Supervisor who answered said he had just sat down; had no idea what we were talking about; said he would do some research and call us back.  5 minutes later he called us back and said; 'After review; the previous Controller showed you slightly high and stopped traffic on the arrival at 12;000 feet (which I thought was at 11;000 based on his advisory call).  Then showed our altitude correct in the climb after he inquired again passing 12;000 feet.  Said there was no conflicts or loss of separation; not a big deal; and that he would just file it as an RA report and close It out; however; we had no known RA's; nor any TA/RA indications for the potential conflicting traffic passing above and behind us?  The ATC Supervisor didn't take any further action or questions; and wished us a safe rest of our day and left It at that.  We thought It would behoove of us to fill out this report regardless.Wrong altimeter setting.  We had a lot of distractions from multiple visitors on the flight deck at the gate while setting up cockpit and during the before start checklist (flight attendants; gate agents; deadheading crew and commuting pilots who we knew who stopped by to visit).  Flight attendants held off boarding passengers who were held up at the door; until catering; who arrived at the aircraft late; had cleared the forward galley and aisle; and got them their snack/sanitary packages set up to hand out.  So this backlogged the jet bridge; had the flight attendants coming in and out of the cockpit along with the commuting pilots; and gave us a lot of distractions.  This back log seemed to frustrate the agent; for It was the flight attendants who were keeping the passengers out of the way until they were ready for them.  For that; the gate agent was rushing to close the flight (We still pushed 10 min early).  The FA A seemed rushed; and just closed the flight deck door before verifying if we were ready or saying 'seated and stowed;' which was nonstandard.  These multiple interruptions (which seem to happen every flight these days) just added up; we had the current ATIS printed off; but when back tracked to get caught up; we missed the altimeter settings; which must have been set from a flight a day or two prior due to the difference in what It actually was at the time.Verify; Verify; Verify; Trap the Errors; Don't let the distractions of the daily operations knock you off your game.  It was a beautiful cold VFR morning; flying with a Captain I had enjoyed flying with in the past; so I felt we were both comfortable and familiar with how each other operates within the SOP's and as a person.  The Aircraft had sat overnight.  I would like to see more operational (non-flying) related distraction/awareness incorporated into training.  The day prior on a separate flight we had a passenger removed by law enforcement for non-compliance/and possible criminal related activity.  Gate agents are constantly under stress to get flights out on time or early.  To top It all off; everyone has been under stress of the pandemic; furlough related; or state of the airline related issues.-"

column121: Departing during the waning stages of an intense storm. Winds were gusting close to 30 kts.. Windshear advisories were on the ATIS; however a flight landing 10 minutes before our departure reported only moderate turbulence with no mention of Windshear. Decided to let FO be the pilot flying. Climbing through 1;100 ft. MSL in a right turn to our cleared altitude of 4;000 ft.; the turbulence got very intense; with large; rapid; +or- 15 kts. fluctuations in airspeed. PF (Pilot Flying) called for flaps one; which I set; and thereafter he announced the autopilot was engaged. I had just changed to departure on the radio and then we were cleared to climb to 10;000 ft.; and to continue the right turn to our first navigation fix. PF called for flaps up; I selected the flaps up and then noticed the attitude of the airplane was falling below the horizon and we were starting to descend. I also noticed the PF trying to select 10;000 ft. on the altitude preselect. He was having difficulty setting the altitude selector as it was so turbulent ; so I stated: 'fly the airplane; we are descending'. The PF disconnected the autopilot and raised the nose after we reached about 3 degrees nose low attitude. During this time; our altitude dropped to about 1;300 ft. MSL (1;200 ft. AGL) and the GPWS 'Don't Sink' advisory sounded. We started to establish a climbing attitude so I directed my attention to setting the altitude preselect; setting the heading bug to our first fix; and the PF asked to also execute this fix in the FMS. After setting the FMS; I noticed our aircraft attitude was dropping below the horizon again and we were descending through 1;300 ft. MSL. Before I could command a correction; the GPWS 'Don't Sink' advisory sounded again; and the PF raised the nose. As we continued the climb; by this time the airspeed was climbing over 250 kts. and the aircraft attitude was raised to control the speed. The speed increased to approximately 287 kts; before starting to decrease. As the speed started to drop; the PF continued to raise the attitude of the airplane; and as we exceeded 25 degrees nose up I commanded the PF to 'lower the nose; our airspeed is decreasing; establish a pitch of 12 degrees'. By the time the airspeed stopped decreasing; our speed was about 5 kts. below the flaps up maneuvering speed. We accelerated and established a normal climb. From this point on; the rest of the climb was uneventful.

column121: Getting radar vectors to intercept the final approach course to Runway 34L RNO;  ATC instructed us to fly direct to SPOON at 11;000 ft and intercept the localizer. The direct routing to SPOON took us on a westerly heading approximately 90 degrees to the final approach course. SPOON is defined as a radar fix on the approach chart and is D24.6 from the field. As such; we were reluctant to use the localizer to guide our turn to final and instead used GPS to navigate to SPOON and turn onto final. Upon overflying SPOON; the GPS commanded an aggressive; yet smooth; right turn to final. Once on final; we intercepted the localizer and descended on the glide path while observing the altitude restrictions at APIME; WAGGE; and EPOSE. The FO (First Officer) and I were fully 'dialed in' for this approach as we had briefed the procedure; identified the surrounding terrain; and associated threats. Landed uneventfully. Three days later I was advised ATC identified our airplane as one that lost acceptable separation with terrain during our approach. The FO was making his first trip to RNO and I had only been to RNO a few times in at least a few years. We were initially planning to fly an approach to the south until ATC told us to expect one to Runway 34L. The routing to SPOON put us at (approx.) 90 degrees to the final approach course with (from memory) an unreliable localizer signal at D24.6. That large angle and our reluctance to use the localizer so far from the field forced us into using the GPS which caused an overfly situation; and thus; and overshoot of the final approach course. I think getting a heading to intercept the final approach course inside SPOON and at a lesser angle would alleviate the overshoot possibility and the resulting loss of separation.
column123: We were cleared to and were proceeding direct to SPOON at 11;000 ft on a track of approximately 070 when we were cleared to intercept the localizer for the ILS 34L.  The Pilot Flying (Captain) and I discussed intercepting the localizer so far from the field (SPOON is 24.6D from the field) and the PF elected to stay in Nav [mode] until we had turned on to the final.  We saw the line the nav was going to take and that it was going to fly over SPOON and then turn us onto final with a slight overshoot and the PF verbalized this.  We had done an extremely thorough review of the RNO brief and of all of the pages in FD Pro and based on the clear weather and our awareness of the terrain hazards we concluded that this would be an appropriate course of action.  We overflew SPOON; 'nav'd' to the final approach course and then selected the approach mode and flew the rest of the approach and landing uneventfully. The extremely steep intercept angle and relatively close proximity to SPOON when we were cleared to intercept the localizer along with the far distance from the field.  Emphasize to both ATC and aircrew the ramifications of a steep intercept angle to final.

column121: Upon being vectored for the ILS approach to Runway XX at ZZZ; ATC cleared us to descend from 3;000 MSL to 2000 MSL. The PNF was distracted while trying to control the cabin pressure that had been wildly uncontrollable since the beginning of descent from FL410. As the PIC and PF; I set the Altitude Alerter to 2;000 and vertical speed to 700 FPM descent; with autopilot engaged. During the descent to 2;000 MSL; I briefly looked up at the Pressurization Control Panel to monitor the PNF progress in controlling the cabin pressure; I noted the cabin pressure was finally close to the aircraft's actual altitude. I directed the PNF to select 'RAM AIR' ON.  That action stabilized the cabin for landing. ATC called to confirm our 2;000 feet clearance limit and I realized that the aircraft did not level off at 2;000 feet and the autopilot was not engaged. I acknowledged our clearance to ATC; manually flew the plane from 1;700 feet to 2;000 feet and reengaged to Autopilot. Since the cabin pressure was finally under control; an uneventful approach and landing were completed. Due to the distraction of the cabin pressure control issues; as PF I briefly failed to monitor the aircraft flight profile. Since I had tasked the PNF to attempt to stabilize the cabin pressure; I take full responsibility for failing to continuously monitor the aircraft flight profile.No matter what cockpit distractions occur; it is incumbent upon the PF to continuously monitor the aircraft flight profile. And if using the Autopilot; PF should continuously monitor that it functions as programed and does not inadvertently disconnect.
column123: The flight went well up to the time of descent when the cabin pressure started to malfunction. All attempts were made to control the pressurization using ADC 1 & 2 and Manual control. As preparations were made for landing; air traffic control issued further descent to 2;000 feet and the flying pilot was in control of the aircraft with the auto pilot engaged. The aircraft did not capture the 2;000 foot altitude because the autopilot was inadvertently disconnected and the aircraft continued descent to 1;600 feet at which time the deviation was noted and immediately corrected.  The aircraft was subsequently vectored onto the final course and the rest of the approach and landing was uneventful.  The pilot monitoring should have noticed the altitude deviation as a result of the auto pilot not being engaged while manually controlling the pressurization and the pilot flying should have been aware that the auto pilot was not engaged. It is imperative that the pilot flying concentrates on flying the aircraft while the other attends to the malfunction and refers to the checklists.

column121: Training on combined sectors; moderate traffic; two practice approach aircraft in satellite airspace all other traffic in departure sectors.Aircraft X came off ZZZ on the published missed approach for the RNAV RWY XX approach; he checked in and was radar identified while in the published left turn towards the missed approach fix; ZZZZZ.  The trainee subsequently verified the pilot's previous request to return to ZZZ1 on an IFR clearance.  The trainee cleared Aircraft X direct ZZZ and instructed the aircraft to maintain 2;000'.  At the time; the aircraft was within a 2;000' MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude].  I believe both the trainee and I anticipated that the pilot would make a right turn direct to ZZZ1; not recognizing that a continued left turn may be more appropriate because the aircraft was already in the published left turn on the missed approach.  With the anticipation of a right turn in mind and the aircraft in a 2;000' MVA my attention as the OJTI turned to the other departure traffic; which was going to require the trainee to merge and weave multiple departures off multiple airports (ZZZ2/ZZZ3/ZZZ4) to get them on course and through our airspace.  This was an area the trainee had shown struggles in in previous sessions as well as earlier in this training session; so I was attempting to stay ahead and have a plan of my own if needed.  Upon reviewing the incident; I became aware that in the moments following Aircraft X's clearance I was suggesting an alternative course of action for one of the trainee's departures in an effort to illustrate a way to expedite getting a departure on course which also got them out of the way of succeeding departures quicker.  Unfortunately; this conversation kept my focus on the departure traffic as opposed to the continued turn that Aircraft X made into the higher MVA.  Aircraft X subsequently continued a left turn towards ZZZ1 and entered a 2;500' MVA at his assigned altitude of 2;000'.  The trainee was aware of the incident almost immediately.  The trainee issued a climb to 2;500' to Aircraft X when the aircraft was only a third or a half a mile inside the 2;000' MVA.  I was not aware of the situation until I heard the trainee issue the climb to Aircraft X.  I subsequently requested that we be relieved.  The trainee and I debriefed; after which I informed management of the incident when I requested time for myself and the trainee to review the incident and fill out our report.  To my knowledge; Aircraft X climbed to the MVA and subsequently landed at ZZZ1 without further incident.Numerous things could have prevented this occurrence.  Had the trainee climbed Aircraft X to 3;000' instead of descending them to 2;000' they would have been above the MVA.  Had the trainee left the aircraft on the published missed approach for even a few miles they would have climbed above the MVA and a subsequent clearance may have included a more appropriate altitude.  Had the aircraft made the anticipated right turn instead of continuing in a left turn they would have remained in the 2;000' MVA.  Had the trainee issued the clearance to ZZZ1 via radar vectors; I believe they would have assigned a vector that would have remained within the 2;000' MVA and avoided the situation.
column123: Recertification time on [positions] (departures) and Article 67 training on[positions](south satellite). Aircraft X departed ZZZ on the published missed from the RNV runway XX  approach. column121: On descent into CLT; open descent; 6;000 selected in the altitude window. Approaching AAIRE on the JONZE 2; I asked the FO to verify our descent clearance as it didn't feel right being cleared to 6;000 with departures at CLT coming off of 18C. As I asked this; I disconnected the autopilot and arrested the descent at 8;820. The frequency was quite congested (CLT Approach) so the FO was unable to get a word in. However; as I continued the climb from 8;820 to 9;000; CLT Approach did ask us to climb and maintain 9;000. To my knowledge; there were no traffic conflicts; however it was a very uncomfortable situation.Flying into CLT has become problematic with the CDA arrivals. The CHESLY has become legendary for altitude busts; and the JONZE 2 isn't much better. The scenario goes something like this; you check in with Atlanta Center and receive a 'descend via' clearance. Not long after; you are turned off of the arrival and given a 'descend to and maintain' clearance. This process usually repeats itself a couple of times (either with Atlanta Center or Charlotte Approach) before you are assigned a final descent clearance. This system makes it very difficult to fly the arrival. Please know that this isn't pointing blame; but pointing out a problem. As PIC; the responsibility ultimately falls on me. However; a smoother process would be helpful.Eliminate the CDA arrivals into CLT. We rarely fly them as published.

column121: I was PF; hand-flying.  On departure; we were cleared to 10;000 feet.  Northbound on the SID; climbing through approximately 7;500; I increased pitch to avoid a small build-up off the nose.  Climbing thru approximately 8;800 feet; I realized that I was going to have a difficult time leveling off by 10;000 feet.  I asked the CA to advise ATC of the potential altitude excursion and aggressively; but smoothly; reduced pitch to level off.  I exceeded our assigned altitude by 450 feet; and promptly descended back to 10;000 feet.  ATC did not seem concerned by our deviation and cleared us to 16;000 feet.This was one of my first sequences after a 6-month leave of absence.  The CA is new to the airplane and new to the seat.  These factors contributed to our poor altitude SA and slow cross-check.Our threat-forward briefing focused on our lack of recent flying.  We needed to be even more vigilant to trap decision and execution errors.

column121: I was flying on an IFR flight plan at assigned altitude of 4000'. After seeing a cell on FIS-B radar (Flight Information System-Broadcast); I requested from ATC if there were any PIREPS for the weather. I then requested a deviation for weather depicted by FIS-B. I was granted the requested weather deviation and was flying outside of the weather depicted by FIS-B several miles in IMC conditions. Apparently; I flew into an embedded thunderstorm cell with both severe turbulence and violent downdrafts and updrafts which was not depicted by FIS-B weather with a 4 minute time stamp.I noticed the IAS had climbed dangerously high into the yellow arc while on autopilot (AP) maintaining an altitude of 4;000'. I reduced power to idle in an effort to maintain a safe indicated airspeed. While the AP was engaged and power reduced the IAS did not reduce sufficiently to the maneuvering speed but was rapidly climbing. I disconnected the AP and pulled the yoke back to reduce IAS. I then encountered severe turbulence and downdrafts forcing the aircraft to lose approximately 500 feet. In an attempt to stabilize the aircraft; I attempted to various throttle settings in an attempt to maintain altitude and heading with little success in controlling altitude or heading.The entire event lasted approximately 2 minutes with several calls from ATC offering assistance. During those calls I requested ATC standby until I was able to regain control of the aircraftThis was an isolated cell whose location was not accurately depicted by FIS-B weather radar returns. In regards to corrective actions on my part as pilot; I'd say to not trust FIS-B time stamps nor the weather depictions as being reasonably accurate. Further I'd extend my safety margin around weather depicted on FIS-B to a greater margin.The flight terminated without incident with my cancelling my IFR flight plan once out of IMC conditions and safely landing at the destination airport.

column121: At XA:28Z; Aircraft X checked on the frequency asking for VFR flight following in the vicinity of ZZZ. He was given a beacon code and I displayed a data block on the radar scope; waiting for it to track up. After a minute I told the pilot that I did not have radar contact; and I didn't have a target in the area he stated. I verified his code and location; and had him reset his transponder after another minute went by. At XA:31Z I told him it might be necessary for him to climb before I could establish radar contact. He reported that he was starting a climb to 7;000 feet.One minute after he started his climb; at XA:32Z; I picked up a primary target in the area the pilot reported. I tried to verify the position of the primary target; but the pilot just responded that he was showing zero oil pressure and having electrical issues. As he was saying this; the data block correlated to the code and I radar identified Aircraft X and verified his location. My standard practice; something that I did less than ten minutes prior; is to radar identify; verify location and altitude; and give altimeter. I do it every time; and in that order. When I radar identified Aircraft X; there was no Mode C data; so I asked him to report his altitude. He reported that he was climbing to 7;000 feet and asked for help to get into ZZZ; he was showing zero on his oil pressure. I didn't circle back to the altimeter at this time.I issued Aircraft X a heading to set him up for a pattern into ZZZ. If his engine was about to quit; I wanted him lined up for an airport; not guessing what was below him. I told the CIC I was working a special aircraft; and the OM was quickly in the area. I didn't feel it was in good judgement to add on to the pilot's stress level by pointing out that he was experiencing an urgent situation. It was being handled as such.He asked as he rolled out if he was on the correct heading. I advised that he was 20 degrees off course; and that he should correct. He told me he was using his backup compass; due to electrical failure. That information made a lot of sense at that moment. The backup compass is a magnetic compass. It's one that bounces around as you turn it. The magnetic compass will continue to turn past the heading and then bounce back and correct as the airplane levels off and the compass stabilizes. This is something that an IFR rated pilot would be more knowledgeable about. No gyro turns; or turns with only the backup compass were part of my IFR certificate training. Due to this; I decided to give him small turns that would create an arc to final; and help him maintain better control and orientation.I told him to descend to 5;000 ft. and that I should still have radar contact at that altitude. He responded that believed he'd be able to poke through. I knew it would be minimal conditions; I still believed getting the aircraft set up for a runway was the safest places. As I gave him a turn to the left he stated that he was going to get into the clouds. I asked if he and the aircraft were IFR qualified. He said they were not. I asked if he could maintain VFR conditions. It sounded like he was trying; but didn't seem sure that he would.I told Aircraft X that he could continue down to 4;000 feet and gave him a heading to get him turned more toward the airport. About that time at XA:39Z; just eleven minutes into the situation; an aircraft inbound for ZZZ1 checked on. I issued the ZZZ1 altimeter. This aircraft would end up being held out for the [situation]. I then told Aircraft X he could descend at his discretion to 3;900 feet; but that was the minimum enroute altitude in the area; and the lowest I was comfortable advising him. He said he was starting to poke through at 4;100 feet. I gave him the position and distance of ZZZ1. He responded that he could see some ground.I had him continue his gradual left turn but saw a much more aggressive turn on the radar. I asked if he was circling down to stay in VFR conditions. He said he saw bases at 3;800 feet and it was an unintentional 360. Based on what the radar showed; it was not a controlled maneuver; and probably resulted from an unusual attitude due to spatial disorientation. I asked him to regain level flight; as to maintain control of the aircraft and not get into another unusual attitude. I asked him his altitude; he responded 3;680 [feet]. Up until this uncontrolled maneuver; every report was that he was in marginal conditions; but always seemed to have some visual capabilities. At this point the inability to maintain VFR was imminent.The aircraft showed a northeast heading; I asked him to make a slow turn. Being an IFR rated pilot myself; and seeing how easily he became disoriented already; I wanted to avoid a stall; spin or turning over the aircraft. In the clouds a turn can make your body feel like you are descending; and a climb can make your body think you are turning. A more abrupt climb or turn only magnifies this effect. At XA:43Z as I maintained focus on keeping the pilot's wings level; I offered the option of climbing back up into VFR conditions. He was in favor of the idea. He added that the engine had been running fine; and believed the zero oil pressure reading to be due to electrical issue; not engine issues. With that information I immediately reassessed the IFR conditions to be the most hazardous conditions in the situation.I saw the aircraft again start a west turn that seemed to increase in rate. I gave the aircraft his location and his observed turn. I advised that he level off and focus on flying straight and level. He did not respond. The maneuver seemed unstable and I tried to relay that he needed to get wings level; then start climbing slowly. Anything aggressive would cause greater disorientation. He said the engine was running fine now; no longer a concern. I told him that we believed it to be clear in ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. He said that sounds nice. I wanted to get him into ZZZ3 if it was in fact clear. It was much closer; and based on his workload; fatigue due to stress; and equipment issues; I wanted him in the air the least amount of time possible. The CIC or the OM; I don't remember which; went up to the weather desk to get the most complete weather information available. Other controllers were also pulling weather at surrounding airports. I was focused on getting Aircraft X oriented and into VMC.I told him to fly his present heading and start a climb; advising that there was no traffic ahead. He responded that he was having trouble keeping his wings level. I advised back to straight and level and asked his altitude. The climb was giving him a sensation of turning and he was having trouble overcoming that. I should have advised him to focus on the instruments over his own sensations; but I did not think of it at the time.He said he was at 4;020 feet. I said give me level straight flight and then we'll start a slow climb. I wanted him to remain calm and know that we were going to work through it. He did not answer. Seeing what appeared to be straight flight on the radar scope I advised a shallow climb. He said he was trying to keep the wings level. At that point a VFR aircraft departing ZZZ1 was checking in. I called the traffic to that aircraft; advised the altitude was unknown; and asked Aircraft X to say his altitude. He did not immediately answer. Instead another aircraft keyed up; saying the other aircraft didn't look good on his TCAS and he needed to level his wings. Aircraft X then responded; he pulled into a stall; but was starting back up. I advised him to take it slow. At that point Aircraft Y verified ZZZ2 to be clear. I asked if Aircraft X was staying level. He said yes; 5;000 feet and seeing sunlight. I saw another turn on radar and had him level his wings once again. A minute later he reported on top of clouds and level. I told him maintain level flight; catch his breath; and if there were any airports he wanted to try to get to; we would get the weather for him. In my experience; it was best to remind him that he could exhale. He still needed to have the ability to fly the rest of his flight with electrical issues. I also offered him the opportunity to request an alternate airport. He had equipment that most likely needed to be repaired or replaced. I didn't want to send him somewhere that he'd get stuck. Aircraft X was maintaining a southeast heading and I asked him his altitude. He responded; 5;860 feet. I offered again; ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. The pilot was happy with ZZZ2 because it was reported clear. I gave a heading for him to fly that would get him started turning more towards either airport as I waited for the weather information. I recommended going to ZZZ3 because it was the closest. The pilot agreed that ZZZ3 would be his first choice; then ZZZ2. Immediately as he said that; the information was back from the weather desk and I relayed it to the pilot. He said he wanted to shoot for ZZZ2 because it was clear and ZZZ3 was overcast. I gave a few more heading changes and turns to get him direct to ZZZ2. I also lost radar contact on him a minute later as well. I received another report that he should expect to be clear of the west edge of the moving weather some time before ZZZ2; and passed that along. I advised him that he appeared right on course; and I was relieved at XB:08Z.Ten minutes later; while talking to the relieving controller; the pilot thanked us all for the help he received and said he was feeling the love. He even asked to get a forwarding address to send me a bottle of good scotch. Additionally; when calling the facility from the ground; the pilot was very thankful for the services he received. He informed the OM that he had to change pants when he landed; and again wanted to send a thank you bottle for getting him to safety. It was not apparent at the beginning of the situation that the engine oil reading was due to an electrical issue. It was possible that it could have been a number of different factors; but I knew that he could lose his engine at any moment; and it may not sound rough right away. I wanted him to get lined up for a runway as safely and quickly as possible. I gave him the option to get down below the bases; but should have emphasized to maintain VFR; even though it is the pilot's responsibility. During a stressful [situation]; that would be a good reminder to give the pilot. Once the pilot gained confidence that the engine was running properly; I did everything in my power; and with all of my flight experience to keep the pilot focused on not getting into an unrecoverable condition; while maneuvering safely into VMC.During an imminent [hazard]; controllers have to make judgement calls on what is the most prudent and time critical course of action. Access to checklists during these situations would ensure that all services are provided. Controllers could check that they had provided all of the information possible without taking as much attention away from the imminent safety issue. An easier to use weather reporting system would ensure more weather reports are forwarded along from controllers. The current GI method can be tedious and the tie up keyboard use during busier sessions. ERIDS (En Route Information Display System) offers weather reporting by tapping on the information and hitting send. Using this system would increase the efficiency and result in more weather reports being available. Even just having paper weather slips that controllers can hand to a supervisor would improve efficiency.A working knowledge of flight instruments and factors of flight would allow better assistance to pilots in [hazardous] situations. Recurrent training that focuses on best practices during imminent situations would enhance controllers on seldom used skills.

column121: On the Arrival into ONT SoCal Approach assigned vectors to sequence behind a 747. We were vectored directly behind and above the preceding 747 for 26L when we were cleared for the visual approach to 26R. ATC advised to maintain visual separation. At that point; due to concerns of descending behind the heavy aircraft; I offset right of course and attempted to parallel the 747. My intention was to remain clear of the 747's wake vortices. As we continued the approach and began to converge with the other aircraft; ONT Tower issued clearance to S-turn to the right if necessary. At that point we were too close to the runway to make any effective maneuvers and still maintain a stabilized approach. We then received a 'Descend' RA and continued descending on the visual approach to 26R while the adjacent aircraft executed a climb and go-around from 26L. In retrospect I believe a better course of action would have been to discontinue the visual approach or ask for delay vectors to increase separation from the heavy aircraft. ATC should have issued more realistic vectors to sequence us further behind the 747.
column123: Descending on the Arrival into ONT; SoCal Approach Control gave a maintain current HDG [instruction]. We visually acquired a 747 at our 12 o'clock position approximately 5 NMs. SoCal then gave us a right turn to a 140 HDG; then subsequently a 170 HDG that placed us at the 6 o'clock position of the 747 approximately 5 NMs behind. Once established on the 170 HDG; SoCal cleared us and the 747 visual approaches; 747 to Runway 26L and us to 26R and told us 'Caution wake turbulence and maintain visual separation with the 747'. The Captain did not want to be in a position to be at a 45 degree angle behind the 747; which would've increased the chances of getting into the wake of the 747; so as we were descending for the approach we received a descend RA and Aircraft Y executed a go-around for a climb RA. When we noticed that it would be challenging to do the approach and simultaneously staying out if the heavy aircraft's wake turbulence; should've asked the Controller for a vector or turn before starting the final portion of the approach.

column121: I take full responsibility for this altitude deviation.  We were in the chocks at ZZZ and there was a slight reroute to ZZZZ.  The FO X said it would not load in the FMC; but FO loaded manually.  FO said the same thing happened on the last flight also into ZZZZ.   I had flown down to ZZZ1 in Month X and had the same reroute.   The FO had over 40 hours total time with XX landings.  I have not flown in over 60 days.  So in the chocks the Departure Briefing I briefed CA designates PF PM states concerns and threats PF states concerns and threats taxi; takeoff/reject departure.  The FO said low time and I said my over 60 days off.  FO is rock solid; what an excellent stick.  You know when you meet someone for the first time; it's going to be a fun flight.  Every time I see FO X's name on the crew list; it will be a fun flight.  For over 40 hours and XX landings FO flew real well.  Talking to ZZZ Center of frequencies XYZ.Z and XYA.B and we're climbing to FL230 and they ask Aircraft X we just want to confirm the route.  FO asks this is a reroute you want me to put on the autopilot?  If I had said yes; I would not be writing the report.  The fault is all mine.  My thinking was this is the same reroute we got in the chocks easy-peasy.  And it was the same route but took three or four minutes to get everything done. ZZZ Center then cleared us ZZZZZ JXXX ZZZ1 as filed.  I spelt ZZZZZ wrong and it was not accepted in the FMC.  Right then the Altitude Deviation warning came on.  ZZZ Center told us switch over to XYZ.Z and I reported FL240 we were at FL238 and our clearance was FL230.  Center than cleared me to climb to FL400.Lots of areas to hit on.  Even though I haven't flown in over 60 days do Company work on most days; I read all the changes; FD Pro X; Airline Pilots; WSI Pilotbrief; and Outlook.  On any day to read all this it takes 45 minutes to and hour and a half.  For this ZZZZ flight; I checked it three days in a row.  What was the routing; did it go over ZZZZ1 Country; and the weather?  FO is an excellent pilot.  Low time like FO is the autopilot should have been on.  The mistake is on me; no excuse; I messed up.It pains me to have made this mistake; I can't remember my last report.
column123: New on the aircraft; I had briefed the Captain I wanted to hand fly the aircraft; which he agreed was a good idea. We departed ZZZ on XXL and was cleared on the ZZZZZ1 4 RNAV SID.  In our turn towards ZZZZZ1 we received clearance to ZZZZZ2 on frequency XYA.B. When we checked in to XYZ.Z we received a clearance to FL230 and to fly direct to ZZZZZ. I believe I spelt the fix out to the Captain and asked if I should I put the Autopilot on; which he responded 'no it's okay'. Just as he was typing it in and he executed it we heard the altitude alert caution and we were at 23;580 feet. I quickly reacted and proceeded back towards FL230 at the same time the Captain called ATC and stated 'Aircraft X at FL240'. ATC then cleared us to FL310 or FL330. The deviation occurred at XA:22Z.I should not have asked the Captain if I should put the autopilot on; I should have just done it. We were obviously both needed to navigate. I should have put the autopilot on while the Captain was trying to figure out and insert a fix that was not on the SID. column121: While on the RNAVM XX in ZZZ1 we encountered a GPWS event. At the beginning of the approach we had a tailwind and the descent angle of the approach caused us to be a little fast starting the approach. As the pilot monitoring I should have caught this issue sooner and brought it to the attention of the PF (Pilot Flying). Because of the speed the PF disconnected the autopilot/auto throttles and slowed the plane to the proper approach speed. During the turn onto final the PF was visual with the runway and let the nose drop which caused a momentary don't sink. He corrected and the warning went away. Still with the airport visual he tried to correct on the VASI and received another momentary don't sink call at around 700 ft. We continued the approach and the landing was normal. I don't have anything to add for [this report].I have learned many lessons from this very short flight. I haven't had much ZZZ experience and my FO (First Officer) who was PF has had very little. We tried to mitigate the possible issues by having a slow cruise speed of 210 kts. and trying to get ready for the approach early. We briefed the 3.4 GP and felt we were in a good position for the approach. With the unfamiliarity of the situation and the weather in ZZZ this day I missed the strong tailwind that was making our situation worse. This put us behind and we had to play catch up. It was turbulent the whole flight and when he disconnected the AP/AT my [situational awareness] went down because I was worried about his flight path at that time. As I look back at the event and if I could do this again I would have us discontinue the approach early and come around to try again. Once we continued and got out of the [weather] and had the runway visually climbing back into it in that terrain did not seem the safest option. But if we had bailed early it would have made the situation easier the second time.

We debriefed after block in and recreated load the FMC. Although the arc portion showed on the route; there was also a vectors line after DRKAR. column121: Volume during this session was not particularly high; but complexity and workload changed quickly; and a sequence of events took my attention away from aircraft that didn't need much of it; including the aircraft in question. Aircraft X descending into ZZZ. My initial descent clearance was to 15;000 ft. An eastbound departure was potentially in conflict with 3 other aircraft; including Aircraft X. Deconflicting this aircraft took much of my attention during this time. Aircraft X ended up being no factor. Once clear of all other aircraft; I gave Aircraft X descent clearance to 11;000 ft. Read back was not as clear as I thought; but I had other things to worry about; including two aircraft simultaneously calling for VFR flight following and a conflict alert between VFR aircraft I was providing flight following to and a Mode-C intruder which took much of my attention because they were tracking to pass about 1 mile apart and the Mode-C intruder was climbing into the other VFR aircraft. Once that situation cleared up and as Aircraft X was descending through 12;000 ft. I received a call from FSS (Flight Service Station) which I decided to answer on the assumption that it would be a faster phone call than it turned out to be.Their request was for a Special VFR departure (SVFR). I had to take time to verify that SVFR was possible from this airport and since SVFR is a very rare request in my area of specialization I then had to look up the phraseology to give the clearance. By the time the clearance was delivered and read back; at least 2 minutes had passed. As I disconnected the FSS call; Low Altitude Alert showed Aircraft X at 7;900 ft.; descending below the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) of 8;000 ft. I immediately issued a low altitude alert with a clearance to climb to 10;000 ft. immediately. After the pilot responded I advised the pilot that his descent clearance had been to 11;000 ft. and asked if he had ZZZ in sight. Pilot responded that he had the field in sight. I cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach and gave instructions to contact Tower. It did not appear that he observed the climb clearance that accompanied the Low Altitude Alert; and the aircraft was at 7;300 ft. when I cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach.It is difficult to recommend any actions or changes to prevent re occurrence. This particular sector is quite complex; with high terrain; military airspace; two approach control facilities; arrivals to and departures from ZZZ1 in all directions. Convergence between ZZZ arrivals/departures to the south of ZZZ and ZZZ1 arrivals/departures to the southeast of ZZZ1. Also ZZZ2 arrivals and departures to the northwest of ZZZ2 all come together in the vicinity of ZZZ3. Also several satellite airports where pilots cannot reach us on the ground resulting in FSS relays. 11 adjacent sectors adjusted for typical sector configuration with multiple combined but the actual number of individual adjacent sectors is much higher and a relatively heavy VFR workload. It can unexpectedly become quite busy; even with a small number of aircraft in the sector. When this happens; it usually entails coordination calls from one or both of the approach control facilities; the military controlling agency; FSS; and one of the 11 adjacent sectors; and often includes aircraft that require a higher-than-normal workload. The timing of these factors is not controllable; so when several things happen at once; it usually can't be predicted; it can become difficult to manage; and it's often over before a D-side (Radar Assist) can make it to the sector to help.

column123: Beautiful day; 30 mile visibility; clear skies; airport in sight 30 miles away. Routine departure from ZZZ. At altitude; we were given direct to a fix and descend to 3;000 ft.
