column121: While flying the ZZZZZ RNAV departure this morning; ATC asked us if we were assigned a heading from the last Controller. The PM replied stating we were direct ZZZZZ1; with ZZZZZ behind us on the FMS legs page. This made us look closely at our legs page and moving map on our iPads; which showed us off course. ATC replied with 'roger.' Shortly following that; we were handed off to the next controller. When we checked in we mentioned our box input error and he said; 'No problem; proceed direct ZZZ1. How's that?' No further discussion with ATC. I immediately knew what happened and why. The FMS would not download our flight plan (not uncommon) so I built in manually. As I looked at the clearance I noticed the departure and selected it; but failed to assign the ZZZZZ1 transition. ZZZZZ1 appeared on our route packet as a different fix; not part of the departure and I fell for it. I had a lot of fixes and airways to type in so I focused on getting them correct and failed to notice how I had loaded the departure; without the transition. Ultimately we were missing 4 fixes in the legs page. I checked the first 5 fixes in the legs page to confirm the altitude restrictions since we were cleared to climb Via. Normally I check all the fixes but the other contributing factors today were no coffee or breakfast at this point. I wanted to get setup and ready so I could get coffee. Due to COVID; food and coffee was not available at the hotel so we catered it for our morning departure. Additionally; the pax showed up XX minutes early which squashed my plans to eat before we took off. Additionally; the lead pax birth date was incorrect on our brief so we were further distracted.Human error. I caused this event during the FMS setup. The pre-flight distractions becoming more and more common place with passenger related issues of catering and name details; today it got me. Another potential cause could be how the flight plan route is displayed on our packets. I'm used to seeing something like 'ZZZZZ.ZZZZZ1 ZZZ2; etc.;' as the FMS shows; but the filed route on our flight plan shows 'ZZZZZ ZZZZZ1 ZZZ2; etc.' Seeing it with the period would have drawn my attention to the ZZZZZ1 transition. Suggestions - For me; all things being the same again; if the filed route on our flight plan packet showed 'ZZZZZ.ZZZZZ1' this deviation wouldn't have happened today. Regardless of this and the distractions; I need to be more careful.

column121: During arrival to HAN; I was a jumpseat observer. We were at 2;000 ft. on the localizer; cleared for the ILS [Runway] 11 Left approach. Just outside the Final Approach Fix; I heard the Captain (Pilot Flying); say glideslope captured; and he set the missed approach altitude of 5;000 ft. in the altitude alerter. I was confused; because looking at the FO's (First Officer's) PFD (Primary Flight Display); I could see that we were below the glideslope; and it was no captured. I could not see the Captain's PFD to verify whether or not the glideslope was captured. The aircraft started descent from 2;000 ft.; even though we were not on the glideslope. I called out to check the glideslope and/or altitude. I did not have a hot mike; and maybe they weren't hearing me. The aircraft passed the Final Approach Fix approximately 500 ft. low. I called out the glideslope deviation again. The other jumpseat observer was also telling them to climb; and I yelled 'Go Around'. Then we got a GS caution with a line strike through the FMA on the PFD. At approximately 1;200 ft.; the go around was finally initiated with full scale deflection indicated on FO's PFD.During the surprise go around; we were instructed to maintain heading and climb to 5;000 ft. At some point the autopilot was disconnected; and situational awareness was deteriorating. The aircraft was veering to the right of track; 20 degrees nose up; and not following the flight director commands of 10 degrees nose up. I called out something like 'Who's flying the airplane; fly the airplane!' The flying pilot then steered back toward the flight director; regained control and the autopilot was re-engaged. After reaching 5;000 ft. we were vectored back for another approach to Runway 11 Left.Also of note; there was runway/taxiway construction at HAN airport that could have possibly created a glideslope anomaly. Though I could not see the Captain's flight instruments; it is possible there may have been a loss of glideslope indication at the start of the event. On the FO's PFD; I could see that the ILS was identified; and localizer/glideslope were displayed at all times.The Pilot Monitoring should have noticed on his instruments that the aircraft was not on glideslope; and should have called out the deviation immediately. When I saw the deviation; I was trying to alert the crew to fix the situation. I should have called out go around immediately.
column123: While inbound on the localizer for RNWY (Runway) 11L; the glideslope was captured and the 'G/S' FMA was active. Shortly after capturing the glideslope; the 'G/S' FMA blinked and had a yellow strikethrough. The glideslope then started to fall beneath us; while the autopilot tried to increase the rate of descent. The Pilot Flying switched to V/S [Vertical Speed]; and rolled in more V/S down to stay on glideslope with a more than normal descent rate. I instructed to 'level off; level off' followed by 'climb back to 2;000 ft. It was then I noticed the glideslope dot had blinked and reappeared at two dots high; indicating we were low. The Captain in the observer seat then said 'Go Around; Go Around'. The Pilot Flying initiated the go around with the 'TOGA' [Takeoff Go-Around] switches and sometime thereafter turned off the autopilot. He then hand flew the go around to 5;000 ft. and present heading. After notifying Tower of our missed approach; we were told to contact Approach frequency. During this event; with my seat position; I was only able to observe the Captain's PFD [Primary Flight Display]. After landing safely and gathering all facts observed between crewmembers; it was apparent that the autopilot tried to capture a false glideslope and failed; thus giving us the yellow strikethrough the 'G/S' FMA."

column121: We were at FL410 in continuous light chop. The seat belt sign was on before we entered the known area of turbulence and remained on till we passed the turbulence. ATC [was] reporting light chop for the next 150 miles. I had the speed intervene window open. The N1 was set for turbulence penetration. The speed was Mach .76. Within a matter of seconds we were in severe mountain wave. The speed increased to Mach .80 and we were in the over speed band. The over speed clacker went off right away. We began losing altitude. I immediately reduced thrust which was ineffective so pulled the speed brake. The speed slowed to Mach .76. We lost 300 ft. quickly. Then the second wave hit and we climbed rapidly back to altitude then 200 ft. above the assigned altitude. The aircraft returned to FL410. The event was probably 30 to 45 seconds. During the event I had the FO (First Officer) seat the flight attendants immediately. I had the FO ask for a descent to FL390. We were given the descent. The FO reported the mountain wave and the trends to ATC. There was no traffic in the area on TCAS and none was reported by ATC. We reached FL390 with no further wave but the light turbulence continued. I checked the flight attendants in and they reported no one was up during the event. I reported the event to Maintenance as severe mountain wave and over speed. I reported the event to Dispatch as well. In my 25 years of flying I have never seen mountain wave this bad.

column121: Please consider changing/eliminating the Deer Valley One procedure!The Deer Valley One obstacle departure is improbable if not impossible in a high-performance airplane.1. Chart does not tell you how close the turn is.2. Turn needs to be completed by 1.6 nm from end of runway! This alone should never never be permitted.3. Turn radius at 200 kts. is likely about 1.3 nm.4. 400 ft. V2 +10 flaps up igniters off Venr takes about 2nm min. And way longer in this scenario.5. And wait until you add what happened to me; a traffic call for departing traffic on parallel runway in the direction of my needed turn.6. That took time to find and alter course to avoid the traffic that was about 500 ft. away at the same altitude!6b. That traffic prohibited a turn to [Heading] 336 as required to occur at about 100 ft. if I was to make the turn in time.7. Then the TCAS resolution screen took time to resolve that first conflict.8. Then the instant that screen was resolved; a second additional 'traffic traffic' call occurred for another item of traffic that I could never visually acquire. Box said above and slightly ahead as I recall. Right near my course; so it was a serious safety concern.9. Then the second TCAS screen took time to resolve that second traffic call.10. Now it's finally time for 400 ft. V2 + 10; flaps up igniters off; recall Venr.11. By this time I'm coming upon 5;000 ft. considering engaging the autopilot; but the Flight Director is not aligned because so close and capturing.12. Stuff it down to capture; but overshot 5;000 ft. slightly.13. And now it's finally time to do the turn; but ATC asked what's up.Well ...How can you design a turn that needs to be completed in 1.6nm which would mean it must be started at about 100 ft. AGL = unsafe & no jet should turn before 400 ft. as trained.And look at the chart; no indication how close that is.And compounding my situation is that the PXR VOR was out of service.I submit it's impossible in a high performance airplane. Do it in the sim without telling the pilot in advance and with and without being a regular at the field; and I estimate you'll get max 10% compliance. Who would design for a 90% potential of non-compliance?Please have them redesign/eliminate this departure!

column121: On arrival into ZZZ from the south; we were vectored off of the ZZZZZ procedure and held high due to traffic. We had been previously queried as to our RVR requirements for [Runway] XXR. column123: Flight was left high on the ZZZZZ Arrival.   ATIS had us landing on [Runway] XXR. column121: Aircraft X was vectored to their final approach course approximately 3 to 4 miles in trail of a preceding Aircraft Y. We were VFR conditions but had low ceilings hovering around 1;000 feet. Aircraft weren't coming out of the clouds until a 1 to 2 mile final. When Aircraft X joined the approach they has an absurdly high overtake speed with the Aircraft Y in front of them of 80 plus knots. There was no way separation was ever going to be maintained. When the realization set in of what was happening Local Control issued instructions to cancel the approach and to climb to 3000 feet and to turn 20 degrees to the left.  I began coordination with Departure Control for a handoff with vectors to bring the aircraft back around for another approach. In the meantime Aircraft X advised Local Control that they were minimum fuel and were continuing the approach. Local Control advised me of this; so I canceled the coordination; and redirected my attention to an aircraft awaiting clearance. Then Local Control advised me that Aircraft X was indeed going around with the 20 degree left turn; and 3000 foot altitude assignment. Traffic was light; so I instructed Local Control to climb Aircraft X to 6000 feet and issue a turn to get them into the dispersal area as per our joint agreement. I again initiated coordination with Departure Control for the handoff; with Aircraft X climbing to 6000 feet and on a 100 or 105 heading.Then I came back to the aircraft on Clearance Delivery and had them read back their clearance. During the read back; Departure was trying to call me and say that Aircraft X needed to climb immediately for an aircraft that was departing southeast bound off a satellite airport. I responded that the altitude had been issued and would find out why Aircraft X stopped their climb at 3000 feet. I relayed the information to Local Control as I was receiving it.  Local Control told me that Aircraft X would not accept the climb due to their minimum fuel situation; which I relayed back to Departure. Departure Control requested we ship Aircraft X to them; so that they could maintain separation with the traffic departing the satellite airport which I relayed to Local. Local was able to get Aircraft X to climb to 4;000 feet before shipping them. There was a loss of lateral separation on final approach; but there may have been altitude separation; although I am not sure about that. The problem is that we are struggling with spacing issues on final and even have a collaborative work group established with Approach to resolve these problems. Approach is continually handing Tower these overtakes;  and less than coordinated arrival spacing for departure gaps; but Tower is always held accountable for the consequences of each event. This is the standard here at  even though the separation problem originates with the Approach Controller. Even our local management tends to initially stand behind Approach and their actions while pointing their fingers at the Tower controllers trying to tell us that what we did was incorrect; even though we are only trying our best to prevent an separation error from occurring or getting worse.  Standardize spacing requirements here at 3 miles or required and coordinated arrival spacing distances and never transfer communications of aircraft on final until there is less than a 30 knot overtake speed. In other words; follow the guidance in the 7110.65 and ensure separation before transferring communications to another controller. And on top of this; performance management to ensure controllers are being held accountable to the basic standards.

During the decent briefing the approach and contingencies were briefed; however; a storm disrupting the approach was not anticipated. A left deviation was started and I decided to proceed direct to point D111G as the best course of action. The FO had his terrain display in terrain mode allowing me to see any conflicts ahead. The FO correctly pointed out that going direct point D254I would be a better course of action and allow more time for the approach. I agreed and we asked for and was given direct to that point by ATC. At this point the situation was less than ideal. The weather was mostly cloudy with only brief glimpses of the terrain. I had the altitude of 10;500 feet in my mind thinking I was heading for my original point (D111G) when in reality we were required to be at 14;200 feet point D254I. I had started the descent when the FO pointed out the error and I immediately started to climb. At this point we were still not on the approach due to the weather. We were still proceeding direct to D254I. I was also slowing and configuring for the landing. I ended up disconnecting the autopilot in order to reestablish myself on to a stable approach. The terrain display never showed any conflicts and no verbal warnings of the system was encountered. I knew approximately where the aircraft was at all times. My error was in the decent altitude while forced off of the approach due to weather. We eventually did get on the approach; were stable when we broke out of the weather and had an uneventful landing. The large cell situated over the UIO VOR forced an unprepared diversion around it resulting in an off route decent in order to land. This in turn resulted in attaining a lower than desired altitude in heavily mountainous terrain. This was my first time into UIO. Although I reviewed the required airport familiar special qualification briefing; in this situation it was not adequate. I consider myself very experienced in mountainous terrain and I believe this particular field should require a Check Airman checkout. 'Picking the brain for gotchas' would have been invaluable.

column121: Just after completing a climb to 12;000 ft in an attempt to get above an icing layer; the company issued iPad mount fell off the windscreen on to the floor. Initially; I reacted to this by reaching down to pick it up; but simultaneously noticed the G600 displayed a GPS failure indication on the moving map side of the screen. At the same time TAWS (terrain awareness and warning system) gave an aural alert 'TAWS NOT AVAILABLE'. There were no additional audible alerts or visual annunciations. I initially thought this was simply a GPS signal failure and was starting to react accordingly; I then observed that the aircraft had entered a descending turn and immediately reacted with an unusual attitude in IMC recovery procedure. Given that the aircraft was in continuous light turbulence; in the clouds; at night; I was momentarily completely focused on ensuring the aircraft remained in a controlled attitude. A few moments latter I began taking stock of what I did and did not have. I observed the GMX200 screen off; GNS530 screen off; the primary GTX330 was off; and the autopilot was off. The G600 was giving associated GPS/AHRS and GAD43 failures. There were no other annunciations on the primary panel; and no audible alerts. My next focus was to re-establish navigation to my next known waypoint; the ZZZ VOR. I had previously tuned the ZZZ VOR into the NAV1 and NAV2; so I had manual navigation and DME via NAV2. Since the GNS430 and secondary GTX330 appeared operable; I immediately squawked 7600 as I had been out of contact with ZZZ1 Center (which was on COM1) and had obviously deviated heading/altitude at the beginning of the incident a few moments earlier. Not knowing what was happening to cause these failures and what might be failing next; setting the squawk may at the very least alert Center that I am having a problem. I also needed a few moments to sort out which frequency I needed to be on; as at this point the stress level was high enough I could not remember the frequency. I had to retrieve the iPad which was still on the floor in order to look at the chart screen for the frequency. Once back in contact with ZZZ1 Center I described the situation as best I could: some kind of electrical and/or communication failure as most of my avionics were now off. I elected for a diversion to ZZZ; now about 17nm away; and worry about troubleshooting the problem on the ground rather in the air in IMC at night. I was given vectors for a visual approach and landed without further incident.Having time to analyze the situation; and noting after landing/parking that the Avionics 1 & 2 were able to be switch back on; I conclude that the root cause of the systems associated with Avionics Bus 1 failing was from the iPad mount falling off the windscreen and hitting the switch on the way down. In personal reflection; I can recognize the irony that simply reaching over to check the avionics switches would have likely resolved the issue. But; the totality of the circumstances I had been suddenly faced with: 'an unexpected flight attitude deviation following an otherwise innocuous distraction; an initial observation of having a GPS signal failure'. Normally a failure of the GNS530/430; even if the failure was a complete loss of the entire unit; would not have resulted in the loss of the autopilot modes. Typically any normal failure of the autopilot is also accompanied by an audible alert. I had no immediate indication that the autopilot was off until observing the aircraft starting a descending turn. This precipitated the human factor contribution to the scenario of dealing with an otherwise unexplainable loss of avionics and uncommanded attitude deviation and no indication to which trained emergency checklist actions would be a prudent course of action. Overall troubleshooting based on system knowledge is a higher level brain function and at the time I did not have the luxury of 'stepping back' to think what might be going wrong. All that to say; there are no checklists specifically for an avionics failure (such as the switch some how getting turned off) or even what to do if the GPS fails. The assumed reactions remain in the realm of pilot knowledge and ability to troubleshoot the problem in lieu of following a checklist... in all likelihood with the assumption that the autopilot is still functional. This isn't a suggestion that we make a new checklist item; but rather the addition of random failure modes such as this during training to either establish situational memory or reinforce what to do if you don't know what to do. Finally; the root culprit of the situation... the iPad mount. This has been an ongoing 'issue' that has been simply tolerated by Company pilots. It hasn't been reported likely because we didn't think it was a big problem; would have never imagined it would lead to any problem; or have not been explicitly told that it is a problem if it occurs. There is also the ongoing back and forth with pilots who do not like having the mount and will remove it from the windscreen. The result is the mount ends up on the floor; getting dirty and damaged to the point that many of the suction cups do not effectively stay on the windscreen. In fact; in talking with another co-worker I discovered that this exact scenario happened to him during an AM departure a few weeks earlier and had hit both Avionics 1 & 2 switches. Since he saw it (and had the benefit of being VFR during the day) he just turned the switches back on and remounted the iPad. It has been my observation the suction cups seem to most frequently fail when climbing into colder temperatures; but this is not always the case. At this point; I believe it is safe to say that the current mounting system does not work... either by nature of system or as a result of the poor care and handling it as received over the past year or so. I will have to admit; the iPad mount coming off is something that I have observed and didn't report... and frankly should have reported and made a big stink over sooner. But I am now: at this point I do not believe the current iPad mounting system to be either effective nor safe.

We were not able to make the restriction at ZZZZZ2. I told the FO to stop descent until we were sure of the instrument readings while we were communicating with ATC telling them of our situation. I took control of the aircraft back from the First Officer and continued the arrival and approach via ATC instructions.We were immediately aware of the malfunction. There were multiple alerts and warnings going off when it happened.After landing the mechanics did a CFDS (Centralized Fault Display System) check which showed a MSC (Miscellaneous Systems Controller) failure. Look like the Captain pitot tube was not being heated properly and descending into the icing conditions cause it to become blocked. column121: Prior to top of descent we briefed the NNCEE 1 RNAV Arrival into IAH.  The arrival says to plan on flying the RWY 8R transition.  So we briefed the ILS RWY 8R approach.  Houston Approach Control then told us to fly the RNAV (RNP) Y RWY 9 approach.  The CA was the PM and told the FO he would change the approach in the FMC. So the CA brought up the second HOWLN fix and entered it into the discontinuity boxes and assumed that this action closed the discontinuity. column121: Descending on the DSNEE 4 arrival from EMLLD; we became aware of congested airport environment with two different TCAS traffic alerts very close by. Approach had us at 190 knots departing DSNEE; and we were expecting the visual to runway 20R. We had gone to flaps 2 configuration. We were handed off late to the final controller; and when we switched over we heard a company call sign with nearly identical numeric as ours; cleared for the RNAV (RNP) Z runway 20R. We heard the other aircraft read back the clearance; we knew a VERY similar call sign was on frequency. We thought we might be cleared for the same approach. We checked in and asked if we were going to get the RNAV approach; and the controller said no; we were going to get a visual unless we asked for the approach. Shortly after; the controller cleared an aircraft to descend to 3000'; but neither of us were sure that it was our call sign. The First Officer (FO) attempted to clarify; but the controller was very busy and talking nonstop. We flew a few more miles; and before we could clarify he repeated the clearance to descend to 3000' and asked if we had the airport in sight. We called the airport; and said we were high. He cleared us to fly through final approach course and intercept from the right. FO read back the clearance; and we both agreed it was going to be tight. I immediately called for gear down and got the flaps to full; I also used the speed brakes as long as safely practical. We switched over to tower control; and I made the glideslope at approx. 1400' AGL; but we were still 40kts fast. I told the FO we were going to do a 'Soft Go'. At 1000' AGL I called for 'Go Around; Takeoff/around (TOGA)' and advanced the thrust levers to TOGA. I then called 'climb' as I brought the thrust levers back to what I thought was the climb position; but was actually the Maximum Continuous Thrust (MCT) detent. The tower initially held us to 2000'; so I reduced our climb rate - we were accelerating rapidly. As we cleaned up and were cleared to 3000'; the FO recognized that we were in MCT detent and brought it to my attention. By then we were clean and rapidly approaching 250 KIAS. I brought the thrust levers back to idle as we passed 260; and we saw a maximum speed of about 280 before we began to slow down again. I selected speed mode and set 220 KIAS; positioned the thrust levers in the climb detent and re-engaged auto thrust. We slowed and turned back into a right downwind for an uneventful visual approach and landing at SNA.Causes(1)	Late clearance to descend. SNA is challenging even when on a normal profile; and a few miles made all the difference.(2)	Task saturation. The L.A basin is one of the busiest airspaces in the world. Two Traffic Alerts and nonstop chatter from the approach controller indicated that he was task saturated; as well.(3)	Call sign confusion. The scheduling shop should never have had two call signs separated by one digit arriving at the same airport at the same time.(4)	Approach expectations. We were going to do a visual; and changed our setup and expectations when we heard preceding traffic approach clearance.(5)	Fatigue. Our FAR 117 duty day limit was 10 hours. We had been awake since 3.5 hours earlier to make sign-in; and were at 9:00 of our 10:00 limit when we arrived at SNA. When we knew we were too high to likely make a successful approach; we could have asked for a vector and more time/distance to descend. Flight scheduling needs to de-conflict call signs so very similar ones are not scheduled to arrive at the same airport at the same time. The ATC controllers seemed very busy; perhaps a few more controllers on-shift would help divide the workload better. Crew scheduling could alleviate fatigue factors by avoiding sequence builds that have crews flying into airports at the back end of their duty periods that are known to present unusual challenges (even if they aren't officially 'special qualification' airports).

column121: Arriving DEN on the CLASH2 arrival from the southeast; I planned and briefed an easterly flow arrival to land 17R. ATIS advertised 17R; 16L; 16R ILS; visual and RNAV Z approaches. I briefed for the RNAV RNP Z 17R. The final point for the arrival was QWIKE intersection and I left a discontinuity between that QWIKE and the QWIKE point starting the RNAV RNP Z 17R. Denver Center gave us a clearance to descend via the CLASH2 arrival landing south.The PM (Pilot Monitoring) and I confirmed that that was what we briefed and the FMC was properly programmed. The PM checked on with DEN Approach and we were told to expect RNAV Z to 16R. The PM installed that approach and I briefed the new arrival points and crossing restrictions on the CLASH2 that coincided with that runway; which were now a west downwind; the final fix being CLFFF. I briefed the approach as well. We did the same thing; leaving a discontinuity between CLFFF on the arrival and CLFFF as the IAF on the approach. The PM pulled the landing data for 16R and we briefed the changes on the engine-out missed approach which was slightly different then 17R. Approximately EVRLY intersection as we were descending through FL180; DEN Approach then said runway change; expect visual or ILS (I can't remember) to 16L. I remember it was at FL180 because it coincided with the altimeter change and the need to verify that VNAV is still able to maintain. The PM installed runway 16L and I did a briefing for the ILS 16L. This changed the FMC to an east downwind; the same fixes as for runway 17R but I did not note the changes in arrival fixes. As we were approaching JURKY intersection; I noticed on the FMC that the next waypoint was not what I was expecting. I had in my mind that we would be on a west downwind for the 16 runways. I said to the PM; it's not the correct fix next for runway 16R. The PM then asked DEN Approach to verify the runway assignment.Approach responded with a frequency change but did not respond to the request for runway clarification. This was at the point where we needed to go left or right depending on the runway. I thought it was 16R; so I went to the next fix for that runway; ROOTZ. As soon as the PM checked on with the next frequency; the Controller asked our runway assignment. The PM said we were trying to clarify. Approach then gave us 16R as a runway assignment. In fact; the previous clearance was for runway 16L. And that runway is an east downwind; not a west downwind even though the runway is on the west side of the airfield. This was absolutely my responsibility to ensure the correct runway and corresponding waypoints for the arrival. Going forward my personal correction will be to write down the runway assignment given by ATC each time it changes; whether on the yoke clip notepaper or on the iPad graphic. I also got complacent after doing 2 full briefings into DEN on a clear day. With the 3rd briefing; I did an abbreviated briefing. A full briefing; stepping through every arrival point would have caught it earlier. Additionally; as suggested by the Jump Seater; instead of clarifying the runway and having to verify the points quickly; I will ask ATC for the next waypoint they are expecting in order to give myself some time to figure out any ambiguities between the FMC and the chart. If we are adding to the data for DEN arrival deviations though...I didn't think this could happen to me. We briefed the threat of runway changes going into DEN. But DEN giving runway changes that impact arrival points without sufficient time for us to properly program and confirm was a contributing factor. Its 11.4 miles from EVRLY where we got the change to JURKY where the arrival splits. To reprogram; confirm; brief; get landing data and brief the engine-out profile changes while monitoring the descent is challenging.
column123: CLASH2 RNAV into DEN we initially planned for a Visual Approach to 17R backed up by the ILS. ATC then came back and said maintain 12;000 unrestricted which in my mind validated the shortcut because usually you get the phraseology 'Climb via the SID except maintain XXX'. ATC then informed us our deviate and asked us if we were on the SID.  I said affirmative except from ZZZZA we were direct to ZZZZZ which was incorrect according to the clearance.  After getting to cruise the Captain and I discussed the situation looking at both the clearance; the FOM and the loaded routing from the CPDLC.  We realized that two errors were made.  When I loaded the SID I did not reselect the runway and SID with the ZZZZZ transition because when I checked it was in the box and because we both missed the period in the printout and ZZZZZ was on the regular routing I thought ATC wanted us to cut that part of the SID off because of low traffic volume.   It was pilot error and it's a difficult lesson.  I am fully aware that a period means a transition but I missed it on the printout and assumed ATC wanted a shorter routing which has become the norm is so many ATC environments with COVID.  I also realize that I will always double check every period on the CDU against the printout copy as it's easier to see.  In addition I will ensure that every modification in the future requires an input of both the runway and SID even when uploading clearances from CPDLC which I'm aware to do but I didn't see the period on the printout.  I take full responsibility for this mistake and I feel really bad I missed such a small but signification part of the clearance.   I know better so there's no excuses for this missed detail.

column121: During normal climb out of ZZZ; passing roughly FL240; we got a single CAWS Overspeed warning; FMA indicated FMS speed; however aircraft had accelerated into the MMO range I Reduced the speed from Mach .81 to .79 and pressed FMS speed to edit a new lower FMS speed. Reaching cruise at FL350 returned to normal FMS ECON Cruise .83 Mach Two hours into the flight; in cruise with no changes to pitch or power with autopilot on; aircraft started to overspeed by roughly 15 kts beyond the MMO in a couple seconds Both Primary Flight Display's indicated the same speed fluctuation We were alerted by the CAWS and the aircraft started to climb The First Officer took the controls as he was first to identify the problem; turned off the ATS reduced the power I pulled the speed brakes and called for the controls; reduced the speed from .83 Mach to .80 Mach Airspeed spread was about 60 kts and we were at optimum altitude Once the aircraft speed and altitude were under control; I reengaged the FMS speed and ATS These previous events; helped influence my decision making for the primary event.......All three crew members had been in the cockpit; with the door closed; together since departure I got up to use the lavatory about an hour west of ZZZ1; 3 hours into flight As I opened the cockpit door I detected a very strong smell of oily fumes I turned on the lights on the courier deck and the main cargo deck Air was hazy I went to the cockpit and got my flashlight turned off the lights on the main deck opened the smoke curtain and confirmed the presence of blueish smoke on the main deck in my bright flashlight beam I asked the Load Master to please come back to the courier station and check She confirmed the presence of smoke and fumes I returned to the cockpit and I ran the Emergency Non-Alert SMOKE/FIRE/FUMES checklist As per the checklist; I determined the source to be the Bleed 3 as the smoke smelled oily; not acrid; and I've heard of this problem in the past on this aircraft; also the Dangerous Goods Form did not list any hazmat on board and all systems were still functioning normally I turned off Bleed 3 per the checklist and started looking at nearby airports in my iPad The smoke began dissipating slowly I asked the First Officer to please go back and make sure the smoke is not coming from a ULD He returned after a few minutes and confirmed the smoke was dissipating and it was not coming from any of the cargo He said it seemed to concentrated above the wing box but dissipating I was reviewing the previous logbooks and current logbook pages for any smoke occurrences during the previous flights to help come to a decision to divert per the Quick Reference Handbook or to continue per the Quick reference Handbook Before I could finish reviewing the logbook Autopilot 1 disconnected; the aircraft started deviating from altitude and we got a LEVEL 2 alert for FCC 1B FAULT; a master caution and my flight director disappeared I immediately switched to Capt on First Officer Flight Director and stabilized the aircraft; checked all the parameters and engaged Autopilot 2 I called for the LEVEL 2 FCC 1B FAULT checklist After the checklist was complete; I consulted with the crew and made the decision to divert to ZZZ1 as it was a Company flight; it was en-route; weather was good; we were very familiar with the airport and we have maintenance there I gave the controls and communication to the FO and began running Checklist I told the FO to advise ATC that we would like to divert to ZZZ1 for technical reasons We were 39 minutes from ZZZ1 and cleared direct to a point on the STAR We advised NCC via ACARS of our diversion On the STAR when we were passing 11;000 ft at 245 kts; we were cleared to 6;000 ft; I reduced the altitude to 6;000 ft on the FCP and selected IDLE and confirmed on the FMA The aircraft began to climb instead of descend; speeds were normal and aircraft was in clean configuration w/ local altimeter set I disconnected the autopilot and hand flew thelast 50 miles We were cleared for ILS On final as we set Flaps 15 we got a LEVEL 2 FLAP DISAG; this was expected as the right outboard flap had been 'X' out since the FCC Fault We set flaps 35 Flaps showing 21/22/20/X on both PFD's I elected not to extend the flaps further or retract and retry to extend them as the airplane was light and controllable; runway was long and insight; weather was clear and winds were light I elected to maintain MIN auto brakes however I informed the crew I was going to use all 3 reverse and to advise tower that we would be rolling to the end Before landing checklist was completed I announced 'no green box' due to flaps not beyond 25 degrees We landed with no further incident and taxied to the ramp. Excellent job from my First Officer and Load Master They were invaluable to me during the flight. I identified the haze/fumes when I left the cockpit to use the lavatory I found the upper deck full of fumes. [Probable cause of the] smoke was Engine oil leaking into Pneumatic system [Probable cause of the] FCC issue is unknown. Followed SOP; make decisions while weighing input of crew. [As my response] recommended Preventative Maintenance.

column121: I departed Aircraft X for takeoff. Once approved separation was anticipated I cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff. I wasn't anticipating the trailing aircraft to be so much faster or the lead aircraft to under perform like it did. Both aircraft were similar types. Another factor could be that I had been medically decertified due to a COVID-19 exposure at the facility. I was not sick but I was only notified the day before this incident that my medical had been reinstated and that I was to report to work the next day. [It] was quite a surprise to me and didn't give me any time to mentally prepare to conduct air traffic duties after [several] weeks away from work.The only recommendation would be a more advanced notification of a return to air traffic duties after a long time off. column121: Captain (CA) was PF and First Officer (FO) was PM. We had a crew alert action of AUTOFLT FCU1 failure not far from our initial descent for the STAR. CA was working the crew alert issue and Center called saying what the CA heard was 'Flight ABC'; Direct ZZZZZ descend via ZZZZZ1' (CA was in the QRH; reading about or looking for the crew alert issue).  After talking with the FO on the ground in ZZZ; after the event; the FO thought the read back something like 'Flight ABC direct ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1.'  Then; PM made sure PF was inserting the bottom altitude of STAR in the FCU (Meaning PM understood the clearance to descend via the ZZZZZ1).  PF did insert the bottom altitude. Then; shortly afterwards; we hit some moderate turbulence and PF decided to start descend early because he could not read the QRH; hoping to get into some clear air.  Then we were told we descended and there may have been a flight deviation.  I did not think so at the time because of the clearance I understood.I believe there were several causal factors on this event. 1) Pilot Inexperience.  The FO was on the Type X aircraft and in March was awarded the Type Y aircraft.  But from March through December; all the FO did was go to Type Y training; and IOE.  This was the FO's first flight since IOE. The FO was going very slow making sure no mistakes were made. The PF was also going very slow to ensure all FO tasks were completed.  2) Task saturation (crew alert event; pilot inexperience; turbulence and clearance understanding). Combined; this put both pilots in a 'caution situation.'  The PF; was trying for something like this would not happen from the moment the flight started by making sure he was slow and deliberate on all his thoughts and actions. 3) Turbulence event. We descended early because PF had a hard time reading the QRH. 4) PF flying and completing crew alert actions.  In this case; it may have made a difference; but; I do not believe it would have made a difference; because the PM understood the clearance from Center was a clearance to descend Via;   and when the turbulence started; the person working the crew alert action would have said descend to get out of the turbulence the QRH could be read. The same outcome would have happened.Suggestions - Verify the clearance; no matter the circumstances...In this particular event; the PF should have verified the clearance knowing the proficiency of the other pilot may not have been 100%.  A pilot may be 'Current' with regards to the official written documents approved by the FAA; but they may have not been proficient...(I do not know how this can be fixed...)
column123: In preparation for descent; Status Page showed an inoperative system the CA/PF noticed. CA was in the process of investigating the crew alert message that caused it. We had a seasoned CA in the Jump Seat who was assisting in the lookup for the crew alert actions; if any; and the code was send to Maintenance. In that time; we received a call from Center to proceed 'direct to ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1.' I read the clearance back 'direct ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1 arrival'. I then conveyed to the CA/Pilot Flying 'direct to ZZZZZ; we can descend via the ZZZZZ1' and I backed CA up to set direct ZZZZZ in the FMS and dialed in the lowest altitude in the arrival for south landings. We verified the altitude. While inbound to ZZZZZ; we were at FL390 and encountered some occasions of moderate turbulence and continuous light chop. The CA/PF commenced a descent to avoid remaining in the turbulent conditions. I contacted the Center to let them know we were descending out of FL390. They called back to ask what was the reason for the descent. I stated we had encountered moderate to light turbulence and needed to descend to avoid it. They called back asking me to confirm the reason for descent was turbulence. I confirmed. Then; before we were handed off to the next frequency; the controller asked us to contact a number for possible altitude deviation. There was a misunderstanding; on my part; of the vertical clearance in the call with Center with the initial clearance for ZZZZZ1 and I passed that misinterpretation on to the CA/PF.It was my first flight in over a month; preceded only by sim events way back in September and just prior to OE. This was a threat up front. Hadn't flown in this environment in over 18 months. We had multiple distractions due to the crew alert and system loss being addressed; icing conditions and turbulence. The ATC frequency was covering high traffic volume so there was a significant amount of talking on the frequency. We had both been up very early in order to be ready at report time. My expectation bias led me to believe we were cleared to 'descend via' when we were cleared only laterally for the approach.We could have briefed the arrival prior to addressing the crew alert and done a transfer of control of the aircraft and radios. I could have had ATC repeat the clearance; once the PF was back with me; so that they could communicate directly what the intended clearance was. I could have stated the clearance exactly as it was read back to eliminate any 'single point' of interpretation; or misinterpretation.

column121: FL360 ISA -54C; REC MAX ALT (recommended maximum altitude) 39.8. MCDU weight 132.8. Green dot speed 229 KIAS. Vls 220 [lowest selectable speed for autopilot]. Takeoff Data Performance derived green dot corrected one knot per 1;000 feet above FL200 equals an under FL200 green dot speed of 213. A 213 KIAS green dot from 3.5.4 of the Performance Manual is the speed for a 141 knot jet (8;200 pound difference). FAC1 (flight augmentation computer) and FAC2 averaged to 140 kts. Flaps full landing. Vls 128 KIAS. MCDU Vapp was 123 (5 knots into the hook). Out of an abundance of caution; we added 10 knots to get to Vls+5. Landed uneventfully and under max landing weight even if you added in the 8-9 kts (worst case scenario). Documented all in the aircraft logbook. For the committee; this is the second 319 that has presented a large difference in MCDU weight vs. calculated weight from FAC1/FAC2 (which generates Vapp and Vls on a basic jet). Either the jets EOW (empty operating weight) is wrong; the software is corrupted or the alpha vanes are out of calibration. I think safety and maintenance need to do a deep dive in to the FAC's and alpha vanes and any software changes of late. The only other explanation is an error in the EOW which is hard to envision. I would like a response directly from the committee about this and [another] aircraft which was previously accepted in to report system. I am concerned that given the increase in the number of pilots who are not flying regularly due to schedule reductions; this could result in an incident or mishap.

I plan to continue to maintain a high level of situational awareness in the cockpit to trap threats before they become errors. I told the CIC (Controller in Charge) to open up monitors; they were trying to find staffing at the time already. I then got Aircraft X above the MVA and vectored them for the approach while continuing to deal with LAX deviations. After clearing Aircraft X for the localizer runway 25; I switched them to HHR tower; monitors had opened at this time. Aircraft X then proceeded to do a left turn southbound on about a 7 mile final without notification to me from HHR tower. Monitor 1 then called HHR and asked what was going on. Aircraft X then checked back on frequency with me heading 160; no coordination. I climbed Aircraft X above the MVA and vectored them for another approach. I also asked the pilot if he could accept the approach and they agreed they could. I was then relieved.[We need] staffing. column121: Aircraft X took off RIL climbing to 15;000 feet; at around 10;000 feet; Aircraft X informed me he was having a landing gear issue; could not climb further and needed to return to RIL right away. I sent him direct to RIL. He had good sight of the terrain and once he got the visual he was cleared the visual approach. Aircraft Y was another aircraft going into RIL north of the airport level at 14;000 feet with no approach clearance. Aircraft X appeared to be circling to the runway so I did not clear Aircraft Y into the airport. Aircraft X then popped back on the frequency saying they cannot land at RIL and need to go to [another airport]. Aircraft X at this point was 8;000 feet climbing eastbound still in priority handling status. I re-radar identified Aircraft X and had them climb to 13;000 feet to try to maintain positive Minimum IFR Altitudes. They affirmed they had good sight of the terrain. I called the traffic to both Aircraft Y and Aircraft X hoping to apply visual separation. Neither saw one another so they both remained 13;000 feet (Aircraft X) and 14;000 feet (Aircraft Y).Once able; I vectored Aircraft X south to get him away from high Minimum IFR Altitudes and the RIL approach corridor. I asked Aircraft Y 'if I turn you direct to RIL; do you think you can get a visual with the airport?' Aircraft Y responded he could. I then said 'Aircraft Y; cleared direct RIL' I then went back to Aircraft X and asked fuel remaining; souls on board; what altitude they could climb to; and then explained why 15;000 feet was not feasible. I offered GJT etc. While discussing options with Aircraft X; I noticed Aircraft Y leave 14;000 feet and begin their descent while still 3 to 4 miles from Aircraft X. I gave a traffic alert to Aircraft Y and told them to climb back to 14;000 feet immediately. I then gave the traffic alert to Aircraft X. Aircraft Y climbed back up; I gained the 5 miles and climbed Aircraft X up and gave Aircraft Y the visual approach to RIL. I issued Aircraft Y advisories.In this session I had two separate situations. A pilot deviation; an arrival rush; a handful of ornery pilots on the ground at RIL clogging the frequency looking for releases off the ground. Had RIL sector been separated out through our split frequency procedures; this may not have occurred. There was a lot of frequency congestion between the sector's two frequencies which blocked transmissions to the priority handling aircraft. We used to do this procedure and have been recently barred from doing it again. This procedure could have helped!

column121: [We were] inbound to Ontario; CA. Prior to the descent the flight was brief following the [approach briefing]. Ontario was landing 8L and 8R; with good VFR weather and a light wind from the west. The crew descended on the Ziggy 7 arrival and was given a clearance to track outbound on 270 radial after Paradise VOR. There was a distraction trying to set up the tracking of a radial in the FMS by the pilot monitoring. As the pilot flying I decided to use the VOR and VOR mode to accomplish this. We complied with clearance and were cleared to 3;000 feet.After leveling at 3;000 feet a traffic report was issued for a helicopter at 1 o'clock and 4;000 feet. We were given a base leg heading of 320. After starting this turn an amber target showed up on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) at our altitude. I was looking out the window for traffic; in a matter of 2 seconds the Captain pushed forward on the controls; we got a TA/RA descend descend warning; I saw a small aircraft at 2 o'clock and 100 yards; I turned off the Autopilot and Autothrottle stopped the turn towards the small aircraft and descended to 2;500 feet. [We were] cleared to remain at 2;600 feet and received radar vectors to join the Localizer and landed 8L. The Captain was the pilot monitoring and the First Officer was the pilot flying. The ATC controller did make some kind of apology regarding the event. There was a minor distraction regarding the tuning of our radios. I had the VOR tuned and needed to make a switch to the ILS frequency. This took a matter of seconds to correct and we had the airport in sight the entire time.The Captain and I debriefed the event and felt we made all the correct decisions. The next day we confirmed how to track a radial using the FMS and LNAV mode. A note regarding small aircraft in vicinity might be a good idea. Knowing how to set up the FMS to track a radial would be helpful. Above all fly the airplane; keep your eyes outside; and expect the unexpected.
column123: Descending on the ZIGGY ARRIVAL ATC gave clearance to fly the PDZ 270 radial after PDZ. PM (Pilot Monitoring) was unable to input the radial to fly in LNAV and the PF (Pilot Flying) flew the radial using raw data. ATC gave clearance to descend from 4;000 to 3;000 with a right turn to a heading of 340 for vectors to 08L. ATC advised traffic (helicopter) in the turn at 3;500 and gave clearance to continue turn to 020. Helicopter traffic was never observed. On TCAS PM saw a target which appeared to be at 3;000 feet on the 020 heading and advised PF to stop turn. TCAS aural warning TA 'traffic traffic' annunciated and PM saw traffic as TCAS aural alert advised an RA 'traffic descend now'. PF and PM both pushed controls forward as conflicting traffic continued to descend and turn into the jets path. PM advised ATC of the new heading altitude deviation due to the RA. Conflict was resolved at 2;300 feet; PF leveled off and started climb back up to 3;000. ATC advised stop climb at 2;600 and continue turn to 020 to intercept 08L LOC with an apology for conflict. PF intercepted GS inside NAROD (FAF 08L) due to ALT (Altitude) assignment by ATC of 2;600 feet. PF and PM had field in site and terrain in site during all phases. ATC reported 'helicopter' traffic at 3;500. Both PM and PF did not observe the traffic on TCAS at 3500 nor saw any helicopter traffic in the initial turn. Controller change during the descent from 4;000-3;000 feet. Weather was VMC daytime.The clearance received to fly the 270R outbound caused PM and PF to be distracted. PM could not get the radial to input in the FMC and therefore the PF flew raw data. This created additional threats which created additional distractions at the low ALT 2;600 with terrain all around. Having had to use RAW DATA the radio panel had mismatched frequencies and MCP had mismatched courses in the selectors which caused FD to give incorrect LOC info. PM was able to configure the MCP/radio panel and EFIS in time to capture LOC before crossing LOC. It caused the PM to be heads down instead of assisting PF in confirming the airport in sight for a visual backup. During debrief both pilots agreed that asking for a climb back to 3;000 may have helped with visual guidance to help with positional awareness. The following leg PM/PF practiced input of radials off VOR stations to create a less threatening environment for the 'next time.'

column121: Departing ZZZ1 for ZZZ2 I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and the CA (Captain) was the PF (Pilot Flying). We planned a low altitude flight due to the shortness of the leg. Some altitudes in the legs page were edited to allow the lower cruise altitude to be selected. The flaps 10 takeoff went as normal (LNAV/VNAV). The PF called for flaps 1 as near as I can recall. I believe this is the case as most if not all of our previous legs had been flaps 5 takeoffs. I was distracted with a radio call or frequency change and I moved the flaps to 1 and did not catch the error. Shortly after that; the FMC changed to the descent phase and the speed bug moved to the flaps 5 maneuver speed; and the A/T (Auto Throttle) mode went from N1 to FMC speed; which resulted in the flaps 5 maneuver speed being the A/T target. As; or just prior to this happening the PF called for flaps up. I moved the flap lever to the up position; and since we were no longer accelerating got a momentary stick shaker. The PF instinctively lowered the nose reducing the AOA (Angle Of Attack). I increased the speed in the MCP window to get the A/T to command acceleration. The remainder of the flight was normal.Suggest crews be alert for unusual mode reversions when using low altitudes for cruise. I would probably use non VNAV takeoff procedures in the future. The big lesson is not new; vigilance absolutely has to be maintained during the 'red' parts of the flight path. The PM job is challenging and can be intolerant of errors.

Between the FD turning and leveling off; it was at this point that I was focused on wanting the aircraft to continue straight on runway heading; and I flew through the 2;000 feet restriction; to my recollection by about 300 feet. The PM attempted to get some sort of instruction from ATC as to what they would like us to do; but struggled to get a word in on the radio. Finally they called and assigned us a vector. I turned the aircraft in trail of a SLC B752.  As I turned the aircraft further north so final turn wasn't so tight; the pilot called the airport in sight. PVU was advertising Visual Approach Runway 13. I cleared the aircraft for the Visual Approach. They turned towards the airport; I shipped them to the Tower approximately 10 miles out when I saw them turning towards the airport. Almost immediately the aircraft started turning further south towards a 8;900 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude descending out of 8000 feet. I called PVU and they said they were talking to him. I asked what they were doing and was advised the pilot stated they were making S turns or something. The aircraft descended to 5;100 feet 7 miles from the airport; elevation 4;497 feet.  At that point PVU called stating the pilot had lost the airport and was climbing to 9;000 feet. The pilot checked in with me heading 180 and climbing to 9;000 feet. I said roger. They then asked for vectors to an ILS and I stated I would when they were at Minimum Vectoring Altitudes. I vectored for the ILS with no further complications. I don't really have recommendations on my end. PVU after this incident continued to advertise Visual Approaches. My Supervisor did not want to fill out any paperwork on the incident; so they said nobody did anything wrong and to leave it at that. I felt like this should be reported somehow. The pilot was extremely low a long distance from the airport trying to scud run the Visual Approach. I knew visuals were iffy because when I descended the aircraft to 9;000 feet they were IMC; I turned them and descended them to 8;000 feet (also telling them to expect the ILS) and they called the airport. It's not surprising they were able to call the airport in sight at that point; the mountain sits below and often they can descend slightly and get the airport in sight. What's surprising is the pilot accepted the approach if clouds were that bad; that we didn't 'declare an emergency' for the aircraft when they lost the airport at 5;100 feet in an 8;900 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude MVA; and that the supervisor wouldn't at least want to follow up with the pilot. I truly don't know why we wouldn't want to look at this further.

I intervened by leveling off and we continued in a managed descent on profile for the remainder of the arrival.My estimation that we were high on the profile was inaccurate due to the fact that the airplane was light and capable of descending very quickly; I had not taken that into consideration. The pilot monitoring was heads down and I did not tell him I was changing the mode of descent from managed to open and explain why I was doing so. Had I done so; he would have caught it. This was my first day back to work after two months of leave. I had prepared to return by studying flows; call; procedures; etc. and had briefed the other pilot hoping to prevent errors from happening.Suggestions - Keep the other guy in the loop. Tell him when making a change especially if he is heads down. Always check the altitude selected when changing modes. Always focus on the next restriction.

column121: I wanted to take a few minutes to relate to you my personal experiences during the events that transpired.  We were at the tail end of a lengthy four day trip; with the usual holiday related challenges; weather; maintenance; crew-placarding; lengthy sit times; de-icing etc. On the third day of the trip; we were waiting in line for departure on [Runway] XXL at ZZZ; when the tower informed us that the operation was shut down for a 'deep-cleaning' at ZZZ1 Center.  Having personally experienced the same the same scenario last year when both the ZZZ2 Tower and ground were shut down for a COVID spread throughout their Tower; it didn't take long for us to figure out the reason for the closure.Like everyone one else in our situation; we opened up the FOM and began compliance with the notification processes for the passengers; the Flight Attendants; and ZZZ Ops. My First Officer (FO) and I immediately began working the 14 hour duty day issue; (FO A was my second FO during the course of the trip; and he had a less restrictive duty day constraint than I did).  After nearly two hours at the hold short line; we began the process of finding a gate; with the intent to avoid the prospective government fines levied for lengthy delays. It was the usual chaos; with ZZZ Ops being overwhelmed by this unforeseen event.  As we approach the two hour FOM deadline for locating a gate; we were assigned DXX via ACARS.  While taxiing to the gate; we made multiple attempts to get guidance from Ops; Ramp; Dispatch; etc.; to see what the intent was for the passengers; my crew; and the aircraft. We were unable to get any specific guidance. Following our arrival at the gate; an Agent opened the main door; and told us that the flight would be cancelled. As directed by the agent; the passengers disembarked with their bags. Since we had seen no changes to our crew schedule; nor had we received any kind of communication from crew tracking; we assumed that the agent was correct regarding the cancellation; and as such; we began reviewing our required duty time obligations. Absent any further guidance; we subsequently put the aircraft 'to bed;' and once again we attempted to contact crew tracking; (no luck there).  Rather than exit into the terminal; we elected to continue to wait on the aircraft.After 20 minutes or so; a new Agent came down the bridge; and asked me if we were ready to board the aircraft. Needless to say; I was a bit astonished.  I asked her what the plan was; and she said that we were going to resume the flight to ZZZ3; ASAP.  I reminded her that the airspace was still closed; and that we had not received any contact from either dispatch or tracking; regarding an updated release; and that we would need additional fuel; lavatory/water service; and a resupply of the delay rations that the Flight Attendants had used for the passengers during our time spent waiting on the taxiway. I also told her that both of us; along with two of the Flight Attendants had duty-time issues that we have to calculate and resolve before departure.  She promptly replied and asked me; 'Captain are you refusing to board the aircraft?'I immediately realized that this was the standard pass-the buck/assign the delay language; that some Agents use in an attempt to intimidate Pilots. I took several deep breaths; before I stated to her in no uncertain terms; that we would need to at least begin to address the aforementioned issues; before we would be comfortable boarding the aircraft again.  Her reply was; 'Captain; are you refusing to board the aircraft?'  I answered that until we get some of these issues resolved; yes.  What was clear to myself; my FO and the number one Flight Attendant; is that this was clearly an attempt at pilot-pushing. [In my opinion]; this Agent had one concern; and that was to make sure that these passengers would become someone else's problem; (namely ours).Long story short; and after significant efforts by all involved; we reconstituted the flight and determined that without further lengthy ground delays that we would likely arrive in ZZZ3 within our respective 14 hour duty day window. We then performed our usual checklists; flows; refueling; new clearance etc.After push-back; start and taxi instructions were received; I made my first mistake of the flight; and turned in the direct opposite direction of ground's instructions on the taxi clearance. It was at this point that I realized I was a lot more tired than I thought.  My FO and I discussed this; and we agreed that though we were both somewhat tired; it was safe to proceed; and that we should just take extra time and precautions going forward.Mistake number two on my part was that when ATC changed our departure STAR; we briefed it at the gate; had it up on our iPads; but I had failed to enter it in the MCDU. After wheels up; ATC gave us direct-to clearance to a fix that wasn't on the legs page. My FO quickly realized that I hadn't entered the new departure STAR; and he rapidly remedied it on the MCDU. I was mad at myself for making this series of unprecedented and inexplicable mistakes. Those mistakes continued as we descended on the type of complex STAR with a series of 'at or above' altitude constraints; that confounds the logic on some of the older 'Basic' airplanes.Needless to say; we landed safely in ZZZ3 later that evening. After block-in; I determined that I was within my duty legality; by 20 minutes or so. It had been a very long day.  We had departed ZZZ4 that morning before the sun had risen; and we had left the gate at ZZZ for the second time; well after the sun had set. In summary; I had made many embarrassing operational mistakes during the course of the last leg; beginning with my pre-flight; push back; all the way through the descent into ZZZ3.  The only explanation for my numerous mistakes was fatigue. In short; I will never; ever; again allow the 'system' to push to me beyond my own personal safety limits. I will take my First Officers counsel more seriously when it comes to considering just how tired we are.Additional factors include that when you consider the cumulative effects of four and five day trips on us; along with a 14 hour duty period; it can be well beyond the average pilot's limitations to safely operate.  And while I don't blame the agent personally; (like everyone else; she was just doing the job in the manner that she was trained); and like everyone else she's just under time pressure.  As time has gone by at our company; it has become clear to me; that the safety culture at the top of this airline; is in many respects; mostly honored and kept in place; by those who of us; who are at the pointy end of the spear.In retrospect; the main causal factor was fatigue due to a lengthy delay.Two suggestions.  The first is that [in my opinion]; we need to take into account the cumulative effect of a lengthy four and five day trip on pilot fatigue.  The other issue is Gate Agent conduct and verbiage regarding flight Ops as it regards to boarding the passengers.

column121: On route to the airport the First Officer's Multi Function display failed. We decided to continue destination airport because it was not required equipment. Then we were informed the weather at the airport was deteriorating unexpectedly. We completed all the required tasks and checklist before the we were cleared for the approach. On approach we realized that we were too high and our descent profile was going to be unacceptable for a stable approach. Around 11;000 ft. the Captain called for the Missed Approach. We executed the Missed Approach with no issues and cleaned up the aircraft and started climbing to the missed approach altitude. We were at the missed approach altitude and Captain called for the auto pilot on. During this time there was a bit of confusion and the right turn and swapping the navigation displays and setting the new course for the back course was slow to be executed. We turned to the heading too slow and never intercepted the back course. Once we figured out that we didn't intercept the back course we had the Course Deviation Indicator full-scale deflection. ATC gave us a new altitude and a new heading to start the restart the approach. We got vectored around to the Initial Approach Fix to restart the approach and completed the second approach stabilized without any issues. Failure to comply with the approach profile and the missed approach profile.
column123: I neglected to call for the First Officer to start our descent. The First Officer noticed my mistake; but by this time we were very high. My initial reaction was to deploy the boards and steepen the descent in an attempt to get back on profile; however I quickly realized it wasn't going to work and we were unstabilized. I called for a missed approach when we were at roughly 11;000 ft.  Because we went missed early; I called for the autopilot on once we reached the published missed approach altitude of 14;200 ft. This caused confusion as to who should complete the tasks of spinning the heading knob to the 300 heading; swapping the RTU's; and setting the course to 303. I decided to have the First Officer complete these to stay as on-profile as possible. The first two tasks; the 300 heading and swapping the RTU's; were completed however the task of setting the 303 course was not. This led to ATC querying us about our progress on the missed approach and soon after issuing an altitude alert with an instruction to climb to 15;000 ft. By the time we figured out our mistake we were showing full-scale deflection on the Course Deviation Indicator. In addition to not setting the course; I made the mistake of accelerating to 200 kts. and calling climb sequence once level at 14;200 ft. instead of waiting until outbound per the profile. I should also add that the First Officer MFD failed enroute and this most likely caused a reduction in situational awareness throughout the rest of the flight. Failure to comply with the LOC/DME 15 approach profile; especially the missed approach segment.

column121: I was using a safety pilot and view limiting device to log instrument approaches to regain IFR currency. I was on climbout/missed approach from a low approach to a practice ILS X at ZZZ. I was told to by the Tower to 'proceed on course' after having previously told the Approach Controller I was headed next to ZZZ1 for the next approach. I was switched to ZZZ Approach at about 1;800 feet MSL on climbout and reported 1;900 feet for 3;000 feet direct ZZZ1. I was told 'Radar contact' and nothing else specifically.On climbout I was trying to set up my Garmin 430W for the next approach; and get a new program on the iPad (Foreflight vs. Garmim pilot I had previously used) to post the selected approach for ZZZ1 on the map. I had trouble with my glasses fogging up due to wearing a COVID mask in the plane and was experiencing updrafts/turbulence. The time to 3;000 feet was shorter than expected and due to the above distractions; I did not notice I was passing through 3;000 feet until I hit 3;250 feet at which point I reduced power and pushed the nose down. I was back to 3;000 feet within 15 seconds. I heard nothing from ATC regarding this; probably due to being VFR and no altitude restriction issued by ATC. I was able to verify all audio and events/altitudes due to a GoPro running to capture the flight.While I was VFR and there was no traffic nearby; if this was IFR; I would have had the same challenges and it would most likely been an altitude bust. There needs to be the same discipline applied to 'practice' instrument work as there is during the real thing in IMC; or the bad habits and distractions you allow during practice will seep into operations in general. I should have left the gizmo programming for level flight and popped the glasses off if the mask induced fogging was a distraction. I should have made the instrument scan primary rather than assuming I had more time than I actually had to program while getting to 3;000 feet.

Our area was not staffed properly; so I had been on position for about 2:40 when the event occurred; and was working my third different radar scope of the session.  I had been moved twice due to partially certified controllers kicking me out of my previous position.  I had also just returned from XX days off.The sector next to me (XY) was very busy; and part of my attention was diverted to that scope because there was inadequate staffing to provide them a tracker or D-side.  I know this is not something I should do; but the controller at XY seemed over loaded.I took hand offs on Aircraft X and Aircraft Y at about the same time.  I saw the traffic immediately; and turned Aircraft X to a 270 heading; and issued Aircraft Y 20 degrees left.  I've been certified at ZZZ1 radar for over X years; and have seen this same scenario thousands of times in my career.  I continued doing other things; then looked back on the situation and saw for some reason my 20 degree turn was not going to be enough.  I am not sure if Aircraft Y actually turned 20 degrees; or maybe wind was a factor.  I issued a 10 degree left turn to Aircraft X; confident that this would resolve the issue.  Upon checking back a minute or so later; I saw that this was not going to be the case.  I issued another 20 degree left turn to Aircraft Y and instructed them to expedite the climb. column121: Aircraft X was on ILS approach to Runway 4 at GSP when a VFR aircraft inbound to GMU went across final under Aircraft X. Traffic was called. GMU [Tower] was called. Aircraft X was below the clouds and stated he would execute missed approach if there was a RA. The pilot seemed to stay above glide slope to avoid the RA. Both aircraft eventually got each other in sight and Aircraft X landed.This is a known safety problem. The closest proximity of 2 aircraft in this situation is zero lateral and less than 100 feet vertical if the GSP arrival is on the glideslope and the VFR is in the GMU Delta airspace. However; it should not be taken for granted that aircraft on instrument and visual approaches will be at or above glideslope altitude. Since the VFR is under the GSP arrival; which is usually a jet; there are also wake turbulence issues.The Charlie and Delta airspace design is flawed. The FAA is either unwilling or unable to redesign the airspace to provide for the safety of the flying public.From my experience; the VFR aircraft involved are always inbound to GMU from SC72 (Chandelle). It is probably less than half a dozen aircraft that occasionally do this. When they depart GMU; they are instructed to fly over VPLOW when GSP Runway 4 is in use. If they were instructed to fly over VPLOW when inbound to GMU; the problem would be resolved. GMU Tower can instruct aircraft to remain outside the Delta and instruct aircraft where to enter the Delta; so there is no reason this solution would not work. It could be agreed to; briefed and implemented in 24 hours.This situation develops quickly and there are no guarantees that the controllers will see it before the RA or collision alert. When it is seen; or when the alarms go off; what does FAA management want the controllers to do?  Should we be breaking off the approach as a preventive measure?

column121: Aircraft X departed Runway 30 on an assigned 270 heading. At that moment; a controller at PCT; I think Departure Control contacted me. My initial thought was that Aircraft X had misunderstood my assigned heading and had not switched to Departure Control and was still on my frequency. While the controller was speaking to me other aircraft were talking on the frequency. The cross-talk prevented me from clearly understanding the information that was being relayed in the coordination. I heard the controller say climb the aircraft to 3;000 ft.; and turn him to the west immediately.Because I did not clearly hear the call sign of the aircraft he was referencing my mind jumped to Aircraft X as the aircraft needing the instructions. Midway through issuing the traffic alerts I recognized that Aircraft X was descending and turning to join final for Runway 1L. In that instance I recognized what Departure Control was trying to coordinate and I sent Flight Number X around and vectored him away from Aircraft X and issued a traffic alert.Aircraft X checked onto my frequency on a mile final. I cleared him to land. Immediately after clearing him to land; the ASDE-X alerted with a taxiway proximity alert. It appeared to me that Aircraft X was correcting back toward Runway 1L. I asked the pilot if they requested priority handling. The pilot said no. The aircraft appeared aligned with the runway and the pilot confirmed they were; but because he was not a priority. I sent the plane around as required by the 7110.65. Coordination would have been easier and clearer had the radar data tag scratchpad entry for Aircraft X been changed to '01L' which would have indicated that he was inbound to land. The scratchpad showed the SID he filed; which contributed to my initial thinking that he was off course and not a priority. Additionally; had Departure Control requested priority handling in the coordination; I believe I would have immediately keyed onto the fact that Aircraft X was returning.The Airport Surface Detection Equipment (ASDE-X) ASDE Taxiway Arrival Prediction Software (ATAP) has had five alerts since its implementation on Date. In every case; the aircraft have been properly aligned with the runway and the alerts have been the result of poorly designed taxiway capture zones. The ATAP enhancement should be temporarily disabled and a full review of the ATAP system should occur.

As we intercepted the course the autopilot flew past the localizer at close to half scale deflection; as it would not correct course timely. We also had to descend and slow down to configure for final approach within 3 miles of final approach fix. As the autopilot was correcting for that we set 3;000 ft for the missed approach altitude. A CAS MISCOMP status message appeared and the altitude alerter came on would not stop ringing. When we changed navigation source to green needles; the localizer would not capture with the autopilot; therefore the glide slope would also not capture. During the navigation source change; my flight director on the first officer's side became erratic and I lost the localizer transmission. We decided to execute a missed approach due to being unstable along with the flight instrument errors. Tower assigned us a heading and altitude and we reconfigured the aircraft for the go around all while the altitude alerter was blaring. During straight and level flight; we decided to reassign the FCP to heading and altitude. Once established; we turned the autopilot on and all instruments worked correctly. The altitude alert ringer was still buzzing so we decided to silence using Data Control Unit (DCU) audio buttons to declutter the situation. After completing proper checklists; we decided to continue on with another ILS XXR and executed approach and landing normally. After shutdown the altitude alerter still continued to ring until AC power was switched from the APU GEN to EXT AC. We wrote up the problem and notified maintenance.ATC giving us tight vectors with a tailwind on base along with our equipment malfunctions. The altitude alerter sounding loudly along our flight directors being erratic caused task saturation to the captain who was PF. As PM I helped the captain de clutter the situation and to reminded him to just fly the airplane which he did well as we tracked the localizer and conducted the go around. Once we silenced the altitude alerter it became much easier to fly the aircraft and we were able to conduct the next approach successfully.Possibly asking for a slower intercept speed or lower from ATC. The equipment malfunctions lead to the approach to become unstable and that's why we conducted a go around. I could have possibly contacted tower a few seconds earlier to ask for a vector and altitude but it was quite difficult with the task saturation being as high as it was; especially with the altitude alerter loudly sounding. Overall it was a great lesson in always being able to maintain control and fly the aircraft regardless of the state of automation it is in which I thought we did a great job of despite the system malfunctions during a high work load environment.
