column121: Descending via the NIIXX 2 arrival for the ILS Runway 35R in CAVOK conditions. Around the BSTON Intersection we were given a westerly to northwesterly radar vector and cleared to descend and maintain 10;000. As we got closer to the final approach course (somewhere between DEANE and DRUMM) we were cleared to descend and maintain 8;000 and cleared direct to the FRONZ Intersection (FAF for the ILS). The Controller asked if we had 35R in sight; after a pause; we had the runway in sight and advised ATC. We were then cleared for the visual approach to 35R. The FAF altitude at FRONZ is 7;000 so that is what we set in the MCP while descending through approximately 8;800 in FLCH. We had just gotten the '2;500' call from the Radio Altimeter and made our call outs. As we descended through 8;000 I noticed the Radio Altitude around 1;800 and descending. A quick look at JeppFD PRO showed our aircraft position just south and east of the DRUMM Intersection. I called out the altitude and the fact that we need to go back up to 8;000 (our last cleared altitude prior to the approach clearance) until we are north of DRUMM. I reset the MCP to 8;000 and verbalized that we need to climb back up. The Captain selected a V/S climb back to 8;000. We joined the approach course and followed the G/S and landed without incident.ATC never mentioned anything to us about violating airspace or going below the DEN Class B. Though it is nice to get directs; etc. However; I believe the direct to FRONZ clearance; if not really familiar with the DEN Class B; can set crews up to possibly violate airspace and even lead to an unstable approach.Once parked at the gate with all checklists complete; we debriefed and there certainly was some confusion as to exactly where we were when we descended below 8;000. We had a jump seat observer who thought we might have been a little low as he has a lot of General Aviation experience in the DEN area.

column121: Description of Event: The aircraft with PIC as above and one passenger was returning to ZZZ from a 1-hour cross-country flight that originated at ZZZ1. The flight was uneventful in VFR weather; with altitude from 2;000 feet to 1;600 feet after takeoff and climbout until approach. Flight path was as depicted in the charted course; following VFR altitude restrictions as required within ZZZ2 Mode C airspace; and with ADS-B Out active on 1200 a required. Visibility was observed to be 10+ miles with a solid cloud cover (overcast) at 9;000-12;000 feet. Winds were variable 6-9 knots at approximately 230-260 degrees from surface to flight altitude. Within 10 nm on the approach to ZZZ on a vector of 220; while monitoring ZZZ voice radio on 123.00; little traffic within the airport operations area was observed or noted on the radio. At approximately 8 nm from ZZZ; an inbound aircraft was announced on my ForeFlight display through the ADS-B In signal at my 7 o'clock; 400 feet below and overtaking. That Cessna 152 pilot announced his intention for a straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX. Communicated directly with that PIC and told him that we would slow down to distance behind him on my own straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX; since he already had a 25+ mph speed advantage. Within 2 minutes; the Cessna 152 had passed us by on our left side and descended ahead of us to line up for Runway XX. In the process; I lost visual contact with that aircraft; and since there was no other traffic in the area; and ForeFlight did not show a blip for its position; I decided to perform a slight S-turn to the left to further delay our landing until the 152 announced he was clear of Runway XX. At approximately 4 nm from the threshold; with our speed down to 62 mph (58 mph Ground Speed); the Cessna 152 PIC announced 'clear of Runway  XX ZZZ'; after which I immediately announced a straight-in approach for Runway XX ZZZ and began to adjust our speed and trim to line up with the two VASI lights on the glide path. At approximately 2 nm; we were high (two white lights) but gradually settled to a nominal (white/red) glide slope on the final approach. We completed visual and verbal cockpit checks and I glanced outboard at the right Flaperon position (there being no flap setting indicator in this CH750 STOL; and no stall warning annunciation); but did not notice anything incorrect; even though I had earlier made a mental note that we would be making a flaps-up; standard landing instead of the full-flaps; STOL landings I usually make. We settled slightly low of nominal (two red lights) as we approached the threshold and at that moment; I made a mental 'flip' or attitude adjustment that we were about to land STOL; and I decreased power for a short-field landing. Our sink rate increased; but mentally; I still had confidence that the STOL nose-up attitude was safe; and did not add power but instead retarded it to idle as we crossed the threshold of Runway XX. Without flaps; our stall speed was 48 mph instead of 42 mph; and we stalled out at approximately 12' above the numbers and fell in a slightly nose-high attitude until impacting on the main and then nose gear. The aircraft bounced up and then impacted slightly nose-down; collapsing the nose strut; blowing out the nose tire; and stopping the engine as the fiberglass prop blades impacted and flexibly shattered.We immediately checked for fuel leaks even though the aircraft came to rest tail-high. I switched off the ignition and removed the key; exited the cockpit; checked again for fuel leaks (none); then shut down the avionics manually with the master switch; and turned the Fuel Selector valve to OFF. After ascertaining that the aircraft was not an immediate hazard and that both Pilot and Passenger were able to move about without difficulty; we called other airport residents; and cleared the CH750 from Runway XX.Conclusion: In summation; distracted flying due to traffic avoidance caused energy mismanagement resulting in a stall upon landing flare with flaps retracted and subsequent nose gear collapse without injuries.

column121: I was providing instruction on new avionics for a client in Aircraft X. An IFR flight plan was filed by my client on his certificate. I briefed prior to engine start that he was PIC and that I was there to provide insight on the use of his new GTN 750. He had flown previously with this equipment; based on what he had told me. This was our first flight together in his aircraft.Prior to taxi; I reviewed with him how to load and activate approaches in his new GTN 750. He seemed familiar with its use and only asked a couple questions prior to departure. His knowledge of the features was adequate when I queried him on the unit.After takeoff from ZZZ Runway XXR; we were given a left turn to a heading of 070 and a climb to 3;000 feet. He engaged the autopilot at about 1;000 feet AGL. My client requested from ZZZ Approach the RNAV Y XXR but asked for a non-standard transition. He stated that he wanted the RNAV Y XXR to ZZZ 'via the ZZZZZ transition.' This is not a published transition and not what we briefed prior to departure. We had briefed previously that he would ask for vectors for the approach and he would repeat that same approach three times to increase familiarity with the equipment and its use in the approach environment. A short time later; we were given the instruction to climb to 3;000 feet and after that; to 'turn left direct ZZZZZ.' The autopilot began turning the aircraft to the right; presumably because he had switched from HDG mode to NAV mode without my knowledge. ATC queried and he once again read back the left turn. By the time I caught the erroneous turn direction and autopilot setting; the aircraft was well into the right turn. ATC then requested that we continue the right turn 'since we were already turning right and I have to keep you away from other traffic.'My client did as instructed and I queried ATC to confirm that we would overfly the ZZZZZ waypoint; then proceed outbound for the full approach. I apologized for the error on that same radio call. ATC responded in the affirmative; then cleared us for the approach. No further communication about the incorrect turn direction was made and the rest of the flight proceeded without incident.My client and I debriefed this issue and shared the lessons we learned. We both looked at this with an eye toward learning and future improvement.First; I reminded him of the importance of flying what we brief and that we will commit to always do so in the future. Second; as his flight instructor; it was my responsibility to catch the turn error and take control -- an effort I began but could not finish before ATC requested that he continue the right turn. Third; reliance on the autopilot worked against us and I suspect he switched from HDG to NAV mode without my noticing; initiating the right turn direct to ZZZZZ. Finally; business has been slow due to COVID and I have not been instructing as much as I normally would. I feel this last point is perhaps the most important one. As the pandemic has continued for nearly a year now; its effect on skills as pilots and flight instructors is being felt industry-wide.

column121: This narrative highlights two incorrect published crossing altitudes on two different arrivals that can lead to altitude deviations and aircraft overspeeds. The first is the PASLY 4 (10-2C) arrival to BNA at GROAT intersection. The crossing is depicted to cross GROAT at or below FL 230. It is always 1000 out of 1000 times given to cross GROAT at FL 220 usually by Memphis Center and has been for at least five years. Sometimes this occurs very late. This can lead to a situation where the aircraft was on the path; is now high; and the aircraft then pitches down at the last minute to meet the unpublished altitude of 22;000 ft. This pitchdown can lead to an overspeed and a situation that still does not meet the crossing. The second instance is on the ENDEE 6 Arrival into MDW (10-2). The fix in particular is KAMBL and the published crossing is between FL 270-FL 240. The unpublished crossing that is given; very late; is to cross KAMBL at 24;000 ft. Now the aircraft is in the same situation as the PASLY 4 Arrival; only you may have a 100 plus kt. tailwind to deal with as well. Both these situations persist but are preventable by simply changing the published altitude. Finally; there are several Pilots who are rusty from not flying; due to low utilization; whose situational awareness and lack of currency make this situation even more grave. Please fix these easy to remedy issues and trap the known errors. Thank you. We did not have a deviation. I am only reporting to highlight these issues.

column121: We were on the ILS 09R at PHL approximately 15 DME when the Localizer exhibited erratic deviations on both the Captain and First Officers  Primary Flight Displays. The Flight Director and Auto Pilot was engaged and attempted to 'chase' the course which started to worsen the situation. ATC advised us that we appeared to be about a mile south of the localizer course; slightly less than 1/2 dot deflection at this point. The First Officer disengaged the autopilot and hand-flew the approach with no further issue. The deviation appeared to subside as we got closer to the field and we were within stable approach parameters from the Final Approach Fix until touchdown. Also; the NAVAID had been positively tuned/identified per company SOP prior to commencing the approach. Course deviation on the HSI followed by ATC advising us that we were right of course. Unreliable Localizer signal at PHL which is apparently a known issue.The First Officer disconnected the autopilot and hand flew. I notified maintenance and was told by multiple maintenance personnel both on the phone and in person at the aircraft that this was a known issue with runway 09R; it happens all the time; and that there's a NOTAM in effect regarding the issue. I searched all of the NOTAMs  and could not find anything remotely related to unreliable LOC/ILS on 09R. I do not believe that the FAA would allow a malfunctioning NAVAID to remain in service and do not think there is any merit in the maintenance department's claim that this is a known problem that we should just accept and learn to deal with. However; if there is a known problem with this or any other NAVAID that necessitates a procedure change; then the company should disseminate that information to the pilot group with an FIL; etc.

column121: While on approach to ZZZ in day VMC conditions; crew was instructed to fly direct 'ZZZZZ' - the FAF for ILS XX - for a visual approach to [Runway] XX. The crew had been left high by both Center and Approach; but was able to reach the 5;000 ft. and slow prior to intercept. The PIC/PF (Pilot Flying) briefed the SIC/PM (Pilot Monitoring) on speed/energy management and airspeed 'windows' prior to the approach. After reporting runway in sight and receiving the approach clearance; the PF initiated descent to 4;500 ft. (the FAF altitude) and began to lessen the intercept angle; and PM prompted gear down and flaps 22. Aircraft still slightly overshot the localizer but was able to capture both LOC and GS which happened simultaneously. 4;500 ft. is within 1;300 ft. AGL of field elevation; and due to the short distance both vertically to the runway and laterally (just outside 4 miles); the PM/PIC anticipated an unstable approach and called a go around. The PF pressed the TOGA (Takeoff Go-Around); disconnected the autopilot; and called 'check thrust flaps nine' and the PM set flaps 9 and checked the thrust to discover the PF had not yet increased thrust to detents. Concurrently with the 'check thrust flaps 9 actions'; and 'Sink Rate' EGPWS warning occurred; and momentary hesitation by PF prompted PM/PIC to take control and initiate the immediate action in response to the 'sink rate' AURAL as required for the EGPWS escape; with a 'Pull Up' Aural warning occurring concurrently with the initiation of the EGPWS escape procedure. (At the time of initiation the EGPWS escape; PIC noted an 1;800 fpm descent rate). Upon reaching a safe altitude; the aircraft configuration was cleaned up in line as normal; and flight continued back for ILS without further incident. One error was made during EGPWS escape; which was PIC only increasing thrust to detents and not to max. Upon completion of the flight; crew debriefed on a number of key items. These included energy management and the approach profile in the AOM; go around procedure and ensuring power is set concurrently with pitch and callout when conducting a missed; and the EGPWS escape maneuver.Crews should act very early to mitigate unstable approach situations; including in a situation like this requesting a lower altitude earlier and a vector out to the IAF in lieu of the FAF; this can alleviate the chances of an unstable approach long before the issue manifests. Missed approaches should be initiated immediately upon identification of an unstable approach. In the event of a missed approach; crews should ensure the action is taken decisively including the increase of power; and both pilots should remain involved in the process. Should a GPWS warning be received; decisive; immediate action should be taken - as per the AOM - superseding normal missed approach actions due to the time critical nature of high vertical speed close to the ground. Captains especially should keep a close eye on FOs conducting operations at outstations - in this situation; having approach offer a better vector to join or taking an actual ILS clearance may have prevented the situation from manifesting at all.

column121: Upon departing ZZZ early in the morning; both the PF and PNF flight directors failed shortly after takeoff; prompting the PNF to quickly reference the QRH after several attempts to rectify the situation. After the completion of checklists; during the climb out and initial cruise; it was discovered that the FMC had also frozen up; not allowing any keypad inputs for route modifications. Shortly after leveling off at our cruise altitude; the PNF continued to troubleshoot the problem and was eventually successful at restoring both flight directors and FMC's back to normal. Meanwhile; during descent into ZZZ1; ARTCC advised us of a crossing restriction that was not complied with. We immediately stopped our descent and apologized. ARTCC then handed us off to ZZZ1 approach; after which; the flight continued on without further incident. It is suspected that the electronic malfunction of both the flight directors and FMC's; may have deleted or affected the altitude crossing restrictions; or; ARTCC may have linguistically confused the pronunciation of ZZZZZ with the ZZZZZ1 arrival into ZZZ1; as our flight plan indicated. Per SOP (Standard Operating Procedure); maintenance was notified of the situation but unable to determine cause or reproduce the fault.As for the electronic equipment malfunction; both the PF and the PNF became aware of the flight director failures shortly after takeoff when trying to engage VNAV. The FMC was determined to have failed during climb out. As for the altitude deviation; this issue was brought to our attention by ARTCC after crossing the fix below the published crossing altitude.The cause of the electrical/ electronic failure involving the flight directors and FMC's was undetermined by maintenance and could not be reproduced. The failure to comply with altitude crossing restrictions at a fix; may have been due to ARTCC assuming we were given the ZZZZZ1 arrival instead of the ZZZZZ arrival; which was listed on our flight release and selected in our FMC. My reaction was calm but assertive in continuing to fly the aircraft as the PNF; troubleshot the problem.As for the electronic equipment malfunctions; these failures are unpredictable. As for the crossing restriction compliance; our flight planning documents indicate that the correct arrival procedure was selected in the FMC but ARTCC thought different. In the future; I will be a little bit more willing to question; and/ or; verify an ATC challenge rather than assume their always right!

column121: Arriving into ZZZ the altimeter setting was showing 0996 mb; so during our arrival brief we covered the VNAV limitation for altimeters lower than 29.70/1006 and put special emphasis on using FLCH (Flight Level Change) when transitioning. Transition level was FL070. ATC began descending us in small steps; they gave us a descend to FL070 but when we were passing FL080 they gave us a descend to 6;000 ft. then further lower to 5;000 ft.; during those step downs I missed switching the altimeter setting to the local 0996mb. Then when we leveled at 5;000 ft. ATC verified the altimeter setting stating that we were 400 ft. lower than we should have. I immediately realized my mistake; set the correct altimeter setting; took corrective action and called for the approach checklist. Since the airplane wasn't reacting as fast as I wanted; I disconnected the auto pilot; corrected the altitude and continued manual flying all the way until we landed. There is no excuse for missing an altimeter setting during transition. There were many factors/distractions that took place for this to happen and they all came pretty close together: long duty day; our bells to the flight attendants; re-route to a point not in our route; use of wing and Engine anti-ice; heavy rain during descent so continuous ignition was set; multiple small step downs from ATC; VNAV limitation; all of them occurring often simultaneously. We; as crew; came together and managed all threats that were thrown at us as best we could to bring the airplane safely to the ground.I will; from now on; better prioritize on the stuff that I delegate and ask my crew to keep an eye on me and remind me of things that could make us incur a deviation like this one. Even though we all had our hands full; I should have asked someone for some sort of reminder about the transition level.
column123: At the conclusion of a long duty day and the second flight leg of the day; I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) en-route. This was my second leg as PM (6th leg as flight crew) in an international theater in nearly 3 years. Prior to descent and during the approach briefing as well as once the relief pilots entered the cockpit; we discussed the lower altimeter setting of 0996mb and the associated procedure per Company limitations from not using VNAV when transitioning from QNH (Height Above Sea Level) to QNE or QNE to QNH when below 1006mb. We felt very prepared for the arrival and descent into ZZZ. The transition altitude of 7;000 ft. was also briefed however as we proceeded; we encountered winter weather requiring extra vigilance (icing conditions and heavy precipitation). ATC descended us in multiple small increments below 10;000 ft. but the last prior to this event was a descent to 5;000 ft. With the added attention to the weather and ensuring proper use of FLCH instead of VNAV during what should have been the transition; both the pilot flying; and the pilot monitoring did not switch the altimeters at the proper time to the local setting of 0996mb. Upon level-off at 5;000 ft.; ATC came over the radio to verify local altimeter of 996mb and stating the observation of being 400 ft. low. I quickly realized my altimeter was incorrect and took corrective action and confirmed the pilot flying did so as well both with the altimeter and the flight path. One of the observer pilots also confirmed and stated the MSA for situational awareness. The pilot flying disconnected the auto pilot and continued to intercept the localizer path while returning to the cleared altitude. The aircraft was hand flown to landing with no further incident.Multiple links in the chain led up to this event and while we thought we had sufficiently briefed the several unique environments (low altimeter/Company limitation; winter weather) we also were distracted by being vectored to a point not on an arrival or the approach expected. It only goes to show that even with the best preparation and briefing that events can change and compound quickly and while attention to detail is most crucial during all phases of flight; extra vigilance is needed for approach and arrival; especially in areas that have not been flown to in recent months or years. Ultimately; the crew worked together to safely return the aircraft to the desired state and ensured a lesson learned for the future when operating in areas with differing transition altitudes.

column121: At 10;000 ft. cleared direct ZZZZZ and cleared visual RWY XXL ZZZ. We both agreed 8;000 ft. was a safe altitude due to terrain then 7;000 ft. after clearing the hills. Flying pilot; FO (First Officer); set 8;000 ft. then 7;000 ft. in the altitude window. It seemed we were high since we delayed the descent so we were trying to get down. I did not notice the altitude was set to 6;000 ft. Approaching ZZZZZ I realized we were low and told the FO to stop the descent. We climbed slightly and joined the Glideslope to continue the approach. We did not get any terrain warnings but it was concerning that we descended lower than anticipated at night into a high altitude airport.The FO was low time in the airplane and had just came back from a 5 year absence. I did not realize he was behind a bit on the automation. While I was trying to figure out what he was doing I lost situational awareness even though we had discussed safe altitudes. It was also the third leg we had flown that day so we were both tired.I was overly depending on the automation to help reduce the work load for both of us. The automation will only help if it is programed correctly so a person has to be very careful to cross check all available information. From now on I think it is best to request an instrument approach when it's dark going into airports you're not 100 percent familiar with. From now on I will at the very least request to join the visual further out on the instrument approach course in order to get more stabilized.

The Tower saw us correcting during the call however and noted disregard. As we were able to re established on glide path and were stable before 500 ft. we continued the approach to land. column123: ILS [Runway] 16R into Seattle; visual conditions; LOC and GS captured with autopilot engaged. After aircraft configuration complete I felt like we were low. ATC was informing us about low altitude alert; then immediately said disregard. I regained glide-slope utilizing PAPI.Not sure why the GS disconnected; if it was something we did wrong or if it was a fluke or something to do with the system. I talked to the Captain taking the airplane about the event and suggested to use the ILS. Lesson learned; at all times monitor glide path and lat/vertical modes. The transition from GS to pitch hold was very subtle.

column121: Accelerated to 250 knots while climbing on the TECKY3 departure out of San Jose while in the Class C airspace but believe we went below the Class B shelf. First Officer was Pilot Flying and as Pilot Monitoring I hesitated momentarily before telling the First Officer to slow down while I checked our position in Jeppesen charts. As we were slowing back to 200 knots we entered the Class B airspace from below. No comments from ATC and continued on our way. Began accelerating to 250 knots above 2500 feet per setting in FMS Departure Limit page.  We had discussed the SID and the propensity for aircrews to encounter non-normal issues during our preflight threats briefing. We had also discussed maintaining 200 knots during climbs away from intended course to destination on a flight leg earlier that day. I recall seeing the 200 knots below Class B note. The First Officer briefed the FMS Departure Limit page set at 2500 feet and I missed the chance to change it.  I thought from previous experience we would remain outside of the Class B shelf. I can only surmise this was a momentary lapse in the preflight setup. Perhaps I got distracted by some Captain's duty during briefing. The First Officer said that seeing the 230 knots restriction in the SID led him to believe 200 knots wasn't a necessary restriction.  That's a reasonable assumption and acceleration to 250 knots isn't prohibited if remaining outside Class B shelf.  We debriefed the event thoroughly and had a chance to redo the departure the next day with proper speed settings.

column121: Enroute ZZZ-San Salvador at FL390 we were able to ascertain through ATC Control that Runway 25 was in use and that we could expect to proceed via CAT VOR and execute the ILS Y 25. The FO (First Officer) was the Pilot Flying and thoroughly briefed the approach and his expectations for altitudes; automation modes and aircraft configuration throughout the approach. We were turned over to San Salvador Approach approximately 70 miles from the airport descending to FL200. San Salvador Approach cleared us direct CAT VOR; cross VOR above 5;000 [ft.] cleared ILS Y Runway 25. Both pilots confirmed clearance; altitudes and automation as we proceeded. As we neared CAT we were around 8;000 [ft.] at 240 kts.; still on the VNAV path. Although the FMC appeared to like the profile we both agreed it was time to slow down to meet the briefed approach profile. The FO selected vertical speed and dialed the speed back in the MCP window. With the selected vertical speed we weren't slowing down so I recommended Level Change. We slowed; configured and continued the approach passing CAT VOR. I set 2;500 [ft.] in the altitude window to fly outbound from the VOR as we completed the landing checklist. Once crossing the fix at [8.0 nm] we turned inbound via LNAV and set the FAF crossing altitude of 1;600 [ft.]; approach mode selected. We were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight on my side of the aircraft. As we turned towards the airport and descended I noticed we seemed low since we were more than 8 miles away and below the glide path. I looked back at the FMC and noticed fix [7.8 nm] with a crossing altitude of 2;500 [ft]. Shortly afterwards ATC asked what our altitude was and I replied 1;600 [ft.]. At that point both the FO and I realized we had missed [7.8 nm] on the procedure and should have crossed it at 2;500 [ft.]. [7.8 nm] is not clearly depicted on the approach plate with a crossing altitude nor is there an altitude depicted for the turn inbound. Also; we flew the procedure properly if the automation was in VNAV; but it wasn't. Although it was nighttime we were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight throughout the procedure. No GPWS cautions. At no time did I feel the procedure unsafe.
column123: I was the PF.  CENAMER approach cleared us to descend out of FL390 to FL 200.  We were expecting the ILSY Rwy 25.  We briefed the approach thoroughly and I explained I would stay in VNAV until lined up on final approach where I would select APP for the ILS.   Well above FL200; we were handed off to ElSal approach.  They told us to proceed to CAT VOR and cleared us for a full approach ILS Y Rwy 25 approach with procedure turn.  HOWEVER; we were high before arriving at CAT so I selected to use vertical speed and open the speed window to control speed.  The CAPT suggested I use LVL CHG instead since it would do a better job getting down and controlling speed.  I did so; while  flaps and gear helped slow us.  I was still well above 3500'; over the VOR beginning the procedure turn outbound to D8.0.  Still in LVL CHG; We were able to fully configure and be on the VNAV PATH at 2500' at D8.0.  We completed the LANDING CHECKLIST.  At this point we had the airport in sight and never lost contact the whole time.  We were both using TERR MODE for obstacle clearance.  After passing D8.0 I asked the CAPT to select the next lower altitude of 1600' as depicted on the approach chart; and he did so.  In my haste to get at the correct altitude; slow down and  configure for landing; I did not  realize I had not reselected VNAV.  The autopilot descended us to 1600' as we turned toward final.  We crossed D7.8 at 1600' vice 2500'..  There was no GPWS warning and we had the airport in sight the whole time.  On final approach I selected APP and we noticed we looked low and at the same time; the control tower queried us about our altitude.  That was when we noticed our error but were already capturing the glideslope at that time.  We continued the approach; landed safely and taxied to our gate without further incident.

column121: While flying a cross-country; I encountered strong mountain-wave action; making altitude difficult to hold. I asked for and received a 'block altitude'. The conditions were VMC all the way to the surface. The aircraft was on autopilot with altitude hold engaged. The autopilot called for 'trim up;' as the aircraft was descending I added power. I asked the other pilot to give it nose-up trim as he had done several times before. (The aircraft only has manual trim.) Suddenly; the aircraft nosed over. I immediately hit the autopilot disconnect button and pulled the circuit breaker. I noticed that the aircraft was very nose-heavy and I struggled to keep it from pitching down further. I called for more nose-up trim; but the problem got worse and I could barely slow the pitch-over even by pulling with both hands.During our descent; the controller queried us about our rapid descent. Given that I was extremely busy; I advised ATC. Finally; I told the other pilot to help me pull the nose up; whereupon the aircraft responded and I began adding nose-up trim and climbing back to altitude. We arrested the descent and leveled off and then I began the climb back to cruise altitude.I checked the aircraft for any control difficulties and determined that there were none; I advised ATC that I was climbing back to cruise altitude. Upon discussion with the other pilot; we determined that instead of adding nose-up trim; he was inadvertently adding nose-down. Because the autopilot had been engaged; we did not notice the wrong direction trim. We continued to our destination to get clear of the AIRMET for turbulence. Upon landing; an A&P inspected the aircraft and found no evidence of over-stressing the aircraft.

column121: On the ZZZZZ6 we were told to level at 7;000 feet for traffic. This was my 3rd trip on IOE and was practicing hand flying the departure. It was turbulent and we were in and out of IMC. Since we were extremely light due to light loads we were climbing at an extremely fast vertical speed. Passing through 6;000 I announced that I was going to use TCS to reduce the rate of climb to about 1;000 since there was traffic above and I wanted to avoid a RA. I corrected the VS to about 1;000 ft/min. I was not quick enough to override and reduce the autothrottles to avoid increasing airspeed. The airspeed quickly and momentarily increased to 270 knots as we were leveling at 7;000 feet. I reduced the autothrottles too late and while reducing them altitude deviated by 140 feet high. Both deviations were short and immediately corrected. Nothing was mentioned by ATC. We were later given higher once the traffic passed. The combination of hand flying in turbulent conditions in IMC and leveling at a low altitude with light loads was a recipe for distraction and error to occur. I could have eliminated some of these variables by engaging autopilot earlier or reducing autothrottles quicker. The CA and I debriefed and talked through what led to the event and how to prevent it in the future.I learned that when possible reduce extra variables that could lead to an error. I am new to flying with the company and new procedures; was hand flying in turbulent conditions and IMC; light loads with good performance; and was given a low level off. That is a lot of variables at once and the ones that I could control are the earlier use of automation to help alleviation some of the task saturation. Hand flying in turbulent conditions and maintaining altitude can be difficult and the autopilot can alleviate and sometimes do a better job to avoid deviations. Additionally I learned not to lag on overriding the autothrottles when using in FLCH mode. From this experience I feel that I can better identify and evaluate a handful of risks in a certain situation and will take prompt action to reduce these risks in a timely manner. The CA and I had a productive debrief and agreed on what variables led to the deviation and how to prevent in the future.

column121: Our flight departed from ZZZ enroute to EWY. Clearance was issued as follows: 'CLEARED TO EYW AIRPORT [via SID] FLY TOWER ASSIGNED HEADING THEN AS FILED MAINT 3000FT (ZZZ..ZZZZZ..MTH..EYW..KEYW)'. Established level at our cruise altitude of 14;000 ft. and on our cleared route we were handed off to MIA Center (ZMA). ZMA cleared us Direct to EYW and we proceeded on the new route. During our descent ZMA issued the cross a fix not on our route at 10;000 ft. We believed we heard GINGA as the controller pronunciation had the hard G sound. Looking at the chart the closest intersection with this sound was GIGIH. However; as we now know the fix was JANKA to the South. We requested clarification of the intersection 4 times from ZMA and received no response. Believing the clearance was to a GIGIH we started out turn to the West and continued our decent to meet the restriction. ZMA asked if we wanted to arrive from the North to EYW and we responded we had no preference. ZMA then issued at turn to heading 180 and we continued our descent to 10;000 ft. ZMA handed us off to Navy Key West Approach and the flight continued without incident. Upon landing and researching the charts in more detail we discovered the similar sounding intersections of GIGIH and JANKA in the EYW area; neither of which were on our flight plan. It is my opinion no violations occurred; and all altitude restriction were accomplished as published; however; the Safety of Flight is highest priority at our company and the crew felt this issue should be submitted as an ASAP report to further pilot education and professionalism. Similar sounding intersection names not on our flight plan. Controller pronunciation and being unable to confirm the waypoint.The ability to confirm the proper waypoint spelling with ATC.

column121: On initial climbout of ZZZ off Runway XXC we experienced loss of power shortly after passing 400 feet and received the 'Landing gear' aural warning. I double checked the gear handle and verified gear position; then verified N1 rollback; momentarily thinking we had dual engine failure. FO exclaimed startle; I replied 'fly the plane'. FO disconnected auto throttle; brought the thrust back up to takeoff position. We momentarily lost altitude and airspeed as Startle and surprise delayed our recognition slightly. Timing of the event was before flap retraction so we were near flap over speed during recognition and recovery; I said 'watch the speed pitch up pitch up' until flaps were retracted. FO later indicated his flight director was not giving correct indications for phase of flight. FO was able to recognize and manually control the aircraft; resuming normal climb out. Once the aircraft was under control; auto pilot and auto throttle engaged normally and no further anomalies were experienced.Unknown; weather was stormy; with moderate turbulence and lightning flashes in vicinity; in full IMC.We teach hand on thrust levers at all times during arrival and landing phase; but not during takeoff...had the FO had physical contact with the thrust levers during the climb; the AT retarding would have been instantly detected. I recommend the same procedure is taught for takeoff as is for landing...one hand on the thrust levers.
column123: After checking everything was normal we lined up on runway XXC in ZZZ. We verified our automation was in the correct mode including TO; ROLL; and FLCH were verified on our FMA as well as the crosshair flight director was up. As I advanced thrust the auto throttles took and the captain confirmed that ATTCS armed and we had normal TO thrust. at 80 knots while verifying the speed I saw the AT were in their normal HOLD mode. At this point everything was completely normal. When I went to rotate and was transitioning in the instruments I noticed that the FD had switched during the roll to the diamond mode which is supposed to happen at 1000'AGL. (Latter the captain confirmed that there's was normal). I had a normal rotation and pitched towards a normal takeoff attitude disregarding the flight director. At approximately 400 AGL the auto throttles commanded idle thrust suddenly. The startle and surprise nature of this took a second to process where we lost approximately 50 feet. At this point I disconnected the auto throttles and set climb power. The automation was still not working correctly including the flight director. Once we climbed through sterile we turned on the auto-throttles and they worked throughout the flight but we watched them very carefully and called Maintenance writing up the experience on the ground. The cause is unknown. before Takeoff we both verified we were in the correct automation modes. Once in cruise flight we verified all out take-off date and departure limits were set correctly and they were. Contributing factors to the loss of altitude was the thunderstorms in the vicinity; night; and moderate turbulence. More effective startle and surprise training in the sims. We are taught to keep both hands on the yoke throughout departure I think at 400 feet though 10;000 we should be guarding the thrust levers like we do on approach to landing.

column121: While on final approach the PF was having difficulty slowing the aircraft and continuing the descent. The headwind we had been fighting quickly turned to a crosswind. The PF elected to re-bug and use flaps 40 well above 1;000 feet. As the PF I selected the new flap setting in the FMC and verbally called out the Vref and target speeds. As we were slowing past our previous target speed the PF called for flaps 40. We had no amber band visible for flaps 40 placard speed; so I verified the placard; 162 knots; and selected the flaps seeing 158 knots and slowing on my tape. As I verified the speed brake was armed he again called for 40. The flaps were still at 30. At this point we were now below 1;000 feet but above 500 feet. We discussed the non-movement and load alleviation. As the PM; I suggested; pitch up and slow; the flaps moved to 40 as we suspected they would. The checklist was completed and we were able to be stable by 500 feet AGL; so we continued the landing. We did not observe any limitations being exceeded on the flaps or in procedure as the PM was able to manage the approach prior to the 500 foot gate.In discussing this event during our debrief we believe that we did meet our approach gate criteria. We were in our first 'heavy' approach in many months as the flight was full. The weight may have contributed. The wind was also a contributing factor as it shifted down the final enough that by the time we departed the traffic flow had reversed.Neither of us were averse to going around but it did not seem necessary in the moment as it seemed we met our criteria to continue. Having said that I'm certain eyes further from the instrument panel may have captured data we missed but I believe we trapped and corrected the situation.
column123: While on final approach I; PF; called for final landing flap (flaps 40) and flaps did not move to commanded position (they were at 30); despite being slower than max speed for flaps 40. Since we were within a few knots of max flaps 40 speed; I slowed further and flaps extended to commanded position. I believe the flap extension occurred right around 500 feet.  The final approach speed was within stabilized approach criteria and the outcome of the approach and landing were not in doubt. Landing was uneventful.We have been flying mostly empty airplanes for almost a year and this flight was almost completely full. I believe the higher landing weight coupled with a significant loss of headwind on final contributed to the airplane taking a while to slow down to an acceptable speed for final flaps. When I called for final flaps; we were 3-4 knots below the max flaps speed and I believe the aircraft's safety system was restricting flap movement until I was a little slower. As we return to Pre-COVID passenger loads; I will have to adjust lead time for decelerating the jet. Today was a good reminder.

column121: We were flying; from ZZZ to QRO (Queretaro; MX). During preflight inspection; the FMC database was current as well as both pilots' Electronic Flight Kits. While in-flight; the weather was reporting clouds at 1;200 feet 5 mile visibility and light winds. The runway in use was [Runway] 09. While in cruise flight; Mexico Center informed us to expect VOR DME 2 for RWY (Runway) 09 approach in QRO. The aircraft was set up; and the Pilot Flying (Captain) completed all briefings. While in cruise flight; Mexico Center gave us a late descent clearance which is very common on this flight that required LVL/CHG mode and speedbrakes to get back on path. While we were descending to our first cleared altitude (around 14;000 feet MSL); Mexico switched us to QRO Approach. Upon contact with QRO Approach about 15-20 miles out; they advised of a traffic on a ten mile final; and informed us to now expect the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 Approach. We were recleared direct to QRO VOR; provided another descent; and then shortly thereafter; Approach cleared us for the approach. The First Officer went into the FMC and configured it to fly direct to QRO VOR. After the aircraft was established on course to the VOR; the First Officer selected the QRO VOR fix in the FMC and inserted the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 approach after verification with the Captain. Because of the angle the aircraft was approaching the VOR (straight in Runway 09); and relative to the approach procedure (an outbound heading 292 followed by a left procedure turn inbound); an additional procedure turn was required just to begin the approach. The procedure turn would normally be done at the VOR. Due to the FMC not having a procedure turn at the VOR to begin the approach for arrivals from the west; it immediately started auto-sequencing fixes to fly the aircraft directly to the outbound procedure turn DME 10 from the QRO VOR. The First Officer had to re-enter the VOR into Direct To and build a holding pattern into the FMC. There was a missed approach holding pattern depicted on the approach chart; therefore; the First Officer built a hold based on the holding pattern published. The First Officer informed ATC that a procedure turn was required at the VOR and also notified approach that the aircraft would enter holding as published to begin the approach. ATC advised us to descend to 11;000 feet and cleared for the approach. ATC seemed confused as to what we were doing. It appears that they were expecting the aircraft to make a hard left after crossing the VOR (almost a 180 degree turn) into unprotected airspace that contained mountainous terrain. The minimum safe altitude for that sector is 12;800 feet and if the aircraft would have flown that; there could have been a CFIT event. Once the aircraft entered the holding pattern; making a procedure turn to enter the crew selected IMM EXIT and the aircraft completed the current holding pattern; just a procedure turn; and exited the hold to fly the entire approach as planned and expected. There seems to be an issue regarding the Jeppesen Charts; and FMC database for this specific approach. The FMC did not contain any proper procedure to join the approach legally. Also the FMC sequencing the approach could have presented multiple issues including CFIT; TCAS; or lost of Situational Awareness.
column123: We were heading to MMQT to shoot the VOR 1 approach from the west. We were headed direct to the VOR with the approach loaded after that. Approximately 9 miles prior to the VOR the airplane started a left turn to join the outbound portion of the approach. This was not appropriate or legal. We turned the airplane back towards the VOR and realized there was nothing loaded to turn the airplane around to join the approach legally. There is also no procedure turn depicted on the chart. There was a holding pattern at the VOR and a missed approach procedure associated with the approach. We decided to enter the holding pattern at the proper altitude and told the controller we were doing that. That allowed the airplane to turn around and we were able to join and commence the approach that way. The rest of the approach was uneventful

column121: Flight was all normal until we were cleared for a visual approach. Approach vectored us about 2 miles outside of the Final Approach Fix. When cleared for the a visual approach the First Officer turned inside of the Final Approach Fix. We had briefed the towers and their height and had them visually. The First Officer turned off the flight directors and turned directly towards the runway; about 20 degrees angle.  At 1;000 feet Tower called and asked if we had the towers in sight and said he had gotten an altitude alert.  At that point we were still visual with the towers and a half dot low on the glide slope. I directed the First Officer to come left and get on final. We continued the approach and landed. Found out afterwards this was the First Officer's first time to this airport and that he really didn't have a good visual on the runway. I felt his turning off the flight directors added to his lack of situational awareness. We discussed this approach afterwards and he felt I should have directed a go around. I believe he was waiting for me but I was in the green.  I didn't know he was lost. I explained to the First Officer that there is a reason we brief instrument approaches at night; to use them.  I shouldn't have allowed him to make the turn directly towards the runway but told him to intercept closer to the Final Approach Fix. The First Officer needed to communicate he wasn't in the green and execute a go around if he felt it was needed.

I had the towers in sight and the Captain gave me verbal commands to help me orient the runway. The landing and rollout were uneventful. I accepted a visual approach based on the beacon alone. I advised Gander Radio that the decent to FL330 had been initiated due to the severe turbulence. We received an approval to descend to FL300 at approximately FL350. No other deviations were noted. column121: We were flying to ASE and I was the Pilot Monitoring. As we approached Aspen; we were given vectors to intercept LOC E into ASE. We accepted clearance to maintain 13;000 ft until established and clearance to execute LOC E approach. As we were intercepting LOC we picked up visual with the airport and commenced descent towards it while having visual reference with the airport and all the terrain around. In the midst of all things happening quickly and the excitement of having visual with the airport; I failed to communicate to ATC my intention of executing visual approach. At some point we lost the visual with the airport due to a cloud layer just ahead of us; but not the terrain. At the same time ATC issued an altitude alert to us due to us being lower than what LOC approach altitudes called for. I advised that we had terrain in sight but lost the visual with the airport and said that we would be going missed and starting a climb. We got another altitude alert from ATC. We advised we are in a climb and asked vectors; until we decide what to do. We proceeded to ZZZ airport afterwards.  At no time we were in IMC conditions and maintained visual clearance from all the terrain. My mistake in this case was deviating from ATC clearance and going visual without communicating that to ATC. And also; not staying on a LOC due to a cloud layer over the airport. At no time was the aircraft in IMC conditions and we were maintaining clearance with terrain at all times. By all means the aircraft was never put in any unsafe condition.  I did learn from this experience to clearly and concisely communicate any and all of my intentions with ATC; so there is no misunderstanding at any point of the flight.

column121: Position was CORKR intersection to directly over SFO [VOR] at approximately 8;000 MSL. Had navigation flag on GNSS from GPS jamming  Was tracking fine up to SFO; Over SFO GNSS made a turn directly to ZZZ or so was thought; however; it was off course; Controller asked what our previous clearance that had been given; which was HOLLR; GRIJO; CORKR; SFO; ZZZ. Original clearance was GPI DIRECT to ZZZ. On the NW side of Nevada; there was GPS jamming was in progress. We reported it; and checked with controllers to see if our course was accurate. They informed us it was; and that if necessary they would give us a heading. Upon changeover to Oakland Center; we advised the Controller that GPS jamming had been in progress; and that we still had a navigation flag. He then issued a clearance to follow the fixes listed above; and we then asked how much longer the GPS jamming would continue. He said a few more miles. we advised him we still had a navigation flag on our GNSS; but apparently he was distracted; and told us to continue without issuing a heading. We were then turned over to another controller who apparently had not been informed of the ongoing issue. Hence once over SFO VOR; was when the issue listed above was encountered. We were not told if there was a near miss; he just gave us a heading to 180 and vectored us to the airport after that. Once on the ground; we were advised to call approach control for a possible deviation. We attempted to call but could not get through to anyone. We advised the Tower we were not able to reach anyone; so he tried to call and failed; but then he got through with another number. They said to disregard; and we then proceeded to ZZZ1 where the flight terminated.

column121: During the approach we were cleared direct down to 8000 feet from 12000 feet. During the descent Autopilot was engaged and following LNAV and VS we were encountering continuous light to moderate turbulence throughout the descent. As we passed through approximately 12000 feet and beginning to slow; we experienced severe turbulence mixed with continuous moderate [turbulence]. When we initially encountered the severe turbulence; the Autopilot disengaged; the aircraft was changing altitude and air speeds abruptly with several hundred feet of altitude change and at least plus or minus 20 to 30 knots airspeed changes. The Captain was thrown hard enough to hit the overhead panel with his head and we received a report one of our Flight Attendants had been hurt and several passengers had hit their heads. I as the Pilot Flying took manual control of the aircraft and flew the remainder of the descent and approach. The aircraft was extremely hard to control throughout most of the descent and approach as we continued to encounter continuous turbulence; strong crosswinds and wind shear. During the ensuing descent and approach the aircraft was extremely hard to control as we continued to experience moderate to severe turbulence; strong crosswind and wind shear throughout the approach. Once established inbound and cleared for the approach we were pushed several degrees off course and had some airspeed fluctuations of plus or minus 20 knots. We quickly discussed missed approach but prior to reaching 1000 feet we had regained the course; were on glide path and stabilized (properly configured) to continue the approach. We continued the approach while receiving some lower wind shear of plus or minus 10 knots down to approximately the 500 foot call. At 500 feet we were still stabilized and continued the approach to landing without further issue. Throughout the approach and landing; we had airspeed; altitude variations and heading deviations that were extremely hard to control due to the turbulence and wind shear events we were experiencing. I do not believe at any point we had any exceedances or violations; however; it was a very task saturated environment. There were no reports of the severity of the turbulence ahead of us and it was a very unexpected event.This was an example of good Crew Resource Management as the Captain and I maintained good communication throughout the event and helped to cross monitor the aircraft systems and instruments. As the pilot flying; I was entirely focused with aircraft control and the Captain doing the pilot monitoring was ensuring all the descent and approach tasks were completed. We kept good crew communication with what was happening with aircraft control and situational awareness. A recommendation is for pilots to ensure they continue to practice hand flying skills for situations like this. The autopilot was unusable; and I was thankful I constantly practice hand flying the airplane. It helped me with confidence to control the airplane to the best of my ability in a situation where the aircraft is being tossed around by turbulence.

column121: While approaching Mt Jefferson area on course direct ELKES at 14;000 aircraft encountered a mountain wave. First indications were not unusual; a loss of altitude followed by the autopilot pitch correction to maintain and resulting indicated airspeed loss. It is not uncommon for a momentary loss of a couple hundred feet and airspeed to drop to 90 KIAS; however; at the point where it would 'normal' the situation quickly escalated into an uncontrolled altitude loss as the autopilot rapidly pitched above 15* and I noted a 90+ headwind on the G600 wind vector indicator. I immediately contacted ATC that I was unable to maintain altitude; which they issued a lower clearance (13;000) and vector away from terrain. With the autopilot turned off; I maintained about 10* nose up at 75 KIAS; flaps 10; full throttle and noted a 1200FPM altitude loss. As I approached 13;000 I informed ATC I was unable and inquired about the MVA. I was fully prepared to activate emergency power; declare; and turn back; however ATC stated that the heading I was on gave me about 9000 for an MVA. I elected to ride the wave as the uncontrolled altitude loss was trending up and was able to stabilize as I approached 12;000. While altitude was stable; I remained below the MEA and published minimum off route altitude unable to climb or increase indicated airspeed above 80KIAS for several minutes. As the aircraft exited the mountain wave to the south; I was able to recover the airspeed slowly back to normal cruise as the aircraft moved over the ridge lines.This is the second time a mountain wave event has resulted in altitude loss of more than a few hundred feet. During the 'normal' events I have always notified ATC that I was encountering a wave and only one time previous did the incident result in the necessity for a lower clearance at 13;000'. However; in this event; I would characterize the resulting altitude loss as uncontrolled at minimum control airspeed and max continuous power for the altitude. I would consider this to be an escalation of what might be a normal inconvenience; and causes me to inquire about alternate routing. In all cases of my experience; these waves seem to be encountered over the Mt Jefferson area and a southerly re-routing of to the south is the normal avoidance procedure when the waves are encountered. But why wait until one is encountered? Might it be more prudent to take a different airway further south to begin with? Might be worth exploring.

column121: I was PF in the left seat and we were cleared for take off on Rwy XL.  As we were lining up on the runway; I heard the Tower clear a helicopter for an eastbound departure from the ramp; but I did not visually see the helicopter yet.  Once we were on the takeoff roll; I saw the helicopter lifting off from the ramp (ahead and to our left); but it appeared to be turning parallel to our runway to I diverted my attention back to the runway.  Right after initiating rotation; I saw the helicopter begin to cross over our runway; left to right; at approximately 200 feet AGL.  Because we were past V1 and already rotating on a short runway; I quickly determined an aborted takeoff was not an option so I continued our rotation.  During these few seconds; there were some communications between the Tower and the helicopter; but I did not comprehend them due to my focus on avoiding hitting the helicopter.  Shortly after liftoff (~100 feet AGL); I had to make an evasive maneuver to our left and reduce our climb rate for a few seconds to avoid hitting the helicopter.  Luckily; there was no terrain or obstacles to the left of our runway heading.  Once the helicopter passed off our right at what I estimate was 200-300 feet; I resumed a normal climb rate and a right turn back to our departure heading.  The Tower controller apologized and then handed us off to Departure.  Looking back on the scenario; I believe continuing the takeoff roll as we did was the right call; as we certainly would have had a runway excursion if we had attempted an abort at that point in the roll - passed V1 and already rotating.  Additionally; I am not sure how I could have anticipated the impending conflict earlier because helicopters maneuver on a dime and it was hard to tell its intending heading after liftoff.  After the event; I listened to the ATC recording on a publicly available website and it seems the controller tried to tell the helicopter pilot to remain north of the runway at all times; but that transmission was not acknowledged.

column123: I was training on the Local Control position. There were 4 VFR aircraft in the traffic pattern for RWY XX and 1 VFR aircraft on practice approach RWY YY. Aircraft Y was VFR in left traffic for RWY XX and given a sequence to follow Aircraft X. Aircraft X was VFR in right traffic for RWY XX. Aircraft Y was given a sequence of number 4; to follow Aircraft X on right downwind. Aircraft Y was extending their downwind until they had their traffic in sight. Aircraft Y asked if their traffic was turning final RWY XX. I visually scanned the traffic pattern to verify Aircraft X position. I saw Aircraft X on final for RWY XX. Aircraft X was the 3rd aircraft on final at the time and was on an approximately 4NM final. I cleared Aircraft Y to land RWY XX after my visual scan. Aircraft Y must have had the incorrect aircraft in sight; the aircraft preceding Aircraft X was an Piper. Aircraft Y flew into the flight path of Aircraft X; cutting them off. Aircraft Y had to make a quick turn north bound to avoid Aircraft X. Aircraft X saw Aircraft Y; after Aircraft Y turned to the north; and Aircraft X made a south turn to avoid Aircraft Y. At this time Aircraft X made a call to Local Control that he was making his north turn to avoid Aircraft Y. I did not see the two aircraft turning to avoid until Aircraft X made his call for the north turn. Aircraft Y rejoined the RWY XX final; in front of Aircraft Y; and was reissued a landing clearance for RWY XX. Aircraft Y was instructed to make a 270 degree turn back to final and rejoined RWY XX final behind Aircraft X. Aircraft X was reissued a landing clearance for RWY XX. Both aircraft landed without further incident. About 10 minutes after Aircraft X landed; the pilot called the tower to let us know that Aircraft Y was within close proximity to him and he would be filing a safety report.

column121: Aircraft X on an IFR flight plan was being vectored for an ILS approach. The weather was marginal but apparently had some very strong winds aloft as the aircraft kept flying off course when given any heading. The initial heading of 115 looked like a 125 heading. I gave him a 115 heading down to 1800 ft. for the ILS approach but when I saw that he was heading toward the higher MVAs; I asked him to turn 10 degrees left. The pilot asked if I was painting any weather but I didn't see anything and I told him that. I also told him to advise if he wanted to deviate for weather. It looked like the weather was clearing up and the winds were calm enough for an approach. Since he kept getting blown off course toward the shoreline and away from the water; I asked him if he'd like an instrument or visual approach instead. He said that he had the shoreline in sight so the visual approach might work.As he got closer to the field; I noticed that he looked like he was heading 145; even closer to the MVA. And so I told him to turn left heading 090 but he delayed his response; much like he'd been doing the whole time. He flew out of the 1500 ft. MVA and into the 2100 ft. MVA and I issued a safety alert and again told him to turn left heading 090 and to climb to 2100 ft. After what felt like forever; he finally turned left heading 090 and climbed to 2100 ft. I then safely vectored him for an ILS approach and he landed without incident. Throughout the conversation there was a major delay in the pilot's responses and I believe that that made a big difference. I could have sharply turned him much earlier though and had I done that I believe that this would not have happened. Given that he was such a small aircraft and was being so greatly affected by the winds; I've learned my lesson. When the pilot departed ITO after landing; he was very thankful; and quite honestly I am too. It was a good learning experience. I know that pilots are quite busy and he was probably fighting the winds more than he knew. I discussed the matter with my Air Traffic Manager who was Controller in Charge at the time and we went over safety alerts. Weather can make a big difference and here in Hilo it is very unpredictable.

column121: ZZZ ATIS advertising ILS Runway XY; winds 24008 favoring [Runway] ZA but it is normal for ZZZ to use 12 until winds are 10 KTS or greater due to terrain and approach undesirability of Runway ZA.Aircraft checked on with correct ATIS descending from Center and asked for RNAV ZA. I only heard RNAV.  The common request from airline is for the RNAV Z Runway XY when we are advertising ILS's because it saves flying miles/time.I should mention that the cleaning/disinfecting person was starting my station so I had to move out of the way and move items away for her cleaning process. This is a nightly routine and is highly distracting.I cleared Aircraft X for the RNAV Z Runway XY approach. To which they read back 'Cleared RNAV' (pause) 'Zulu; Runway XY' (the XY was dropped and due to the cleaning I only heard Y which I assumed was part of X-Y) [Note: there is NO Runway YA at ZZZ].I observed the aircraft making a right turn at ZZZZZ intersection instead of the left turn for Runway XY this alerted me the aircraft was following the Runway ZA approach path. I immediately canceled the approach clearance; assigned an appropriate altitude and heading and informed the pilot it appeared he was on the wrong approach and I was now vectoring for the correct approach. The pilot was still above all MVA's so there was no immediate danger. There was a short discussion with the pilot and he set up for the correct approach which was completed with no issue.1st; Cleaning/Disinfection of control position and its immediate vicinity by contract staff should be done only when the position is not being worked at that station. Our facility closes the TRACON at XA:00 and has a 5hr XX min window this could be done in with no distractions and eliminate the danger to the NAS is currently poses.2nd; this was a clear hearback/readback issue with expectation bias on both the controllers and pilots part.A- Because of distraction; I failed to hear the initial request for Runway ZA and followed up by issuing a standard clearance for the RNAV Z Runway XY with no other warning to the pilot such as 'Unable Runway ZA' as I would normally do with an opposite direction request I was unable to approve.B- The pilot readback a completely wrong clearance in many ways; The RNP approach he wanted to Runway ZA is called 'RNAV Runway ZA'. It does not have a Z and is to ZA not YA. By reading back 'Cleared Rnav Z Runway YA' it greatly increased the chances of my hearing it as I expected.C- In listening to the recording the pilot obviously was unsure of the clearance he got as there was a long pause between RNAV and Zulu; which leads me to believe the pilot had a flag going off in his head that he neglected to properly follow up on.  Had I not been involved with dancing around the cleaning person to be able to see my scope I probably would have picked up on this better. As it was I must have had a flag of some kind in my own mind because I did give extra vigilance to ensure the correct turn at ZZZZZ so there must have been something warning the back of my mind as well.In the end the system did work as it ultimately should and the error was caught and corrected with no risk. I know a last minute correction like this can cause stress on a flight crew and this crew handled it with high professionalism and safety was insured by both them and myself.

column121: Aircraft X called Local Control for departure IFR. The aircraft was cleared via the SID and this was reiterated at Local Control when they were released. With their release; Local Control also advised them to remain north of the runway for an aircraft rolling out as well as the next arrival. The aircraft departed and was transferred to TRACON. I observed an unsafe proximity to terrain as this aircraft was climbing form 800 ft. to 900 ft. on the update when it grabbed my attention. The aircraft was approximately 3 miles northwest of the airport and approaching the hillside. I called over to the coordinator fir the two departure sectors and brought their attention to the aircraft and asked if they check on them. This seemed to startle the coordinator who said they would check. About twenty seconds later the Low Altitude Alert went off showing 1;100 ft. and I can only assume Aircraft X was IMC as I could not see them out of the window. Still progressing towards the hillside. The aircraft then began to turn to the west and away from the hillside. The coordinator called back; which goes directly to Local Control; and said the pilot understood they were to remain north of the course. Local Control explained what they had told the aircraft and all was back to normal. With the wind we were having they would have drifted north a little anyway; but this was a lot of drifting; so this statement made sense. Around this time; the Supervisor came back; as I was starting an incident report. I called TRACON Supervisor and asked if they were filing anything on this event. They said no because there is no climb gradient on the SID. But there is and I do not believe this aircraft was meeting it. I left it at that and said I was filing a report. When I filled out the report I entered 800 ft. for the required and observed altitudes because that was the first altitude I saw. The pilot should have understood what was issued and to not over fly the runway. I do not know if this would be considered a Pilot Deviation; but I have a hunch it was: The vector SID has a required climb gradient. They were near that; but I do not believe they were legally meeting it and off course.

column121: I was the pilot monitoring and my First Officer was the pilot flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  The First Officer briefed and the flight computer was programmed for the ILS XXR.  We were flying to ZZZZZ waypoint on ZZZZZ4 RNAV STAR.  When the Approach Controller assigned us the ILS XXC approach; the First Officer incorrectly executed the secondary flight plan.  He asked for my confirmation; but he had already executed the secondary plan before I had a chance to tell him not to do so.  And; he misinterpreted the FMA on his PFD; which led him to make an incorrect turn using the heading mode selector.  This caused a course deviation.  He was confused.  So; I reprogrammed the flight computer to rejoin the arrival route.  Soon after; ATC gave us a heading to intercept the localizer for XXC.  The flight was completed safely and normally.  After the flight; I briefed him on the importance of confirming with the crew before executing the flight computer program; not to be in a hurry; to take time to correctly interpret FMA; and to know how to correct your own mistake when you make one.  During this COVID pandemic period; he has moved from this fleet to XXX fleet then back again to this fleet.  That might help explain his getting confused on this flight computer system.  He took the post flight briefing professionally; and I believe it will help him in the future.  However; I must say that we cannot keep using the pandemic as an excuse for errors and mistakes made on the job.  Professionals should; regardless of the root cause; be able to recognize his or her own deficiencies; and continue to put effort into doing a better job every time.

column121: The flight was cruising at 35;000 ft. (FL350) in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC). The flight attendants had been briefed earlier about turbulence along the route of flight. When the turbulence became constant moderate; the flight attendants were informed via the public address (PA) system to 'take their seats.' The flight was deviating around weather and needed a left deviation and attempted request a deviation from ATC; however; due to frequency congestion this was causing a delay in deviation. The Captain executed the deviation out of safety (emergency authority) and had the First Officer announce the deviation to ATC; not long after the deviation severe turbulence was encountered lasting approximately one minute. The aircraft was out of control with large airspeed; attitude; and altitude deviations. The severe turbulence caused a 500 foot altitude deviation (35;500 ft.) which triggered a TCAS alert. All automation disconnected in the turbulence and the Captain assumed manual flight control. The second aircraft was acquired visually; and the Captain manually maneuvered to regain control; avoid the aircraft; and return to 35;000 ft. Once clear of the turbulence; the auto-throttles and autopilot were re-engaged; and ATC informed about the location and magnitude of the severe turbulence. The First Officer was tasked to check on the status of the flight attendants and passengers. There were no flight attendant or passenger injuries. Both during flight and upon landing; Maintenance Control; Dispatch; and Operations was kept informed of the severe turbulence encounter along with crew and passenger status. A combination of active weather with turbulence across much of the central United States; high workload environment; saturated ATC frequencies.One cannot control the weather; gather as much information as possible about the route and possible threats along the way.

column121: I received the relief briefing from the previous controller and was briefed that an aircraft wanted to do multiple practice approaches at a satellite airport. The aircraft was on the climb out instructions when I instructed him to turn right heading 180 for vector for an ILS. The aircraft replied to that instruction and began to fly that heading. A minute or so later I noticed that the aircraft was veering to the right of the assigned heading. I instructed them to turn 10 degrees right. He didn't reply and I gave him the instructions again. He did not reply this time either. This is when I first became aware of this aircraft being NORDO (No Radio). I began to reach out multiple times to the aircraft and after a little time I heard him reply that he went back to the tower. I then questioned him as to why would he return to the tower frequency and gave him another instruction.The aircraft again did not respond. I also asked him to ident if he could hear me transmitting and that failed. Now I was becoming worried as I was aware this aircraft was level at 2;000 ft. and there is a Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) south of him 5 to 6 miles that is 3;000 ft. I reached out to Tower to ask them if they could try to reach out to the aircraft. I also had another aircraft in the vicinity that I inquired if he could hear me and if that aircraft could transmit for me and try to contact the aircraft. Both of those attempts failed as well. I was now getting nervous as he was headed towards the two antennas with the MVA's at 3;000 ft. I then reached out to him on guard frequency and stated that if he heard me to climb immediately to 3;000 ft. I also alerted the Supervisor what was going on. Now I was seeing the aircraft entering the MVA area of 3;000 ft. and I transmitted in the blind a MVA alert and for them to climb immediately. There was still no contact with this aircraft. Now another aircraft was also trying to reach the NORDO aircraft as they heard the concern in my voice. After some time the pilot called me and said he was ready for the vector onto the ILS. Thats when the other aircraft transmitted the climb information and they began to climb. The aircraft then called me and stated he is having a serious problem with his radios and wanted to return to their departure airport. I then gave him vectors to return where the aircraft landed safely.I have no recommendations. This was an event that as a controller I did everything I could think of to get in contact with the aircraft but he was truly NORDO. In conclusion it was a equipment issue that caused the incident.
