column121: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X from ZZZ2-ZZZ1. I flew the RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach with rain and wind in the vicinity. I attempted to configure early but a strong tailwind made it challenging. I encountered a wind gust which caused me to counter increasing airspeed by pitching up and slightly reduce power to maintain airspeed and continue configuring. This resulted in a position higher than anticipated. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) noticed this also and we articulated that. About that time; ATC directed a go-around. We executed the missed approach and climbed to 3;000 [feet] on vectors for another approach.Noting the conditions; I configured early for the second RNAV RNP XX approach. Rain and wind were still predominant throughout the approach but fewer gust excursions and we remained stable throughout the approach all the way to minimums. At minimums; we both had the approach lights and runway environment in sight and I continued the approach. As I turned final aligning with Runway XX; I lost sight of the runway environment due to the weather. The PM called go around and I initiated go around procedures. We climbed to 3;000 feet on vectors as directed by ATC. We communicated with one another and ensured we were both in the green; we had ample fuel; and agreed to attempt a third approach. On the third RNAV RNP XX approach; I configured early again and remained stable throughout the approach. The wind was still a factor though and required careful monitoring and aircraft correction to maintain a stable approach. Fully configured and in the vicinity of arriving at minimums; ATC advised a wind shift on the field of 330 degrees at 26 knots of wind. ATC asked for our intentions. Due to airline limitations on Maximum Tailwind Component for Landing; the PM told ATC we could not land and we would go-around. ZZZ1 Tower handed us off to ZZZ Departure and they advised us that they 'turned the airfield around' and they would give us vectors for the ILS RWY XY approach and we would be 'number 1' to the field. Again; the Captain and I communicated that we were both in the green; we noted that we had ample fuel; and we prepared for an ILS approach to Runway XY.After intercepting the localizer for the ILS to Runway XY; I configured fully and continued down the glideslope from the final approach fix. It was raining outside and was windy but we remained stable. Shortly prior to 1;000 feet AGL; it grew increasingly difficult to maintain a stable approach. I told the PM that I didn't feel comfortable; the weather was worsening; and it was likely that we would not be stable at 1;000 feet. We agreed and elected to go-around. Just as I began the go around procedure; we encountered a Wind Shear Warning and I proceeded with the Wind Shear escape maneuver. We exited the conditions quickly and transitioned to ATC's directives. We quickly agreed to divert to ZZZ3 and the PM informed ATC of our intention to divert. We climbed to 3;000 feet and flew vectors to ZZZ3.We flew the ILS RWY XYC approach and landed safely at ZZZ3 and taxied to the gate. We shut down the aircraft with approximately 7.4k pounds of fuel remaining. During the deplaning process; the Captain coordinated with the Maintenance and Dispatch and agreed to continue on to ZZZ1 as the weather cleared the area. We added fuel departing with 11.8k pounds of fuel. The Captain flew as the PF and I was the PM for the return flight to ZZZ1. The Captain maintained appropriate communication throughout the event. He communicated with the passengers explaining as best as possible what occurred and what we were doing to ensure their safety while doing our best to land at our intended destination. He kept the flight attendants apprised of the situation after each approach and we discussed each approach; verified we were both in the green; and maintained situational awareness at all times.
column123: Flew RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying) and was configuring the aircraft early. He was at gear down; flaps 15; and we encountered a wind gust that drove the airspeed indication almost to redline. The FO raised nose slightly and reduced power to slow the airspeed in order to continue configuring the aircraft. As this occurred; aircraft got a little high. As PM; I noticed this and was in process of informing FO when ATC said that we looked a little high and to just go around. We executed the missed approach as directed by ATC and climbed on a heading to 3;000 ft. to vector for another approach.On the second RNAV RNP XX; FO configured the aircraft early and shot approach to minimums. At minimums; approach lights and runway lights were visible; but as we turned to final approach; visibility was lost.  I called go-around; and FO initiated go-around. We climbed on a heading to 3;000 feet. We communicated with each other that we were both in the green; had plenty of fuel; and prepared for another approach.On the third RNAV RNP XX; the FO had fully configured the aircraft; when ATC advised that the wind had shifted out of the north at 330 degrees and we had 26 knots of wind at our tail. ATC asked our intentions; I told them that we could not land with those winds and that we were going around. At that point; ATC handed us off to departure; and departure immediately advised us that they had turned the airport around and could give us an immediate left downwind to be number 1; shooting ILS Runway XY. FO and I communicated with each other that we were both in the green; had plenty of fuel; and prepared for an approach using the new runway.On attempt to Runway XY; we intercepted localizer and G/S. We had continual high winds indicating to me that the aircraft would not be able to remain stable throughout approach and landing. As PIC; I called for a go-around. FO communicated to me his agreement; and I immediately notified Tower of our intention to divert to ZZZ3. FO initiated the miss. As he did; we encountered a brief Wind Shear Warning. FO finished cleaning aircraft up and we diverted to ZZZ3 without incident.We were vectored to ZZZ3 and landed on Runway XYC and taxied to the gate with 7.4 pounds of fuel. I called Dispatch and she said we had plenty of fuel to get to ZZZ1 but as a precaution due to the frontal weather passage; she added more fuel and brought us up to 11.8 pounds. After the front passage; I flew the aircraft as PF uneventfully to ZZZ1. During all of the approaches and the divert I kept the flight attendants up to date and communicated with the passengers at all times. We exercised good situational awareness and followed SOPs during the entire flight.

column121: Accidental cutoff of aircraft in traffic patternI had recently gone flying as I hadn't been up much lately; and maintained closed traffic at the airport to re-familiarize myself with the aircraft and work on my landings. Since this airport is the main airport for a flight school; multiple aircraft were joining and leaving the pattern; necessitating Tower to have aircraft extend on departure and downwind legs of the pattern. As I was in a left downwind for Runway XX; Tower instructed all aircraft remaining in the pattern to extend upwind 3 miles after takeoff; and I made note of this as I was planning to do a couple more loops in the pattern. About 30 seconds later; Tower asked if I had the traffic (a PA28) on short final for Runway XX in sight. I did; and Tower cleared me for the option. I performed a touch and go and began climbing on the departure leg.As I was finishing the climb and extending the departure leg; I noted a call from Tower to the PA28 asking for their position; with the PA28 reporting they were in the crosswind leg. Tower then called me to tell me to extend upwind 3 miles and do right traffic for Runway XX. I estimated as having already done about 1.5 miles due to Tower's notification about doing so earlier; and the delay from Tower informing me again was due to the influx of traffic into the airspace. I continued on for about another minute and then began my right crosswind turn. While on the crosswind leg; Tower called the PA28 to inform them that they would be number 4 in the pattern and following traffic on the left downwind. The PA28 reported that they had been cut off on crosswind and would follow the traffic in front of them. Tower called and asked for my position; which I reported as right crosswind; and Tower asked the PA28 if they observed a Skyhawk in front of them. The PA28 responded with an affirmative and Tower informed them to follow me. Several seconds later; I turned onto the downwind leg and was able to observe the PA28 about 3/4ths of a mile behind me and finishing a turn from crosswind onto downwind. Nothing else of note happened after and I chose to make this my last loop in the traffic pattern; and performed a full stop landing a few minutes later.At the time; I knew that I had missed whether or not the PA28 would be right or left traffic. I had heard their report to Tower of being on crosswind as I started my departure leg and felt that they would not be any conflict no matter which pattern they were in. While I do recognize that it is the pilot's responsibility to maintain separation in the Class Delta and that Tower's workload had increased with the amount of aircraft in the airspace; I did not receive any calls notifying me of traffic (earlier in the flight Tower had informed me of traffic ahead of me on upwind and I did not turn crosswind until I was able to verify that they had finished their crosswind turn and passed me on downwind). Since I had cut off the PA28; I figured the only possibility was that I had turned into my crosswind turn too early. However; I was confused about this as the PA28 had reported being on crosswind at least a full minute before I had even started my crosswind turn; and I could not figure out as to how they would then end up behind me.I did end up pulling both my flight data and the PA28's flight data from FlightAware.com and the ATC audio from LiveATC.com to try and piece together what happened; and it seems several factors played a role in this. For starters; I had missed the call to the PA28 informing them that they would be right traffic. This was something I knew I had missed during the flight; and listening to the audio showed that they were told this after I had been cleared to land initially on Runway XX; meaning that I was likely focused on my touch and go instead of calls to other aircraft. I recognize that I need to work on still listening fully to Tower on this phase of flight if I will be rejoining the pattern; as it is importantto have a mental picture of where other aircraft are within the airspace.I also likely did start my crosswind turn early; as the data from FlightAware seems to pinpoint my turn as having started no further than 2.5 miles upwind. This is likely due to me misjudging my timing and distance in the aircraft after takeoff and is something I will need to also work on.With those in mind; the data from the PA28 also shows that it played a major factor in this event. After takeoff; the PA28 extended about 4.5 miles upwind while also drifting left of the runway. As such; their position report to Tower of being in the crosswind was likely when they just started their turn and the amount of time spent in the crosswind would be lengthened due to their drift left. The longer upwind extension would also explain how they ended up behind me once I turned onto the downwind leg. I am unsure if Tower recognized that the PA28 had drifted left and extended so far out; but I am assuming that they did not as no call was made informing me of their position or the potential for conflict.Overall; my own misjudgments of my timing and distance; mistake in missing calls for other aircraft to have an idea of what is going on big picture (as I would have been able to recognize that I would essentially be following an aircraft in the right traffic pattern); and the PA28's over extension and drift on the departure leg contributed to this event.

column121: During climb out of SMF; everything was normal with some occasional light chop. We had asked the Flight Attendants to remain seated due to crossing the Sierra Mountains. We were climbing at approximately .76 Mach. Upon leveling at FL 370; we experienced moderate bordering on severe mountain wave. Our airspeed began decreasing rapidly and the F/O (First Officer) disconnected the autopilot; applied full thrust; and began a shallow descent to regain airspeed. The airspeed decayed to about .70 - .71. It was about a 30 knot decrease. I may be a little off on the Mach numbers. We descended about 500' and the airspeed began increasing.  I reported the encounter to ATC and we began climbing back to FL 370. The wave climbed us to FL 375; and at that time we requested a descent to FL 350. The Controller cleared us to descend to FL 350. We did not encounter any additional mountain wave and nothing more than a little light chop. We checked with the Flight Attendants to make sure everyone was alright; and the remainder of the flight was uneventful. I would like to add that the F/O did an excellent job of recognizing and reacting to the situation.
column123: We had just leveled off at our cruise altitude of FL 370. (Filed for FL 390 but we were too heavy at that time.) During climb we had anticipated and encounter some light turbulence. Nothing more significant was encountered. WSI (Weather Service International) and Jeppesen weather showed areas of turbulence covering about the first 45 minutes of our flight. Our clearance was on the SCTWN 3 RNAV Departure. We were level at FL 370 when suddenly our airspeed had dropped from M.76 (250 KIAS) to 220 KIAS this was approximately 10-15 above the yellow maneuvering bar on the airspeed indicator and the green vector bar was indicating that the slowing was continuing and at a significant rate. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle and pitched down to keep airspeed. I also increased thrust to max and I was able to recover airspeed about 500' low at FL 365. In my attempt to climb back to FL 370 we started climbing at a significant rate and stopped the climb at approximately FL 376. The Captain reported to ATC that we were in MVA (mountain wave activity) and that we were unable to hold altitude. I continued to hand fly until I was sure we were passed the MVA and re-engaged the autopilot. The rest of the flight was uneventful.

column121: This was me and the First Officer's first flight together.  He hadn't had a landing for approximately a month and hadn't been flying a lot recently.  It was a beautiful day in ZZZ and we were cleared for the visual to XXL at about 7;000 MSL.  We were established on the localizer as a backup and had the runway in sight holding around 210 knots.  Approach control handed us off to tower and I checked in.  We were cleared to land and told that there would be fighters departing out of ZZZ1; but they would stay below us.  The First Officer started too slow and I extended flaps to 2.  I started searching for the fighters and saw 2 of them takeoff.  I keep my eyes on them to make sure we were clear.  First Officer called for the gear and I extended it.  I noticed we were still at flaps 2 and we were too fast for flaps 3.  We were inside the FAF by this point and it was going to be close for a stabilized approach.  The first officer had previously selected the approach mode and we were on course about 300 feet high on the glide path and fast so not correcting.  I noticed the power on the engine instruments was not at idle which was strange because we had the approach selected in managed speed and the speed tape showed the target speed well below our current speed.  I pointed the power setting out to the first officer and it was also confusing to him why the power was still up.  We got to flaps 3 around 1;000 AGL and were still high on the glide path.  We leveled off a little to get the flaps to full and then started to correct to glidepath.  When we got to 500 feet we were still a good 200 feet high and 15-20 knots above our target speed.  The First Officer asked me if I wanted him to go around.  There was no traffic and the runway is 2 miles long so I said to continue.  We ended up touching down at target speed well within the touchdown zone and cleared the runway.  After getting to the gate and shutting down the engines we debriefed the approach.  The First Officer said that all along he thought he was setting himself up nicely for the approach and thought it would work.  I agreed and then I took myself out of the SA loop when I started searching for the fighters and didn't pay close enough attention to our energy status.  When I finally did get back into it I wasn't forceful enough to help.  When I pointed out the engines not being at idle I assumed he would disconnect the auto thrust and put the throttles at idle.  When he didn't I should have told him too and that alone would have probably made us stable as there was still some time.  At any rate I didn't and we were clearly unstable and we both knew it.  The only correct option was to execute a go-around.  Fuel was not an issue as we ended up landing with 6;500 pounds.  I told him that I should have told him to go-around but he should have just executed a go-around without asking.  That is the procedure.  You don't need permission from the other pilot and permission not to go-around is still wrong anyway.  We agreed that the biggest factor that got us going down this path in the first place was his recency of experience and that in order to fix that he should in the immediate future at least; slow down and configure earlier then he thinks he needs to.  Going back to our departure briefing I should have taken the first leg anyway since I knew he hadn't flown in a while.  This way he could have eased back into it.

column121: We were being vectored to final for the visual to Runway XXR in ZZZ. Descending out of 9;000 feet in the right downwind of the ZZZZZ arrival we were then given a vector 'Turn right heading 030; descend and maintain 7;000 feet.' It was clear that the Controller was very busy and was working approach for three parallel landing runways with many inbound flights that morning. Our next instructions were; 'Turn right heading 090.' Shortly after the turn to the east we were assigned; 'Turn right heading 150 to join the [Runway] XXR LOC.' This last instruction was given a minute too late. It was already apparent that we were going to fly through the final approach course with parallel traffic joining up for [Runway] XXL. The Captain had been saying prior to this; 'Controller needs to gives us the turn... Controller needs to turn us already... we are going to fly through final.' Sure enough the turn was way too late and the aircraft automation was too slow to make the tight turn. The Captain immediately informed ATC that the vector was issued too late and that we would be flying through the final approach course and correcting west bound to rejoin. I disengaged the autopilot as the automation was not reacting fast enough to recapture the final approach course. ATC then issued us a 190 heading to rejoin the localizer and a traffic advisory to the aircraft that was flying the parallel; saying we were at their 3 o'clock same altitude and correcting west to rejoin [Runway] XXR LOC. Just seconds after the heading to rejoin was issued (We were already in the turn at this time) a TCAS Traffic Advisory went off due to the proximity of the aircraft on the [Runway] XXL parallel visual. Nothing further happened from this event. We were able to rejoin the [Runway] XXR LOC maintain 7000 feet until descent for landing was necessary and we completed a stabilized approach to landing.The cause of this event was due to task saturation for the Air Traffic Controller. Controller was working one approach frequency with dozens of aircraft needing vectors to final for the triple parallel visuals landing south at ZZZ. The automation lag didn't help when trying to join the LOC with the last second instructions however that was mostly mitigated by disconnecting the autopilot and hand flying a more abrupt turn to re-intercept and avoid further deviation.As a pilot (and never having been in to see a behind the scenes look at an ATC approach facility) I cannot tell you exactly what was going on or any; if at all; distractions may have existed behind the microphone at ZZZ Approach that morning. However; I can tell you based on my perception that the controller was talking non-stop with zero breaks between Controller and aircraft transmission and that Controller may have been overloaded during this event.

column121: On a vector to final; about 20 NM south of CLT; I observed the flight mode change from HDG to LNAV; then about 10 seconds later the flight director commanded a turn in the wrong direction. It starts with a vector to the intermediate approach course; arming the LNAV mode; and shortly after switching modes the computer steers the airplane across the approach course; over-corrects back in the opposite direction; and then chases the CDI to a normal alignment.This error in navigation; even though semi-random in frequency; is of such concern that I have been briefing the risk of TCAS activations and NTZ [No Transgression Zone] incursions that could be caused by this computer glitch. At this airport; it is fair to assume that there is always traffic on the simultaneous parallel course. Today; I briefed this possibility with the pilot flying while at cruise; and his reaction when it happened; although not as fast as mine; was understandable. He thought the turn was at first a subtle deviation in the direction of the final course.

I truly showed the aircraft side by side and waited as long as I could to climb to ensure I would clear Aircraft X; I thought I was legal. Choose the lesser of the evils. I wish I wouldn't have descended the Aircraft X to 070 either; but he read back the turn; I saw the turn start with the PTL and pushed him down because I needed to with Aircraft Y coming fast behind; and already being extended from Aircraft Z I had to break off in the earlier situation. column121: Good VFR day; cleared departure out of ZZZ to TEHRU; then direct MTJ. Just prior to TEHRU we informed the DEN Center controller that we would be requesting the ILS [Runway] 17 and was expecting to be vectored to the localizer. Instead; we were given 'direct DIRDY; Cross DIRDY at or above 13;000 feet; cleared for the ILS 17.'Loaded that into the MCDU; which inserted the procedure turn depicted to the north; after BRUUK. As the track from GEJYU to BRUUK is 78 degrees off the localizer course we figured this was the only 'legal' way to fly it; based on our clearance; so wasn't surprised. (Coming from the west side of the localizer there is a DME arc with a lead-in radial depicted to account for that steep angle; but not from the east. Again; we assumed the procedure turn was the only legal way to turn onto the localizer.)Although the crossing altitude for GEJYU is 10;800 feet the initial procedure turn altitude is 12;500 feet so we crossed GEJYU somewhere above 13;000 feet on our descent to 12;500 feet. Unfortunately; when we visually picked up the airport this made us too high to ask for a visual approach so we decided to just fly the procedure turn; as planned.After becoming established in the procedure turn outbound; the Controller asked us what we were doing and said most flights just join the localizer and go directly toward the runway. After some back-and-forth about this; while we were in the turn back toward BRUUK; he said 'low altitude alert; climb and maintain 13;000 [feet]' (we were still at 12;500 [feet]; and VFR). We climbed to 13;000 feet; called the runway in sight; and were cleared for the visual approach.Long story short(er); there was obvious confusion on our part regarding how this approach was supposed to be flown; as well as; I believe; based on our conversation; the Controller's. After landing we looked over the chart for 5-10 minutes; looking at all the various notes; etc.; before finally noticing the 'NoPT' note depicted under the 9;000 feet MEA listed for the leg from GEJYU to BRUUK.I saw the altitude and NoPT but when looking at the routing in the FMS and the procedure turn altitude assumed it wasn't intended for flying the full approach. I also don't understand why we would expect to intercept a localizer from a 78-degree angle when; I believe; while being vectored to an intercept; the intercept heading given by ATC is required to be within 30 degrees of the localizer course. If we had flown the depicted track from GEJYU to BRUUK as apparently expected on this approach; I believe the airplane would have overshot the turn onto the localizer by at least 1-2 miles. As for the low altitude warning the airplane was flying the published procedure turn on altitude which would lead one to believe you were in protected airspace?

column121: This was the first leg of a 3-day trip and my 2nd trip in several months. I had not flown in several months due to COVID scheduling (but I have remained current with a PC simulator).  I was having difficulty in clearly hearing ATC and through the interphone in flight.  I was the pilot flying at the time of the event.  My First Officer has been enduring a highly antagonistic situation in the home life; which may have found its way to the flight deck; creating an unanticipated stressor.  My First Officer was distressed over these interactions; resulting in a secondary distraction.On approach; my First Officer (the pilot not flying) believed we were issued a clearance down to 2;400 feet and read back the misunderstood altitude of 2;400 feet.  I did not catch the altitude clearance.  Descending below 3;400 feet; ATC advised us of a low Altitude Alert and informed us that we were meant to be at 3;400 feet.  We apologized and explained it was a misheard clearance.  ATC asked us to climb back up to 3;400 feet and advised us we were still cleared for the approach.  We complied and continued without incident.We discussed as a crew the intention to submit a report that evening.  Being a bit rusty on operating in the physical environment and with the remainder of a 3-day to focus on (including a line check); I inadvertently forgot to write the report.  After our first 2 legs; I was scheduled to split from my First Officer to fly with a line check pilot (per my request prior to the trip) out of an abundance of caution; due to being out of the physical environment for so long.  It may be because we were no longer operating together that my First Officer and I forgot to submit our reports in a timely fashion (without having each other as a reminder).My job as a Captain is to ensure the aircraft is flown in a safe manner and that we comply with ATC instructions. The responsibility comes down to me to maintain total situational awareness in all phases of flight.  I became inadvertently disconnected from the communications loop as pilot flying.  This resulted in a breakdown of a good multi-crew concept; as well as an unsafe situation and unintentional deviation from ATC instruction.  I must remain more diligent and vigilant as a crew member in all aspects of flight; regardless of assigned duty in order to maintain safe and compliant operation.It is also imperative that I participate in SMS in a timely manner; consistent with company standards.  To be an effective team leader; it is also my duty to ensure my crew members take part in SMS.  This can only enhance safety for our colleagues and industry as a whole.  It was never my intention to neglect to submit a report; but unfortunately it was mistakenly forgotten.  I should make reminders for myself to stay on task with necessary reports.  In the future I may find it helpful to set reminders in my phone whenever issues like this arise.
column123: On approach to land; as the First Officer and PM for the leg; I responded to ATC's instruction to descend to 2;400 feet. column121: We had a charter flight to ASE. The passengers wanted to go to Aspen but the weather and winds prohibited us from going there. We filed a flight plan to RIL and proceeded. I was the flying pilot. About 30 minutes away we saw the weather in ASE had improved so that we could get in and out. We called ATC and let them know we wanted to make the change. We changed the destination in the FMS and started the new routing to ASE. At one point we had trouble loading the approach into the FMS and I allowed myself to get involved in fixing the FMS. We were given a descent to 13;000; but 12;000 got set in the altitude selector. We were in visual conditions and were looking for the field. passing 12;600 we were told by ATC that we needed to climb to 13;000 as the MSA in our area was 13;000. I began a climb back up When ATC call back and said climb now low altitude alert. While climbing We immediately called the field in sight and were given a clearance for a visual approach. The approach was stable and we landed without incident. As we were taxing in we were given a phone number to contact for a possible deviation. I called the Tower and gave them my name certificate number and contact phone number for their paperwork. I believe that being the flying pilot and allowing myself to get involved in an FMS issue distracted me from catching the wrong altitude being set in the altitude selector. Following company procedures of flying the aircraft while letting the non-flying pilot program the FMS would have allowed me to recognize the altitude error and correct it.
column123: We were filled into RIL airport but passengers wanted to get into ASE. The weather cleared out of Aspen so we changed flight plan to arrive into ASE. Resolved by getting back to altitude and calling airport in sight and cleared for the visual.

column121: The Deviation event occurred over or around the HLMET intersection on the LDA Runway 35 approach into Salt Lake City International. ATC instructions were to proceed direct to HLMET; Cross HLMET at 11;000; cleared for the approach. Somewhere just seconds before or after crossing HLMET I descended to an altitude of approximately 9;600 MSL. The altitude on approach after crossing HLMET is 10;000 MSL until crossing the nest fix PEDLE. However after becoming distracted (which I will explain later); I noticed my altitude got down to that approximately 9;600 MSL for which I knew was not right; and immediately began corrective action while simultaneously ATC queried my altitude and I made mention of correcting. I saw I was just passed HLMET and quickly climbed back up to the crossing altitude of 10;000 MSL. Shortly later the controller mentioned the possible pilot deviation may have led to a loss of separation; although no TA/RA's were issued by either aircraft. Here is where I want to bring to attention the possible safety issue as related to the situation and what resulted in me becoming distracted and task saturated. Starting at an ATC controller back before TRACON; which was Salt Lake Center and while on the QWENN 5 RNAV Arrival off the MLF VORTAC transition; I was left extremely high by the center controller; for which I was expecting to receive the 'Expect' crossing restriction at FRNZY intersection at 15;000 MSL on the chart. I could hear multiple aircraft in front of me getting the FRNZY at 15;000 MSL restriction; but also complaining of being left very high and possibly not being able to make it. As I started to see the FMS computer show a required 3;500 FPM decent to make that restriction; I thought I better ask the controller for a descent; however the frequency was congested and it took many more minutes until finally the controller just issued me to now cross FRNZY at 16;000 MSL and 250 KTS. I replied that I would do by best; but it would be tight to make. Mind you that this new altitude required my attention to reprogram the altitude into the FMS as I anticipated and setup for 15;000; and still it showed a required 3;800+FPM decent to make it. I immediately initiated the decent for which I used the VNAV mode in the FMS/autopilot to make the crossing; which also required idle power and the activation of the aircraft's speed brake system to induce drag to not over-speed in the decent. During the decent on the arrival there was also light to bordering on moderate rime icing in IMC and snow showers. When the engines are at idle power they do not produce enough bleed air to keep the Anti-Ice/De-Ice systems operating; for which I got warning that they were not being kept hot enough; so I was trying to introduce small amounts of power to try and get more bleed air flowing to those systems; all the while trying not to over-speed and setup for the instrument approach. Being single-pilot this induced a very high work load; which caused me to become task saturated and behind on preparing for the approach. After finally passing FRNZY at the 16;000 MSL altitude and still in icing conditions and IMC I was simultaneously passed to TRACON approach control which issued me the direct HLMET; cross at 11;000 MSL; cleared approach restriction. I continued the decent down out of 16;000 MSL to 11;000 MSL still using VNAV on the autopilot (more on that later). I noticed I was still nearing around idle power and adding what I could but was still having trouble keeping the speed under control and still behind on setting up the approach. Somewhere around 12;000 MSL I got an indication that the speed brake panels went down; even though I didn't select it. Wondering what happened I looked out the pilot side window at the wing and noticed they were in fact still up; just no longer indicating it in the cockpit. This distracted me; as I knew I needed them extended to maintain my speed and help to try and keep power up and bleed air flowing. It took mybrain a few moments to try and figure out what was going on as there is no abnormal procedure for that in the checklist. I decided to recycle the speed brake switch; for which they then operated normally (retracted and extended); and then gave all normal indications. Throughout that situation is when the altitude deviation occurred; as after I was confident there was not a problem with the speed brakes and they just needed a reset; I accidentally went through the 11;000 MSL attitude down to the approximately 9;600 MSL altitude. Upon speaking with Maintenance later on the ground they feel that the system was activated for so long throughout the decent continuously; they work trapping hydraulic pressure to hold it up; that logically that pressure must have bleed down some; causing them to blow in-trial/down just enough to give an indication in the cockpit that they were sent fully down; and that this was not a malfunction or cause for investigation for repair; especially since they functioned normally after the reset. The indication only looks for full up or full down deflection; so if they blew down a little due to reduction in trapped pressure; it made sense to them. Again they continued to function and indicated correctly the rest of the flight. Back to the VNAV function I used on the autopilot to meet the crossing restriction; as that is the recommended function to meet crossing restrictions; and the function I always use to reduce pilot workload. Somewhere during the sequence of the approximate 3;800-4;000FPM required descent the VNAV system apparently kicked off and defaulted back to just a raw pitch autopilot decent; in which with everything else going on I failed to notice. I can only attribute this to it not liking or taking issue with that rapid of a required decent; and thus defaulted out of it. With 1500+ hours in type; I cannot recall ever descending so rapidly; to were I would have seen or noticed its inability to function through that rapid of a decent. Had VNAV stayed activated; it would have saved the deviation from happening as the approach was loaded with all crossing restriction altitudes and it would have followed them; for which I was also expecting it to do. Although this 'event' happened in Tracon airspace; I feel the safety issue started back in Salt Lake Centers airspace by being left very high on the arrival. ATC needs to be cognizant especially when icing conditions are possible/present some or most aircraft cannot descend that rapidly and keep critical anti-ice/de-ice systems operating properly with idle power descent. Additionally; giving instruction to meet a crossing restriction that requires 3;500+FPM descents is unsafe and not conducive to being able to setup and properly execute a stabilized approach; and leads pilots to get behind. After giving this event thought I am recommending to our flight department to not use the VNAV function of the FMS/autopilot for required descents over 3;000 FPM; but rather use vertical speed mode and monitor carefully. In addition; we will no longer accept any crossing restrictions from ATC that would require over 3;000 FPM; and rather state unable and require a re-sequence back on the arrival via a course reversal to help lose altitude and keep from the pilot getting behind the aircraft and task saturated. Us pilot use the term 'slam dunk' when ATC tries to do this; where they keep you very high and then plop you right on the arrival/approach. This condition does present safety issues due to the above mentioned items.

column121: I was training a Controller on the sector. He gave a descent to an aircraft from 4;000 feet down to 3;000 feet. When the pilot read it back multiple aircraft keyed up at the same time. One of them was the correct pilot; another was another aircraft checking in; and the third was a C17 that thought the transmission was for him to descend to 2;000 feet. The Controller gave the instruction very clearly; and the descent was to a different aircraft to a different altitude. When the pilot called later he said that he always gets a decent to 2;000 feet there so he thought that's what the call was. When [the C17] descended to 2;000 feet that dropped him into a 2;000 foot (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). The altitude was recognized but not before penetrating a 2;500 foot MVA. A climb was issued and the pilot said he could maintain his own terrain and obstruction clearance. But that was after the MVA was already violated. It was obvious when the altitude read back was happening that more than one aircraft were keying up; it wasn't obvious that 3 were. Let alone an aircraft with a very different call sign descending to a very different altitude. This was a pretty clear case of expectation bias. The pilot was made aware of the situation. He said it was a very clear VFR day so he saw all the terrain just fine; and he just thought that is where aircraft got their descent to 2;000 feet.

column121: Aircraft X was holding at 4;000 feet at the missed approach fix (and also initial approach fix) for several instrument approaches at. They had already executed the Missed Approach Procedure once because of weather below minimums. The pilot advised me that they wanted to try again. Since they were already established in a holding pattern published for the ILS approach; I cleared them for the ILS approach and issued the altimeter.The procedure is clear that the only route of flight allowable from holding is via the 10 DME arc to a straight-in course on the localizer. That is what I expected them to fly. I quickly redirected my attention to a sequence of three other aircraft I was trying to shoot a gap with; through a band of weather. At the same time; I had another arrival that was opposite direction; outbound from the same gap. When I was able to finally scan back to Aircraft X I noticed that they were not on the 10 DME arc; and had strayed into a 4;000 foot Minimum IFR Altitude at 3;000 feet. My first thought was that they decided to shoot a different approach; but when queried; the pilot responded that they still planned the ILS. However; their current position did not correlate to any possible point on the Approach.When questioned further; the pilot said that they were direct to a fix to intercept the localizer. They had received neither a direct clearance nor a descent clearance. Without any more questioning; I informed them that the Minimum Vectoring Altitude (technically minimum IFR altitude) in that area is 4;000 feet; and issued a 'cancel approach clearance' and 'climb immediately; maintain 4;000 feet.' The MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) did not activate. Because there was no audible alarm; and the fact that I knew 3.000 feet was still a safe altitude; I chose to not use the 'low altitude alert' portion of the phraseology. Later; after discussion with; and as recommended by the Operations Manager; I issued a warning to the pilot.Because this occurrence was a pilot deviation; there is not much from the ATC perspective that would have changed the outcome. Undoubtedly; the pilots' workload was high; due to the missed approach and bad weather. The design of the approach is also somewhat complicated because there are variations including the arc; published holding; and an outbound course on the localizer (which they apparently wanted to fly); but they don't all connect logically. However; the pilots should've queried if unsure.

column121: As pilot monitoring; I was handling the radios. Center cleared us for the 'RNDRZ 1 arrival Runway 26L' which I read back. We had set up for that arrival and runway; validated it; and briefed it thoroughly to include the issues with turning early if cleared for the visual which presented a terrain problem. Upon selection of the Runway 26L runway and the RNDRZ 1 arrival in the box; the aircraft automatically selected the Runway 26L transition which we understood we were cleared for. The Captain and I both verified with the other that we were cleared for the transition and we agreed that what the box presented to us was what we were cleared for. At the waypoint BERBN the jet turned onto the Runway 26L transition as planned. We received a radio call to turn back to a 130 heading and then given subsequent vectors to final and landed without incident. We were told by ATC that we should not have turned onto the transition. Looking back over the arrival and approach plates again and again; I still think we did what we were cleared for. If receiving the clearance for the 'RNDRZ 1 Runway 26L' doesn't mean clearance for the Runway 26L transition I'm not sure what does. Such verbiage at other airports indicates clearance onto the transition. The arrival plate is confusing however because at BERBN it directs the reader to 2 different things at once. It directs the reader to the Runway 26L transition found on the approach plate and also the possibility of continuing on the present heading to expect vectors to final. Even with that; to be cleared for the arrival and runway has always meant cleared for that runway's transition. Furthermore; the transition does not connect with the approach to Runway 26L giving greater weight to the fact that one need not be cleared for an approach to be cleared for the transition. I believe the Captain and I did exactly what we were cleared to do and that our understanding of that clearance corresponds to our experience and training.Causal factors were incorrect chart depiction and the aircraft navigational system automatically linking the Runway 26L transition when that arrival and runway are selected.Chart needs to be revised to make clear when the transition is to be used and when not. The aircraft navigation system needs to be updated to reflect how ATC wants the approach flown.

ZZZZZ1 departure. There was a fair amount of turbulence due to the strong westerly winds flowing over the mountains. On the departure you are supposed to cross the fix ZZZZZ2 below 10;000 feet MSL. We were climbing in VNAV Path and the FO was hand flying. We ended up going thru 10;000 to approximately 10;400 feet MSL due to VNAV not commanding the FD to level off. As the FO who was the PF was returning to 10;000 feet MSL the Controller told us to level off at 10;000 feet MSL; which we were already doing. It was clear and VMC at this time. There were no targets on TCAS and nothing was said about any loss of separation. I immediately rechecked the box to ensure the departure was there and the rest of the altitude constraints were correct; which they were. The flight continued to ZZZ2 uneventful and nothing else was said by the Controller.Last minute runway change was a contributing factor as we more thoroughly briefed the Runway X departure at the gate. The moderate turbulence on departure affected aircraft controllability and instrument scan. The fact that we departed from a field elevation of XXXX feet MSL and 10;000 feet MSL came a lot quicker than normal (flying from home base). The fact had I recently transitioned to the aircraft and have only flown less than 50 hrs since October 2020 and often go 2-4 weeks without flying.   Another contributing factor is my lack of HUD experience and the division of duties when looking thru the HUD but not having any navigational information presented on the HUD. Long sit time in ZZZ Departure airport.Take more time to rebrief a departure after runway change. Emphasize the high field elevation and how much quicker we will be at 10;000 feet MSL than what we are typically used to flying out of ZZZ1. Use the HUD for the takeoff but develop a better scan with the navigational display to enhance situational awareness on a departure procedure. Consider the use of a higher level of automation to reduce workload in turbulent conditions.

column121: We were cruising at FL390 and we called the back for a break. I was the second pilot to exit the flight deck and while in the main cabin I noticed the pitch of the aircraft.  I then made a brief break and called to return to the flight deck.  Once the flight deck door opened and the A came out I noticed the thrust levers advancing to max power and the airspeed indicator slowly approaching the amber band.  I then immediately called for a lower altitude as I took my seat and once I was in my seat I looked at my First Officer and said we need lower now.  My First Officer then dialed a lower altitude on the FMC and selected descent via V/S (Vertical Speed). I then gathered all info on what we were experiencing and thought either we had an unreliable airspeed or runaway stabilizer.  As I looked back at our altitude; I realized we weren't descending and our airspeed was slowly approaching amber pole.  At that time I disconnected A/T (Autothrottle); A/P (Autopilot) and started a slow descent and requested my First Officer to call in our descent to ATC.  ATC then notified us that we needed to stop descent at FL370 due to lower aircraft.  My training kicked in and I figured if this went back we would need around 10;000 feet to recover so I then requested a vector off course.  We then were given 10 degrees left and I leveled off at FL370 continued to hand fly and one by one acquired A/P; HDG; VNAV.  Our Airspeed gained approximately 30kts and we were stable at FL370 on a heading.  ATC asked why the need to descend and I replied we encountered mountain wave and could not hold altitude. ATC then replied that we were the first to complain of mountain wave. Seconds later an aircraft at FL470 notified of +/- 1000 gain/loss and another airliner requesting lower due to mountain wave. We were then given direct to a waypoint on our flight plan and landed at destination without further incident. Be more vigilant while single pilot operations.

column121: Somewhere after Burns Flat (BFV) at 38;000 ft. and until ZUN VOR; we had encountered first an ATC Fault EICAS message. Oddly then on both transponders. First Officer was the Pilot Flying. So; we discussed and went into the QRH and complied. I had then though to ask ABQ ARTCC if they were able to see us on their radar scope. The controller had replied yes. So when I remarked of our issue; he knew right away that jamming was taking place. Now I didn't clarify if this was any kind of military exercise and if this was normal. He acted as though it was. Shortly after this; we started slowly seeing other EICAS messages. I can't remember the exact order though. I believe the next was EGPWS TERR or so. Then L GPS appeared not too far after this. Maybe R GPS as well; maybe. Eventually we saw UNABLE RNP. So we definitely knew GPS jamming was making sense. The RNP ANP scales on the Pilot Flying Display bottom was like RNP 2.00 ANP 2.93 in amber color. It was clear our GPS was in an inertial mode. I did select radio updating eventually per the QRH's procedural instructions. Center never seem too concerned as nothing else was said. The weather was quite good and while concerned; I had a good idea as we made our way towards ZZZ1; the start of the RNAV star; the GPS navigation would probably return to a normal state and it did. There wasn't any flight safety breaches or traffics conflicts as this event happened entered at cruise. Although; I did forget to make a maintenance log entry required by mandatory reports. I may have been more fatigued than I was aware. Sleep was fragmented in chunks of multiple 2 to 3 or so hrs. on this day. Intentional GPS jamming I suppose. I've never encountered this in my entire career here. Wondering if the military does these exercises; but I would expect we'd be notified via a NOTAM and on our [flight plan] if it was known. I suppose if we knew we could of had a different routing? I don't believe compromised safety as in this case was an issue. It never degraded to a more severe off course deviation and didn't cause traffic conflicts. Don't get me wrong we were concerned and a bit miffed. I will file a security report and read more on the subject of GPS jamming interference's.

column121: Descending into ZZZ; we received an RA from a VFR traffic crossing our path below us at approximately 5;500 ft. MSL. We were descending to initially 3;000 ft. MSL to setup for landing on Runway XX (VMC conditions prevailed and the ATIS advertised a visual to Runway XX); but then were told to maintain 6;000 ft. MSL by Center for VFR traffic she was not talking to in our path. Hearing and seeing this scenario develop we shallowed our descent rate to level at 6;000 ft. MSL in an attempt to mitigate a predictive RA scenario. Once level and seeing the traffic was continuing in our direction; we also attempted a turn to avoid the traffic prior to the RA; however the frequency was congested and the turn was too late. Once we received permission to turn and initiated it; we ended up receiving the RA. We complied with the RA; disengaged the autopilot; and also climbed to approximately 6;500 ft. MSL to avoid the traffic showing at one point 400 ft. below us and advised Center of the RA. We were given permission to climb and; once clear of the conflict; to proceed to ZZZ without further issue.The event occurred due to a few factors coming together. The main issue is that the VFR aircraft was maneuvering without talking to ATC so as to avoid traffic. It was also a beautiful day; so there was a lot of GA aircraft the Controller was working with causing the frequency to become very congested. Secondly; the Controller should have issued us a vector or higher altitude to maintain to avoid the traffic as we never had or called aircraft in sight. We could have tried to turn earlier; but the congestion on the frequency prevented this from happening as well.I feel that this issue could have been prevented had the Controller issued us a higher level off altitude; or given us a vector once it was determined that the VFR target could become an issue. I feel that we tried our best to avoid this scenario by shallowing our descent and even requesting a turn. It just came down to the VFR traffic had an unpredictable flight path; the frequency was very congested; and once we received our clearance to turn it was too late.

Prior to this we were given delete speeds and at some point; I think we were assigned 210 knots.  Weather was clear VMC.  We were looking for traffic.  At some point traffic was called to us. ATC asked us if we were turning and then asked if we could land.In the 10 months preceding this incident; I have 18 hours of block time.  I have 2 hours of block time in the last 90 days. column123: Arrival into ZZZ during daytime VFR conditions with excellent visibility. Our FMC was programmed for the arrival as well as the RNAV RNP Z to XXR with the transition at ZZZZZ intersection. Our primary error was that we did not close the FMC discontinuity between the arrival and the approach. The result was that we overflew ZZZZZ1 intersection and corrected immediately after recognizing that we were not turning at the appropriate time. In hindsight it appears that multiple distractions contributed to our failure to remove the discontinuity. The change in speed assignments as well as a request by the Controller to watch for Aircraft Y traffic on a parallel runway and the timing associated with the issuance of our approach clearance.We were able to visually identify the Aircraft Y parallel traffic and kept visual separation. Once established on the extended runway centerline we received TA/RA warnings associated with the proximity of the Aircraft Y on XXL.  Also; there was never any indication that our aircraft deviated laterally of the extended runway centerline that would have compromised separation.Immediately after arrival at the gate I called approach control to discuss the late turn on the approach. (I was not asked to call.) I requested to speak with a Supervisor and we had a 5-10 minute discussion. I was told there was 'nothing on their end' in the way of a complaint. We also had an additional discussion about the traffic advisories associated with our approach given the close proximity of parallel traffic.One of the challenges of flying into ZZZ is that we typically are issued our runway assignment; approach; and transition in the latter stage of our arrival. Also; once issued; it seems to be relatively common to be reassigned to yet another runway; approach and transition. It is also common to receive speed modifications on the arrival.We were prepared for the RNAV Z to XXR and per company procedure we had the default arrival transition programmed. In hindsight I believe that if our clearance to fly the approach had come earlier in the arrival phase (when we had less distractions) that we would have been more likely to close the link between the arrival and approach and avoid our error.

column121: This flight was a planned departure from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  Weather was overcast; rainy with relatively calm winds and temperatures decreased during preflight from around 10C to 4C prior to departure. Pushback was delayed due to ramp congestion but only delayed takeoff slightly.  The Captain was operating as Pilot Flying (PF) for this flight.  The First Officer was Pilot Monitoring (PM).  Takeoff was uneventful. The departure was flown autopilot off.  While heading toward ZZZZZ and climbing at 280 KIAS; sometime after passing FL180 and climbing to FL230 in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC); Boeing 737-800 aircraft experienced extreme airspeed indicator swings on both sides of the cockpit.  Indications wildly fluctuated between 300 KIAS down to 180 KIAS.  The PF asked the PM if his indications were normal and the PM responded that his indications appeared erroneous as well and he had an airspeed disagree indication. The pitot heat was verified ON. The autothrottles started to chase the airspeed fluctuations and were subsequently turned off.  PF maintained the climb power and pitch angle and asked the PM to get a higher altitude from ATC.  ATC responded with a 'standby for higher' response.  The PM attempted to select Vertical Speed and it would not engage.  All vertical guidance was unavailable.  The PF asked the PM for a groundspeed and the PM responded that he did not see one.  There was no groundspeed on the Captain's (PF) side as well.  The Standby Flight Instruments were difficult to read as they had been dimmed for the takeoff and now the sun was coming up. Simultaneously; we were approaching a turn from ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1.  PF elected to maintain wings level and continued straight ahead as to not compound the problem by turning in IMC conditions with obvious airspeed errors.  Since the sun was just rising we could see the top of the weather was very close. As we approached FL230 we continued to climb and notified ATC.  ATC cleared us to FL380.  After reaching an altitude; probably FL240/FL250 in Visual Meteorological Conditions (VMC) the aircraft returned to nominal limits.  The flight continued under VMC to ZZZ1.  The aircraft flew normally after the event and landed safely.  Discrepancies were noted in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) and maintenance personnel were debriefed by the Captain. Recommend a third air data inertial reference unit (ADIRU) on the B-737 so the bad ADIRU can be removed from the equation during a failure and still have a comparator feature.
column123: Early morning departure out of ZZZ to ZZZ1. During climbout on the SID just after passing through the transition through FL180 I noticed we had lost the flight director and a yellow 'speed disagree' flag on the PFD (Primary Flight Display). I then looked at the MCP and VNAV/LNAV was off. Tried to re-engage and it wouldn't due to the PFD flag. About that time I noticed the speed had dropped from 280 KIAS to about 260 KIAS and we were off course having missed a slight turn on the SID. The Captain then said his was not right and asked me what mine said. I had said mine didn't seem correct either. Then he asked me what our ground speed was and I looked and mine was blank; not showing and wind/GS/TAS. At that time I told Center that we were having a problem with our instruments since we were off course and altitude. He came back and gave us present heading and FL230. The Captain then asked me to see if we could continue our climb since we weren't far from being on top of the weather; I asked and was told to stand by. A few seconds later Center gave us FL380. At this time I notified ATC having noticed we were getting further off our heading and the situation was getting worse. As we started to climb everything came back; air speeds matched; flag went away; was able to re engage LNAV/VNAV and flight directors. Few seconds after that we were on top in VMC. Everything came back just as quickly as we lost it. We were cleared to our next fix and resumed normal operations. We discussed our options and mutually decided that since there was clear weather for the rest of the way to ZZZ1 and everything was working that it was best to continue rather than turn back into the weather and return to ZZZ. The rest of the flight was uneventful and sent an ACARS message to let Maintenance know we would be writing the aircraft up when we landed. We landed in ZZZ1 and the Captain made the entry in the logbook when we got to the gate.

column121: There were storms in the area; and we were given a reroute by ATC; to go south to the coast; and then follow the coast west to IAH. The FO (First Officer; Pilot Monitoring) had made a passenger announcement telling them that we were expecting storms along the route of flight; and that we were anticipating a bumpy ride. I; the CP (Captain; Pilot Flying); had advised the FA that it was going to be bumpy. In the climb out; we encountered light turbulence. Upon reaching cruising altitude of FL280; it was smooth; so we briefly let the passengers up. Upon reaching the coast; ATC advised us of multiple storms and cells along our route of flight; and had mentioned that several aircraft ahead of us had gone south of these storms; had stayed within 50 NM of the coast; and had reported nothing worse than light turbulence; and advised we do the same. After discussing with the FO; we agreed that flying south of our route; and staying within 50 NM of the coast; was our best option. At this time; I had my radar up; and the FO had his terrain map up. We advised the passengers and the FA to expect a few bumps; turned the seat belt sign back on; and to remain seated. We also decided to slow to turbulence penetration speed. We were painting multiple red and magenta cells which we were staying south of; and had a lot of green all over the radar. We were dodging and avoiding the cells to the north; while staying within the 50 NM range of the coast. We then must have hit an embedded cell that the radar did not pick up; as it was only reading green. Almost instantly; we went into severe turbulence; and lost approximately 400 feet. The aircraft did not go into any unusual or upset attitudes; and the Auto-Pilot remained on. During this turbulence; we also had a suspected lightning strike - we saw a flash of light all around us; heard a bang; and smelt the 'fireworks' smell that you usually smell associated with lightning. After being struck; we got a Stall Protection System advanced master caution message appear. It disappeared within 5 seconds of it showing. As quick as the severe turbulence hit us; it disappeared. ATC queried us regarding our loss of altitude; at which point the FO reported the severe turbulence and suspected lightning strike. ATC asked if we needed further assistance; to which we replied no. As previously mentioned; this happened very quickly. All in all; I would say it lasted no longer than 30 seconds; and closer to 20 seconds. Once we were back at FL280; we had completely exited all weather (which we had been in for a majority of the time upon reaching the coast); and were in clear blue skies. I spoke to the FA; and asked if she was OK; to which she replied she was. She then asked if it was OK for her to check on the passengers; which she did. There were no injuries; and the only thing she mentioned is that the passengers were staring at her wide eyed. ATC asked if there were any injuries onboard; we replied with none. The flight continued with no further incidents. Upon landing; both pilots thoroughly inspected the outside of the plane on the walk around; noting a black mark on the right side of the nose which may be the entry point to the suspected lightning strike; but with no damage seen. I wrote up the plane with 3 write ups - Severe turbulence; Lightning strike; and Lock out/Tag out installed.CRM was effectively utilized during this event; with the PF using the radar; and the PM using the terrain. With the information available to us at the time; with ATC advising us of going south of the cells; as opposed to north; the decision; at the time; to go south was the correct one. That being said; I think it would have been smarter to go north of the cells; but we did not have that information. Utilizing the radar was key during this event; by staying out of the red and magenta cells. However; the radar has its limitation; especially considering they are older pieces of equipment; and can not 100% accurately paint embedded cells; of which we hit. After the event; ATC began recommending to other aircraft to go north of the cells. Ultimately; I would say the crew were stuck between a rock and a hard place - staying within the 50 NM boundary of the coast; but staying as far south as possible of the mega cells to the north. Additionally; I would like to mention the extraordinary job that the company did after the incident. Upon reaching the gate; multiple members of both [safety teams] reached out to me and the crew; checking that we were OK; and that the passengers were OK. I feel our company truly encompassed themselves with the company values; of which we stand for; and has made me thoroughly proud and joyful to be a part of.

column121: While in cruise at 35;000 feet and in excess of 90 knots of wind from the tail; the flight had been in constant light and occasionally moderate chop. I requested 37;000 feet after confirming performance capability; and hearing ATC advice that higher altitudes were better than lower and the closer we got to 40;000 feet the better the ride. We were told 'Aircraft X; I have your request' and we were handed off to three subsequent controllers each assuring us that the next would assign our climb. Both PM (Pilot Monitoring) and PF (Pilot Flying) recognized the flight path was taking us directly into a cloud bank; and the turbulence levels were becoming more of a solid moderate chop. As a result; PM (the Captain) advised the Cabin Crew to secure themselves and instructed the passengers to take their seats and securely fasten their seat belts. This event took place less than 10 minutes from entry into extreme turbulence.On the last handover; we had a converging aircraft 1;000 feet above us and traveling in the opposite direction. When ATC called the traffic for each of us; we were just entering the cloud bank into IMC conditions. Almost immediately; we encountered an increase in turbulence to solid moderate (changes in aircraft attitude and altitude occurred; but the aircraft remained in positive control). However; within seconds; we encountered severe turbulence including large abrupt changes in altitude; attitude; airspeed; as well as wind shear and updrafts. The result was initially a traffic alert. Within a few more seconds; we were in extreme turbulence and the aircraft was being tossed about violently; control was practically impossible; and the aircraft was being pushed upwards.The PM called the increase in speed and retarded the thrust levers as the aircraft was being shaken so violently that it took both hands of the PF to maintain positive control. Then a TCAS RA alerted us with a 'LEVEL OFF' command with the converging traffic icon in the PFD illuminated yellow. Almost immediately after; the icon turned red and PF pressed the FORCE TRIM INTERRUPT" button and shoved the yoke forward into the RA box to comply with the given guidance. The turbulence continued so violently that the autopilot was fully kicked offline; and the aircraft remained in a diving attitude per the TCAS guidance.During this period; and as a result of the wind shear and turbulence; the aircraft's speed fluctuated between a momentary illumination of the green PLI (Pitch Limit Indicator) and the triggering speed for a stick shaker activation. PM continued to apply speed brake and retard thrust levers to maintain the aircraft speed within limit (at no time did we encounter either a yellow or red PLI; or the stick shaker). At 30;500 feet we came out of the most violent turbulence and were able to reestablish a climb back to assigned altitude. Immediately after; the Captain contacted the cabin crew for an evaluation on any injuries or known damage. Beyond all the drinks and unsecured items being thrown around; none were reported; so we continued to the assigned destination. After landing; the post flight walk around revealed what appeared to be abnormal alignment or misalignment on the right outboard aileron."

column121: Turning final ZZZZ fully configured at 150 knots I armed the Localizer first than the Approach mode. First Officer inquired and received the landing clearance. I noticed that the glide slope didn't capture and that we were going above the path. I tried to descend in Vertical Speed; but it didn't come active; so it wouldn't work. Approach mode light still on. I disconnected the Autopilot; lowered the nose and started a descend using the VGSI (Visual Glideslope) path indicator and the outside PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator). During the descent we tried to reset the Approach/Glideslope unsuccessfully. The approach was pretty bumpy with some good downdrafts. The aircraft went below the glide slope and I started to correct back when the pull up warning came on then stopped right away. Then the glide slope warning followed. I was just under the path recovering and had 3 red lights and 1 white on the PAPI. Speed around 10 knots above Vref and decreasing toward Vref. I was very focused on the approach and continued to an uneventful normal landing.We were configured early; ready for approach; but the Glideslope not capturing and the uncertainty concerning the landing clearance created a distraction that put me behind the aircraft and I developed some tunnel vision trying to remedy the approach. I became fixated and continued when I should have discontinued the approach and gone around. After landing the First Officer said to me that she had mentioned going around; but it hadn't registered with me during the approach. I tell First Officers that there is no mission; but today I didn't follow my own advice. It's easy to become over focused without realizing it. When in doubt; go-around.
column123: The event began while beginning the ILS Approach. The company notes on the approach dictate not to arm the ILS until reaching a certain position because of the possibility of false localizer signals. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring.  I remember thinking that the Pilot Flying armed the approach later than I would have since we were well beyond the designated point. My best guess on what happened is that because of the delay the localizer armed but the glideslope never captured because we were already too high. Whatever the reason for the automation not doing what we had expected; the result was that we realized that the Glideslope never captured and were trying to get the aircraft to come down.Not only were we distracted with being above the intended glide path; but we were handed over to tower late and I was busy with getting clearance to land while the Pilot Flying was flying the plane trying to get back to a stabilized approach. As the aircraft was getting back to a normal glide path (3 red; 1 white on PAPI) around the 500 foot mark I gave my stabilized approach callout and realizing we were slightly above speed and correcting; but the vertical speed exceeded what is acceptable. At this point I said 'I think we should go around'. I can't remember if it was just before or after I said this that we got a 'PULL UP' alert. The Captain elected to continue the landing. Later after discussion; I learned he may have had tunnel vision to the point where my go around call didn't register with him.My unfamiliarity with ZZZZ did not help our situational awareness as well as being distracted with getting switched over to tower (late) and attempting to get landing clearance around the same time we realized the automation did not perform as expected. As a FO/PM not being assertive enough when a go-around was needed.Abiding by company SOP to the letter. No matter what; at 500 feet if stabilized approach criteria aren't met; it's an automatic and firm 'GO AROUND'.

column121: I had just assumed responsibility of the position about a minute prior when the pilot of Aircraft X informed me that they were 'Over HOMAI; what do you want?' The previous controller; still observing the 2-minute overlap; confirmed what she stated in the relief briefing; that Aircraft X had been assigned direct HOMAI; which ties into their flight plan routing of the LNDHY1 STAR into OGG. I responded to the pilot that he should track outbound of HOMAI on the LNDHY1 arrival; which publishes a 204 degree track. The pilots were obviously confused; but began to correct. In the process of doing so; the aircraft may have clipped the boundary of a higher 6;300 ft. MVA. Aircraft X was level at 4;000 ft. in a 3;500 ft. MVA; and would have had no problems remaining so if they were established on the STAR. In an effort to salvage the situation; I asked the pilots if they had the airport in sight for a visual approach. They replied in the affirmative. Then I asked if they had traffic to follow in sight. They replied in the affirmative and I issued the visual approach clearance. The MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) did not activate and I did not issue a low altitude alert. The pilots did not question the 'direct HOMAI' clearance they received from the previous controller until they were about a half mile past the fix. If there was any question about their routing; they should've clarified much earlier. But the confusion is not infrequent; and I have had pilots question the routing before. The published STAR clearly shows a 204 degree track after HOMAI on both the visual layout and written description. When I state this fact to querying pilots; the confusion is resolved. But the lack of a fix after HOMAI may cause pilots to ignore the track; or (as some controllers suspect) cause the track to drop out of the FMS when an approach is pre-loaded. My recommendation is for another fix to be added on the 204 degree track after HOMAI; to resolve the confusion; and to help ensure that aircraft don't fly on a free heading toward a higher MVA.My other recommendation is to look into how the LNDHY1 STAR is being programmed into FMS displays; and whether the addition of a (yet to be assigned) approach (e.g. RNAV Z RWY 2 from HOMAI) erases or otherwise obfuscates the 204 degree track outbound of HOMAI.

column121: We were level 5;000 feet 250 knots approaching ZZZ VOR on the ZZZZZ2 Star. Approach gave a heading 280 and slow to 180 and asked if we had the field in sight.  We were heading 330 and I was thinking a turn to 350 was coming so 280 heading caught me a little off guard. I (FO) was pilot flying. The sun was just above the horizon as I looked west and across the cockpit for the field.  Simultaneously I was looking cross-cockpit and programing the speed and heading change into the FMC. I could make out the field so I said to the Captain (PM); 'I can see the field; you can call it in sight.'  I noticed another aircraft on TCAS at our altitude on TCAS and then saw them visually less than ten miles away; also headed west toward ZZZ [Airport]; I noted the  paint scheme and relayed to the PM all that information and that they were probably headed to the north side of the airport.  In my head I was thinking that our airplane was not slowing down as fast as I would like when the PM said 'where is that airplane; I think we need to turn.' I pushed the localizer button on the FMC but the airplane did not turn so I turned the autopilot off and manually turned to intercept final for [Runway] XXR. As I did; we received at TCAS TA then a few seconds later a TCAS RA to climb.  The ADI showed a red boxed area from level flight down (I was descending) so I just leveled off until we heard 'clear of conflict.'   Then Approach gave us a 180 heading; paused; and then said 'you guys can't do that;' and switched us to Tower.  I was able to correct the high energy level of the airplane using gear; flaps; and speed brakes and continued the approach and landed uneventfully.Fast close to the airfield; sun in eyes; failure on my part to use automation.Something from ATC that I was going to turn towards the runway instead of downwind in the [Runway] XXR pattern or an advisory where we were in the sequence.  My recency of experience led to not arming the localizer; while I did brief that at the start of the first leg I could have reemphasized it during the approach brief.

column121: Intended to land flaps 30 in windy conditions with add speed of 14 knots.  Visual approach on Visual Approach Slope indicator and slightly below ILS glide slope. We received a Ground Proximity Warning alert for 'too low terrain'. Rechecked landing gear was down and landed. We realized on very short final that flaps were actually set to 25 instead of 30. We did not select flaps to 30 since we were so low. With the extra speed we had added for the gusty winds; I felt we were safer to leave them set at 25 and land.
column123: While on final approach  we experienced a Ground Proximity Warning 'Too Low Terrain' aural warnings. Knowing that we were on glide slope and Precision Approach Path Indicator and the runway was in sight in VFR conditions; we decided to continue the landing. We ensured that the landing gear was down and that we were free of terrain; however; on short final the Captain noticed we were at flaps 25 instead of 30. It was decided to safely complete the landing since we were stable on speed and path. We already had built in a 14 knot wind additive for the windy conditions. The entire approach was stable including at the 500 foot 'Stable' call out point. I take responsibility for misreading the flap gauge; and will certainly give it more focus in the future. One potential factor; not an excuse; is there was the distraction of balloons going by our aircraft around the time of the landing checklist. I reported the balloons to Tampa Tower.

column121: On the ZZZZZ X arrival into ZZZ; we were given a descent to FL230.  As PF; I re-cruised for FL230.  Prior to ZZZZZ1 we were told to descend via the arrival.  I dialed in 6;000 feet for the Runway XXL approach.  Initially the descent point was visible and looked normal.  After flying several more minutes it became clear that we were past the descent point.  It was about this time that the descent point disappeared from the ND.  We started an immediate Open Descent with full speed brakes.  We were unable to get relief from the altitude/airspeed requirement at ZZZZZ2 (250/110) due to radio congestion.  We were given a frequency change and got relief from ZZZ Approach who gave us a descent to 6;000 feet which we accomplished.  The rest of the approach and landing was uneventful.  When the PF re-cruised he inadvertently typed in '320' instead of '230'.  There was not an immediate erroneous depiction on the ND.  Everything looked normal; however we continued past the descent point.  Just as we realized there was something wrong; the ND descent point disappeared.  The PF has been on reserve and has flown very little in the last two months.  The next two flights went well with no problems.The two pilots were on the first leg of the trip.  It was the first time they'd flow together.  They were working well together and both were attempting to follow policies/procedures.  This was a dumb mistake by one pilot that was not caught by the other.  By re-cruising; the goal was to have the ND provide usable descent point information.  I listed this as a 'Moderate' risk rating because we easily received relief from ATC.  If they had not assisted us; the risk would have been higher.
