We selected the ILS XXL in the FMC; and upon executing the selection; we received an Autopilot Disconnect message; and an A/P Disconnect Caution light. The aircraft went into Control Wheel Pitch. I; the Pilot Flying; immediately selected Vertical Speed to keep the aircraft in a state towards the impending crossing restriction. I also reset the Altitude Alerter for X;000 feet; as we now were in Vertical Speed and needed altitude protection at ZZZZZ2 [fix].A few seconds later we passed over ZZZZZ2. The Autopilot Disconnect Caution light illuminated; and the Autopilot Lateral Mode switched to Control Wheel Steering; and the aircraft didn't turn and follow the still illuminated and displayed LNAV PATH. I immediately engaged heading mode; and turned to rejoin our intended course. Approach gave us a heading; as the minor deviation from our path was most likely noticeable.  The rest of the flight proceeded uneventfully.  We assumed we programmed the FMC incorrectly; in some way; and we needed to be more vigilant.  ZZZ to ZZZ1 [airport]; we were on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV; Autopilot B engaged; on PATH. We were given an intercept heading to join final for [Runway] XX. Heading mode was selected. The aircraft flew heading and was in VNAV. The final approach course was entered into the FMC; and upon executing; the Autopilot B Vertical mode disengaged; with the A/P Caution light and the aircraft descended in Control Wheel Pitch.  We selected a pitch mode and proceeded without further incident.My concern:  I don't know why these disconnects happened. If they are normal for the -800 MAX; I am unaware of this. I thought all of our fleet types were programmed and responded to Pilot programming the same; in this scenario.  I've never experienced [other model] aircraft revert to CWS Pitch or roll; even with faulty Pilot programming.  We both assumed that perhaps; since neither of us had flown a MAX in a few years that we missed some training; or company notice.  We assumed that the error was a Pilot programming error.   I called the Chief Pilot on Call and told him of the occurrence the first time; and he was unaware of such a thing happening normally. We confessed that we actually had more experience than him in the MAX. He indicated I should call later and talk to the MAX programming expert and he perhaps could explain why the MAX behaves in this way. That is why we flew the aircraft a second leg with the anomaly; I assumed it was Pilot programming error.  A few days later; I was contacted by a Chief Pilot; who informed me that our experience was a malfunction; and that a logbook entry and maintenance resolution should have taken place.  I assumed it was a MAX anomaly; but it was a malfunction.

column121: Severe turbulence encounter on climb after departing.  We conducted a full and normal briefing in operations prior to the flight. During that briefing we identified a threat of possible turbulence around 20;000 feet based on a PIREP. Upon arriving at the plane; I briefed the lead Flight Attendant. That briefing included a discussion on turbulence. I directed that the Flight Attendants stay seated for the departure until I call. Ground operations through takeoff and climbout were normal and uneventful. Departure cleared us to 17;000 feet. We leveled there awaiting hand off to Center and were in light turbulence. After a short delay we were cleared to climb to approximately 25;000 feet and to contact Center. I initiated the climb via VNAV. Almost immediately we encountered severe turbulence. The airspeed was fluctuating and the plane banked +-25 AOB (Angle of Bank). The autopilot remained engaged and made appropriate corrections. However; I put my hands on the controls in anticipation of needing to take control. The ride was so violent that my First Officer could not get his hands on the radio knob to change frequencies. By 18;000 feet the ride eased to moderate turbulence. When I deemed it safe; I then picked up the PA and asked 'Flight Attendants check in.' They checked the cabin and reported all passenger; crew and plane were safe. The First Officer made the check in with Center; reported the severe turbulence.At an appropriate time; I notified dispatch of the event. He published our PIREP. Later we submitted the log entry for maintenance. Further down line ZZZ1 Station was notified and I discussed with them an appropriate response upon landing. The remainder of the flight was uneventful; not even a ripple of turbulence. Once blocked in and checklists completed; I greeted passengers in case any were still concerned. They all seemed very appreciative; and thankful. Many even commented on the smooth landing and offered thanks for a safe trip. Customer Service; Maintenance and Flight Operations and met us at the gate. I provided full debriefs to each. The flight operations manager said we did a great job but also advised we submit a safety report. I want to offer that I believe the system; Standard Operating Procedures; and tools made available work. While I could not foresee the severity of the turbulence that awaited us; we knew a rough ride would be encountered in that area and took precaution. The result was no injuries to crew or passengers or damage to the plane. I offer this report mostly to help improve the system. And I am happy to answer any questions if necessary.
column123: WSI (Weather Service International) indicated a narrow band of turbulence on our route from roughly 17;000 to 20;000 feet due to shear below a jet stream.  Larger jets reported moderate (PIREP symbols) turbulence on WSI so the Captain had the flight attendants remain seated after takeoff until we called them.  At the time of the event the seat belt sign was ON and everyone on the plane was seated.  As we climbed through 17;000 feet the turbulence worsened from moderate to severe.  Large and rapid airspeed deviations of +/- 25 knots and sharp rolling moments of roughly 25 to 30 degrees occurred for roughly 2 minutes; all estimates.  As Pilot Monitoring it took me awhile to tune the ATC radios for a frequency change as I couldn't grab the tuning knobs in the turbulence.  I believe ATC instructed us to climb from 17;000 to 19;000 feet and that put us into the worst of the turbulence.  Once we were cleared to climb higher (above 19;000 feet) the ride improved quickly.  I believe a hand off from TRACON to Center caused much of the delay but I am not certain.Again; the seat belt sign was on and all flight attendants were seated per the briefing.  No injuries and no damage.  We did not make the 'be seated immediately' announcements as everyone was still seated since takeoff.  We were focused on getting a higher altitude and a better ride. Once we were clear of the turbulence we asked the flight attendants to 'check in' per our turbulence training.  We filed a PIREP with ATC and notified Dispatch.

Shortly there after; Aircraft Y separated from the tanker without communicating to me; and what I assume was descending back to the fighter cap altitudes of FL230-FL240 of which he was initially cleared to be at. Aircraft Y turned at the southern portion and descended; and then I saw him at FL227 below his assigned altitude. Aircraft X; was at FL220 right underneath him. I immediately asked the pilot if he was FL230-FL240; he responded that he was. At the same time the altitudes on the data block went back to FL230-FL240. The Sector 19 Controller; who was working Sector 18's airspace (even thought Sector 18's airspace was assigned to me sitting physically at Sector 17); said that Aircraft X was responding to an RA and descended. I immediately called the traffic to the fighter jet at that time. Filed previous reports regarding the Presidential airspace over Delaware. Procedures are not defined; there is no LOA or SOP; and the workforce was not properly briefed. There are many sited violations FAA Orders associated with this unsafe operation in addition to automation issues that can cause unsafe situations with Sector 18 not being utilized correctly. Request an LOA for the procedures; and for the boundaries; altitudes; refueling operations; and reroutes to all be negotiated with affected parties and implemented correctly in an LOA. A fighter jet got too close to an airliner jet in this situation; and the pilot did not even seem to understand the issue or care. column121: Coming into IAD the errors started when we were intercepting the localizer for Runway 1R. I was the pilot monitoring and the FO (First Officer) was the pilot flying. Approach cleared us to intercept when we were basically already crossing the final approach course so we had to navigate back to the localizer on our own. At the same time we had been getting hit with some minor wake turbulence from the airplane ahead of us which Approach informed us was a Boeing 777. We were then cleared for the visual approach and advised of the caution for wake turbulence and to maintain 170 kts. until 5 miles out. At this time we configured gear down flaps 20. I had just recently had training in the sim for wake turbulence and remembered how dangerous it could be so I advised my FO to use caution and I believe I recommended maybe staying above their path since we had already hit a small portion of their wake prior when we were on downwind. He elected to turn the autopilot off and hand fly slightly above their glide path. We then continued down and around 100 ft. got a terrain warning. Our first reaction was this was because we weren't on glide path and the FO called out; 'visual; landing.' around 50 ft. we got another aural message stating 'too low terrain'; at this point I realized something was wrong and quickly scanned and noticed we were still at flaps 20. At this point I immediately called for a balked landing. The FO restated in a question; balked landing? I said yes and he immediately executed the maneuver. We advised ATC of the go around and they asked for the reasoning and I stated we were unstable. We continued the go around and came back to land on [Runway] 1R after some vectoring without further incident. To add to this and to summarize; we did not complete a landing checklist; we were not fully configured and were at gear down flaps 20 degrees; and our speed bug was still at 170 kts. We received a terrain aural warning that we misinterpreted followed by a second aural warning and executed a balked landing at a medium energy state with lower power setting but high airspeed. Our attention started deviating from standard starting with the poor intercept angle of the localizer. I further complicated the situation by over concentrating on the wake turbulence from the 777 and focusing too much on the FO's glide path and what I would call tunnel focusing on his flying. I believe my statements to him about the wake turbulence also led to distracting him from normal flight operations as well. He was talking through his thought process on staying a half dot high on the glide path and I was responding with statements like I agree; not necessarily breaking sterile cockpit but also causing more distraction on both of our parts. This was the first time that I had not completed a landing checklist. It has made me realize that while being aware of threats like wake turbulence is important; it's even more important to maintain a greater situational awareness and take a step back and not tunnel focus on one threat while other threats could arise. While I am glad we did not try to force a landing. This is a mistake I never thought would be possible or would happen to me. I have definitely learned a lot from this experience.

We continued climbing and turned further right (net 180 by then); while it appeared target was still at their previous altitude (now -700 thanks to our climb) and maintaining a roughly easterly heading but still in a right turn. After we continued our right turn (now heading west); I for the first time caught a visual on the other aircraft at roughly our 4:00 position and 700 feet below (where ADS-B said they were at that moment). They appeared to be still turning right; perhaps practicing 360s -- I don't know. In any case; we were continuing to put distance and altitude between us such that we resumed our northerly heading back to home airport without further incident other than perhaps a minute during which our altitude was 3;800 MSL -- not a legal VFR cruising altitude -- while we made sure the other aircraft was not trying to chase us. We were now overtaking a B777 ahead; so our approach clearance was canceled. We were given vectors for spacing and vectored back onto the localizer and then re-cleared the ILS 25L. Neither the First Officer no I recall hearing the 210 knot speed assignment. We had only heard 250 knots and read that back. The 210-knot speed assignment probably occurred about the time the Flight Attendant called us about the passenger feeling ill again and just as we hit the wake turbulence.
column123: A bunch of things happened at once which led to us missing a slower speed assignment. On the arrival to LAX; cleared the approach to 25L and told to maintain 250 knots. The gear was already up and the Captain; Pilot Monitoring; was just checking in with departure. Both of us weren't sure if we had hit a bird or something else. We had another rapid succession of three bursts with associated ECAM that almost instantaneously cleared the screen. The Captain quickly recognized the right engine (#2) indications were 'rolling back' and stated so clearly. He then ensure positive aircraft control by verbally stating; 'Your aircraft'. I responded with 'My aircraft'. The right engine ECAM message went away just as quickly as it displayed. The right engine then showed normal parameters and 'parallel' with the left engine. The Captain reviewed the Quick Reference Card and determined no action from the QRC required. He [advised] ATC while I simultaneously flew the aircraft on crosswind and turned downwind. The thrust levelers remained at CLB setting and flaps 1 on downwind with no other associated engine indications at approximately 2;500 feet MSL. We both agreed the best resolution was to land the aircraft ASAP. Our current weight was below max landing weight. I very quickly briefed a visual approach to Rwy XXR while the Captain loaded an approach in the FMGC. With gear down; I made the right turn on a base leg. I pushed the SPD button for managed speed as I thought we were in APPR Mode however; I quickly pulled the SPD button for selected speed once I noticed the engines were increase thrust for a higher speed. At this point we experienced one more rapid succession from the right engine which quickly resided again with speed now selected and winding back to approach speed. We configured final flap setting to 3 and briefed our potential go-around if required. The Captain successfully ensured our Descent and Before Landing checklist were completed with clearance to land. Upon a successful landing; the Captain ensured the passengers and crew were informed to remain seated while we taxied to the gate. ARFF did a complete review and temperature check of the engines with nothing significant to report. Noteworthy items...the aircraft was hand flown until downwind. Auto pilot was engaged briefly once at 2;500 feet MSL. The autopilot was disengaged when turning base leg and hand flown for the visual approach.Definitely a startle factor; particularly since it happened just above 1;000 feet AGL while thrust levels are normally set to CLB mode. Additionally; the initial confusion as to whether we had hit something (bird?) since the ECAM did not display an action. Furthermore; once the ECAM action did display it was nearly instantaneously gone as the engine continued to attempt to resolve the problem.Since ENG Stall isn't on the Checklist; this scenario could be used in future training events to increase awareness and action based on a low altitude scenario during take-off phase.

column121: I was working the Eagle Lake sector. Our area was getting all of the west arrivals as well as our normal arrivals due to weather. I had been coordinating with Houston Approach as to what was working best for them in terms of arrivals and how they wanted them situated since we could not get in on a normal flow. He had also indicated that all of the aircraft were deviating upon check in with him. At this point I told him I would take care of it.Because of the weather building and starting to slowly close in I shut our corner post off. We had about 15 inbound and in terms of safety and using my best judgment I thought it would be smoother and safer if we took everyone to the southeast corner post. After I had made the decision and told the supervisor this is when the issue really began. The Supervisor; along with TMU (Traffic Management Unit) did not like this plan. They specifically told us to continue pushing these aircraft through the weather because it 'Wasn't bad enough yet'. That is a complete and utter lack of regard for safety. The mentality at Houston Center is to push aircraft through as much weather as humanly possible until a pilot decides they physically cannot make it happen. This has been the mentality for years and needs to be corrected immediately. I cannot in good conscious work airplanes through an unsafe situation just because someone with a higher position than me thinks it's OK.Ultimately when I am on position the decision should be mine on what is safe and what isn't. I am the Controller talking to the pilots; getting PIREPs and watching the weather develop real time. No one in TMU is talking to airplanes real time. They do not know the flow of the sectors real time. Houston Center's TMU is ungodly bad. They have been for years. There is never a plan and the Controllers are the ones who suffer for it. This needs rectification immediately and needs to be taken to the top of the food chain. Its not a matter of if; but when something happens because of poor judgment on managements part. This needs to be taken very seriously. It has gone on this way for far too long.Management needs to listen to Controllers when they are being told something isn't working or something isn't safe. Yes; any Controller can make a bad plan work. That doesn't mean we necessarily should.This unsafe mentality of pushing aircraft to the limit through weather will result in a safety event and it needs to get fixed before that happens.

column121: This was not a good flight because of compounding errors that happened and the negative effect that they had.  The good part is that the flight remained safe; but here below are several things that I learned.  The events started when on decent into ZZZ when the lights on the autopilot mode selector began to flicker erratically; however the autopilot appeared to perform normally.  This was in IMC descent thru layers with occasional moderate turbulence.  (The was second flight after the power supply to the EFIS system failed resulting in loss of the primary attitude indicator and HSI which was repaired and return to service.  I mention this only because it attributed to my increase lack of trust in the flight instruments.) The autopilot was on altitude preselect with a vertical speed selected.  During the decent I was evaluating the autopilot issue and I think; after the fact; I pushed the altitude capture twice; resulting in me disengaging the capture and descending below the desired altitude.  At the time I attributed this to a malfunction autopilot and I decided to disconnect the autopilot and manually flew the plane.  This increased the workload.  Weather was also a significant factor.  There was a line of thunderstorms that were moving over ZZZ (destination) and I was watching the satellite radar utilizing a portable GDL52 communicating to Garmin pilot on my I pad. For this flight I was using ForeFlight for navigation/charts and Garmin Pilot for weather; because the GDL would not communicate satellite radar information to ForeFlight.  I have been using ForeFlight for charts and weather in previous aircraft for many years; but this aircraft has only ADSB-out and is scheduled to have an avionics upgrade to a GDL69a (sat WX) and Garmin 345 (ADSB IN/Out) installation in Month.  I was also utilizing the onboard radar; but am learning to use this system.  Bottom line was too many nav / weather systems in use that resulted in unnecessary and additional workload. Another factor was that I had transitioned from a piston to a turboprop and had about 80 hours in the TBM time at the time of this flight. So I was still low on the TBM experience curve.   Based on the weather I requested GPS XX and activated the approach on the 530s. However; as I proceeded to ZZZ GPS XX; the weather changed and the IAF for GPS XX was near the line of thunderstorms and center offered ILS XY and left turn to heading for the IAF - I made a right turn to that heading.  I should have recognized that I was starting to make small mistakes. During this time I also was varying from assigned altitude due to increase workload.   I entered ILS XX in to the 530S and activated and Center vectored me to the approach.   I began the approach and was able to see the ground occasionally.  I was handed off the Tower and I waited to capture the glideslope. I continued the approach; my position and altitude were not cross checking; and I began try to determine why.  I was high when I was on a 2-3 mile final.  While making this evaluation; I was able to see the runway lights and able to make a visual decent and landing.  I was not confident after this flight; there were too many mistakes in this flight.  When I was on the ground I contacted my flight instructor and went over flight and discussed the avionics and my reaction/ decision I made.  We made a plan of how to determine the effect of the flickering light on the mode selector and insure that it was safe for flight.  I altered my plans so that weather would have a minimal impact and returned back to ZZZ1.  To learn and avoid these errors in the future; I did a full debrief with my instructor when I return home.  This focused on both the avionics and cross reference that he recommended to determine status of the navigation system.  We also spent a considerable time on how I responded to the apparent situation and decision making.  It was at this time; I realized how much some minor errors in my part had a large impact onthe flight.  The avionics have also been evaluated by Company in ZZZ2 and determine that the malfunction was limited to the mode selector display and that the autopilot is functioning normally. It is schedule to be repaired.   Further I have also flow approaches in VFR conditions to verify operations of the navigation and autopilot systems and apply some of the procedures that my instructor and I discussed.

column121: IFR flight to ZZZ. Weather was not a factor. Departed PHX from Runway 7R; runway heading assigned. After approaching 1;000 feet AGL; assigned heading 050. Switched to Phoenix Departure on 119.2; then 120.7 within a minute or two. Controller gave me instructions to 'turn left heading 360; vectors to intercept the PXR 350 radial.' Knowing I was on a diverging path away from my flight-planned route; I was waiting for at least one more turn that would take me toward the radial. This turn occurred within the next few minutes with the controller saying 'turn left heading 270'. Now on an intercept heading with the radial; I made a right turn to join the PXR 350. The Departure Controller quickly gave me instructions to fly heading 260 (which I immediately complied with) asking why I had made the turn north. The remainder of the flight occurred without incident.In hindsight; here's what I learned during this exchange. Despite the numerous flight hours operating in the PHX ATC system; I somehow mistakenly interpreted 'intercept' with 'join'. I knew a 360 heading would not intercept the planned radial. So; I was expecting that next turn to put me on course to do so. What I wasn't told; was the 270 heading was for spacing from other traffic; not necessarily to intercept or join the PXR 350 radial. Had I known why (traffic) I was being turned to a 270 heading; then my thought process would've completely changed and I would've known; without question; to continue on the assigned heading. Instead; I was thinking this was simply the heading that would allow me to intercept the 350 radial. Despite my error; I should have questioned the heading as the intercept angle was 80 degrees; not the standard 30 degrees one would expect. In doing so; the Controller would have simply advised me to remain on the 270 heading and expect another turn to intercept and join the airway. As pilots; we must deal with many human factors on a daily basis. Some of those factors thwart our efforts to fly safe and reasonably. I feel this was a situation where 'if it doesn't look right or feels oddly different' then say something. Questions are always free. Accidents are costly. Routinely flying the same routes and hearing the same instructions from ATC can also create a unique set of issues. We don't always hear what was said; we hear what we expect. And this human factor is one that all pilots must concentrate on avoiding.

column121: There was a momentary unreliable airspeed followed by a brief failure of the PF's (Pilot Flying) PFD. Once the PFD was restored; airspeed was still momentarily unreliable.While operating the flight from ZZZ to ZZZZ; I was the pilot flying. After deviating for weather; we were proceeding directly to ZZZZZ to perform the VOR DME 2 [approach to] Runway XX at ZZZZ. Approximately 20nm from ZZZZZ and descending; we encountered IMC and light precipitation and light turbulence which gradually increased to moderate turbulence. We were partially configured at flaps 1 and gear was down at 200 kts and beginning our turn for the arc when my airspeed began having deviations of +/- 15 kts; I attributed this to the increasing turbulence and precipitation we had encountered. While banked and descending; the PLIs (Pitch Limit Indicator) presented and I had a loss of airspeed below the green dot and a gain of airspeed that presented amber digits. At this point my airspeed completely went away; as if I was on the ground; a grey box was present where the digits would be but there was no V-Speed information. Shortly after this occurred; my PFD went black for a moment; but never reverted to a different display. Once this happened; I transitioned to the IESS (Integrated Electronic Standby System); rolled the wings level; advanced the thrust levers; climbed to ensure terrain clearance; and we returned to VMC.Nearly immediately after establishing the climb; the PFD and all information on it returned; although there were errors with the airspeed. Initially; the airspeed showed faster than we were; as if we had been repositioned in the simulator; and we received one aural 'High-speed' until the airspeed settled back to what the IESS was showing. Our altitude at this point was approximately between 17;000 ft. and 16;000 ft. with a high peak around 9827 ft. in our vicinity. From our descent; I knew I could find VMC around 19;000 ft. so I directed the pilot not flying to tell ATC we would be present heading and climbing to 20;000 ft.I did not direct the PNF (Pilot Not Flying) to declare an emergency as we were busy figuring out what just happened and coordinating a plan between each other. In the climb; we cleaned the aircraft up and ran an after takeoff checklist. Once we were in VMC; we worked with each other to determine that all of our instruments matched and were reliable. We also determined that we could remain mostly VMC by performing the approach from ZZZZZ1 and asked to proceed directly to ZZZZZ1. We successfully performed the approach and landing at ZZZZ. Upon exiting the runway; we received both AFCS (Automated Flight Control System) Fault; and ADS Probe 1 Fail messages. We felt that we could have been struck by lightning; but we could not find any strike points on the aircraft; and all static wicks that were visible to us were found intact. We entered both messages above in the AML as well as an AML entry for a possible lightning strike.I feel my actions were appropriate given that we were not in radar contact any longer. I was unsure if I could trust any pitot or static instruments and I knew where I could find visual conditions away from terrain. I should have declared an emergency but at the time I felt that doing so with the language barrier would have broken down my communication with my First Officer when we needed to focus on flying the aircraft. Additionally; he was able to secure a clearance for the same heading up to 20;000 ft. as soon as I asked him to do so.

What is my elevated level of risk from deviating from flight planned route due to ATC ERROR . Should I query ATC? Is ATC error of immediate danger to me? As I was pouring over charts trying to determine if there was some charted military air space at my altitude that I was simply missing ATC advises turn right 30 degrees . I turn right 30 degrees. ATC advises that I was off course and had appeared to proceed from KITTN direct to OAL rather than KITTN KATTS OAL. I reviewed FMS and ATC was correct. Although I had entered the revised routing in the FMS ; the FMS glitched and sequenced in error from KITTN Direct to OAL .I explained what appeared to have happened to ATC . Controller said I had come within 1 mile if penetrating this military airspace which I still could not find on any government or Jeppesen chart at my altitude. I took down the Controller's telephone number and agreed to call him after I landed to discuss this and the reason for me being issued a revised clearance. When I called the Controller he explained that the government has lots of military airspace that represent a hazard to normal flights which they purposely do NOT publish on government Enroute charts. He explained ATC was aware of these uncharted portions of military airspace and it was their job to keep the public away from this hazard. I was somewhat shocked by this admission that the government is publishing knowingly false Enroute charts that do not show military airspace hazards which the controller said in fact do exist and around which they had given me a revised routing. My FMS glitch resulted in a deviation from revised routing. But what I am concerned about is that the Enroute charts we rely on are being willfully and purposely falsified and do not reflect what controller described as many military airspace hazards that do in fact affect the flying public.

column121: Denver airport is becoming hazardous to fly into due to non-specific ATIS; poor communication between DEN Center and DEN Approach; and the normalization of multiple arrivals and approaches being programmed during a normal arrival into Denver. This has increased substantially in the last few months and is resulting in aircrews being nearly continuously heads down reprogramming and briefing arrivals/transitions; approaches; taxi plan; getting appropriate landing data; briefing such changes; reviewing NOTAMs associated with these changes...etc. This is usually done while dodging weather; and mitigating turbulence; while descending into high terrain and congested traffic into an airport with multiple; parallel; similarly named runways. I feel there are three root causes. 1) ATIS is not very useful. Basically; a direction of traffic flow and a listing of all available approaches DEN has. 2) There seems to be a system now where approach tells Center what runway transition to assign aircraft. This transition frequently doesn't make sense and was not anticipated; programmed and briefed. Then; upon handoff to approach; the transition to another runway is often assigned. Then when the actual runway and approach is assigned; it frequently results in another reprogramming. This is acceptable during rapidly changing weather...it is commonplace all the time; however. On Aircraft X we programmed and briefed the FLATI 2 RNAV; RWY26 transition; RNAV Z Runway 26 approach. (Winds were 25024G34.) After starting the descent; we were given direct BYYKE; for the LONGS RNAV arrival. We programmed the LONGS arrival; Runway 26 transition; Runway 26 RNAV Z approach. We told Center that we were requesting Runway 26. Center directed us to fly the Runway 16R transition. (even though we were planning not to accept this approach). They said they are directed by DEN approach what transition to assign). We reprogrammed the ILS R16 transition and approach (we are now well along in the descent...moderate turbulence; and a VNAV discontinuity resulting from the reprogramming not being executable because of an approach transition altitude in-congruence) This was resolved quickly and safely and flown uneventfully with a 25 knot crosswind landing. The forecast approach winds were spot on; the ATIS hadn't changed substantially in an hour (Though there were about 5 or 6 of them). The point is; there was no significant change in weather driving this. I could have written the same report the last time I arrived to DEN on my last [arrival] from the east. On the flight today; we planned and briefed two different arrivals; one of the arrivals changing the transitions twice; two different RNAV Z approaches; an ILS approach and two different runways/performance numbers; NOTAMs; engine failure procedures taxi plans etc. I wouldn't spend time filing this report if it was a 'one off' It is becoming the norm and accepted scenario into Denver. It is also a contributing factor with DEN historically having issues with RNAVs. Each of these arrivals is complicated with at least 5-10 different altitude or speed constraints associated with them.

column121: When I came into the area; the controller working [Sector X] asked me if I would sit down on the D-side. It was obvious the controller was feeling busy. I asked him if he would like the sector split and he declined. I sat down on the D-side and attempted to get a briefing but the controller was too busy.During the stint; the controllers work was sloppy; he did not seem to have any idea what was happening in the sector at any given time. Several times throughout the stint he did not use positive separation between IFR aircraft and had what I would describe as 'separation by luck.'The reason I decided to report this stint is because the controller nearly caused a midair collision between Aircraft Y that had departed ZZZ1 and Aircraft X that was descending for ZZZ1.When Aircraft X called for a clearance airborne off of ZZZ; the controller did not issue him and IFR clearance but instead instructed the pilot to remain VFR and take up a westerly heading for active military airspace. The only problem with this plan is that the airspace didn't start until 17;000 [ft.]. The aircraft should have been given the clearance to 170 and a heading to get out from under the airspace.Aircraft X was on a heading (for the military airspace) and was descending quickly because he had been left high.I made the following suggestion to the controller. Clear Aircraft Y on a 190 heading and leave Aircraft X on his present heading until they pass.The controller instead cleared Aircraft X direct ZZZ; putting him in conflict with the climbing Aircraft Y that had not yet received a clearance. I just don't understand why he would do this. Direct the airport wasn't even a good way to set the airplane up to land had there not been traffic.When he finally saw the conflict (did not respond when I pointed it out to him). He froze. The control instruction he gave was 'UHHH Aircraft Y maintain VFR' He then called the traffic to Aircraft Y which was at 12'oclock and 10 miles (estimated) opposite direction. Descending.He then followed up the instruction to Aircraft Y to maintain VFR at 8;500. At the time he issued the instruction; Aircraft Y's indicated altitude was 082 and he had been climbing in excess of 3000 ft. per min. The pilot said he could not stop at 085 but could go back down. The next radar hit was at 094. The controller then said 'UHH just maintain VFR.' He should have left Aircraft Y climbing and turned him. It would have cleared the conflict quicker.He then turned Aircraft X 15degrees right for traffic. But when he issued the instruction; he didn't say it with any urgency at all.I don't remember if he eventually issued Aircraft Y a turn or not; but I do remember thinking I was about to witness a midair collision because a bad controller was sitting on the sector.The traffic was not busy; it had some complexity due to the military airspace; but it wasn't bad. It could easily be worked by a competent controller without a D-side.In summary: Bad control judgement; Bad control technique; lack of control instructions; inadequate control instructions; failure to scan the radar environment; and a controller being completely overwhelmed by traffic nearly lead to a collision at near 10;000 ft.

Crew was able to correct aircraft back to RNAV path and complete the approach + landing. If this was another crew with little or no experience flying this RNAV Arrival to RNAV (RNP) Approach into RIC with actual weather; there is a high probability they would not successfully complete the approach and landing (would have to go missed approach; other altitude/speed deviations and/or compromise safety).

column121: While serving as PF (Pilot Flying) into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ arrival; I was flying the aircraft with autopilot; autothrottle; and VNAV. We had programmed the STAR along with a transition to the ILS XXR into ZZZ and reviewed all the fixes and block altitudes on the Pro Line Fusion MFD screen. The aircraft flew the STAR without incident from FL280 all the way down to about 13000. The VNAV and autothrottle were working. I became distracted when the autothrottle failed to reduce 'FMS speed' for ZZZZZ1 to 250. I manually selected 250 and slowed. I reactivated the FMS speed function and verbally announced that we would monitor the speed and to make sure it made the next speed slowdown proactively at ZZZZZ2. What I failed to properly notice is the VNAV set a floor altitude of 13000 and leveled off. I did not think much of it since the next fix was an 'at or above' 9000 so I thought it was a level-off in lieu of an overly shallow descent.While being distracted in over-monitoring the FMS speed reduction; we got caught in an undesirable aircraft state. To make the alt window at ZZZZZ3; 9000-8000; I manually selected VS and adjusted the descent rate and flight spoilers in order to make that fix's alt window. I believe it was too close to notice if we made it or not and we did not seek relief with ATC since the Captain seemed unsure how to query ATC since he too was interested in watching the VNAV and FMS speed since he had little time on this Pro Line Fusion avionic suite. I flew the remaining alt windows in VS mode since that higher level of automation was not trustworthy or compatible with my state at that time. Later in the arrival; before ZZZZZ4; ATC gave us relief off the arrival and gave a descent to 3000. I dialed 3000 into the FGCP and the Captain confirmed the ALT. Continued down in VS. Since the previous UAS - Undesired Aircraft State - was around 10000; it impeded on the 'in-range check' being completed. We were at about 6500 when the in-range check was started and it distracted us from noticing the aircraft was still in VNAV and had captured the floor of the arrival; 6000; and did not continue [the] descent to 3000. ATC would query us shortly and again I would notice that the aircraft in a UAS. I noticed VNAV still active and disabled it; and continued down. We intercepted the approach and landed without further incident.In hindsight and a word of caution; this is the first avionics suite I have seen where altitudes on a STAR can be superseded by altitudes on an approach. In this example; the ZZZZZ STAR with the ILS XXR ZZZZZ5 transition. There was a discontinuity between ZZZZZ6 and ZZZZZ5. I want to know why in what world should VNAV look ahead of a discontinuity and block the VNAV windows on the STAR. All the stepdowns on the ILS XXR were there for reference as there no way knowing how far in the downwind ATC would take you before a base turn. I don't have a lot of VNAV-capable aircraft experience and I see tremendous issues with not being properly trained in how the aircraft will respond based on what is programmed into the FMS. In general; the avionics differentiation training was lacking and laughable and the differences from the standard avionics in the CL604. It seems half-finished and very retrofit. Having to train on-the-line with the suite to new crew members is frustrating at best and dangerous at worst. I will continue to step up and down levels of automation as my comfort and knowledge adjusts and will try to look for any potential red flags in FMS programming beyond the basic comparing to the approach plate.

column121: On left base for visual Runway (RWY) XX; slowing to full configuration and turning final; flaps were extended to 45 degrees while flight spoilers where deployed at 1;500 feet. Speed trend vector was decreasing although thrust setting was at expected thrust setting for approach. Captain called for increased power and crew realized that the flight spoilers were not fully retracted while turning final. The aircraft speed was approx. 150 knots which was below the SOP maneuvering speed of ref + 17 knots with spoilers deployed. At this time the stick shaker activated for approx. 2 seconds and the angle of attack was lowered. The flight spoilers were immediately retracted and the stick shaker stopped. Continued to join the localizer and were on a stabilized approach by 1;000 feet and landed without any incident.While slowing to configure for final approach; Pilot Flying (PF) believed the flight spoilers were fully retracted and called for flaps 8 and 20 at 200 knots. Then the call for gear down and flaps 30 at 180 knots. PF was approaching the localizer course; called flaps 45 at 160 knots. To reduce automation workload the autopilot was disconnected and was preparing to make a left turn to intercept the localizer and glide slope. The stick shaker activated at this time because the flight computer detected a pending stall with the flight spoilers deployed. Immediately after the flight spoilers were fully retracted; the stick shaker stopped and the aircraft was on speed with flaps at 45 degrees. A left turn was made intercepting the localizer and the aircraft was on a stable approach by 1;000 feet.ATC gave direct to the final approach fix for the visual to RWY XX while still descending out of 6;000 and needing to slow to configure for landing. PF could have anticipated needing more distance to reduce airspeed; possibly without flight spoilers; and fully configure the aircraft by 3 miles of the final approach fix by descending sooner and leveling off earlier. This would have reduced pilot workload and automation management allowing for a more thorough scan of the aircraft and its systems before deploying flaps and slowing to final approach speed.

column121: On arrival at ZZZ; winds were variable and began to favor Runway XX for landing. We were set up for landing on Runway XY. I; acting as Pilot Monitoring for this leg due to special qualification airport; suggested to Captain that we swap our planned arrival runway due to winds and additional available landing distance (approximately 500 feet) for landing on Runway XX. The FMC was reprogrammed correctly; briefed; and we accepted a heading to intercept final Runway XX. With approximately a 30 degree intercept; approach control cleared us for the ILS XX. Captain selected approach mode early. This caused the aircraft to capture a false glideslope and the aircraft began a descent prior to capturing the localizer. I called this to the Captain's attention; of which he was also aware.Prior to localizer capture I recommended a discontinued approach. Altitude was well above Minimum Safe Altitude and the approach was salvageable but due to my experience level in the jet; I suggested a soft go-around. The Captain elected to continue; to which I agreed and remarked that our subsequent protected altitude would be 2;600 feet; which we were currently above; and that I would monitor. The Captain; slightly flustered about the false glideslope capture began to fiddle with Auto Pilot disconnect; Flight Director reset; and approach mode was re-armed. The new capture mode now is LOC but with a failed Glideslope. The aircraft has defaulted into the current vertical speed. I call slightly below glideslope; Captain again resets Auto pilot; Flight Director; and re-arms the approach mode. Localizer captures; Glideslope has been armed; and we are currently in a 700 to 800 FPM descent; very slightly low on Glideslope; at a safe speed; and safe altitude.I call attention to our protected Final Approach Fix altitude and glideslope intercept at ZZZZZ 2238 feet. If I remember correctly; we were approximately 3 miles from ZZZZZ when I remarked that at our current Flight Path Angle would have us slightly below our target altitude without any correction at ZZZZZ. Let me be clear; the aircraft was; based on our current descent rate; projected to be only slightly below 2;300 feet at the Final Approach Fix. A minor correction would have rectified the approach path angle and captured the glideslope. I called our altitude to the Captains attention once more approximately 1 to 2 miles prior to ZZZZZ; where we had now reached 2;300 feet; the charted approach value. Right as I was going to call for the Go Around at ZZZZZ; the tower controller issued a Low Altitude Alert; the Go Around was called and initiated; and the aircraft was at approximately 2;100 feet; a little less than 200 feet low at the charted glideslope intercept altitude; as well as above 1;000 feet above ground.The Go-Around was accomplished without error and a subsequent ILS was flown to Runway XX without any additional complications. Upon debrief; I became aware that the Captain was unaware that he had not captured the Glideslope. I re-framed the situation for us to consider alternate action and explained my reasoning for a requested discontinued approach prior to localizer capture. I am still low time and in consolidation. I had no reason to expect that we could not become stable with glideslope capture prior to Final Approach Fix. Hindsight is exactly that and this event began and ended all within 4 miles. The Go-round was completed to qual standards with safety and stable approach criteria in mind.False glideslopes capture prior to localizer capture due to not allowing the aircraft to capture in LOC or LNAV prior to arming the approach mode. Again; I believe I was very clear about our impending altitude deviation; however I don't believe I heard any response from the Captain from 3 miles(my initial call) and 1 to 2 miles(my second que). I could be wrong. The whole event spanned a time frame of less than 3 minutes from 'looks good' to 'doesn't look so good' so I could NOT have fit many more altitude callouts in that span. Due to my low experience in the jet; I incorrectly expected a correction that I did not receive. The go around was initiated at or just seconds after the Final Approach Fix. An assumption of understanding is not the greatest way to handle approaching a go around. I do not believe I was hinting and hoping but I will be more aggressive with my descent planning awareness callouts so as not to enter into a [undesirable situation] in the future. However; the correct decision was made concerning the safe operation of the aircraft and the proper response was executed.
column123: Trip was third leg of the day.  Landed from second leg at around XA:40 local and got to sleep room at XB:10L.  Awakened 30 early of show time at approximately XB:40L.  Weather was marginal regionally and at ZZZ. ZZZ1 was filed alternate but also monitored weather at ZZZ2 for second option.  First Officer has less than 75 hours and ZZZ is Special Qual field. Identified the CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) hazard; short runway; marginal weather; etc.  Pre briefed the ILS XY enroute as winds were favoring that runway.  Also talked about EFVS (Enhanced Flight Vision Systems) and auto land contingencies.  Upon contacting ZZZ approach; they asked if we wanted ILS XX due to a wind shift.  Initially decided to stick with XY but reversed the decision seconds later due to shorter usable runway on XY due to displaced threshold and winds favoring XX slightly.I was flying the approach while the First Officer set up and briefed the ILS XX.  We re-accomplished the approach checklist and accepted a clearance direct to the Final Approach Fix to cross at 2;600 feet and maintain until established; cleared for the ILS.  We put the 2;600 foot hard restriction at the Final Approach Fix and were navigating LNAV/VNAV.  Just prior to Final Approach Fix I mistakenly selected the approach mode.  The aircraft immediately intercepted what I believe was a false glide slope and begun to descend before intended.  I turned off both flight directors and attempted to get the aircraft out of approach mode. The aircraft stayed in approach mode because I did not disengage the autopilot.  So; after re-engaging the aircraft tracked the localizer in LOC mode and Vertical Speed with Glideslope Flight Mode Annunciation struck through as a failed mode.  Realizing the error; I disconnected both flight directors and autopilot and immediately re-engaged and re-automated.  At this point I believe the aircraft momentarily intercepted a glide path; and almost immediately and simultaneously with the Tower Controller realized we were about 250 feet low of the glide slope intercept altitude.  We immediately performed a discontinued approach and climbed to 3;000 feet.  We received vectors for another ILS XX and auto landed uneventfully.Fatigue was undeniably a root cause although not the only issue here.  Flying two legs and then getting only 30 minutes opportunity to nap between legs was just a little too much for me despite 'feeling pretty good' ahead of the flight involved. In retrospect I should have used LNAV/VNAV to get solidly on the ILS final before selecting approach mode.  And; also; I should have and will in the future decide to discontinue an approach as soon as any serious mode switching starts happening on the final approach. In the light of day and after a nap I know this solidly; but it is much more difficult with a foggy brain at XF:00.  So; in the future; I'm going to use LNAV/VNAV more and not use APP until later in the approach. Revision of the flight pairing to allow for more rest time...even an hour nap; would help.  Also; making sure to use LNAV/VNAV and protect GSIA (Glide Slope Intercept Altitude) at 1 NM prior to the intermediate fix.

column121: Departed ZZZ 4L in windy gusty conditions with a normal takeoff. Passing approximately 500 feet; a Rudder Ratio EICAS caution message appeared. I followed the QRH procedure after doing the 'after takeoff' checklist. This procedure stated: Above 160 knots avoid large or abrupt rudder inputs; Crosswind limit is 15 knots; Do not autoland. I made a maintenance write up and we continued. Climb was in IMC with light chop since there was a weather system moving into the east coast.Approximately an hour and half into the flight at FL340 received a Cabin Alt EICAS warning along with Cabin Altitude light and aural warning. We performed the immediate actions: Donned the oxygen masks and established crew communication. I followed the Cabin Altitude checklist and when I came to the decision tree: Cabin altitude is controllable (I switched to the other alt controller without any change) or Cabin altitude is uncontrollable; I felt that I was in between the two since the cabin was slightly above 10;000 feet and HOLDING STEADY. I advised ATC and asked for a lower altitude to the mid 20;000 feet thinking the cabin would decrease below 10;000 feet. I was also reluctant to go any lower because there was weather and turbulence below us. I called the purser and asked if the cabin oxygen masks had dropped and she informed that they had not confirming that cabin altitude never got above 14;000 feet. The cabin altitude decreased below 10;000 but the EICAS message was still illuminated so I asked for lower again. Passing 20;000 feet the Cabin Alt warning went out and the cabin showed approximately 6;000 feet so I elected to stop at FL190. This kept us right above the weather with the FO deviating around the tops.I informed the purser of the situation and made a preliminary PA. Contact with Dispatch was next with Maintenance Control on the line. Maintenance Control was not able to rectify our situation so the Dispatcher and I started looking for a divert airport. Due to the weather and the cross-wind limit of 15 knots due to the Rudder Ratio issue I was very limited in airport selection since the cross winds were in excess of 15 knots in ZZZ1; ZZZ2; ZZZ3; ZZZ; ZZZ4. ZZZ5 was the only option with calm winds; 400 Feet broken; 3 MI visibility and rain.I made the decision to divert to ZZZ5 with dispatch concurrence. I informed the purser and made another PA.We began planning for landing into ZZZ5 and was told of moderate turbulence ahead. I seated the flight attendants. Approaching the IAF for [Runway] XXL ATC informed us of an aircraft ahead of us Going Around since they were unable to see the runway at mins. I inquired about XXR and was told there was another aircraft on approach for that runway. That aircraft landed and we proceeded to a normal landing. Fire and rescue greeted us and after getting the all OK we taxied uneventfully to the gate.

column121: Planned fuel was 6;040 and got fueled to 6;200. We took off with roughly 6;000 pounds of fuel and minimum fuel was 5;564. So we left with well above minimum required fuel according to release. We were enroute and about halfway to 2/3 of the way through as I monitored our fuel burn. I noticed based on current conditions at that time (winds aloft were greater than planned and ATC requested Mach .77 or greater while .76 is planned); that we would be about 700 pounds under planned landing fuel. So as a crew we quickly setup for long range cruise and contacted ATC that we needed to slowdown even though they insisted we maintain a high speed. So we slowed to Mach .63 for long range cruise and then ATC descended us to 27;000 feet from 31;000 feet starting down early because we were slower than surrounding traffic.Then we get instructions shortly after to change arrivals keeping us away from other traffic. Once we finally got situated with the changes; dispatch beat me to notifying them and sent us an ACARS asking about the route changes and fuel. So we told them current plan and situation and based on the information back from dispatch; we had sufficient fuel as long as we maintained LRC (Long Range Cruise speed) to ZZZ allowing us to land with just 100 pounds of fuel more than planned and dispatch had us landing at roughly 1;850 pounds. At some point ATC also queried us asking about why we would be taking off with less fuel than we need to do the flight; even though we didn't. We actually took off with more fuel than planned. ATC was actually being unprofessional about the whole thing and giving us a hard time; because we asked to slow down to conserve fuel as stated over the radios in order to avoid getting into a bad fuel situation later or having to declare minimum fuel; and then he put us on different arrival and etc. It just created more workload and pressure by his attitude and questions as if it was our fault than it needed to be and ATC did not help with that even though they're there to help us.He made us sound bad on the radio as if we didn't know what we were doing about our fuel. Then sometime later while setting up for new arrival; ZZZ does a runway change as well after we got our LDR (Landing Distance Required) and brief; so that added more workload trying to update everything and re-brief in addition to ACARS taking longer than usual to respond. During all of that; Center then instructs us to level at 19;000 feet after getting the first descend via due to VFR traffic at 17;500 feet!  After traffic passes Center then gives us descend via again with immediate handoff to Approach in the same transmission. So First Officer does the handoff while I'm assessing and starting down seeing how quick we need to descend.  I saw we needed to do 6;000 feet or more a minute in order to meet the crossing restriction. I knew that wasn't going to happen so right as I was going to tell First Officer to let ATC know we can't make the restriction because of the level off earlier due to traffic as he was checking on; Approach immediately on initial contact asked if we would make the crossing restriction and we said no.He immediately then got upset and asked if we told the previous controller who would be Center and we said no because we didn't have time as we literally just switched and got the clearance at the same time and literally a few seconds later discovered we couldn't make it work. So we explained that to Approach but he wasn't accepting that and blamed us for not making the restriction or notifying Center before talking with Approach. But we literally had no time between the clearance and handoff at the same time and during the frequency switch that's when we noticed the issue and first transmission with Approach we weren't given the time to tell him that before he asked and queried us. So Approach then gives us two small delay vectors and rejoin arrival. But Approach said we should've told them early on we couldn't make itbut again we explained the situation and that we were not given that chance to do so. So we then continued on after that with no further issues.Insufficient fuel planning on release as it never reflects the actual fuel burn since release doesn't account for delay vectors or vectors on approach. The issues with ATC and last second changes to arrival and runways were a result of not having enough fuel at normal cruise followed by slow ACARS affected our ability to fly the planned arrival causing a higher workload for us and ATC which then caused the hiccup with crossing restrictions and with crossing traffic as well.  For fuel; we slowed for LRC and got a couple shortcuts once on the banker arrival. We were able to gain most of our fuel back because of LRC and landed with 2;200 pounds. For the crossing restriction; we just explained the situation to ATC and along with Center; Approach gave us a hard time and we notified them we couldn't do it; then we carried on with no further issues after that.For fuel planning and fuel contingency; we should be doing a minimum of like 500 pounds and 750-1;000 pounds extra on IFR days. Also for holding fuel; that should be 600 pounds minimum as we realistically burn more than 400 pounds on a go-around on a VFR day. As far as ATC goes after discussing with my First Officer as the situation that unfolded after another as a result; we maybe should have declared Minimum fuel early on knowing we wouldn't have enough unless we slowed down. But because of LRC and little to no delay vectors we determined to have enough hence why we never declared. However; if we declared min fuel early on that would've maybe given ATC more understanding even as frustrating as it may be; and allow us priority to slow and not have to descend via and etc. And that maybe would've avoided the issue with crossing at ZZZZZ1 and etc. One thing led to another; so next time maybe declare min fuel and decline a descend via to stay up high longer and to reduce workload. It was a good learning experience except for lack of professionalism and help from ATC.

column121: After flying a practice RNAV (GPS) approach into ZZZ; I was climbing through 2;000 feet on the missed approach when I checked in with Approach. Approach provided an altimeter setting (30.12; which had changed since my last check-in of 30.11) and a few seconds later provided a heading for vectors for the ILS at ZZZ1.  I leveled off at the assigned altitude of 3;000 feet and shortly after; ATC asked me to maintain 3;000 feet.  Considering my altimeter was reading 3;020 feet; I knew this call meant something was not right.  I scanned the instruments and saw the altimeter setting was now set to 29.92. I requested the altimeter setting again and when I entered the correct setting; I was approximately 300 feet above my assigned altitude.  After landing I was able to determine the sequence of events that caused this deviation.My airplane has an Aspen Avionics Evolution 1000 PFD.  I have had this for the last X years and feel I am proficient in operating it.  It has a feature that; in my piston powered general aviation airplane; is not used.  If you press the 'baro' button and then push the right knob; the altimeter setting will change to 29.92.  Since I never climb to FL180; I have never used this feature. In this situation; when I contacted ATC; they gave me the altimeter setting; and since it was different; I pushed the 'baro' button and turned the right knob to the correct setting. When ATC then provided me a vector; I needed to move the heading bug almost 180 degrees (it had been set during the southbound approach and now I was flying northbound).  Instead of spinning the heading knob (the same right knob) 180 degrees; I pushed the knob which automatically sets the heading bug to the current heading.  What I didn't realize was that when I pushed the right knob; the 'baro' function was still active and therefore set the altimeter to 29.92.  The heading bug also aligned to the current heading; however since I was in turbulence; I assume I bumped the knob twice instead of once.  I didn't notice the change in altitude because I was in a climb.  When I reached 3;000 feet; I leveled off like normal without being aware that I was higher than I should be.Moving forward I will need to be more careful and aware of what function is active in the PFD before making changes.  However; my fear is that it may be another X or more years before something like this happens again and as time moves forward; we tend to forget these events.  I do think this is an opportunity for Aspen to make a software revision.  If this baro reset feature is meant for aircraft passing through 18;000 feet; it would be nice if this feature could be disabled for installations in aircraft that cannot reach that altitude.  Alternatively; if this feature is meant for aircraft passing through 18;000 feet and it is utilized at an altitude well below that; a flashing yellow flag (similar to what happens when approaching the selected altitude) would help to visually annotate the change that was just made. I'm not trying to remove responsibility from the pilot; but the pilot has hundreds of things to remember when flying.  Modern avionics should not be adding to the list of quirks that need to be remembered.

column121: I departed ZZZ; climbed normally; received vector for a right turn to a heading of 290 and a climb to 10;000. I complied with all of the uneventfully. West of the airport was cell of precipitation that I couldn't see through. It was depicted as yellow on my weather display. The precipitation was west of the airport and oriented along the axis of about 290 to 300 west of ZZZ.I was doing the ZZZ4 departure. The tower controller advised in the initial climb that in substance that I'd be boxed around on vectors for the climb before being going to the route.A previous departed reported the ceiling at about 6;500 which was basically true. I changed frequency to ZZZ TRACON and got a heading of 290. When I entered the IMC the rain was very intense and it was turbulent. I noticed changes on the vertical speed indicator up and then later down. The temperature was near freezing; but I did not see any actual ice. While climbing in IMC; the radio frequency began to screech such that I couldn't hear anything. That ultimately occurred on both radios and both frequencies. The marker beacon lights were flashing. I received a traffic alert for traffic on my left. It was very turbulent; but I stayed at 10;000 feet as assigned. With no communications (coms); I squawked 7600.I decided to turn 90 degrees right still in IMC because that resolved the traffic; would get me out of the precipitation; was a heading basically on course; was consistent with the expectations from the departure briefing and ZZZ4; and would restore coms. The precipitation was aligned with the vector so remaining on that heading was not viable. There was traffic there. I didn't change altitude (I was at 10;000 ft. the whole time).After the right turn; I exited the side of the precipitation; I was able to hear ground responding to one of my calls (on COM2 on the bottom antenna); so I went back to the departure frequency on COM1 (on the top); re-established communications and departed.The ATC TRACON controller was upset seemed to think that I was in VMC and just turned randomly or something. I've flown through 'yellow' precipitation many times uneventfully. The lost coms procedure when you're on a vector is to either stay on the vector or turn on course. I turned on course because it solved all of the problems; but seemed to surprise ATC. I think that the confusing thing for ATC was that it was fine weather straight over the airport; which is probably what he has on his computer. But west of the airport was unexpectedly intense rain.I'm not sure that this incident could have been avoided given what everyone knew at the time; although once I squawked 7600; the turn on course shouldn't have been a surprise.

column121: On the arrival into the ZZZ area; ATC kept us high due to departing IFR traffic. We heard the departing traffic calling ATC on the radio after departure; but got no response. Because we were getting very close to the airport; we elected to reduce speed in order to make the impending descent easier to manage. We were monitoring both the ATC Center frequency and the CTAF frequency at ZZZ. There was a significant amount of General Aviation traffic operating in the vicinity of the ZZZ airport. As the speed was reduced below 200 knots; the First Officer; who was the PF; asked for Flaps 8 and 20. I verified that the speed was below 200 knots and selected Flaps 8 and 20. As soon as I selected Flaps 20 I realized we were still at 16;000 ft.; and said; 'We can't do that yet;' and immediately retracted the Flaps back to 0.  At this point we were only six or seven miles from the airport; still at 16;000 ft. We had identified the traffic threats on TCAS. In order to initiate our descent to the airport; we canceled IFR. After descending through 15;000 feet the First Officer again asked for Flaps 8 and 20. Because we had extended the flaps earlier above 16;000 feet; I was focused on the altitude. Due to the fact that we had slowed to below 200 knots the first time we extended the flaps; I failed to look at the airspeed indicator; thinking we were still below 200 knots. We were discussing the maneuver we would need to make to circle around and descend to the airport at the time. ATC and CTAF radio traffic was also heavy at the time. As soon as the flaps were selected the overspeed clacker started up. I looked at the airspeed indicator; saw that we were above 200 knots; and reached for the flap lever with the intent of retracting the flaps. At this point I'm unclear what EXACTLY happened next.  There was some turbulence; we were beginning our turn; and there was a lot of radio traffic.  We were also focused on the traffic displayed on the TCAS. All of this created a great deal of distraction. My hand was on the flap lever at the time; with the intent of retracting the flaps. Whether it was because of turbulence causing me to inadvertently move the lever; or me simply moving it the wrong way because of the distractions; I did; in fact; move the flap lever to 45. The overspeed clacker; interestingly enough; added to the momentary confusion. In fact; at one point I believe the First Officer said; 'What the hell is going on?' I was mortified to see the indication that the flaps were at 45; because there was no intent; plan; or call for further flap extensions. It was simply a mistake. I immediately retracted the flaps to zero. We did not receive any message associated with a flap problem; i.e. 'Flaps Fail'; etc. After everything calmed down and things were back in order; we continued the approach; which ended up resulting in a go-around because a general aviation aircraft cut us off on short final. After landing and proceeding to the gate; I wrote up the flap limitation exceedance. Maintenance arrived later; inspected the flaps; performed functional checks; found no irregularities; and returned the aircraft to service.In my opinion there were several factors contributing to the event. Distraction was probably the primary cause. We were distracted by all the radio traffic on the CTAF frequency. Sometimes it was difficult to differentiate between the CTAF traffic and the Center traffic. Also; being left so high so late on the arrival created a self-imposed sense of immediacy...'We need to get down'. Interesting to note that this urgency was never 'real'; but rather something we imposed on ourselves. Assumption was another contributing factor. Because we had originally slowed to below 200 knots; I assumed we were still at that airspeed when flaps were requested the second time. This assumption caused me to neglect the airspeed indicator before selecting the flaps because I was more concerned about the altitude.This is primarily an exercise in self-discipline and patience. The training and procedures are all in place to help prevent these types of events from occurring. It simply becomes incumbent on each pilot to be disciplined enough to not allow external factors to get in the way of simple; straight-forward procedures that can and will keep the aircraft; passengers; and crew safe.

column121: We were flying the ZZZZZ RNAV arrival into ZZZ inside of the ZZZZZ1 waypoint when ATC instructed us to descend via except cross ZZZZZ2 at 10;000 ft.; 2000 ft. higher than published. We informed ATC that if we comply with the assigned crossing restriction that we will have trouble making ZZZZZ at 6;000; [which was] only 8.2 miles from ZZZZZ2. ATC then replied; 'If you will be high on the arrival let me know.' We then decided to slow down the aircraft to prepare for making the crossing restrictions and recalculate our descent inside of ZZZZZ2 to advise ATC if we will be high or if we can comply with the ZZZZZ restriction.Once the Honeywell FMS reached waypoint passage over ZZZZZ2 and cycled to the next fix; we started down to make the next crossing restriction. Within a few seconds of starting our descent; we received a TCAS 'TRAFFIC' alert followed by a TCAS RA. I immediately disconnected the autopilot to comply with the RA and resolve the conflict. After the resolution advisory was resolved; [the Pilot Monitoring] noticed that the FMS had cycled to the next waypoint early and found that we were still a few tenths of a mile from ZZZZZ2 during the event. The assigned altitude at ZZZZZ2 was 10;000 ft.; we leveled off during the RA around 9;750 - 9;800 ft. There was no communication from ATC to us regarding the event. The rest of the arrival and approach was flown successfully and we landed safely.The Honeywell FMS cycled waypoints early; leading us to believe that we had reached waypoint passage. [I suggest] finding a solution to prevent the Honeywell FMS from making premature smart turns/waypoint passage cycles.
column123: Operating [the] flight as SIC (Second in Command) and PM; we were assigned to descend via the ZZZZZ [arrival] but cross ZZZZZ2 at 10;000. We leveled off at 10;000 prior to the fix and set the next appropriate altitude. At about 2.5 miles prior to the fix; the Honeywell FMS prematurely sequenced to the next waypoint. We began an initial descent and quickly noticed the discrepancy in distance between current position and waypoint. [There was] an RA to 'monitor descent' annunciation. The Pilot Flying immediately climbed back to 10;000 and we waited until the correct DME was displayed. [The cause of the crossing altitude deviation was the] Honeywell FMS [working improperly]. I have noticed this problem in almost all company aircraft containing Honeywell FMS. The airplane will sequence to the next waypoint prior to the actual position. This can; and does lead to; altitude deviations and potential RAs and possibly worse. I would like to either see the problem itself fixed or the company to implement an SOP or training that covers this issue.

column121: As PM; the Captain and I were nearing BERBN intersection on the COKTL 1 Arrival into LAS. After receiving the ATIS for LAS; and before beginning the descent on the COKTL 1 Arrival; the Captain briefed the COKTL 1 Arrival; along with the visual approach; backed up with the ILS to Runway 26L. Conditions at the time were VMC DAY (15;000' few/10SM vis). Prior to reaching BERBN intersection; Approach Control asked us if we had the ILS loaded. I looked over to the Captain and we both nodded; at which time I stated that we did indeed have the ILS 26L LAS loaded into the FMC (from the direction of PRINO intersection). The Approach Controller cleared us to fly the ILS 26L with a clearance to cross BERBN at or above 7;000 feet MSL. I then queried the Approach Controller about whether or not they would like me to call our base leg for Runway 26L.  The Controller replied that our base leg would be visible on their radar; and that a call was not necessary. Not realizing that there was INDEED a transition from the BERBN intersection to HUXAR on the ILS 26L; we proceeded turn north whilst descending to intercept the Runway 26L localizer just outside of RELIN intersection (D7.2 IRLE) Runway 26L.Shortly thereafter; we were told by the Approach Controller that we had initiated the turn too soon; and we were given a heading to the East in order to avoid traffic (other carrier) that was already established on final for Runway 26L.  We did receive a TCAS TA (no RA); and after completing the turn to the East; the TCAS TA was resolved. After the turn to the East; and with proper separation between our aircraft and Aircraft Y; Approach Control vectored us back to the north to join the localizer and clear us for the visual to LAS Runway 26L. We were then handed-off to LAS Tower. Landing was uneventful. After landing; we were provided a phone number to call LAS TRACON. The COKTL 1 Arrival and the latest ILS 26L charts for LAS are dated (date). I can tell you that I was certainly not familiar; nor had I ever been assigned the ILS 26L from the COKTL 1 Approach (I wasn't even aware that there was a transition from BERBN intersection; as that transition is located on the new ILS 26L Approach chart). My apologies to the LAS Approach Controller for our misunderstanding.As an added measure; I would prefer to see more information added to the COKTL 1 Arrival; like a ball note referring Pilots to the BERBN transition on the ILS 26L LAS.  An added note within our company pages may help bring attention to this transition as well.

When double checking the pitot heat was on I notice both Engines Electronic Control (EEC) were in soft alternate mode. During the entire time the aircraft was in IMC the airspeed indicator was erratic and EEC remained in soft alternate. A few minutes later; at level off at cruising altitude (low 20;000s) and out of IMC the airspeed indicator returned to normal along with EEC. Remained clear of clouds and landed uneventfully at ZZZ1. We did not return to ZZZ after [Notifying ATC] because we were more than half way and the squall line was over ZZZ.Unknown as to why airspeed indicator was unreliable and erratic in IMC turbulent air and then returned to normal when clear of clouds.
