column121: The incident happened during our descent on the ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ. As far as I remember; we had been cleared by the previous Controller and told to do the XXL transition. I had already programmed the FMS for that specific arrival and pre-loaded the ILS XXL. The weather was not an issue with a clear sky and great visibility. I briefed a visual approach for XXL; backed up with the routing of the ILS for that same runway; and made sure we had the discontinuity between the last point on the arrival - ZZZZZ1 and the first point on the approach - ZZZZZ1. We were then told to contact the next Controller and assigned different altitudes on the arrival while maintaining the routing. For some reason; at one point; I thought/assumed we were cleared for the visual and got rid of the discontinuity by linking the first point on the approach with the last point on the arrival - ZZZZZ1. I turned to the Captain to ask him to 'confirm' and proceeded by removing the discontinuity. Because we were not cleared for the approach yet; the aircraft proceeded past ZZZZZ1 on a XXX as expected; but because it was now programmed to fly the approach it started turning at ZZZZZ2. The Controller asked us if we were flying the RNAV; we responded that we were doing the XXL transition and as the Captain said these words we realized we had made a mistake by leaving the XXX. The Controller kindly reminded us what we were expected to do and gave us a heading to intercept the localizer for the visual XXL. What led to this mistake is mostly my fault. I was fixated on flying the visual; and I forgot to actually make sure we had been given the clearance before getting off the arrival. My mind was too focused on the preconceived idea of what was expected rather than what we had actually been cleared for that I failed to properly communicate with my Captain. I was complacent; and this led to confusion in the cockpit and with the Controller.
column123: During our descent on ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ; we were cleared to descend via ZZZZZ ; XXL transition. We programmed the FMS for that particular arrival and transition and preloaded the ILS XXL. The weather was good with clear sky and great visibility. Pilot Flying; briefed the visual approach XXL back it up by ILS. We made sure the discontinuity between the last point on the arrival ZZZZZ1 and the first point on the approach ZZZZZ1. We were told to contact the next Controller and assigned us different altitude on the arrival while maintaining the routing. I contacted the next Controller and for some reason we thought; we were cleared for visual via ZZZZZ1 transition. As we past ZZZZZ1; we continue to fly heading XXX as we approached ZZZZZ2 the plane was about to transition to the new fix. At this point ATC assigned us a heading 350 and asked us if we are flying the RNV transition? Which responded yes and I realized the error. At this point he assigned us 310 heading to intercept the localizer and cleared us for visual to XXL.We were both fixated and our mind was set on the preconceived idea of what was expected rather than what we had actually been cleared for; especially when the proceeding traffic receives that clearance. I (we) failed to confirm and communicate with each other and ATC. I got complacent and side tracked; the combination of these two led to the confusion in the cockpit and with the Controller.As a (Captain/Pilot Monitoring) I should have communicated and confirmed that we are both on the same page and understood the clearance and when in doubt ask the ATC for clarification. I want to make sure and get the confirmation before removing the discontinuity and not to rush. Do not assume if previous aircraft receives particular clearance we will get the same and avoid complacency. I will emphasize this on my future arrival briefings to ensure this doesn't happen again; FOOLISH ASSUMPTION/MISTAKE.

As I was doing so; ATC gave us a notification of opposite direction traffic 1;000 feet above us which we had on TCAS and immediately saw visually.  All appeared normal and I believed ATC was simply letting us know why we had not been cleared higher and was giving a normal notification of traffic.  The transmission was partially garbled; and the Pilot Monitoring (PM) requested that ATC repeat it.  ATC simply responded with 'maintain 16;000' which the PM acknowledged.  The PM then noticed that our altimeters did not agree and informed me that my altimeter was set at 29.92 instead of the local altimeter setting.  I reset the altimeter and discovered that I was actually at 16;180 ft; which likely had prompted the call from ATC.  We were just short of 200 ft high.  I descended and was at 16;000 before passing under the opposite direction traffic.  We did not receive a TCAS TA or RA.  I have no memory of resetting my altimeter to 29.92 but surmise that I must have done so as it would be very difficult to have hit the button accidentally.  While allowed to set 29.92 once assigned a climb above 18;000 ft; my normal practice is to wait until the altimeter setting flashes approaching 18;000 ft to reset it.  Normal practice meaning I don't recall ever doing it differently.  I cannot explain when I reset it to standard; except that it was after the pre-start check and prior to leveling at 16;000.  My best guess is that I did so at 10;000 for some reason; as that was the only altitude I passed that I would have considered significant; although I was on profile in a 250 knot climb both before and after 10;000 ft.  In this case; the local altimeter setting was close enough to standard that I did not exceed the 300 feet limit for a flight violation or cause a traffic conflict.  This was just luck however.  Had the altimeter been significantly different from standard; I don't believe I would have been more likely to notice the error and could have been responsible for a conflict.I'm not sure what the cause was except that I simply made an error.  Why; how; or when escapes me.  However; I did have to call in fatigued that morning as we were on a late in the day pairing but had been delayed overnight to a morning departure two time zones to the east.  When I called in fatigued unable to fall asleep early; I was given my 10 hours and a later show time; though to make the later show time I still needed to get out of bed two hours prior to when I was accustomed.  After I woke up to my alarm; I was notified that the aircraft was still in maintenance and was given an even later show time; and I took a short nap.  In the end; the error happened during a time I'd normally be awake; but I did not get my normal sleep routine.  I had legal rest and did not feel particularly fatigued; but I can't discount that fatigue very well could have contributed to such an unusual error.  I utilized the Fatigue Risk Management Plan (FRMP) to the extent I felt necessary and neither Crew Scheduling nor the company pressured me in any way to fly fatigued.  Perhaps I should have insisted on an even later show time.  My feeling of responsibility to our customers who had already been delayed over 12 hours was a factor in making a show time that was earlier than normal for me; considering time zones; but again; I didn't feel overly tired at the time. Obviously; having made this error for the first time; I'll be more cognizant of when I hit the button to bring the altimeter to standard going forward.  As far as the possible fatigueaspect; our promise to our customers to transport them to their destination at the time we say can sometimes conflicts with our promise to transport them as safely as possible.  I have availed myself of the risk management plan several times in the last year and have never received any negative feedback or pressure to fly fatigued.  There are times when I feel the probability of losing pay has pressured other pilots to fly with less rest than they needed; but in this case pay was not a factor as I was the only pilot available to fly this leg to an outstation serviced only once per day.  So; I was going to be paid for the leg no matter when I flew it.  Therefore; I can't recommend any changes to the risk management plan.  I simply need to do a better job of anticipating and assessing my own fatigue level.
column123: Climbing out we were assigned to maintain 16;000 ft. First Officer (FO) was pilot flying. Altitude was verified at '1;000 to go' call. As we went through 15;000 feet; I said 15;000 climbing 16;000. FO was hand flying; as we near 16;000 (about 100ft to go) I noticed he wasn't slowing down the climb rate. I looked over and his altimeter was set to 29.92 instead of the altimeter we've gotten when I checked in of 30.16. As I looked over ATC asked if we had the 16;000 ft altitude assigned which I replied affirmatively. As I was done talking to ATC I told the FO he had the wrong altimeter setting; and that our Altimeter was 30.16. FO did level off at 16;000 ft but he had a wrong altimeter setting. FO may have pushed the standard 29.92 altimeter inadvertently at some point after initial departure. As the altimeter were set and cross checked for departure on the ground. We had checked our level off altitude on the 1;000 to go call. But I didn't notice at that time he had a wrong altimeter setting. I think on the 1;000 feet to go call we should have notice this discrepancy; but I was looking at my PFD and not his. FO should have mentioned that his altitude did not match with mine at the 1;000 to go call.

column121: On arrival into EDF we were on ANC Approach. After initial contact; ANC asked what approach we wanted at EDF. The Pilot Monitoring replied the Visual 34. ANC instructed us to turn left heading 260 and descend and maintain 8;000 (we were at 13;000.) While rolling out on a 260 heading and still descending; ANC came back and said they were going to take us the other way and to turn back right heading 330. We rolled out on 330 still descending. At around 9;000 descending; ANC asked us if we wanted Runway 16 and that the winds were 330 at 5. Taking into account our position and high altitude relative to EDF Runway 34 and our weight; I decided that this would be acceptable; but wanted the IRO to double check the numbers before accepting this change. I said 'standby' and the Pilot Monitoring transmitted 'standby' to ANC. ANC immediately instructed us to descend and maintain 3;000. At the same time of ANC transmission; we were leveling at 8;000; and I was asking the IRO to run the numbers for 16. The Pilot Monitoring replied '3;000; Aircraft X'. I reset the altitude selector to 3;000; verified the altitude with the Pilot Monitoring; engaged FLC; set speed and we began to descend. This clearance seemed logical considering we were clearing terrain; there was no traffic on TCAS; no terrain indicating on the HSI (I was in terrain mode) and we needed to lose altitude to make the airport. There was no further contact with ANC ATC until they instructed us to maintain 8;000.Descending through approximately 6;700; ANC contacted us and instructed us to maintain 8;000; low alt alert and that the MVA in that area was 8;000. After landing and block in; I was notified by EDF Tower (via the military) that ANC TRACON wanted me to give them a call (which I did after speaking to the Chief Pilot.) They took my info and said he would be forwarding to quality control (assurance?) and they may contact me as they were looking into it. There was either an error by ANC Approach or we mistook instructions for another aircraft. After the flight while discussing with the crew; myself and the Pilot Monitoring thought we heard the same instructions. Considering we may have accepted a clearance for another aircraft on frequency; I later looked at the flights in and out of ANC at the same time. There was another flight that arrived in ANC shortly after we landed. It is possible that the instruction were meant for them. It is also possible instructions were meant for an entirely different aircraft and we mistook it for us. There was high workload at the time while considering a runway change; configuring the aircraft and checking landing data.The Pilot Monitoring immediately replied to maintain 8;000. I rolled the altitude selector back to 8;000; clicked off the autopilot; added power and hand flew the airplane back to 8;000 and then reengaged the autopilot. If in fact we did accept a clearance from a different aircraft; caution must be used when similar flight numbers are on the same transmitting frequency; especially during high work loads. Unfortunately; we were unaware of the other aircraft at the time of the event.

column121: Upon arrival to the aircraft; an ACARS message from our dispatcher was already on the printer asking if we had Revision X to our flight release.  I opened and downloaded the flight release to my iPad.  The release was indeed Revision X.  We replied to the Dispatcher telling him that we did have Rev X onboard.  I never saw the original Rev Y.  When uploading the flight plan to the FMC; the route that loaded was consistent with Rev X.  This route was: BLZZR4 BLZZR BAF Q480 CANDR RAV J64 [...].  I logged into the CPDLC and we received the clearance via CPDLC.  The CPDLC clearance was: 'CLEARED TO ZZZ ARPT BLZZR4 THEN AS FILED. [...]' We accepted the clearance.  From this point the flight progressed normally.  After departure while flying the BLZZR4 departure we were talking to Center; we had not yet reached the BAF waypoint.  The controller gave us a shortcut and cleared us directly to TRIBS intersection.  We couldn't find that fix on the legs page and replied that we were not showing TRIBS on our route.  The controller inquired as to what our route was and I replied with the route that was on our release (noted above).  Controller replied that they had a new route for us and cleared us from our present position direct to TRIBS Q406 BWZ J6 HVQ J78 FAM SGF [...] to ZZZ. We accepted the new clearance; entered it into the FMC; then notified Dispatch via ACARS of our new route.  Later in the flight; while talking to the next Center; the controller notified us of a possible pilot route deviation and gave us a phone number to call Center upon arrival in ZZZ.  The flight continued uneventfully to ZZZ.  Enroute to ZZZ; the Captain and I discussed what possible route deviation could have occurred.  We could only speculate that there was a difference between the flight plan on our Rev 01 Flight Release and the route that Center had cleared us via CPDLC and expected us to fly.  We were confident; however; that we were never off course since both the CPDLC clearance and Rev X flight plan had us flying the BLZZR4 departure; and the shortcut and subsequent reroute issued by Center occurred while we were still on the departure route.  At BAF (Barnes VOR) is where Q480 & Q406 diverge).After the Captain called Center from ZZZ; we suspected that the cause of the problem was that the Rev 01 route wasn't processed by BOS prior to issuing us our CPDLC clearance.  Since both the Rev X route; and the original route that BOS expected us to fly both began with the BLZZR4 departure; we had no idea from the CPDLC clearance of 'CLEARED TO ZZZ ARPT BLZZR4 THEN AS FILED.' that there was any discrepancy.  We are unsure why the updated route wasn't processed by BOS prior to issuing our CPDLC clearance.   Perhaps there is a cut-off time where changes are no longer accepted or processed. Even when being issued a 'Cleared As Filed' CPDLC; listing the entire filed route at the end of the message would be another way to confirm that the ATC facility has the same route as the crew does on their flight release.  In addition; being able to print the entire CPDLC message would also be helpful to not only have a hard copy of the clearance; but also to avoid having to step through multiple pages on the FMC and potentially miss something.  This would be especially helpful when there is an unexpected reroute as part of the CPDLC clearance.

column121: Training was in play at Local and Ground all day.  There was flow with delays to ZZZ.  Aircraft Y was taxied to Taxiway L short of M for eventual taxi via M to 1L for departure. Aircraft X was taxied to Runway 1R on the SSTIK4; which requires a red 'R' if requested/required by the pilot.  It is unknown at this point if that was the case.  My only assumption is that the Ground CPC-IT taxied the aircraft incorrectly to Runway 1R and the OJTI did not notice.  As their flow time came up; Local CPC-IT taxied Aircraft Y across Runway 1R at M and LUAW Runway 1L.  Aircraft X was given Runway 1R LUAW.  The CPC-it then; unbeknownst to the OJTI; launched Aircraft X on the SSTIK4; and shortly thereafter launched Aircraft Y also on the SSTIK4.  The only reason I became aware is when I heard the CPC-IT issuing visual separation and the Local Assist coordinating the same with NorCal.  When I looked up at the display; the aircraft were approximately 2 miles in trail with Aircraft Y lower and following to SSTIK.  Of note; with OJT occurring on both Local and Ground simultaneously; and Local Assist open; but apparently not engaged dynamically; the FLM could not possibly monitor both positions and all that the Local Assist was doing.  Subsequent discussion by the Local Control OJTI dictated that they were sorry; as they missed it and 'Use of RNAV To... will save you every time.'  This has been my complaint about people who refuse to use it and ignore that its use will in fact keep this exact scenario from occurring.  The numbers of neigh-sayers are reducing thankfully and we will eventually have the majority compliance.The traffic has picked up over 700 operations a day a few days of the week and is expected to get busier by the month this summer.  Use RNAV To... and; when working as OJTI; pay attention to what the CPC-IT is doing.

column121: On the departure; the First Officer (FO) had requested Heading Mode (HDG); Flight Level Change (FLCH) during the climb out as we were given a heading.  It was bumpy and he was trying to comply with the SID instructions to speed up to 250 KIAS while hand flying in bumpy air.  As we approached the 5;000 foot altitude restriction; he started to slow his climb for the level off; but didn't pull back on the thrust levers. The autothrottles were on; but we were not quite close enough to the altitude for the flight director to switch to 'ASEL' on the FMA and begin capturing. In a climb; the auto throttles remain at full thrust in green FLCH until ASEL is annunciated; and since the FO was hand flying and beginning the level off before the Altitude Select (ASEL) annunciation; the speed began to pick up.  As pilot monitoring; I noticed the airspeed at 255 KIAS with an increasing trend and I called out 'airspeed' to alert him to the airspeed.  He seemed confused and did not make any corrections. I then called for him to 'pitch up' which he did slightly; but he mentioned the level off altitude that was approaching.  I said to 'pull the thrust back' and he seemed confused again and replied that the auto throttles should do that.  I then pulled the thrust levers back myself to slow the aircraft down as the speed was starting to go past 260 KIAS.  ATC gave us a 'climb and maintain 7000' and a direct to one of the fixes.  The FO pitched up for the climb and I was able to let go of the thrust levers as the speed was again under control.  As we were climbing; ATC instructed us to climb to 16;000 and the FO called for 'Autopilot On' prior to the next level off so there were no further issues.  I reminded him that there is no speed protection in the level off for the FLCH mode if he is hand flying it and levels off early.   ATC didn't seem to notice the increased airspeed;  and the flight continued without further incident.The FO said that he finished IOE and for the next month was unable to get any flying from crew scheduling.  He had less than 30 hours on the aircraft.   The following month; he had to be in Country to check on family due to the COVID pandemic.  He said that he had flown earlier that day and seemed to be comfortable in the plane.  It became clear that he was rusty on the details concerning the FLCH mode.  After I spoke with him about what happened; he said he understood and he did not make the same mistake on his flight the following day. Any time a pilot has less than 100 hours (consolidation) on an aircraft; and doesn't fly for more than 30 days; they should be given a trip with an IOE instructor both to give them recency of experience and to refresh any forgotten material.
column123: During take off climbing to the assigned altitude of 5;000 in flight level change plane accelerated to 250K; during last 1;000 ft I shallowed the pitch as climb was getting a bit bumpy due to builds up around [the] area and I was trying to avoid flying through a cloud straight ahead. Captain advised me of speed increasing and passing 250 and I assumed the auto-throttle would have compensated for that as it was engaged. Leveling off to 5;000 speed past 260 and the Captain reached out the thrust lever decreasing power avoiding further deviation. Soon after cleared to 7;000 climb and flight continued with no further deviation. After IOE I was put on reserve and didn't fly for about a month; I then was able to pick up a line and fly just one sequence as a tragic event forced me to drop the rest of the month and travel overseas; as a result in 2 months I only flew 19 hours and that was my first day flying after a long stop. As newly typed on a new airplane I didn't immediately recalled the different ways the autothrottle responds; however soon after the event my Captain explained [to] me what happened and refreshed my memory on it. After IOE it would be good to assign some extra flight to help consolidate; maybe assigning more frequent flights and not letting more than 2 weeks without flying would avoid skills deterioration until the first 100 hours are reached.

As we approached our base leg; tower told us the base turn was our discretion; and we began turning base. Tower approved and notified them that once they completed their 360 to watch out for us; and that they would be now following us (making us now #2 for the runway; and them #3).My student turned final and we were on an approximately 1.5 nm final; descending through 700-800 feet; when my student stated; 'I think they're turning right at us!'Simultaneously Aircraft Y had apparently just completed their 360 turn and Tower inquired if they had us in sight and were to follow us; they stated they were looking for traffic.I looked up to suddenly see the other aircraft heading directly across our final approach path; and almost on a head-on course; coming at us approximately from 45 degrees off of our left nose.  As I looked; I also simultaneously received an ADS-B traffic alert from Foreflight on my iPad; indicated the other traffic; heading directly at us and at the same altitude.I immediately stated 'my controls'; took over control of the aircraft; and quickly began a descending turn to the right to create distance from the other traffic; I looked up again and saw the other aircraft also start a sharp bank to their right; while simultaneously telling the tower that they now had us in-sight.  I remained in control of the aircraft and executed an (otherwise) uneventful landing.Tower did not acknowledge the event.  It seemed that the controller was very task saturated with the five aircraft in the pattern.  It seemed they were also distracted by a King Air 350 that was handed over to tower from ZZZ Approach and setup for a right downwind for Runway XX. Initially tower had told them to enter left downwind; but they were adamant that they wanted right downwind; which I believe both added to the confusion; as well as tied up the tower frequency unnecessarily with their continued back and forth communications. It did not help that the King Air had requested and was then doing a 360 turn for spacing of their own; right on the upwind leg of Runway XX when there were multiple other aircraft in the traffic pattern.It should be noted that while we were on short final; the Aircraft Y involved in this incident had once again turned base too soon; and I noticed that they were less than 0.5nm behind us.  They were so close that they in fact were ordered to go-around by the Tower because we had just touched down and were still rolling out when they crossed the runway threshold behind us.I believe contributing to the incident were: The pilot of Aircraft Y failing to maintain situational awareness resulting in inadequate spacing thus requesting multiple 360 turns; their failure to adequately scan for traffic and maintain a proper rectangular course in the traffic pattern causing them to cross our final approach course at a 45 degree angle; tower controller being task saturated with multiple aircraft in the traffic pattern; and the King Air traffic adding to the confusion by adamantly requesting to enter the right downwind (which conflicted with the other aircraft already in the traffic pattern for Runway XX; which is right traffic.)

column121: I was Pilot Flying. I triggered a stick shaker/pusher at the Final Approach Fix. I recovered per SOP.[There was] a northbound squall line west of the field. A last minute wind shift caused us to switch runways. Although it was fast; we were able to set up and brief before intercepting course. ATC forgot to turn [us] on the ILS; so we went through the localizer course. This led to reactionary vectors and the aircraft doing S turns until we passed the final approach fix. At this point we were flaps 30 with the power reduced. I called for the go-around; but when I pressed the autopilot disconnect button; I became fixated on the lack of a missed approach course. (I didn't press the TO-GA button.) While troubleshooting; the airspeed continued to decrease leading to a simultaneous stick shaker and pusher. I lowered the nose and recovered per the training; paying special attention to the radar altimeter. I briefly oversped flaps 8 on recovery.Stall recovery training works. I was able to accomplish the recovery quickly without having to think about it. However; it shouldn't have gotten that far. It was my first go-around since OE. I was task saturated and in the moment couldn't remember where the TO-GA button was. We were able to handle weather; ATC error; runway changes and an instrument approach at the same time. However; because our go around was triggered at a relatively untrained aircraft state/position; I missed a critical aspect of the maneuver. I don't believe this is a common problem; but incorporating go-arounds during recurrent in various positions may be beneficial.

column121: While in cruise at FL400; I noticed cabin altitude display illuminate Amber on upper EICAS showing cabin altitude of 8300 feet and rising at 300-400 ft/min.  Aircraft was dispatched with one pack deferred; two operating. I brought up the ECS schematic to verify Packs 2 and 3 were both supplying pressure and in High Flow. They appeared to be operating normally; but I then noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault; cabin altitude was already 9;000 ft. and still climbing. At this point I requested a descent from ATC to FL 360.  They gave us a vector for descent.  A minute later; with Cabin altitude of 9300 ft.; I informed ATC we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend.  We were given FL390 and then a few minutes later; FL360.  Pressurization stabilized at 8;500 ft.; but began to climb again at 100-200 ft/min. We requested and were given FL 320.  I notified Operations Control via ACARS (SATCOM inop); that we had a Pack 2 issue and that we had descended as cabin altitude had been increasing. They were given our fuel and told I would keep them advised. We were at FL 280; where cabin altitude at stabilized; but showing slight increase. I recommended to divert to ZZZ along our route of flight; but they informed me they wanted the airplane in ZZZ1.  I informed ATC that we needed to change our destination for 'maintenance' from ZZZ2 to ZZZ1.  We were given proceed direct ZZZ1; about 350 miles away; where we landed uneventfully.Cruise flight when cabin altitude appeared amber on Upper EICAS.Strictly a maintenance issue with the aircraft. We had Pack 1 deferred and any issue with the remaining Packs was going to cause pressurization issues.To assess the situation; attempt to bring pressurization under control; and descend as necessary to reduce cabin altitude.  QRH was utilized to validate what pressurization reading we should have at the various altitudes.Aircraft was dispatched to pick up freight in ZZZ2; and then proceed with a Pack deferred.
column123: Pushback; taxi; takeoff and climb were completely normal. Weather on departure were calm winds and decent VFR in the terminal area. The weather became more marginal upon leveling at cruise. On this leg I myself was the First Officer and Flying Pilot. The Captain was the Pilot Not flying. We also had a Relief Pilot on board and loadmaster.  The event began somewhat early in cruise at FL400 when the Captain noticed a cabin altitude display Amber on the Upper EICAS display. He then immediately selected the ECS page and we both were made aware of a 8;300 foot cabin and rising at 300-400 fpm. The aircraft was dispatched with Pack #1 deferred; therefore packs 2 and 3 operating normally. After diagnosing the situation via the ECS page; both packs 2 and 3 appeared to be supplying pressure and in High Flow as designed when one pack is selected off.  However on the Lower EICAS we both noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault. Cabin altitude was still climbing and at this point showing 9;000 feet and still climbing. At this point we agreed to suggest a decent to FL360 and were given a vector for decent. About a minute later with Cabin Altitude of 9;300 feet the Captain informed ATC that we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend now; we first were given a decent to FL390 and shortly after to FL360. At FL360 we observed the cabin initially stabilizing at 8;500 feet; but shortly afterwards began again climbing at a lower rate than previously of 100-200 FPM.  We again agreed to request a lower altitude of FL320 and ATC cleared us to FL320. The Captain then notified Operations Control of the situation via ACARS (SATCOM Inop) that we had a PACK 2 issue and we were descending with a cabin altitude still slowly increasing. The Captain requested further decent to FL280 and ATC complied. At FL280 we experienced a cabin altitude almost stable at around 8;000 feet but still trying to climb at a slow interment 100 FPM. The Captain notified the rest of the crew including the Relief Pilot and load master. The Relief Pilot was taking his rest but immediately returned to the cockpit to help in CRM and dealing with the situation. I suggested the Relief Pilot pull up the cabin altitude chart showing what the cabin altitude should be for our current altitude so we would know how far off from normal we were.  All 3 crew members talked about possible diversion airports and relayed our ideas to Operations Control. After communication between Operations Control and us it was decided by Operations Control to divert to ZZZ2 to address and fix the situation. The Captain immediately requested to divert to ZZZ2 and informed ATC as to why; and I put us on a course to ZZZ2 via ATC instructions. At this point we were about 350 miles north of ZZZ2 with plenty of fuel and sufficient weather for landing. We landed at ZZZ2 uneventfully and maintenance was made aware of the present maintenance issues.While in cruise flight the cabin altitude appeared amber on the Upper EICAS.Pack 2 was failing for unknown reasons. Pack 1 was already deferred on departure so any remaining pack issues was going to cause a pressurization issue.Crew did their job in noticing the system fault and working the problem. We were dispatched with Pack 1 deferred so any further pack or pressurization faults would cause a pressurization issue.Dispatching an aircraft with a pack deferred which would and did cause a pressurization issue when any further pressurization problems would happen. In this case pack 2 also failing to perform up to specification; therefore; causing an increasing cabin altitude at a higher level cruising altitude.

column123: We were approaching Harrisburg Int'l from the west when we were instructed to intercept the final course for a visual approach to RWY 13. Its RWY 12 is oriented similarly to RW 13 at MDT; so when we were asked if we had the airport in sight; we said we did.  The airport was closer by a few miles than our FMS was indicating so we configured for landing and steepened the approach. MDT Tower then asked if we could be approaching Capital City as we were lower than we should've been. At that point; MDT was also visible. The pilot flying applied power and climbed enough to conduct a normal approach to RWY 13.The haze contributed; as did the vector for a visual. column121: I have departed ZZZ airport to the south to practice landings in ZZZ1. On the way back to ZZZ I have contacted ZZZ Tower around 7NM to 8 NM south of the field; the Tower has replied standby so I have tuned to easterly heading so I will not enter the airspace; a few minutes after that the Tower has instructed me to join mid left downwind for Runway XX and to report when established on the downwind; after I have established on the downwind I have notified the Tower. To the best of my knowledge and memory the Tower has replied the following instruction: 'you are number 3 for Runway XX continue'; I have given the Tower read back and then I looked forward to visually scan for the traffic in front of me; I remember clearly that I saw 2 aircraft in the final for Runway XX; the first one was an airplane in the short final and the second one was a helicopter that was also in the final behind him. I remember that I have pointed the 2 aircraft to my students and explained to them that these are the aircraft that are in front of us and we will follow them as we are number 3 in the sequence. After the helicopter was abeam to my position; I continued to fly on the downwind for an extra 30 seconds to 1 minute so I will allow some extra spacing between myself and the helicopter as I'm flying with students on their first ever fly day. As I was told I'm number 3 in sequence and I visually saw the 2 aircraft that are in front of me I have continued the traffic pattern and turn left to the base leg; and then when I was in the appropriate position I have turned final. Between 30 seconds to 1 minute after I was established on the final for XX the Tower has instructed me to 'immediately turn heading 090 and break the approach'; I have immediately took controls from my student and turned to the heading 090 while giving a read back to the Tower. As I have established on the heading 090 I saw that there was a jet aircraft on the final approach behind me; approximately 1;200 feet horizontally and 300 feet vertically in my evaluation. after that I have continued to comply with the Tower instructions and followed a different traffic that was on the downwind to join the final for Runway XX again for a full stop. Before landing when I was on short final I have verified with the Tower that I had clearance to land.I have strong belief in self critic and self evaluation and after this event has occurred I have come up with the following safety measures that can help prevent this situation from reoccurring:1. When you have been instructed to follow traffic while on the downwind; you should always verify with Tower that you can start your turn towards the base leg.2. When you are told that you are number 3 in sequence and you see the 2 aircraft in front of you; that absolutely does not mean that you should stop looking for other traffic in the area; you still need scan for traffic very frequently.3. When flying on the base leg; even in a controlled airport; you should always try to look for more traffic coming on the final; both behind you and in front of you; and make sure that there is no traffic that can jeopardize the approach before actually making the turn to final.4. Do not think that just because you are flying in a controlled airspace under ATC supervision; you are protected. Always actively scan for traffic and verify ATC instructions.I believe that if I had used these safety measures that I have mentioned above this event could have been prevented. I am glad no damage has been done in this event; and I'm committed to learn from this experience and actively seek to improve myself as a pilot and as flight instructor.

column121: I was the Relief First Officer sitting in the right aft seat with a very limited view of the PFD;s and MFD;s of the aircraft. Shanghai Approach Control issued us a different arrival than what the company had filed and what we already had planned. The communications were ambiguous at best and we all agreed to get a clarification on which arrival was being issued. There were four arrivals that had the suffix '81A'.  The pronunciation was tough to understand.  It took some clarification but we all confirmed the new arrival as the 'DUM 81A' arrival. At some point after DUMET there was a transmission from Shanghai Approach to 'comply with all restrictions' At the same time the PF was slowing down and trying to get down with deploying the speed brakes to meet the restrictions of PD230.  Shanghai approach made the same transmission again. I unbuckled my seat belt to stand up see what the displays were showing and wanted to confirm the altitude in the alt window was correct. It was set correctly to 6;980 feet which was equivalent to 2;100 meters issued to us. The aircraft showed a little high on the path but was correcting and it showed very close to the speed restriction of 230 kts.  I sat back down and verified the restrictions on my tablet. There was a lot of foreign language chatter on the radio. Upon crossing the fix; Shanghai issued a clearance direct to MPI which was the IAF for the approach to [Runway] 16L.  It wasn't until after we landed that the PF and PM were talking about being high over the PD230 fix however they agreed they were on speed.Understanding which arrival they were trying to issue took more time than necessary.  The pronunciation of the arrival was very hard to understand. This complicated things more than usual and it cost time. The frequency congestion in a foreign language complicated things when trying to get them to repeat the clearance.  On a side note this was the first time I've ever heard an approach clearance to a runway with a Left designator as 'Cleared for 16 Lima' ...the PM was corrected to say 16 Lima after she responded with 16 Left.  it didn't make sense.  When passed on to the Tower Controller; they correctly said 16 Left.My only suggestion is if you look high on a path; Flight Level Change works pretty good to hustle down to the altitude.  I can't say for sure if this descent was done in PATH or FLC.  The language barrier is what it is and probably won't change much.

column121: As this report is not timely; it is to the best of my recollection. Approach phase of the flight to DEN. Briefed and installed the SSKII 2 RNAV/ILS 16R. On arrival we a received multiple speed and heading changes but we were back on course and LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. At some point prior to CLIFF; for whatever reason ATC changed clearance to RNAV 16R for us and the Aircraft (AC) behind us. I was Pilot Not Flying (PNF) so I installed the approach/transition. The AC ahead of us was in sight and was on the arrival but still assigned the ILS 16R. The approach was verified by both the First Officer (FO) and myself. LNAV/VNAV were still engaged and the speed window was open as ATC had already been assigning speed changes. The FO located the Approach briefing guide for the RNAV/RNP approach and RNP values for the approach were line selected and installed. All altitudes for the approach were verified.  I made the comment that 'Since ATC has been messing with our speed so much; the speed window is already open'. So far the approach was flawless and the aircraft (AC) was on the vertical and lateral profile.Upon reaching CLIFF the AC began a descent as it should have. TDZ had been set and VNAV Path was engaged. As we approached CEPEE the MCP/FMA's had not changed SPD/LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. The magenta track depicted CLIFF;CEPEE;AAGEE;JABRO;JETSN; RW 16R; as it should. It was upon arrival at CEPEE that the event occurred. The AC continued to descend and VNAV path remained engaged. But; the AC continued to track straight ahead. CEPEE had not become active and the vector leg out of CLIFF was still engaged. I had been so concerned with the vertical profile that I failed to notice CEPEE was not active. Realizing what had happened I went to the FMC to LS AAGEE; but ATC noticed at the same time and assigned us either a 080 or 090 heading. ATC also canceled the RNAV approach clearance for the AC behind us. We landed without further issue. Once inside the terminal; still pissed that I allowed this to happen; I located the Captain of the AC that landed behind us to apologize. He informed us that ATC had mistakenly given him the # to call. I took the number (#) and called immediately. After a conversation with the supervisor I was informed that there was no safety issue; no loss of separation; and no need to file a report.Looking back; how this could have been avoided... first of all; I could have just said 'unable' when ATC switched us to the RNAV RNP 16R. Although not a big deal at the time...after flying all night; briefing and installing one arrival and approach then; at the last minute being reassigned to a RNAV/ RNP approach which requires lots of briefing and changes; and programming; was probably not the thing to do. What else could I have done...I allowed myself to get distracted. I should have continually monitored the lateral path to insure the AC was doing what we thought it was going to do. It was very clear and it was easy to look outside to follow traffic. It was also the FO's first Pilot Flying leg so there was instruction taking place and attention was diverting to multiple places.The FO did a great job when we were reassigned to the RNAV RNP Z 16R. He did not miss a checklist; procedure; or setting.I'm disgusted that I allowed this to happen. I am unfortunately or fortunately very familiar with the airspace and lateral/ vertical deviation issues in the area. I'm not the first and sure won't be the last; but I know what I will and won't do next time.
column123: During the SSKII 2 RNAV Arrival phase; we were advised by ATC to expect the ILS 16R approach. A few minutes prior to CLFFF; the last point on the SSKII 2 arrival; we were assigned the RNAV (RNP) Z R16R approach. We were on a northerly heading in HDG mode at this time for vectors for the previously expected ILS. The Captain; as Pilot Monitoring (PM); selected the correct RNAV Z 16R approach as well as the correct transition (CLFFF transition) in the FMC. I verified the selected approach and transition after he did so. I then set up the approach per all steps of the Approach Briefing Guide and briefed the approach. We were then given direct CLFFF and selected LNAV. We were cleared for the RNAV RNP Z R16R approach shortly before arriving at CLFFF. Upon arriving at CLFFF; I verified that the CLFFF waypoint sequenced in the FMC to ensure we were now on a published segment of the approach. I selected LNAV; VNAV; opened the speed window for the appropriate speed; requested the PM set touchdown zone elevation (which he did); and verified that the ENGAGED FMA's were in green LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft began a descent per the VPATH glide slope. I ran through the items again to verify that the approach was proceeding correctly. I verified again that the FMA's showed an engaged green LNAV and engaged green VPATH. The approach was proceeding as expected. At the CEPEE waypoint; the aircraft should have begun a right turn towards the AAGEE as part of the track towards the final approach point and final approach course. The aircraft did not turn and continued in a straight course after passing CEPEE. I immediately checked the FMA's again to ensure it did not revert to HDG mode. The FMA's were still in green; engaged LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft was also still in an expected VPATH descent to the TDZE. Within a few seconds; and before we could figure out why the aircraft did not turn; ATC called to cancel the RNAV approach and gave us a right turn for a visual approach to runway 16R and gave clearance for the visual approach. We proceeded uneventfully for the visual approach and landing. After arriving at the gate and leaving the aircraft; a pilot from another aircraft that was behind us during the arrival and approach advised us that he was mistakenly given a phone number by ATC to call regarding the RNAV Z 16R turning issue that we actually experienced. We got the phone number from him and the Captain called. The ATC supervisor said that no report would be required; there was no loss of separation; there was no safety issue; and how just wanted to know what happened. The Captain and I reviewed everything we did in setting up; preparing; and executing that approach and could not figure any reason why the aircraft did not initiate a turn at CEPEE and continued straight while engaged in LNAV with the proper approach waypoints; altitudes; and sequencing verified in the FMC.

column121: We were taking off from ELP on Runway 22 and had an initial clearance for the TDOWN3 RNAV Departure.  Tower cleared us for takeoff with revised clearance to turn left to 200 and climb to 17;000 [feet].  I was the flying pilot manually flying.  As we were accelerating and getting the aircraft to a clean configuration we were issued a frequency change to Departure.  Upon checking in we were immediately given further instructions which included a right turn after reaching 6;200 feet to 060.  Both of us misunderstood the turn right part of the clearance.  The FO (First Officer) read back 'passing 6;200 heading 060' and had no response from the controller.  We climbed through 6;200 and turned left. We were about half way through the left turn when the controller saw the mistake and told us it was a right turn; but then told us to continue the left turn.  He later asked us to call them for possible pilot certificate action. There are several causal factors [due to direction of turn by flight crew].  First; having a clearance for an RNAV departure that has a left turn from Runway 22 sets you up to expect a left turn out for protected airspace even after receiving a last minute change to the departure plan using radar vectors.  Because the radar vectors are given last minute the old departure stays in the FMC showing the original route on our map displaying that left turn; so even though we were not following the route displayed it probably influenced our thought pattern.  There is no published departures turning out to the right from Runway 22 due to mountainous terrain if you are departing east.  Secondly; we also had prebriefed the engine failure procedures that have you turn out to the left for the same reason.  Third; from a 200 heading to turn right to 060 is counter intuitive because it is more than 180 degree turn. All of these factors I think caused expectation bias to turn left and not hear the right turn instruction.  Fourth; the controllers failure to emphasize the right turn part when it is more than 180 from current heading and his not ensuring the read back was correct. Controllers need to emphasize the direction of turn especially if it's more than 180 degrees and ensure they get a correct read back.  On the phone the controller said this was normal to avoid traffic from Mexico.  If this is a common procedure to use radar vectors to turn us out an opposite direction of our assigned clearance then there needs to be some notes somewhere in our charts so we can prepare for that ahead of time.  This non published procedure could cause conflicts with terrain in the event of an engine failure.
column123: The missed approach and takeoff engine failure profiles for Runway 22 tell you to turn left.  The TDOWN 3 SID; we were assigned; tells you to turn left off of Runway 22.  The reason all of the departures turn left on Runway 22 at El Paso is because there is high terrain if you turn right.  On takeoff; we were told to climb to 17;000 feet and turn left to heading 200.  When we contacted Departure; the controller quickly blurted out a long; involved clearance.  I responded; 'Passing 6.2; turn to 060.'  He did not respond back to my radio call.  On a heading of 200; the heading of 060 is to the left.  As we entered the left turn to 060; the controller informed us that he had told us to turn right to 060; he also told us to expedite our left turn and continue to a heading of 010.  When we rolled out on the heading; he told us to call a phone number because of a potential violation.  I read the phone number back to him and asked him to verify.  He did not respond because he was working two frequencies; and was talking to another aircraft on the other frequency. When we called the phone number for El Paso Departure Control; they told us that left turns off Runway 22 often conflict with traffic at a Mexican airport.  So; they often vector you to the right.  The Captain and I have both been in and out of El Paso numerous times; and have never gotten a right turn off Runway 22.  None of our guidance for El Paso says to expect a right hand turn.  Expectation bias caused us to hear 'turn to 060' instead of 'turn right to 060.'  Also; the Departure Controller was working two frequencies and did not catch that we said 'turn to 060.'  Here is what he blurted at us at 1;000 feet AGL while we were retracting the flaps; '[company name]; radar contact; turn right to 060 and climb to 17;000.'  He also had a thick; Hispanic accent.  If the keyword was 'right'; it didn't help that he placed it in the middle of a sentence with no emphasis or follow up. If left departures off Runway 22 conflict with Mexican air traffic; perhaps they need an updated departure procedure.  The ATKNN 5 Departure off Runway 22 turns right; but it continues west bound.  There are no departure procedures for Runway 22 that turn right initially; and then continue to the east.  Also; none of our guidance tells us to expect a right turn off of Runway 22.

column121: Aircraft X was on route to ZZZ going northbound at 7;000 feet. I took the hand off. I called out to him and the aircraft was sitting on my frequency. I called the Moderate to Extreme Precipitation between him and his destination and he acknowledged. After a talking with a few other aircraft I went back to Aircraft X to call the weather again and told him it looked as though he was going to go through an area of moderate precipitation but here was extreme precipitation to the east and west. Again; the pilot just simply acknowledged me. It looked as though the aircraft climbed about 300 feet but leveled back off; I asked how the ride was; the pilot responded bumpy. Shortly after; the aircraft began losing altitude; I called the aircraft a few times; gave a low altitude alert; no response. It also appeared the aircraft was in a spiral. A VFR aircraft could hear Aircraft X but attempts to communicate failed. I took a handoff on an air carrier that I asked to help. At that moment I could finally hear Aircraft X and he informed me he lost his vacuum. I asked if he was in control of the aircraft and if he could see the ground; he said yes and that he was below the cloud layer in VFR conditions. Afterwards; I lost communication again. I tried all my transmitters (main/standby/Backups) but was unable to reestablish communications. We watched him proceed very low towards ZZZ and I learned afterwards he did land safely.
column123: I was flying direct to ZZZ. I was IFR in clouds; rain; and turbulence at 7;000 feet approximately 35 miles from ZZZ. The plane started making turns to the right ; which I corrected a few times. I was trying to figure out why it was happening. Suddenly the plane did a hard right. I noticed the artificial horizon had 'tumbled' and the 'vacuum' warning light came on. I turned off the auto-pilot and attempted to level the wings with multiple left and right corrections. Also noticed I was now in a dive. I saw the ground through an opening in the clouds and aimed for that. I broke out of the clouds at approximately 3;000-3;500 feet. Once I regained control below the clouds I tried contacting ZZZ Center. They were very difficult to hear/with broken reception. I notified them I had a vacuum pump failure; was below the clouds in VFR conditions and would call when I landed in ZZZ. Not sure if they heard me. I maneuvered the plane as necessary to stay out of the clouds and rain showers to ZZZ. Once on the ground I called Approach and Center to notify them of what had happened. I guess you can never know when a vacuum pump may fail; but it sure does affect many crucial navigation equipment. My assumption would be to have a secondary vacuum pump or artificial horizon as a safety back-up. I will be checking into that.
column125: A Center Controller; and a PA32 pilot flying through rain and experiencing turbulence reported the aircraft had a vacuum pump failure causing a temporary loss of control of the aircraft. The aircraft descended below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude but recovered and landed safely.

column121: Upon taking the aircraft; the number 3 MFD was inoperative which; per the MEL; required the Captain to complete all flying duties. While at ZZZ the Captain noticed that the GPWS Inop; Windshear Inop; Terrain Inop; and Terrain fail message were indicated in the EICAS. The Captain called maintenance who immediately deferred the issue and the Captain completed the logbook entries. Prior to push I entered the appropriate information into ACARS which did not match the PERF INIT which the Captain entered. We verified the numbers multiple times and determined that the ACARS had to be inaccurate. We also verified our numbers with the updated AOM. After calling Dispatch it appeared that their was a fleet wide issue with ACARS. It appeared to me that some information that is generally manually input may have already been calculated in the zero fuel weight of ACARS (85lbs for crew bags). Prior to the ACARS issue we notified Ground Control to receive an off time into ZZZ1 which we were given a departure time. At that point the Captain decided to complete the paper form X. We notified the ground crew of the delay who informed us they had to leave for another aircraft and would not be back for about 30-40 minutes. The Captain decided to have them push us from the gate in the event our issue was solved prior to their return. We completed the appropriate checklists and pushed but did not start any engines. Then notified ATC of the delay to void Off Time. The Captain then called the company for approval to open the cabin window to hand the form paper copy to the ground crew. Once the form was completed we called ops; handed the W&B out the window; and re completed the before start checklist all the way through. We also discussed not utilizing ACARS W&B throughout the flight (added workload). We then notified Ground that we were ready to verify off time prior to starting engines (fuel management). They gave us an immediate wheels up time so we started the engines and taxied to [Runway] XX. I used my IPAD to verify weather at ZZZ1 prior to push which was reporting calm winds ; few 050 TCU and 10 miles vis and again I checked prior to taxi which they were reporting calm winds; 046 CB; 10 miles. On departure from [Runway] XX we were given a turn to the west and eventually a heading to the north with a climb to 8;000 [feet]. When given direct to ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ4 Arrival we had to vector around a few storms. We also had to vector around storm clouds on the arrival and were given vectors off the arrival by approach due to flow into ZZZ1. Within this period we both discussed the weather; verified the TAF; and discussed needing an alternate and potential fuel issues. After updating the D-ATIS we verified that the field visibility had dropped below 3 miles so we messaged Dispatch asking for/if we needed an alternate due to visibility. Dispatch responded that the TAF was good and we didn't need an alternate. The Captain started to become concerned because he was showing extreme areas of precipitation along the arrival and approach. Other aircraft ahead reported heavy rain. There were multiple discussion with ATC about getting in to ZZZ1 but I don't remember if they advised aircraft were going missed. We received normal vectors into the approach to Runway XYL and my first awareness of wind shear is when the aircraft in front of us called wind shear and missed. With our Windshear capabilities inoperative we were both paying very close attention to the aircraft's instruments. After intercepting the localizer and passing the Runway XYL FAF the precipitation was worsening. Somewhere between 1;700 and 1;200 feet the aircraft instruments were showing increased gains and losses and began to vibrate significantly. The Captain called wind shear and we completed the wind shear procedure up to the missed approach altitude of 3;000ft. Tower gave us runway heading and eventually turned us to the west with a hand off to approach. Prior to the handoff we began discussing fuel and alternates. The Captain suggested ZZZ2 which we messaged to Dispatch. Dispatch recommended ZZZ3. I recommend that we not go to ZZZ3 because of all the weather that was building between ZZZ1 and ZZZ3 and it also appeared weather was building at ZZZ3 per my IPAD. We asked ATC about ZZZ3 and they indicated that ZZZ3 had similar weather to ZZZ1 so we determined based on fuel and ATCs information that ZZZ3 was not an option. It seemed to me that Dispatch was adamant about diverting to ZZZ3. We also discussed other airport near ZZZ1 (off field) that could be potential alternates. After the check in with Approach they asked us our intentions which we replied stand by and began rough fuel calculations to ZZZ2. The Captain quickly determined that fuel to ZZZ2 was inadequate due to a 15-20 minute flight and approximately 2200lbs of fuel on board. (Increased fuel burn at lower altitude; storms in the area; and potential unknown issues on arrival at ZZZ2). We then asked ATC about aircraft success in to ZZZ1 which they replied that some aircraft were making it in and some were not. We then requested Runway XYR because it was the closer runway and informed ATC of our minimum fuel situation. The Captain notified the Flight Attendant; we ran the appropriate checklist (ATIS; build it; bug; brief it) and continued vectors to Runway XYR. There were two aircraft in front of us which one was able to land and another missed (aircraft in front of us) due to wind shear. After recalculating fuel requirements the Captain determined that a missed would put us in an emergency fuel situation therefore we [advised ATC]. I believe that upon intercepting the localizer we were somewhere around 1700-1800lbs. During the approach the gains and losses of altitude did not seem significant but it appeared to be difficult to maintain the localizer although I did not see anything greater than one dot. There was also added pressure to continue the approach due to the fuel situation. During the approach tower asked the aircraft that made it in where they broke out and they replied 'right at mins'. At around 800 feet I called out that I could see the ground which was not visible as we got to 500 ft. At 300 feet I called approach lights in sight 12 o'clock and continued to call out the approach lights. The aircraft began to drift right and I called the runway environment insight at 11 o'clock. Throughout this period it was apparent that the Captain was having difficulty seeing the runway. When he finally looked up and determined that he did not have adequate references; and the aircraft was not in a safe position to land; he called the missed. Immediately on the missed it was apparent the at least 90 percent of the airfield was VFR. We could see all of Runway XZ/XA; including approach paths; so we made a decision request XZ and due a VFR pattern into XZ. Tower provided we could use whatever runway we needed so we continued with XZ; entered the left crosswind; base; and landed. During the miss we did not climb to the missed approach altitude; left the gear down; and kept the flaps at nine because of the immediate landing after the missed to Runway XYR. We updated the FMS with Runway XZ and extended a line for reference because there are no approaches in our pubs for XZ. We did not rerun the performance information again because the field length was 10;500 [feet] which was longer than Runway XYR and it was an immediate landing. We also received fuel EICAS alerts during the missed and a fuel critical prior to landing XZ. All approaches were conducted with flaps 22. Emergency vehicles were on scene which we did not require. Upon taxiing into the gate the field went in to a ground stop due to lightning. In all the entire flight segment from door closed to door open was 3.4 hours. I would say that this flight provided the crew with several threats. To name a few; my PFD was inop so only the CPT could fly; windshear; GPWS; and TCAS were inop; pop-up weather wasoccurring throughout the flight route; fuel considerations; ACARS not accurate due to new AOM changes; delays prior to departure; delays in route; other aircraft encountering wind shear; and potentially an inexperienced dispatcher. There was also a significant pressure to land the second approach. I felt that we handled the situation very well as a crew and discussed and analyzed any and all potential alternatives but were cornered due to the fuel situation. I do wish I had analyzed the winds better throughout the duration and been more aware of the weather at the field during the Runway XYL wind shear event. With most of the airfield being VFR it was absolutely possible to successfully complete approaches to the XB runways and XZ/XA [runways]. The only area impacted by the weather was the XY runways approach segments. Therefore; if winds were within landing limits we could have immediately requested an alternate runway from ATC.
column123: While conducting the setup check in ZZZ; the GPWS Inop; Windshear Inop; Terr Inop; and Terr Fail messages appeared on the EICAS. Maintenance was called and the affected system was deferred per MEL. The aircraft also had an MEL for the First Officer MFD; and an NEF item in the cockpit. ACARS would not produce accurate weight and performance numbers; and Dispatch informed us that this was a known issue. We elected to perform a manual weight and balance with the Form X. The TAF for ZZZ1 was forecasting VFR and radar looked fairly benign. The First Officer obtained the D-ATIS for ZZZ1 which showed Winds Calm; visibility 10SM; Few at 5000; Scattered at 8000; with no other weather (information M). Due to this; extra fuel for weather was not considered by us or Dispatch. While in our initial descent the First Officer and myself noticed the weather in ZZZ1 was deteriorating and sent an ACARS to Dispatch asking if we should get an alternate. Dispatch replied that no alternate was needed; and we assumed that they had more up to date information than available to us in the air. Our radar was depicting areas of extreme return (red and purple) blanketing the approach and airport with other aircraft saying it was a smooth ride; but heavy precipitation. While outside of the final approach fix on the ILS Runway XYL; other aircraft were heard going missed due to windshear. ATC informed us that some aircraft were landing and some were going around. We elected to continue the approach as we were not experiencing any abnormal flight conditions. Inside of the final approach fix; I was unable to maintain positive aircraft control on the approach path due to airspeed; altitude; and course fluctuations. I made the determination to execute a windshear escape/go around. The Flight Attendant was notified of our situation. We contacted Dispatch to request a diversion and suggested ZZZ2. Dispatch replied that ZZZ3 was a better option; but ATC informed us that ZZZ3 was having similar weather to ZZZ1. I used the FMS to determine a rough fuel burn to ZZZ2 as 1400 lbs not including any deviations or approaches. We were also low on fuel; approximately 2;200 lbs after the missed approach. We discussed and agreed that we did not want to end up in ZZZ3 with such low fuel and similar weather issues. We decided to attempt a second approach at ZZZ1 after ATC stated that some aircraft were landing successfully. It was apparent that we would be below divert and possibly final divert on the second approach so we declared Minimum Fuel. We requested ILS Runway XYR due to perceived improved conditions and the closer approach for that runway. During the approach; the Flight Attendant called and said that a passenger was in the bathroom and asked if we could delay the landing. I advised her that due to our fuel situation; it would not be possible. She was able to get the passenger back to his seat before final approach. While on the approach; we overheard the aircraft in front of us go around for windshear. Our fuel level was low and a go around would put us in a fuel critical situation. We [advised ATC] and continued the approach. We experienced difficulty in maintaining the approach course and I used my PIC authority to continue the approach since a missed approach would leave us with inadequate fuel for much option. The First Officer called approach lights in sight; and we continued to 100 feet above the field. The First Officer called Runway in sight; and when I looked up; I did not see a runway and was disoriented due to the extreme precipitation and reduced visibility and immediately executed a go around. We were now showing a very low fuel level; and it was unlikely we would have enough fuel to get to another airport or reattempt an approach. I used PIC emergency authority to request a circle to land Runway XZ. We were able to maintain visual contact with Runway XZ during the maneuver. We had no time to get any type of performance numbers; and reasoned that since itwas longer than Runway XYR we could land. The landing was conducted without incident. As we engaged E/TO Reserve on the windshear escape; I entered this in the logbook and contacted maintenance. See attachments for reference if needed.Many threats existed in this incident including: pop up weather; weight restrictions; the need for paper performance calculations; an inoperative MFD; an inoperative Windshear system; and lack of an alternate. The weather and TAF looked ok during the planning portion of the flight; it was not until enroute; that everything deteriorated. I believe we acted in the best manner possible given the stressful situation and lack of backup options (fuel and/or alternate). It was a unique scenario that required a unique response. I believe we made safe decisions based on the current parameters. In hindsight; I would have been more assertive about requesting an alternate enroute. I do not believe we could have forecasted such bad weather; which is why we did not ask to remove passengers to add fuel in ZZZ. As we could not find a suitable alternate; we had little choice once we were low on fuel than to attempt to land on any runway. A third go around would have likely had us considering an off field landing.

column121: During the terminal phase of a single pilot IMC maintenance ferry flight to MRN (Foothills Regional) I requested the RNAV (GPS) Runway 21 Approach into MRN. ATC approved the request and cleared me to the CIKIS IAF. Scanning the preloaded route of flight in my G1000 PFD; I inadvertently selected the CICAC FAF as the desired steer point and turned in that direction. ATC observed the aircraft tracking to the wrong fix and directed a heading change in the direction of the IAF. At that instant; I detected the switch error and made the appropriate correct selection. The approach continued and the flight terminated without further incident. There can be no excuse for my having failed to confirm the exact GPS steer point selected; but in the interest of preventing a future incident such as this; I might question why two of the fixes on this approach would be labeled with identifiers so similar in spelling and pronunciation that this error could almost have been predicted; especially in the high workload environment of single pilot IMC during the terminal phase of the flight. I suspect that I'm not the first pilot to bite on this one; and the controller was probably spring-loaded to detect and correct my error. Can't TERPS label these fixes with less ambiguous identifiers?

column121: I set up for a visual approach with an ILS back-up to Runway 13L at DAL.  We were in good shape from a speed and altitude standpoint at NNATE.  I was hand flying.  I was distracted by the localizer guidance which showed me well right of course when I was actually slightly left.  I mentioned that to the Pilot Monitoring.  While troubleshooting the lateral guidance; I got behind the jet for getting flaps 15 and gear down and we ended up high.  As I regained my crosscheck; I subconsciously followed vertical guidance; which now was taking me erroneously higher. I called for flaps 30; and realized we were now 800 feet. The Pilot Monitoring called out the PAPIs (Precision Approach Indicators); which showed all white; but the glideslope guidance was taking me higher.  I called for a go-around.  My go-around was sloppy; but the Pilot Monitoring brought his A game; so it was manageable. On the second approach; a visual approach backed up by the ILS 13L; both lateral and vertical guidance were erroneous.  I had to fight the tendency to cue on the vertical guidance; which again was taking me high. The Pilot Monitoring turned off both flight directors. On short final; we got an audio glideslope alert. The glideslope raw data showed me way low. The PAPIs were three white and one red.  We should have also turned away from the ILS on the NAV tuning panel. On both approaches; an Aircraft Y was parked right at the hold short line in front of the glideslope antenna.  I suspect we will see more aircraft stopped at the hold short line with the runway closure at DAL; and so we will see more ILS interference.  I have seen similar ILS behavior at other airports with an aircraft stopped at the hold short line.  We did not write up the aircraft.  An ILS test was completed and passed prior to the flight. NOTAM (or other reminder) that the 13L ILS may be unreliable with aircraft in the ILS critical area. More training on go-arounds.

column121: On the ORCKA 5 Departure; after passing the 160 SMO radial and DOCKR below 3;000 feet. We were given heading of 030 and climb to 12;000 feet as prescribed by the SID (expect vectors). As we were climbing and turning he gave us direct 'KLIPR at or above 10;000; climb to 15;000.' I could not find KLIPR on the legs pages. I checked several downline pages; went back to page 1/9 and then checked the route page to verify the ORCKA 5. It was loaded but still no KLIPR. I told the controller it isn't apparently on our route. He spelled it out. I was moving too slow. He gave us 030 heading and told us to let us know when we are heading there. I though we were heading in the right direction but the intersection is now behind us. As I was jamming the box; perhaps KLIPR got eaten or dropped out as we passed it. It's location is right by DOCKR.  I can't figure out why it wasn't there initially as we turned. We were going through 10;000 feet easily so he then gave us direct KEGGS and to go to next frequency. The next controller gave us direct NNAVY.  Altitudes were no issue; if anything our climb rate was quicker than my cumbersome effort towards KLIPR. What could we have done better. I had expectation bias from the old Loop departure. If I remember after DOCKR you loop back to LAX at or above 10;000 feet. With this departure giving an initial vector and our climb rate much better than my 737 experience.  I was looking for KLIPR to be farther down the road than between LAX and DOCKR. I still don't know why I didn't see it because I was looking at the' top of the flight plan' legs page. I was just too slow for the expectation of the controller so he vectored us on down the line. Although I haven't been to LAX in two years I am comfortable there and fell behind unexpectedly during this event. Errors were automation Management; FMC / CDU and similarly spelled waypoints.
column123: The following narrative describes events that occurred over a very short period of time; perhaps only a few minutes in total. It is my sincere intention not to cast blame; but to offer an explanation for what happened from my biased point of view as the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X. Our flight began normally from LAX; with the exception that we were pushing back about 45 minutes late due our aircraft's late arrival into Gate 77. Preflight duties were performed fairly routine; but under some time pressure to complete everything thoroughly but as quickly as we could in an attempt to make up some of our delay. This time pressure was self-induced; as no other employee was pushing us for an on time arrival in ZZZ. Red flag #1. During the pre-departure cockpit preparations; we received notice that the passenger boarding was complete; followed shortly by ramp informing us that they were ready for the parking brake release and pushback. At this point I gave a cursory PF brief from the briefing card we all carry - too cursory. Red flag #2. Taxi and takeoff were normal from Runway 25R on the ORCKA5 Departure. I was manually flying; enjoying only my second flight as PF in over a month. We switched from Tower frequency over to SOCAL Departure; and shortly after checking in we received instructions to continue climb I believe to 5;000 feet and turn left to a heading of 030 degrees. Quickly after that we were given further climb to 12;000 and direct to KLIPR.  At this point things went wrong; rapidly. The Captain; as PM (Pilot Monitoring); couldn't find the KLIPR intersection on the legs page; and informed ATC that it did not appear to be on our departure. SOCAL spelled out the intersection phonetically; and then I think confirmed that we were on the ORCKA5. Things were happening fast. While hand-flying; in the turning climb; I tried to locate (unsuccessfully) KLIPR on the 10-3 page displayed on the iPad. Red flag #3.At this point; I should have turned on the autopilot to assist with the FMC and MCP inputs; as I could detect the stress and frustration in the Captain's voice in being unable to find KLIPR on the legs page; or on the departure plan view. Red flag #4. In my divided attention between flying the aircraft and searching for KLIPR on my iPad; I failed to find it as well. I was looking too far down the flight segment to see that the this waypoint is located right off the departure end of the 25s at LAX. This was the key moment; I think; and the last opportunity to correct the error. All I needed to do was put on the AP (autopilot); join the Captain and assist with the repair. But I did not; at least not immediately. The Captain inserted KLIPR on the legs page; got my confirmation; and executed the entry. When I had looked at the route modification; I thought it was correct. The waypoint showed in the correct direction (I thought) but much further down line than it should have; off the scale of my selected range on the navigation display. Red flag #5. Passing around 10;000 feet I engaged the autopilot at the Captain's urging to finally get back in the cockpit as a crew and together correct the problem. I engaged LNAV; but we were not turning fast enough for ATC and the controller gave us a new heading of 010.  I'd like to add at this point that our controller was patient; helpful and professional throughout our fiasco. The only way he could have helped us more is if he teleported into the cockpit and handed us our crew meals. Somewhere in the fray I had suggested that we reload the departure and that would bring KLIPR up; and now the legs page had a discontinuity and we had lost the LAS transition. Also we were given further climb; and now the KEGGS intersection to get us back on the departure. It was at this point I saw we had not been heading to KLIPR at all; but to 'CLIPR'! How did I miss that?! I had set up that problem by not giving proper confirmation of the legs page entry; having not used proper procedures (see Red flag #5). Further climb; and now direct to NNAVY were issued; but we first had to reload the lost LAS transition. After that was competently accomplished; our 'helmet fire' was apparently extinguished; and we were switched to the next Departure Controller. He gave us direct Las Vegas; and kindly spelled 'LAS' in the clearance for the lost crew.What followed was probably a good 2 hours of discussion and self-examination of what went wrong and why. I believe that two primary factors set us up for these errors. The first was my too-brief departure review. This was the first time the Captain had been on this departure; and only my second. Although we both verified the FMC route and legs page; and had confirmed the proper altitudes; we were not familiar with all the new (to us) waypoints; such as KLIPR. A more thorough review on the ground was paramount; and I failed to do it. The second was my desire to manually fly the aircraft during what rapidly became a complex departure. At the first sign of things getting too busy; it became mandatory for me to engage the autopilot; and thereby engage my brain in helping eliminate the threat. I failed in that regard. Adding mistakes such as 'CLIPR' vs. 'KLIPR'; was due to my attention being more in the HUD than on performing proper FMC verification procedures. That was entirely on me. I still have no explanation for why KLIPR was not on the legs page. I had displayed on my CDU the Takeoff Ref page; and did not give due diligence to the ND or the legs page on the Captain's side. What I saw was '_ _ IPR'; and a magenta line in the direction I wanted to go. Not good enough!  Additionally; in my attempt to find KLIPR on the Jepps I zoomed in and slid the page right-to-left; taking the desired waypoint right out of sight. Using the autopilot undoubtedly would have enabled me to do this search more thoroughly. We had only seconds; it seemed; to prevent this entire undesired event.
