column121: Working 4 sectors combined; and Controller in Charge. SLC was in a South Operation; Visual Airspace; Visual Approaches. Weather was VMC but visibility was diminishing and was marginal. There are thunderstorms throughout the sectors in my airspace. Lightning reported on the finals to all Runways; airspeed fluctuations reported on final; audible Wind Shear Alerts continuous all runways; 15 knot wind shift approaching the SLC Airport. Light to occasional moderate chop reported in the area. Tailwinds on final.Aircraft Y vectored to a 15 mile right base; cleared for Visual Approach to Runway 17 at SLC; switched to Tower. Aircraft X at 210 knots given descent to 8;000 feet abeam the SLC Airport; expecting Runway 16R; on the RNAV arrival being sequenced with other traffic within my sector(s) and on final. Traffic Management Unit calls down to TRACON through speaker in the Supervisor's console that Aircraft Y had a Lightning Strike and coordinated a heading 270 at 9;000 feet. I responded Radar Contact. Tower initiated the Heading 270 on a 9 mile final at 9;000 feet; which you never do; however; Aircraft Y was coordinated at 9;000 feet.  I kept Aircraft X expediting to 6;000 feet; which would not be an issue as long as Aircraft Y leveled at 9;000 feet. This was not the case as I observed Aircraft Y continuing descent through 8900 feet and continuing.  Recognizing this immediately; Aircraft Y appeared to be an Emergency aircraft not knowing what altitude he would be stopping at; I issued traffic to Aircraft X followed by a Traffic Alert with a heading 270 immediately to avoid a mid-air collision; all the while I was still not talking to Aircraft Y performing evasive maneuvers in my airspace.As soon as Aircraft X was past Aircraft Y I would then have divergence. I turned Aircraft X to heading 340; and issued a Low Altitude Alert and climbed him immediately to 7800 feet; while doing so I see Aircraft Y turning to the same north heading 340 at 8000 feet; with Aircraft X just West of Aircraft Y on a parallel course; and not talking to Aircraft Y in my airspace; not having lateral separation; I immediately turned Aircraft X to heading 310; all the while trying my best to achieve some sort of radar separation; and avoid a collision; until I find out who is talking to Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y at 8;000 feet is not what coordinated nor approved by me in my airspace; and a Heading 270 off the finals is never performed; for this exact reason. This is an unsafe operation with traffic in the downwind. Aircraft Y at 8;000 feet leaves no options at all.After determining the adjacent sector controller; who is only certified on those positions; was working Aircraft Y; in which Tower switched him to my airspace; when I had conflicting traffic. The adjacent sector controller provided zero communications to me; even though I repeatedly asked who was working Aircraft Y and what is he doing?  After I had Aircraft X squared away; they just happened to say 'Aircraft Y had your Aircraft X in sight and was maintaining visual separation.'This would have been nice to know.When an aircraft is coordinated to be 9;000 feet then have the aircraft be at 9;000 feet; not at 8;000 feet; which leaves the final sector Controller absolutely no way out. No attempt was made to by Tower who assigned 8;000 feet; or by the adjacent sector who received the aircraft at 8;000 feet to advise the sector who owns the airspace with an aircraft in direct conflict. When a heading of 270 and 9;000 feet is coordinated with another sector; a Departure Only Sector; then make sure he enters the airspace for which that specific coordination was originally made; and not another sector that has conflicting traffic with that type of coordination.No coordination or even a point out was attempted to be made to the appropriate sector in which the vital coordination directly impacts. When Visual Separation is applied between two aircraft that are in direct conflict with each other; it is absolutely a top priority to ensure that all parties involved receive this valuable bit of information.When a Controller takes it upon themselves to accept the responsibility of an aircraft in someone else's airspace at an altitude that is in direct conflict with an aircraft that you are not in communication with and at a different altitude than what was previously coordinated; then it might be a top priority to advise Controller working the aircraft in his own airspace that he is in direct communications with that visual separation is being applied. When a controller is taking evasive actions to prevent a mid-air collision with an aircraft that you are talking to; that is not in your airspace; and you are providing control instructions to; don't sit quietly when you hear 'Who is talking to Aircraft Y'?

ATC vectors and my attempts to maintain an airspeed that buffered against the rapid ups and downs of the green line and the rapid fluctuations of the indicated airspeed left us high and fast on our first attempt so we initiated a go-around missed approach. There was a significant tailwind down the valley that sheared to a headwind at the surface this contributed to us being high and fast.While we were climbing out we were instructed to climb and maintain 15;000 feet and were given vectors back to TOCUD. Approaching TAKBE the Captain requested a turn direct to TAKBE from ATC. Being at 15;000 [feet] we couldn't lower the flaps [so] the Captain instructed me to set 12;200 [feet] for TAKBE and start down. I complied with these instructions and as we dropped below 15;000 [feet] we began lowering the flaps and configuring.Shortly after starting our descent ATC issued a low altitude alert and stated that his minimum vectoring altitude was 15;000 [feet]. We were visual with both the mountains and airport in sight but failed to get proper approval from ATC for the visual approach before descending. As a side note we were being shook pretty good by the continuous moderate turbulence and I was really having to work the thrust levers to maintain a safe airspeed. We informed ATC that we were visual and we were cleared for the approach to Runway 4. We successfully landed on our second attempt. At no time was the safety of the fight or terrain clearance an issue and no EGPWS cautions or warnings were issued.Confusion on my part of the Captains instruction to 'sneak / start down'. It was the last leg of long hot sweaty day with multiple Captain swaps delays and MX issues; heat fatigue and dehydration were setting in and the turbulence and windshear created a very challenging flight environment.Once we goofed up and should have made sure that we were cleared for the visual prior to initiating a descent from a clearance altitude. The clearance to turn direct to TAKBE was not a clearance to descend even though we were visual. Mountain airports and strong winds are a difficult mix and other than adopting overly restrictive limits these difficult approaches will continue to be part of the job.

column121: I was flying on an instrument flight plan from SEE in San Diego to ZZZ1 outside of Denver and filed via Foreflight. The flight plan of direct was accepted but I assumed a SID. Given that SEE was MVFR I studied the departures including the Mission Bay Two (obstacle) Departure which seemed the most likely. I noted that this was a procedure which required tracking multiple radials of different VOR's; and I know from experience that modern glass panels (Garmin G600 and Garmin GTN 750) do not recognize these departures and they must be manually configured tuning the VOR's and radials.Shortly before departure; Foreflight via cellular connection gave me an expected route which was an odd route as it contained over 20 waypoints; but I programmed it into the Garmin GTN750 after engine start. There was no SID assigned. Normally when a SID is assigned its included in the expected route. So; I assumed SEE direct the MZB VOR. The weather was good VFR. So; I did not brief terrain clearance. When I called Ground Control; I was told it was a complicated route and asked if I was ready to copy it all down. I also advised that I had also received the route electronically. To make it faster I wrote the expected route on my knee board and followed along as the Controller gave it to me. I believe the route was the same; but I cannot rule out confirmation bias. I read the route back and received a 'readback correct'I took off on runway heading and noted that if I made an immediate turn to MZB I would not be able to out climb the terrain so continued on runway heading. It was VFR and I had the terrain in sight at all times. When I was handed off to Departure I was asked by the Approach Controller why I was not turning right. (presumably to follow the  obstacle departure). She further immediately called a terrain alert. I advised the terrain was in sight and was not a factor. The  Approach Controller then directed me to fly a heading and advised of a possible pilot deviation. It [is] possible that the Controller specifically called out the obstacle departure and I missed it due to confirmation bias. However; I believe the obstacle departure was not mentioned either due to it being a VFR day or common practice for the field and part of an unduly complicated clearance. The obstacle departure definitely did not populate as the Foreflight expected clearance like other SID's. I have screen shots of this. As a corrective action; I believe that obstacle clearances need to be built with waypoints and published like any other SID so they worked  with automated clearance delivery mechanisms and integrated avionics

column121: On approach in to ZZZ; we were cleared direct ZZZZZ intersection and to descend to 3;000 feet There was a thunderstorm cell between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 (Final Approach Fix) on the approach to Runway XXR to ZZZ. We asked ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) for direct ZZZZZ1 to avoid the thunderstorm cell. We were anticipating a visual approach to Runway XXR because the most recent ATIS (weather report) was reporting only Few and Scattered clouds at the airport with adequate visibility for a visual approach. The TRACON Controller asked if we would be able to 'get the airport?'My First Officer and I were slightly confused by his phraseology and tried to discuss what the Controller meant. At that time; we were within a few miles from ZZZZZ and just about to level off at 3;000 feet. The Autopilot Mode Control panel was in Vertical Speed (Altitude Acquire) and LNAV to ZZZZZ. I was anticipating going to ZZZZZ1 and was ready to change the altitude to 2;800 feet in MCP for the autopilot. We were then cleared on a 160 degree heading to join the final approach course of 128; and cleared for the approach. I didn't hear the Controller say 'maintain 3;000 feet until established.' I selected VOR/LOC and dialed 2;800 feet into the autopilot Mode Control Panel. Because we were in a descent and in Altitude Acquire; the autopilot continued to descend towards 2;800 feet.My First Officer said we were supposed to maintain 3;000 feet. I had missed that part of the clearance so I dialed 3;000 feet into the Mode Control Panel; but by that point the aircraft had descended below 3;000 feet and was continuing to descend and would not ever capture 3;000 feet. I was also trying to slow the aircraft and get it to capture the localizer. Seeing that we weren't going to level off; I tried to use Vertical Speed to make the aircraft climb back to 3;000 feet; but it was continuing to descend. Our descent was exacerbated by the fact that I still had the speedbrakes deployed almost to the flight [descent]. ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) said he he had a low altitude alert and his MVA [Min Vector Altitude] was 2;800 feet. We were now at about 2;300 feet. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles; started a climb and we decided to go missed approach. I finally stowed the speedbrakes; climbed to our clearance altitude and we then got re-vectored by ZZZ TRACON for another approach to Runway XXR and landed safely.
column123: We were being vectored around some weather coming into ZZZ and were given a descent to 3;000 feet and direct ZZZZZ outside of ZZZZZ1 on the ILS XXX. There was some confusion as ATC asked if we would be able to get the airport. I wasn't sure if he meant visually or altitude wise. After a pause; as I pondered his meaning; I responded that we were IMC. At the time; I didn't think we were high; so I assumed he meant visually. Just a couple miles outside of ZZZZZ; Captain asked for a turn to ZZZZZ1. I paused because I was anticipating a vector shortly to intercept the final approach course. I then asked ATC for the turn inbound; and ATC responded that he was just about to give us a vector and then provided the clearance. We were given a 160 heading to join and maintain 3;000 feet until established and cleared for the ILS to [Runway] XXR. This extra communication ultimately caused a delay in getting turned in. Because it all got really busy; I didn't see that Captain dialed in 2;800 feet. So; I don't think it acquired 3;000 feet and was now descending below it. Then I think 3;000 feet was reset into the MCP and yet the aircraft was still descending. All of this was happening while I was replying to ATC and I didn't realize what happened until after we talked about it later. We triggered a low altitude alert; and ATC informed us that we were to maintain 3;000 feet until established. I responded that we were correcting. Captain was climbing back up to 3;000 feet and we were slightly south of the localizer. I figured by the time we got back to 3;000 feet; we would then be high for the approach and not being established on the localizer; I said we should go-around. Captain agreed; and we did. This whole thing took me out of the Green; made me feel rushed and got behind in my responsibilities. A go-around was the best decision.

column121: Wind was gusting to 15 knots at ZZZ; and the Citation seemed unsure on if they wanted to land at ZZZ or go somewhere else. They got all the way to about 3 minutes from the field before they stated that they had the field in sight and wanted the Visual Approach. They had been assigned present heading and to maintain 9 thousand; but then I cleared them for the Visual Approach. Shortly after the aircraft informed they were VMC and were just going to do local maneuvers while they 'come up with a plan'. They had not begun their descent; and I asked if they were cancelling IFR; and they said no. I told them 'approach clearance cancelled; maintained 9 thousand' and I neglected to give them routing. A hit (radar update) or two goes by and they make a slight left turn and I assign them a heading for terrain. A few hits later; they made a turn into the 9700 foot MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) at 9 thousand feet. The pilot was cleared for the Visual; and the last thing I expected them to do was to turn about 160 degrees away from the airfield. They're allowed to climb; descend; and turn; on a Visual Approach; but they're required to keep the field in sight; which they obviously can't do on that easterly heading; so I'm not sure why they turned that far east. Additionally; I don't think a Visual Approach clearance enables an aircraft to just hold and 'come up with a plan'. I get updates every 12 seconds; and I kept waiting; and hoping; that the pilot would fly their assigned heading. I'm not sure how long it took for him to be established on the turn; but if I had updates every second; I would have known he wasn't taking my turn; and climbed him. This airspace area needs an Approach Control. I believe that if there had been faster updates on the data block; I would have taken different action.

column121: In VFR conditions and clear of clouds on final approach to Runway XXL in ZZZ. ATC vectored us behind two other aircraft on final for the same runway and assigned us a speed of 160 kts. The aircraft was already configured with approach flaps and slowing. Tower advised that the aircraft in front of us had slowed further and advised us to slow to minimum approach speed. We fully configured the aircraft for landing and continued to slow. Tower advised we were still 60 kts faster than the preceding aircraft and requested us to do an 's' turn to the north to provide further spacing. The Pilot Flying; using the autopilot; initiated a 90 degree turn to the north (right) and continued to descend. We were clear of any traffic. The parallel runway was closed. About 80 degrees perpendicular to the approach course; using the autopilot; the Pilot Flying turned the aircraft back towards the runway. I; the Pilot Monitoring advised him to slow his descent rate; we were continuing to descend while maneuvering; using the autopilot the Pilot Flying slowed the rate of descent. At about the same instant at 2.5 mi from the end of the runway. Tower stated that he had a 'low altitude alert' on us and he advised us to 'initiate a climb'. The altimeter showed 860 ft above the water. The electronic glide path showed one dot low. The Pilot Flying immediately disengaged the autopilot pilot and applied back pressure to the controls. The aircraft immediately recovered to 1;100 ft agl. The Pilot Flying continued the turn towards the runway and descended on the glide path. At 1;000 ft agl; I; the Pilot Monitoring; reported 'stable'. I confirmed our landing clearance. At 500 ft agl; I reported 'stable'. We continued and landed. There were no TAWS warning triggered by the event. No alarms 'glide slope' or 'terrain to low' triggered.Less automation. Had the Pilot Flying turned off the autopilot for the maneuver and hand flown the aircraft; responding to the rate of descent would have happened in a more timely manner and an altitude low waning would have probably not been triggered. Hand flying would have managed the rate of descent better.

We were passing through FL200 for FL230 when we noticed another aircraft on TCAS at 10-15 miles range reach 300 feet below our altitude before descending back down to FL 190. No TCAS alerts were initiated and no conflict occurred.The primary factor is the fact that ORCKA and ARCUS; two consecutive points along the ORKA5 SID sound similar over the VHF radio. I recommend that Jeppesen change either ORCKA or ARCUS naming on the SID.  2. When waypoints on a SID sound so clearly similar ATC should phonetically spell out the fix cleared to.

column123: While being vectored for ILS approach to RWY XXL at ZZZZ; the Pilot Flying momentarily began an early descent through required altitude of 2;600 feet. Aircraft descended to approximately 2;420 feet as the Pilot Flying regained situational awareness and applied corrective action to include resetting the MCP altitude; and then reverting to manual control.  The recovery was smooth and controlled.  As the aircraft was returning to 2;600 feet; ZZZZ Radar Control called to direct climb to 2;600 feet.  I responded to ATC while the Pilot Flying completed the recovery.  Approach and landing were completed uneventfully.   This was the final segment of a 2 leg international flying pairing nearing 17 hours of duty.  All crew members were not at their best state of alertness.  Original arrival setup was for a STAR coupled to an ILS approach.  Flown arrival was very non standard. The aircraft was vectored off arrival path and given clearance to disregard many published mandatory altitudes.  This complicated arrival descent planning and may have led to the Pilot Flying losing some situational awareness.  ATC Traffic on approach ahead was a potential conflict.  This diverted my attention during the approach.Delays in positive corrective action which could have lessened/prevented the altitude deviation were potentially caused by distraction due to traffic call; lessened cognitive performance due to overnight/long duty period; lack of urgency due to VMC weather with runway in view.

column121: We were descending on the arrival into ZZZ. We were descending at a high speed programmed into the FMC. I have over 10;000 hours flying the Next Gens and am comfortable with that descent profile. This was my first MAX flight. Somewhere in the descent the FMA changed without warning to MCP SPD (Mode Control Panel Speed). It went unnoticed. I have witnessed many Next Gens revert to VNV SPD (Vnav Speed); but never MCP SPD. There is a significant difference; in that MCP SPD gives no altitude protection. I have never seen anything like this. Somewhere around ZZZZZ/11000; we received a radio call and became distracted as the aircraft descended through 11000. I did not catch the deviation until 10;000 and momentum and recovery took us to about 9;500 feet. I disconnect all automation and hand flew the recovery as I tried to figure out what had just happened. We reported the deviation to ATC and continued to ZZZ without incident.I do not know why this happened. I can only guess that somehow LVL CHG (Level Change) was inadvertently selected. Another theory is that VNV could not keep up and reverted to MCP SPD. This happens sometimes in the Next Gens; but it always reverts to VNV SPD; which is much safer.

column121: While at cruise at 35;000 feet in Cairo control airspace; we began to receive a series of Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting messages- ATC Fault; Unable RNP and Terrain Position.  We referenced the Quick Reference Handbook for each message but were unable to clear the faults. We asked ATC if they saw any issue with our transponder and they replied that they saw no problems. Shortly after crossing from Amman control to Jeddah on airway Y415; we received the FMC message 'Verify position'. We saw that we were off the airway to the left and ATC asked if we were on the airway. The First Officer and I put our range scales to 5 miles and noted that the left side showed us approximately 3 to 5 miles left of course; First Officer side showed the same distance to the right of course.We checked the FMC position reference pages and saw that GPS position was blank and substantial errors on the other positions - FMC; IRS and Radio. We advised ATC of the GPS failure and could not determine which source was accurate. ATC said we were showing right of course. I selected GPS off then on; selected HDG (heading) select to manually steer to course. Reselected LNAV. Nothing seemed to be working. I asked for direct to a fix further down the airway. column121: I knew it was going to be a struggle getting out of ZZZ with all passengers on board when I saw the take-off performance. At 40C the margin between PTOW (Planned Take-off Weight) and MTOW was 1100 lbs. My First Officer (FO) was terrific; but it was his first trip since IOE; he had 18 hours on the airplane at the start of the sequence; and had not flown prior to training for about 8 months. In addition; it was only my second time flying the ZZZZZ departure; which has three at or above altitudes on it; which is a new thing in ZZZ.  I live in ZZZ; and consequently fly out of there a great deal.  All previous RNAV departures used to have at or below altitudes on them (to keep clear of inbound aircraft); so it never used to be an issue worrying about making altitudes on the SID.  At the aircraft; I was already concerned about two things: brake temps and having to bump passengers.  I asked my FO to pull us up numbers for 41 and 42C; just in case it got hotter; as it was likely to. In addition; I believe the winds were swinging around - runway XXR had a tailwind component at one point; so I was also looking for numbers for XYL; but due to terrain; the only runway that worked at all was XXR.  I noticed that we would be unable to make the restrictions and asked the FO to ask for altitude relief on the SID as soon as he contacted ground.  In my experience; asking for altitude relief at other airports was never an issue; so I was not overly concerned. We pushed back; and naturally were over PTOW.  I asked the FO to request a new take-off performance for 41 and 42C.  We eventually landed on a Flaps 1 take-off performance requiring thrust bump which got us legal for takeoff.  All this occurred during the short taxi from the terminal to runway XXR.By the time we reached number 1 holding short of the runway; I realized we had forgotten to ask for the altitude relief on the SID. I asked the FO to do so as we were taking the runway.  The controller; upon hearing the request; told us to taxi clear and get a new clearance.  By this time there were 6-8 aircraft in a queue for takeoff; and our brake temps were over 150 degrees.  My main concern was that if we had to leave the runway; it would get too hot to accommodate the load; and by the time we taxied for another 30 minutes; the brakes would be too hot for takeoff.  So; glancing down at the FMS; which showed that we would miss the altitude restrictions by 5-700 feet; I knew that if we delayed cleanup; we could easily make those restrictions.  I told the controller that we could manage the departure; and he again cleared us for takeoff.  I told my FO that since we were at the max performance envelope of the airplane; he should rotate very gently.  As we were rolling down the runway; my attention was fixed on the EGT; as I had not done a bump takeoff before; and the engines were exactly on the edge of the red.  He did as I asked; and as a result; we were very fast on the initial climb segment.  As we climbed out; I was fixated on the altitude.  Once it became clear that the 5;000 ft altitude (I think around 4;500 feet MSL) I relaxed a bit and told him we could clean up.  He set climb power (which was a much greater reduction than normal due to the thrust bump) and I reached for the flap lever and set flaps up.  At this time we were still wings level.  I was so fixated on the altitude; and our airspeed shortly after takeoff was so much higher than usual that I didn't take a good look at the airspeed indicator.  I believe that I retracted the flaps very early. VLS (lowest selectable speed) jumped by perhaps 40 knots; and we ended up about 20 knots below VLS.  Naturally; we were now facing rapidly rising terrain; and the SID commanded a right turn.  My FO started to turn; and now instead of being below VLS; we were in alpha floor.  I instructed my FO to lower the nose; but it wasn't happening quickly enough; so I grabbed the side stick and pushed the nose over; at the same time requesting him to let go.  There was a momentary DUAL INPUT" annunciation and a momentary noticeable low speed buffet which lasted perhaps a second.  We lost perhaps 300 feet of altitude as I got the airspeed back.  We were able to make all of the altitude restrictions and I don't believe there were any deviations from the SID.  Once we recovered; the only other item remaining was how to get the auto throttles out of alpha floor.  Eventually; we turned them off (match and mash) and back on again and that got the system back to normal.I was using my knowledge of past experience flying the old SIDs.  They didn't have airspeed or at or above altitudes; and my experience in the past that asking for altitude relief on a SID was not a big deal.  In addition; I was flying with a brand new (very sharp) but inexperienced FO; who was relying entirely on my experience.  I was also pushing to accommodate the load without having to remove passengers and/or cargo; and was worried about the brake temp issues; causing me to push to get off the ground as soon as possible.I made several errors.  The first one was not notifying clearance delivery early of our inability to make the altitude and/or airspeed restrictions on the SID.  In the past; ZZZ used to have a procedure for A321 aircraft to delay climb power/flap retraction to 3;000 AGL.  I think if we had used that procedure; we probably would have been able to make the altitude and speed restrictions on the SID.  That procedure is gone.  Second; when we finally did request relief on the SID (by this time we were on the runway) and the controller told us to clear the runway and get a new clearance; I should have done so; even if it had caused us further problems with brake temp and/or takeoff weight.  Third; having taken the decision to take off because I was certain we could delay cleanup; thus making us legal for the SID; I should have taken over flying duties.  This would have alleviated my FO's task saturation; as I was far more experienced in the airplane.  This would still have been sub-optimal; but I am confident the takeoff would have been uneventful.   Fourth; once I retracted the flaps and we were below VLS; I should have put the flaps back to Config 1.  So; there were many errors on my part; but an early intervention with clearance delivery would have solved everything.  I believe there should be a warning to the A320 Fleet about the new SIDS; and that at high temperatures careful note should be taken of the danger of not being able to make altitude restrictions on any SID with at or above altitudes; especially early in the SID; and that relief should be requested at the gate with clearance delivery. Also to note: green dot speed (min maneuver) was 245 with flaps up; so the only way to maintain 230 knot speed at ZZZZZ waypoint is at config 1.  Again; the old requirement to clean up at 3000 AGL would have solved this."

column121: After takeoff; during a turn to a heading of 270 degrees; we received an ALT and IAS cross-side miss-comparison. The autopilot also would not engage when commanded and I hand flew up to 5;000 ft. After leveling off; and receiving instructions to climb; I called for the autopilot again and it connected. During the climb; we kept receiving the IAS and ALT notices and leveled off at 16;000 ft.; FL260; and FL320. We also noted a 200 ft. discrepancy between altimeters at one point. We leveled off at these altitudes because of the miss-comparison. After leveling off; for a minute the miss-compare would go away and we would continue the climb. During the climb and at one of the level-offs; we tried using our alternate static sources. This seemed to work on the Captain's side but the miss-compare came back when we started to climb again. The Captain then ran the airspeed unreliable checklist to see if it would be any help but nothing in the checklist seemed to be a fit for the problem we were encountering. The cause of the problems was not obvious and the checklist did not seem like it was of any help. Also; during the climbs; the FCP was not usable. All of the windows for airspeed; heading; and altitude only showed - - - -.With the problems we were having and not being able to identify the cause combined with the prospect of having to hand-fly and the encounter weather; we felt that continuing to ZZZ1 was not an option should the problems become worse. If we did in fact have an unreliable airspeed; we would be directed to disconnect both AFS and FD switches off which would mean having to leave RVSM; which would lead to higher fuel burns and hand-flying in heavy thunderstorms. [The problem was identified] when the amber IAS and ALT alerts were presented on our PFDs (Primary Flight Display). If I had to guess I would say that the aircraft had some sort of computer issue that was presenting the airspeed and altitude to the displays with differing data and a comparator caught the difference and alerted us. Our first reaction was to fly the plane. I started asking the Captain what his airspeed was as I figured that was more important than altitude. Once we were at a safe altitude and maintaining a safe airspeed; we began to troubleshoot and discuss the problems. There is nothing that we could have done as pilots to prevent this.
column123: On the climb out the EIS detected intermittent ALT and IAS miss-comparisons between Captain and FO's (First Officer) PFD (Primary Flight Display). Stopped climb at 16;000 ft.; the issue went away. We then decided to continue to climb but had to stop at FL260. I had the FO put his STATIC AIR to ALT. Problem went away for about 1 minute and then came back. I then selected Captain STATIC AIR to ALT. This time; the issues went away for a few minutes. We decided to continue the climb but had to stop at FL320 because the problem came back. I ran the emergency non-alert AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE checklist; but the issue was not resolved. At 27100 ft.; Captain's IAS/MACH 336/.830; FO's IAS/MACH 330/.816. At every level change attempt FCP window indicated - - - -. The altitude difference between [the] Captain and FO was over 200 ft. Since AP (Autopilot) #2 was deferred and if we disconnected AP #1 we would not be able to remain in RVSM; we contacted company and returned to ZZZ. No emergency or special handling was required. [The problem was identified by the] amber IAS and ALT on Captain's and FO's upper left-hand corner of the PFD. [The cause was] failure annunciations… cross-side miss-comparisons generated when the EIS detected significant differences between the displayed data of the Captain's and First Officer's instruments AIRSPEED and ALTITUDE. [The response was to] climb to [a] safe altitude; maintain speed; and attempt to address the issue at hand. Maintenance issues cannot be forecasted.

column121: We [were] on the Vanze 2 Arrival into MEM and I was flying. After reviewing the arrival and expecting a south landing; we got a new ATIS with the airport now landing to the north. This required a change of FASOP Intersection to 10;000 and 230 knots. I put this in the FMS. I also read the North arrival on the RNAV approach to the FO. When we got to the top of descent; we had not been given a descent yet; so we requested lower. The FMS showed us high as we continued to ask for lower altitudes to make the crossing restriction. Eventually the controller gave us direct to FASOP Intersection. I told the FO we were already going there. Then the FO realized that we were not going to FASOP Intersection; but were going to FASON Intersection. We realized that I had put the crossing restriction in the FMS at FASON Intersection; and not FASOP Intersection!! This was the reason the FMS showed us high. This error was because there are two almost identically named intersections on the arrival; With the change of runway from South to North and having already verified the points; the names being so close in spelling make the error one that could easily be repeated by other crews. Once we corrected the crossing restrictions to the correct FASOP Intersection; we were very low and we slowed our rate of descent.Because we had already verified the points on the arrival; when we got the runway change; we verbally reviewed the changes and the need to insert the crossing restriction in the FASOP Intersection.  It was night and when I looked at the FMS; the first point that came up was FASON; which I mistook for FASOP.  Both the FO and I did not catch it.  We did not realize the mistake until we were given direct FASOP because we were requesting a descent because we thought we were high and were not going to make the crossing restriction.  I did mention the two intersection name similarities to the Controller; and told him it was a potential problem.  He said he agreed; but the fix was above his pay grade.The names of FASOP and FASON need to be changed; especially when there is a crossing restriction that needs to be entered in to the FMS. With both names so similar; it is easily to put the crossing restriction at the wrong point like we did. The runway change was the key here; as we were already set up to land to the South. Then the runway changed to land North; prompting the change to put the crossing restriction in the FMS.

column121: I was proceeding northbound on a VFR flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with flight following (ZZZ2 or ZZZ3- I can't recall which). I had observed an aircraft on my ADS-B traffic that appeared as if it would be slightly to the right of my flight path but presented no conflict (blue vs red indication). It was very hazy and as I was concerned with the varying cloud layer conditions ahead; I scrolled my flight display forward; located the AWOS for ZZZ1 and had just dialed it into my #2 comm (monitoring flight following on comm 1). Before I could scroll the ADS-B driven display back to my immediate area and so that I could re-acquire the ADS-B traffic target I heard the beginning of an urgent alert for traffic conflict from ATC. I heard the traffic alert warning and the words 'Immediate turn...'. Simultaneously I had a traffic alert alarm flash with audible warning on my ADS-B flight display (but no display of the target itself; just to have the AWOS I had dialed in come blasting in over comm 2; completely blocking comm 1 ATC instructions beyond the words 'immediate turn'.  The volume had been set too high on comm 2. Since my last view of the oncoming target I had on ADS-B seemed to indicate that it would pass on my right; I immediately and automatically turned left and visually scanned as it was no time to have my head in the cockpit or fiddle with radios. The Controller repeated the warning and that time I heard his instructions to 'turn right' (his second warning) during the AWOS lull. I heard the 'turn right' about the same time I visually acquired the oncoming aircraft. I saw it at my approximately 10 to 11 O'clock at about a mile or so; opposite direction at what appeared to be 200 feet lower than me (very rough; estimate) about 5;300 feet MSL; I think. I immediately turned hard right. The target was a Cessna (C152 I think) flying on a roughly parallel course by then on my left wing at the incorrect altitude for their direction of flight. I was flying at about 5;500 feet MSL on a north-northeast heading. After shutting down the background noise from Comm 2; and resuming course; ATC asked me if they had clearly communicated the instructions to 'turn right' which they had transmitted twice. I replied; Yes" as this as the Controller certainly had transmitted clearly; but due to the audible interference from comm 2 and the ADS-B traffic alert; I could not hear the communication clearly until the second warning; after I had already initiated a left turn. Given the last known position of the other aircraft and hearing only a partial warning from ATC; and the need to immediately react; I initially turned into (left) instead of away from (right) the traffic conflict as per ATC transmission."

column121: APU fire return to field. Boarding and pre-flight normal. Once the packs were turned on the cabin cooled down easily; but we were not able to get the flight deck under 80 degrees until after engine start. Taxi was also normal; from [the gate] onto Taxiway 1; Taxiway 2; and to RWY XXL. To fly the departure up to and maintain 3;000 ft. Takeoff normal (full thrust takeoff per Maintenance request on maintenance release). On the climb out approaching 3;000 ft; in LNAV; we hit ALT CAP (Altitude Capture); and PNF (myself) rolled the speed to 230 knots. Right at this moment the APU FIRE EICAS message displayed; and the Fire bell alert sounded. Captain took both flight controls and radios; put the auto pilot on and addressed ATC. [Advised ATC] and requested an immediate return to the field for landing. I ran the APU QRC paper checklist. Which reads; Pull the APU Fire handle and rotate to the stop for 1 second. I completed the QRC items; and then turned to the electronic checklist to complete the full APU FIRE checklist. Which stated 'Choose one: APU Fire warning light stays illuminated (which it did); land at nearest suitable airport'. Captain then handed flight controls and radios to me; so that he could consult with the Flight Attendants and the Company. After doing so he took back over the role of PF (Pilot Flying). Captain then made a turn with ATC instruction back toward field for a downwind to RWY XXL. Still level at 3;000 ft. ATC requested where the fire indication was. We set up for an ILS approach; with appropriate frequency and FMS arrival selection for XXL. We were then given a descent to 2;000 ft. by ATC as well as a turn to base leg. Captain began to slow to configure for landing. Using speedbrakes to slow the aircraft. On this turn in the descent with Flaps 1; while retracting speedbrakes; and the MCP (Mode Control Panel) speed in the window set to minimum flaps 1 speed; we had a momentary shaker activation; less than 1 second; and I immediately put out Flaps 5 and we continued to slow and configure from there. We were cleared to maintain 2;000 ft. until established; and cleared for the ILS approach. We continued to add flaps to 15; then 20. Gear down; flaps 25 and 30 without event. Landing data was requested for landing on XXL; overweight 235k lbs; Auto brakes 2 was set for sufficient stopping distance. Also performed a small dip low on GS for touchdown to use full runway length. We touched down with 200 fpm descent. Rolled to Taxiway 3. Exited runway at 60 kts. Continued onto Taxiway 2 to hold short of Taxiway 4. At this time the [it was] assessed that no heat was found in the tail or any other part of the aircraft. The flight attendants also assessed no smoke or heat in the cabin. The decision was then made to taxi to a gate expeditiously to deplane passengers and get maintenance on board. Taxied to the gate; shut down the left engine to allow the jet bridge to be attached to the airplane; then shut down the right engine once ground power was established.
column123: APU Fire Indication after takeoff. Flight was the first segment on day one from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was the flying pilot for this leg. Loading and boarding were normal with a mostly full flight. The cabin of the aircraft had been cooled nicely; but we were having a bit of a challenge cooling down the flight deck; with temperatures hovering in the high 80's. The ZZZ weather was 340/10; 10SM FEW 040 SCT080 BKN250 28/18 29.86. We pushed off the gate on time. [We taxied] to Runway XXL and contacted Tower. We accomplished the before takeoff checklist items and were cleared to takeoff Runway XXL on the ZZZ Departure. The maintenance release noted that a Max power takeoff was due; so we did so; at a TOG weight of 238;192 lbs and the flaps 5. During takeoff roll as we accelerated; water dripped out of the overhead panels which was interesting; we took off; cleaned up the gear and flaps as scheduled. Somewhere between 2;000 ft and 3;000 ft. in the climb in a left hand turn to heading 290; we had a Master Warning and an EICAS annunciation APU Fire. I continued to fly the aircraft; took the radios; and while the First Officer accomplished the APU Fire QRC. It is important to note that the fire light remained on and did not go out after running the QRC with no other indications of a fire. Also; it is important to note that the APU was shut down on the ground after engine start during the after-start checklist; and had been off for approximately 20 minutes. We ran the appropriate checklists; notified Dispatch and spoke with the flight attendants. The Purser was informed that we had an APU Fire indication and was asked if there were any fire indications in the aft cabin? They said they did not have smoke but noted a slight odor (possibly the fire extinguishing agent that was fired into the APU during the QRC). I told them to prepare the cabin quickly as we would be on the ground in 8 minutes. My FO (First Officer) and I spoke about the overweight landing; briefed the approach; and identified the ILS. We planned a flaps 30 ILS to Runway XXL at a weight of 235;000 lbs. as 235;000 lbs. was below our performance limit weight of 259.9; so a 30-flap landing was appropriate. Fortunately; we discussed the possibility of an overweight landing prior to takeoff; so we were already familiar with the requirements. Although we suspected an erroneous APU Fire warning; time was still a driving factor as the fire indication never went away. We maintained 250 kts for as long as possible then configured using flaps and speed brakes to slow the aircraft. We were configured with flaps 1 and were decelerating with the flaps tracking to 5 and the speed brakes out. We decelerated to flaps 5 maneuvering speed; and just as I started to retract the speed brakes for literally a split-second I heard a sound that was so brief I could not tell what it was. The FO told me that it was a split second of the shaker due to the boards being out at the flaps 5 maneuvering speed. We continued configuring with gear and flaps 30; accomplished the landing checklist. We flew the ILS to Runway XXL with the autopilot and auto throttles engaged until 500 ft when I disconnected the autopilot. I disengaged the auto throttles around 100 ft. I briefed that I would slightly duck under the glideslope with a planned touched down early in the landing zone.We touched down approximately 1;200 ft. down the runway with auto brakes 2 selected. The touchdown was extremely smooth with a VVI (Vertical Velocity Indicator) of less than 200 fpm. During the landing roll; we queried the Tower to see if they could see any smoke trailing the aircraft; and they said all looked normal. We rolled clear of the runway on Taxiway 3 and stopped on Taxiway 4 where the ground personnel looked us over. The ground personnel informed us that they could see no indications of a fire and that their thermal imaging scan showed no heat in the APU area. We ran through our after-landing flows and taxied to the gate. We shut downthe left engine so they could start deplaning the passengers. When ground power became available we secured the right engine and secured the aircraft. I proceeded into the cabin to chat with maintenance; passengers etc. Maintenance opened the APU area and said that they suspected a faulty fire loop; as there was no evidence of a fire. Maintenance later found that a faulty APU fire control panel was the cause of the warning. Also; the total flight time from wheels up to wheels down was 11 minutes. That is extremely fast when considering all the factors to evaluate. All in all; I feel that this was a well-executed event; and resulted in the safe return for passengers and crew.

column121: While preparing for departure we noticed we would not make the departure crossing restrictions on the ZZZZZ1 departure. Our plan was to bring this to the attention of ground so departure could be made aware. They seemed unwilling to help as did clearance and our overworked dispatcher. We went back and forth and finally were given a 'modified' ZZZZZ2 departure and proceed to ZZZZZ. While doing this departure we stayed in NAV and the plane turned east towards ZZZZZ. ATC gave us headings and informed us that it was not correct. Had we reviewed the departure closer we would have noted the headings and briefed better. Also; that departure is not in the FMS database.[The causes are] a long list. First cause is [the company] operating an airplane under conditions that it should not. An Airbus 321 weighing 192;000 lbs. in 38 Celsius temperature should not be allowed. The plane barely makes it off the ground and we have to climb out in unfamiliar configurations to get climb performance. I do not believe we will have an acceptable outcome if we ever lose an engine. 90+ Fahrenheit cockpit temps doesn't help and cabin temps of mid 80's are a distraction. Constant interruptions by FA's (flight attendants) due to pax getting up is a threat while attempting to find an acceptable departure. Uncooperative ground and clearance controllers who seemed irritated to even interact with us. Overloaded dispatcher which seemed to be the norm lately and was confirmed to me by 2 dispatchers riding the jump seat. Incorrect verbiage in the performance manual regarding the IAE (International Aero Engine) bump feature which was unfamiliar procedure to me. That was a distraction because it was a green B next to the EPR gauge; not a blue B next to the N1. Missing SID from our database (that would have prevented this event). Operating an aircraft under conditions that are borderline unsafe and expected to do so. The climb was so poor the aircraft started a 1;000 - 1;200 RPM descent upon flap retraction because of the temps and lack of power. Good CRM and PIC experience was our biggest asset managing the aircraft. Of course weather close to the airport was yet another factor. Make sure bump description is correct in the performance manual. Use of A321 under heavy and hot situations need to be reviewed out of ZZZ. Continue training emphasis for CRM because it made ATC and aircraft management seem minor.

column121: I took the position with a Cessna that had just departed SMO airport. At around 1200 feet he made a right turn back to the VOR. I immediately told him to stop his turn and turn back on to the departure heading. He said he was given a 250 heading.  I pulled up the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) map and decided that because of his low altitude and position; it was better to let him continue his right turn into a lower MVA rather then try to put him back to a left turn leading to a higher MVA. I then told him to expedite his climb as he was now below the MVA. I asked him who gave him a heading to the VOR and he said the tower did. The Supervisor checked with the tower and they listened to the tapes and he was not given a turn to the VOR.  I was then told to brasher the pilot and I did. No low altitude alert ever went off on the scope. We've had many occurrences of pilots turning incorrectly off of SMO airport. I would suggest the departure procedures be revisited as there are a lot of inexperienced pilots that depart from there. If this many are having issues; it should be addressed.

column121: I was working the Traffic Management position.  I saw that we were going to have a couple of hours of high volume in the Center; as is normal on a day shift.  I received a briefing from my fellow Traffic Management Coordinator (TMC) in which he relayed that the Central Weather Service Unit (CWSU) had informed him we could expect to lose the East Coast routings through the state of Florida by XA:00Z.  The Atlantic Routes; which normally service much of our volume between the Northeast and South Florida were closed due to weather.  Sealord was planning to activate all airspace to FL500 and the Joint Air Traffic Operations Command Center (JATOCC) was planning to activate W470 to FL600.  This would mean we would be left with one hole through which we would be forced to route all aircraft.  I called the Severe Weather line at the Air Traffic Control System Command Center (ATCSCC) and voiced my concerns and that I thought our best option would be to put an Airspace Flow Program in place to slow the volume through ZJX due to the lack of available airspace and the increased complexity caused by the weather.  I was told we didn't need that because there was not enough volume.  The weather built up; much as anticipated.  Planes were deviating all over the sky.  I received a phone call from Severe Weather wanting to put out a playbook routing for ATL landing traffic in response to my request to ZMA via the National Traffic Management Log (NTML) to route all aircraft on the HOBTT Arrival to keep them off of the east coast.  I told them that at this point it was better to handle it tactically and reiterated that if they had helped me slow the volume on the East Coast earlier; we wouldn't have to ask ZMA to reroute aircraft.  This was disregarded.  To my understanding; the East Area got absolutely overwhelmed and had sectors so inundated with aircraft that they were almost out of control.  We also have repeated issues with ZTL either refusing to comply with requests they have accepted or flat out refusing to accept them at all and arguing with us.  Lately they have begun to send retaliatory restrictions that they don't actually need in response to our requests to tuck aircraft due to tunnel procedures necessitated by severe weather.I would recommend that the FAA and ATCSCC realize that the traffic flowing through ZJX has increased drastically and our Controllers are consistently working Level 12 traffic day in and day out.  We have severe weather literally every day between May and October which shuts off routings.  Most days; unless it is a holiday; military airspace is active on both sides of our airspace; making much of our airspace unusable. Many days we are unable to split sectors off or provide a radar associate or tracker to assist the controllers.  Every single time we call the ATCSCC for assistance we are denied.  It is a rare occasion that an Airspace Flow Program (AFP) or structured routing is actually issued to help us as we attempt to funnel over 100 aircraft per hour through holes in thunderstorms and active military airspace.  We are seeing increasing reports of severe turbulence as we force aircraft full of people through small holes in between severe weather cells. Our facility has been subject to numerous Corrective Action Plans regarding severe weather events as a result of us sending them through severe weather.  Controllers are expected to call depicted weather to each and every aircraft; and are reprimanded when they are unable to; however their workload is completely absurd at this point and when we try to help slow the volume to provide them with more time for additional duties beyond separating the aircraft deviating to avoid weather we are denied!  Sealord calls their airspace active to FL500 early most days and keeps it active until well into the evening; as do the military squadrons who utilize the warning and restricted areas on the Gulf Coast.  As a TMC I am forced to watch sectors become saturated to the point Controllers are overwhelmed after I have initiated the Traffic Management Initiative (TMIs) at my disposal to slow it.  This situation in unacceptable and has to change.  I have been a Controller for XX years; X of those as a TMC; and I have never seen it so bad.  People are working this intense traffic 6 days a week every week; often 10 hours a day; and they are burned out.  They don't have any more to give and the system is failing them as they continue to work under adverse conditions to maintain the world's safest and most efficient system that the FAA and NATCA are so proud of.

column121: Landing Runway 28 GDL; night VMC with bright moonlight. Set up to land Runway 28 using the ILS DME 2 with the ILS DME 2 transition from IKBAN. At the last minute; Control told us to descend via the LIVRI 1D Arrival.  We quickly put this arrival into the FMC; but did not change the approach. Shortly after starting the arrival; we were given direct to PLADE with continued descent to the mandatory altitude of 9;000 ft at PLADE which is the point leading into the ILS Approach to Runway 28. There was a discontinuity between PLADE and CI28; which I closed up. Once we reached PLADE; I asked my FO (First Officer) to set 7;100 ft. in the mode control panel which is the minimum altitude at CI28 and started a VNAV descent with the intention to arm the ILS just prior to CI28. At approximately 7;600 ft. we received a warning 'too low terrain'. We could visually see the terrain and started to level off; then; very quickly received 'terrain; pull up' with amber showing on the terrain display.  I immediately complied by going into the CFIT recovery procedure. We climbed to approximately 8;000 ft. and leveled off seeing that we were well clear of all terrain (no more warning and terrain indicator showed us to be clear). We then reassessed. At that time; we were very close to CI28 and had plenty of light from the city and a very bright moon. We were also in a good position to continue to the airport; so I continued to an uneventful landing.
column123: We were landing Runway 28 in Guadalajara. Night VMC conditions with moonlight provided adequate visual references. We were set up to land Runway 28 using the ILS DME2 or localizer Runway 28 with the transition for the ILS DME 2 with the IKBAN transition. At the last minute; Control told us to descend via the LIVRI 1D arrival. After changing to this arrival in the FMS; we realized that we needed to descend quickly. To complicate matters; Control give us directions to go direct to PLADE. I estimate Control shortened our arrival by 40 to 50 miles in giving us the arrival change and direct PLADE which greatly compounded our decent plan. This caused us to have to execute an expedited decent while having to re-program the FMS and plan for this new routing. I verbalized terrain that was to our right as we were turning direct PLADE and both the CA (Captain) and I correlated this to what we were seeing on our terrain displays. Prior to reaching PLADE; Control cleared us for the ILS Zulu Runway 28. However; we heard cleared for the ILS Two. I attribute this miscommunication to language barriers. CA asked me to set 7;100 ft.; which would've been correct for ILS 2 but 7;700 ft would've been correct for ILS Z. We got the 'too low; terrain' oral warning followed by the 'terrain; pull up'. CA commanded auto pilot off; stow speed brake (Even though they weren't in use); pitched up and added full thrust. We had the terrain in sight the whole time; as well as the Runway environment. We climbed approximately 500 ft before determining that we could safely continue the approach without incident. We landed on Runway 28 without incident.

column121: We were doing a late night flight to Evansville on the visual approach for Runway 22 and the FO (First Officer) (Pilot Flying) drifted below the glide slope as he went to full visual not cross referencing a glide slope. column123: While hand flying the approach around 500 ft. to Runway 22 in Evansville; I allowed the aircraft to drift below glide slope. The Captain; who was PM (Pilot Monitoring) noticed and informed me I was getting low. I also received a 'glide slope' aural warning. I quickly corrected pitch and power to get back on glide slope and landed without any further issues. The Captain informed me I was getting low; and the 'glide slope' GPWS aural alert. I believe the cause was my insufficient scan of the flight instruments; as well as transitioning from the glide slope to scan the runway environment. Since it was nighttime; and since Runway 22 in Evansville has no VASI or PAPI; I believe my sight picture was incorrect; and I judged the aircraft to be higher than it was. I corrected pitch and power and returned to the glide slope for a normal landing. I believe I can do a better job of scanning the flight and navigation instruments while on approach; especially to an airport with no VASI or PAPI.

From there I determined that in order to conduct a standard pattern entry; I should overfly the airport at 1;700 ft. MSL or 500 ft. above pattern altitude; and then perform a 225 degree turn to enter the left downwind from a 45 degree angle to Runway XX. At 10 miles; I began to announce my intentions regularly at intervals of approximately 2.5 miles.At a distance of around 5 miles from the airport; a Piper Pawnee preparing to tow a glider announced that they would be making a right downwind departure from Runway XX; towards the east. This would be the only transmission I noted from this aircraft until I would be touching down on Runway XX. I continued approaching the airfield and I had the two aircraft in sight. As the Pawnee turned downwind; I noted that my flight path would create a collision hazard; should I have continued my descent. As such; I immediately applied full power and climbed to 2;800 ft. MSL. I continued to watch as the Pawnee; with its glider in tow passed underneath me by approximately 500 ft. Climbing was likely the best evasive action in this case because I was in a high wing Cessna; while he was in a low-wing Pawnee. Had I descended; we both would have lost visual contact with each other and no additional action could have been taken should it have been necessary. The factors which appear to have contributed to this event appear to be the Pawnee pilot's lack of communication when departing; thus preventing me from restructuring my arrival plan so that I may safely avoid him. Additionally; he utilized a non-standard right downwind departure that was not charted at the airport for Runway XX. I believe that the Pawnee pilot could have extended their crosswind leg so as to remain well clear of me. On my own part; I should have taken earlier action to increase separation such as maintaining 3;000 ft. over the airport; as I was indeed aware that he would be making right traffic and climbing out of the airport. I had misjudged the climb rate of the Pawnee; and as such suspected that I could pass in front and above them before there would have been a collision hazard.

Aircraft Y is at this point 100-200 ft. above Aircraft X; and enters Aircraft X's field of view high and crossing to the left.ATC spots the deviation right as I did; and issues instructions to Aircraft Y to proceed and enter a left downwind.Aircraft Y then turns right- and begins entering final when ATC again contacts Aircraft Y to issue corrective action.During this time I have expedited my descent by going engine idle and adopting a slightly nose down attitude. Due to low AGL; nearby towers and already having 20 degrees of flaps in; I am hesitant to enter a forward slip and descend faster (aircraft type placards state to avoid forward slips with flaps). It's possible that I'm also reaching the end of my endurance- coming back from an hour of pattern practice at ZZZ1 where conditions were gusty. My flight time at this point was around 1.6 hours; and my flights up to that point at typically max of 1.8.I have debated if I should have immediately turned right or even left. While I had the right of way (a lower craft engaged in landing); the right of way isn't going to help me if I end up in a midair. In the end I think it was correct not to turn- the pattern was extremely busy; there were higher towers to the right and planes on extended down wind to both sides. I could have caused another NMAC by turning suddenly. ATC was aware of the situation; issuing instructions to Aircraft Y and I was going to pass safely- although close- below.While I pass under (300-400 ft. estimated?) Aircraft Y either completes a right 360 or an S-turn; and ends up in an extended left downwind.Because I am below the ideal approach path to Runway XX; I put power in and arrest my descent. I actually end up too high for the runway and decide to do a go around. The go around is uneventful and I land safely. I believe Aircraft Y actually landed in between my go around and actual landing.
column123: Moderately heavy traffic relative to ZZZ; training in progress; everything under control of the Trainee until I noticed an aircraft turning base without any sequence or landing clearance yet. This aircraft was initially part of a flight of two who had just separated in the downwind; because we have to issue separate landing clearances at ZZZ; the AID (Aircraft IDentification) is Aircraft Y. Multiple inbound aircraft on either downwind and on straight in.I key up and say 'Aircraft Y and flight; both of you guys; Don't come in on base; there is traffic at the [VFR reporting point]; so don't come in on base right now; you are going to follow the guy on a 3 mile final' The [VFR reporting point] is 3 mile final; Aircraft Y is starting a 1 mile right base so this is plenty of time to catch and correct this pilot. The second aircraft from the original flight of two responds traffic in sight and immediately corrects back to the downwind. I respond to 2 other calls then scan back to ensure Aircraft Y was correcting; he wasn't; I say 'Aircraft Y it looks like you are doing exactly what I said not to do; unless the radar is deceiving me here.' Pilot responds 'Aircraft Y was already on base'; I respond 'OK; well I just said don't go on base; you missed that part; so let's go right turn back to the north downwind for both you and the other guy (his flight wing man; who was following instructions)' Pilot responds 'Affirm; right turn; north downwind; Aircraft Y'. I tell the original wing man to now turn base; he correctly responds; I then scan back and see Aircraft Y not following instructions; again the pilot does the opposite and starts a left turn towards final before correcting right and continuing for the north downwind. I then say 'Aircraft Y are you literally on final right now cutting someone off?' Pilot responds 'No; I'm trying to get out of here; we're turning; Aircraft Y'I advise the traffic on final 'Aircraft X; the guy in front of you is moving out of your way; Runway XX cleared to land' His response seemed to be partially blocked but I heard 'Aircraft X'.All aircraft eventually land; brasher warning was not issued. The pilot of Aircraft X called the tower a couple hours later and said he wanted to file a NMAC. He said he was aware of the situation developing and heard the controller (me) several times tell the other aircraft not to turn base and issue instructions which the pilot of Aircraft Y repeatedly disobeyed. I should have issued a traffic alert to both aircraft; but at the minimum to Aircraft X.

column121: When we arrived at the airplane the flight deck was around 34 degrees; but it soon cooled to around 28. Everything else was normal until the Captain stepped out to use the restroom. As soon as he sat down the ground crew pulled the ground power; but we had not yet switched over to the APU; so everything shut down. The Captain switched to the APU; but the right FMC did not start back up; and we got a R FMC FAIL status message. After about five minutes it did come back on without incident. We pushed back and started normally; but after about two seconds after I selected the status page on the lower EICAS we got a PACK 1 status message. The Captain reviewed the procedures; but because we had already blocked out and did not get any EICAS messages we continued. After starting up with the packs all off the flight deck warmed up quickly; but we knew as soon as we took off it should start cooling. At around 1;000 ft. the Tower gave us the Departure frequency and I checked in successfully. By the time we reached 5;000 ft. we were concerned by how little airflow there was; and the observer pilot asked for the ECS page to verify that the airplane was pressurizing. It seemed to be normal; and we monitored the air; but still figured as we climbed the flow would increase. Around FL180 Departure called us on guard and said; 'Aircraft X; if you can hear this transmission contact...' The Captain and I agreed that she hadn't called prior to that and I dialed in the frequency. I couldn't reach them; so I asked for another frequency. I didn't realize how much the heat was affecting me; but on the third frequency I asked the Captain to attempt to call. When he transmitted; I could hear that his call wasn't going out; and I finally recognized that we had lost the left comms. I didn't want to change the right radio from guard; because that seemed to be the only way they could reach us; so I used the center radio and was able to reach ZZZZ Control. Shortly after that we got an EQUIP COOLING EICAS message; and the third seat pilot began to run the checklist; and I asked for a level off altitude of FL300. ATC came back with FL290; but we were at FL288 and empty; so I said we would do our best. We ended up climbing to FL295 before we could get level; and promptly descended back to FL290. At this point we began to discuss returning when we noticed that the secondary attitude indicator was leaning to the right; but our wings were level; so we all agreed we should return. We told ATC we needed to return and explained that we were having equipment cooling issues. They assigned us the arrival and Runway XXR; but the workload was continuing to accelerate; and we were all sweating profusely; and told them we would like to get vectors to the ILS for XXR. I gave them the fuel remaining; souls on board; and tried to explain that we were safe; but needed to return soon. We completed all checklists; and uneventfully landed; taxied; and parked the airplane. I didn't realize until we were on the ground how much the heat in the flight deck was affecting me. Even with the lack of traffic in the vicinity; I am surprised how long it took me to recognize the radio failure. In the future I will be more cognizant of the heat and it's affects not only in seeming to increase workload; but also decreasing focus and clarity.
column123: I had gone to the lavatory on the ground prior to departure. Before I returned to my seat; the external power was pulled without my permission; and the power to the aircraft was interrupted; as I sat back down; I selected the APU power source and after waiting a bit; the R FMC would not come back. We called Maintenance up and the FMC returned to normal. We ensured all of the data that we had input was correct and then continued onward to push. The aircraft was extremely hot; and we know that they had just established air as we were arriving at the aircraft. The interior cabin was at 36 Celsius and we agreed that the aircraft should cool after takeoff. After starting we noticed a Pack 1 status message; but there was never an associated EICAS message. We followed our checklists and proceeded with taxi. After takeoff; the airflow never increased and the FO (First Officer) selected the EICAS page as we all were wondering if we were even pressurizing. The gaspers were blowing at about 5%; but cool air was coming out. It was still extremely hot in the aircraft; and the 3rd observer seat first officer said that he had hardly to no air coming out of his gasper. At around FL250; we began receiving radio calls on 121.5 and it was at this time with trying to transmit out; and different frequencies that we realized the radios were not working; except for the center. The Pilot Monitoring was able to get the right radio to work intermittent; and immediately we got the Equip cooling EICAS caution message. I continued to fly the aircraft while the crew ran the QRH and attempted to maintain contact with ZZZZ. At this point; we all agreed the best course of action was to return to ZZZZ. We were given a level off to FL290 after an initial climb clearance. We were given this rapidly; as were already in a climb; but I arrested the climb and descended back from FL295 to FL290. We were given vectors and further descent. At this point with descent power; there was almost no airflow. We [received priority] to get on the ground as safely and quickly as possible. My standby instruments were also showing erroneous. We landed in ZZZZ without further incident. After touchdown; the airflow suddenly increased to normal. Maintenance was briefed with the logbook; but I was not given the nature of the aircraft's issues before we headed back in to rest.

column121: On the way back from the practice area with a student after practicing steep turns; slow flight and stalls; I called ZZZ Tower 12 miles out asking for full stop taxi back intending to do some landing practice with my student. We were advised to report our position when we are inbound over the landfill. As we are about to report the landfill inbound when my ADS-B traffic lit up and advised me of traffic same altitude opposite direct less then half a mile. Looking up I immediately saw the Piper twin on a collision course and immediately began a hard right turning decent. At the time I was aware of a TBM aircraft behind and faster then me on an GPS approach for an avionics check; as well as another aircraft 500 ft. below me passing right to left. Tower was extremely busy at the time and I was unable to report the near miss immediately due to frequency volume and traffic. Adding to the confusion there was another aircraft in the area with the abbreviated tail number being Aircraft Y; while my tail number being Aircraft X. Tower told me to turn base which did make sense to me considering I was 5 miles out. I reported to Tower that there were two [similar N-numbers] on frequencies. He then told Aircraft Y to turn base followed by an instruction to me to turn to a heading of 070. I read back 070 but confirmation bias; and still rattled by the near miss; I turned to a heading of 170 thinking that he wanted me to turn an extended base to final; essentially cutting off the faster TBM closing on me. Tower asked me to read off my current heading and I reported flying 175 only then realizing the mistake. I was advised to make a right turn to intercept the final of Runway XX and report turning through 270 degrees. Already heading south this happened in less than 30 seconds. Now inbound on final for landing I was advised to copy a phone number on the ground for a possible pilot deviation. Finally on a half mile final I asked Tower twice if I was cleared to land Runway XX; and they advised me that I was 'still cleared to land XX' when I had not previously been given a landing clearance. Once on the ground I contacted Tower via phone and we discussed the situation; agreeing that parties were at fault a that a lot of events contributed to the situation.I believe that there were 3 main human factors causes that led to this incident.First the Tower was overloaded with inbound; transit; and outbound traffic and was unable to properly give traffic advisories to inbound and departing traffic.Second that Tower instructed me turn base when an aircraft with a similar call sign was the intended recipient even though it didn't make sense to me and at the time. Lastly that because of confirmation bias I expected to receive a base to final clearance when in reality he wanted me to intercept a left downwind entry into the pattern.
